Timely discussion of the Dhamma (kālena dhammasākacchā) means, in the early evening or at dawn, two monks who are experts in the Suttas discuss the Suttas with each other, or experts in the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya, or experts in the Abhidhamma...
33:
Monks who are bearers of the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma; those who are experts in the Jātakas discuss the Jātakas; and those who are experts in the Commentaries discuss the Commentaries. Or, they discuss at various times to purify the mind when it is overwhelmed by hesitation, distraction, or doubt. This is called 'Timely discussion of the Dhamma' (kālena dhammasākacchā). Such discussion is called a 'Blessing' because it is the cause of qualities such as proficiency in the scriptures.

Thus, by this verse, four blessings have been taught: patience (khanti), amenability (sovacassatā), seeing ascetics (samaṇadassana), and timely discussion of the Dhamma (kālena dhammasākacchā). Their nature as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective places.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Khantī ca' is finished.

Now, in the verse beginning with 'Tapo ca', it is called 'tapa' (ardor/austerity) because it burns away evil unwholesome states. It is called 'brahmacariya' because it is the noble conduct or the conduct of the noble ones; it means the supreme conduct. Seeing the Noble Truths is 'ariyasaccāna dassana'. Some teachers recite it as 'ariyasaccāni dassanaṃ', but that is not good. It is called 'Nibbāna' because it has departed from the entanglement (vāna) of craving. 'Sacchikiriyā' means realization. Realizing Nibbāna is 'nibbānasacchikiriyā'. The rest is as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā).

The explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) should be understood thus: 'Tapa' refers to the restraint of the faculties (indriyasaṃvara) because it burns away covetousness, grief, and so on. Or it is energy (viriya) because it burns away laziness. A person endowed with that energy is called 'ardent' (ātāpī). This 'tapa' should be known as a blessing because it is the cause for abandoning covetousness and so on, and for attaining jhānas and so on.

'Brahmacariya' (the Holy Life) is a term for abstinence from sexual intercourse, the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), the Dispensation (sāsana), and the Path (magga). Indeed, in passages such as 'Having abandoned unchastity, he is a practitioner of the Holy Life', 'brahmacariya' refers to abstinence from sexual intercourse. In passages such as 'Friend, the Holy Life is lived under the Blessed One', it refers to the practice of a recluse. In passages such as 'Evil One, I shall not pass away until this Holy Life of mine is successful, prosperous, widespread, and well-known among many people', it refers to the Dispensation. In passages such as 'Monk, this Noble Eightfold Path is itself the Holy Life, namely: Right View...', it refers to the Path. Here, however, since the Path is included later by 'seeing the Noble Truths', all the remaining meanings are appropriate. This brahmacariya should also be known as a blessing because it is the cause for the progressive attainment of various special distinctions.
34:
Seeing the Noble Truths (ariyasaccāna dassana) means seeing the Path through the penetration (abhisamaya) of the four Noble Truths, whose meanings were stated in the 'Questions of the Boy' (Kumārapañha). Seeing the Noble Truths is called a 'Blessing' because it is the cause for transcending the suffering of saṃsāra.

Realization of Nibbāna (nibbānasacchikiriyā) here refers to the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) as 'Nibbāna'. This is because the Fruit of Arahantship is also called 'Nibbāna' due to its departure from craving, which is called 'vāna' because it entangles the five destinations (gati). The attainment of that Fruit of Arahantship or the reviewing of it is called 'realization' (sacchikiriyā). As for the other Nibbāna, its realization is accomplished simply by seeing the Noble Truths; therefore, that Nibbāna is not intended here. Thus, this realization of Nibbāna should be known as a 'Blessing' because it is the cause for dwelling happily in the present life and so on.

Thus, in this verse also, four blessings have been taught: austerity (tapa), the Holy Life (brahmacariya) consisting of the practice of a recluse, the Dispensation, and the Path, seeing the Noble Truths (ariyasaccāna dassana), and the realization of Nibbāna (nibbānasacchikiriyā). Their nature as blessings has been clearly shown in their respective places.

## The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Tapo ca' is finished.

Now, in the verse beginning with 'Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi', 'phuṭṭhassa' means touched, contacted, or encountered. 'Lokadhammā' are the conditions that occur in the world; it means the conditions that do not cease as long as the world's process continues. 'Cittaṃ' means the mind (mano, mānasa). 'Yassa' refers to the mind of a new monk, a middle-seated monk, or an elder. 'Na kampati' means it does not shake, it does not tremble. 'Asokaṃ' means without sorrow, having the dart of sorrow pulled out. 'Virajaṃ' means free from the dust of defilements, having the dust of defilements destroyed. 'Khemaṃ' means fearless, free from affliction. The rest is as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary (padavaṇṇanā).

The explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) should be understood thus: The mind of one who is not shaken when touched by the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss—whose mind is not shaken, does not move, and is not agitated when touched and overwhelmed by these conditions—that mind should be known as a 'Blessing' because it brings about the supramundane state that cannot be shaken by anything.

Whose mind is not shaken when touched by these? Only the mind of an Arahant whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), not anyone else's. For it has been said:

'Just as a solid rock is not moved by the wind,
So too, all forms, tastes, sounds, smells, and contacts (do not shake the mind of an Arahant).'
35:
Pleasant things and unpleasant things do not shake the Arahant who is endowed with the quality of 'tādi' (steadfastness). The mind of that Arahant, who repeatedly contemplates dissolution and is liberated from defilements, remains firm.

'Asoka' (sorrowlessness) belongs only to the mind of an Arahant. That sorrow is called 'sorrow, grieving, the state of grieving, inner sorrow, intense inner burning, the state of the mind being consumed' according to the method shown in the Vibhaṅga Pāḷi; because of the absence of that sorrow, it is called 'asoka'. Some teachers say it refers to Nibbāna, but that assertion does not connect with the preceding word (cittaṃ). Just like asoka, 'viraja' (passionless/dustless) and 'khema' (secure) also refer to the mind of an Arahant. Because it is free from the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called 'viraja'; because it is free from the four bonds (yogas) and is safe, it is called 'khema'. Since this mind is taken in various aspects at various moments of occurrence and pointed out accordingly, these three states should be understood as 'blessings' (maṅgala) because they bring about the supreme supramundane state free from the round of existence and the aggregates, and because they bring about qualities such as being worthy of offerings (āhuneyya).

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are mentioned: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a passionless mind, and a secure mind. Their nature as blessings has been clearly explained in their respective places.

The explanation of the meaning of this verse beginning with 'Phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi' is finished.

Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the thirty-eight blessings through the ten verses beginning with 'Asevanā ca bālānaṃ', now spoke this final verse beginning with 'Etādisāni katvāna', wishing to praise the blessings he himself had taught.

The explanation of the meaning of that verse is as follows: 'Etādisāni' means these blessings of such a nature as not associating with fools, etc., which I have taught. 'Katvāna' means by doing (having done). In meaning, 'katvāna', 'katvā', and 'karitvā' are the same. 'Sabbatthamaparājitā' means not being defeated by even one of the four enemies—the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), and the Māra of the devas (devaputta-māra)—but rather conquering those four Māras oneself. Here, the letter 'ma' should be understood as merely for the sake of euphonic junction (padasandhi).

'Sabbattha sotthiṃ gacchanti' means that by performing such blessings and not being defeated by the four Māras, they go safely in all places, in this world and the next, and in all postures such as standing and walking. Those taints (āsavas) that would arise due to associating with fools, etc...
36:
...because of the absence of the distress and fever born of unwholesome states, they go happily. It means they go without calamity, without oppression, in safety, and without fear. Here, it should be understood that the nasal sound (anunāsika/niggahīta) is used for the sake of metrical ease in the verse.

With this verse-quarter, 'Taṃ tesaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ', the Blessed One concluded the teaching. How? 'O deity, those who perform such blessings go safely in all places. Therefore, consider those thirty-eight factors, beginning with not associating with fools, as the supreme, praised, and especially noble blessing for those who perform such blessings.'

When the Blessed One thus concluded the teaching, one hundred thousand crores of deities and Brahmas attained Arahantship. The number of those who attained the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning was incalculable. Then, on the second day, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, last night a certain deity approached me and asked a question about blessings. Then I taught the thirty-eight blessings to that deity. Ānanda, learn this discourse on blessings; having learned it, teach it to the monks.' The Elder Ānanda, having learned it, taught it to the monks. This discourse on blessings has been carried down through the lineage of teachers and exists to this day. Thus, it should be understood that this Dispensation (Sāsana) is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, and well-proclaimed among devas and humans.

Now, for the sake of proficiency in the exercise of knowledge regarding these very blessings, the connection (yojanā) from the beginning is as follows: Thus, beings who desire happiness in this life, the next life, and the supramundane state, having abandoned association with fools, relying on the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor; being urged toward the occurrence of merit due to living in a suitable locality and having performed merit in the past; well-establishing themselves, adorning their personality with great learning, arts, and discipline; speaking well-spoken words in accordance with the discipline; as long as they do not give up the lay life, clearing old debts by supporting their parents, and incurring new debts by supporting their children and wives; reaching prosperity in wealth and grain through unconfused occupations; taking the essence of wealth through giving and the essence of life through righteous conduct; performing the welfare of their own people by supporting relatives and the welfare of others by blameless actions; avoiding harming others by abstaining from evil and avoiding harming themselves by restraint from intoxicants; increasing the side of merit through heedfulness in wholesome states; and having increased merit, having abandoned the outward appearance of a layperson and remaining in the state of a monk, fulfilling the perfection of duties through respect and humility toward the Buddha, the Buddha's disciples, preceptors, and teachers; through contentment...
37:
Abandoning greed for requisites, standing in the ground of a virtuous person through gratitude, abandoning mental sluggishness by listening to the Dhamma, overcoming all dangers with patience, making oneself a refuge by being easy to admonish, seeing the application of practice by seeing recluses, dispelling doubts regarding doubtful matters through Dhamma discussion, fulfilling the purification of virtue through the practice of sense restraint, the purification of mind through the practice of a recluse's life (brahmacariya), and subsequently the other four purifications, and through this practice reaching the purification of knowledge and vision which is the method of seeing the Noble Truths, they realize Nibbāna known as the Fruit of Arahantship. Having realized that, like Mount Sineru which is unshaken by winds and rains, they have minds unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, and are sorrowless, stainless, and secure. Those who are secure are everywhere undefeated by anyone and go everywhere in safety. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Having done such things,
Everywhere undefeated,
They go everywhere in safety;
That is their supreme blessing.”

## Thus the explanation of the Maṅgala Sutta in the Commentary on the Suttanipāta,
## in the Minor Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, is finished.

## 5. Sūciloma Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The words “Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth constitute the Sūciloma Sutta. How did it arise (uppatti)? Its origin will become clear through the method of explaining its meaning. In the explanation of the meaning, the words “Evaṃ me sutaṃ” etc. have the meaning already stated. In the passage “At Gayā, he dwelt on the Taṅkitamañca, the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma,” what is Gayā? What is the Taṅkitamañca? And why did the Blessed One dwell in the abode of that yakkha? It is said: Gayā refers to both a village and a bathing place; here both are appropriate. Even if dwelling in a place not far from the village of Gayā, it is said “he dwells at Gayā,” and that Taṅkitamañca is near the entrance, not far from that village. Even if dwelling at the Gayā bathing place, it is said “he dwells at Gayā,” and that Taṅkitamañca is at that Gayā bathing place. Taṅkitamañca is a stone bed made by placing a flat stone slab on top of four stones...
38:
...it is a stone couch. Depending on that stone slab is the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma, like the abode of Āḷavaka. Alternatively, on that day at dawn, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion and surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, saw the support (upanissaya) for the fruit of stream-entry in both the yakkhas Sūciloma and Kharaloma. Therefore, taking his bowl and robes, even before dawn, he went to that Gayā bathing place where the ground was wet and defiled with various impurities such as saliva and mucus from the people gathered from various directions, and sat on that Taṅkitamañca in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma. Thus it was said: “At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Gayā, on the Taṅkitamañca, the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma.”

“Tena kho pana samayena” refers to the very time when the Blessed One was dwelling on that stone couch. The yakkha Khara and the yakkha Sūciloma approached the vicinity of the Blessed One. Who are these yakkhas, and why did they approach? The answer is given: Among those two, first, one yakkha (Kharaloma) in a past life took oil belonging to the Saṅgha without asking and smeared it on his body. Due to that unwholesome deed, after being cooked in hell, he was reborn in the yakkha realm on the bank of the Gayā pond. Due to the remainder of the result of that kamma, his limbs were ugly and deformed, and he had skin with a rough touch like roof tiles. When he wanted to frighten others, he would raise the skin-scales that were like roof tiles to frighten them. Thus, because of that rough touch, he received the name “Khara” (Rough).

The other yakkha (Sūciloma) had been a lay follower (upāsaka) in the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. He used to go to the monastery eight days a month to listen to the Dhamma. One day, while he was tending his field at the gate of the Saṅghārāma, he heard the announcement for the Dhamma talk. Thinking, “If I bathe, it will take a long time,” he entered the Uposatha hall with a dirty body and disrespectfully lay down and slept on a costly floor covering. (The reciters of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, say that this person was a monk, not a lay follower). Due to that unwholesome deed and other deeds, after being cooked in hell, he was reborn in the yakkha realm on the bank of the Gayā pond. Due to the remainder of the result of that kamma, he became ugly to look at, and there were needle-like hairs on his body. He would frighten beings who were to be frightened by acting as if piercing them with needles. Thus, because of having needle-like hairs, he received the name “Sūciloma” (Needle-hair). Those yakkhas, for the sake of their foraging ground...
39:
Those yakkhas left their place, went for a moment, and returning by the same path they had come, passed near the Blessed One while going in another direction.

Regarding "Atha kho" (Then indeed): Why did those yakkhas speak thus? The yakkha Khara spoke upon seeing the appearance of a monk. Sūciloma, however, held this view: "He who fears is not a monk; because he merely adopts the appearance of a monk, he is a mere monklet (samaṇaka)." Therefore, thinking of the Blessed One as such, he said hastily, "This is not a monk, this is a mere monklet." Yet, wishing to investigate further, he said, "Wait until I know." From "Atha kho" and "Sūciloma yakkha" up to the words "Indeed, your touch is evil," the meaning is clear. Specifically, "the body of the Blessed One" (bhagavato kāyaṃ) should be understood in connection with the phrase "he brought his own body close to the Blessed One."

Then, seeing the Blessed One without fear, he said, "Monk, I will ask you a question," and so on. For what reason? That yakkha thought: "Even though he is a human, he does not fear my rough yakkha-touch. Now, I will ask him a question within the domain of a Buddha. Surely he will not be able to answer it; then I will harass him." Hearing this, the Blessed One said, "Friend, I [will not fear] you..." and so on. All this should be understood in all its aspects according to the method stated in the Āḷavaka Sutta.

Then Sūciloma the yakkha addressed the Blessed One with a verse: "Lust and hatred..." Therein, lust and hatred are as previously explained. "Kutonidānā" means what is the source? What is the cause? "Kuto" should be understood as the substitute "to" for the nominative case, and there is no elision in the compound. Alternatively, "nidānā" means born or arisen; thus "kutonidānā" means from where is it born? From where has it arisen? "Arati, rati, and lomahaṃsa, from where are they born?": "Arati" is discontent, the state of being discontented, lack of delight, lack of enjoyment, boredom, and anxiety, as analyzed in the Vibhaṅga regarding secluded dwellings or various superior wholesome states. "Rati" is delight in the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Lomahaṃsa" is the mental terror that causes horripilation. From where are these three states born?
40:
[He] asks: "From where do they arise?" means from what state do they arise? "Mind" (mano) refers to the wholesome mind (kusalacitta). "Thoughts" (vitakkā) refers to the nine types of thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, mentioned in the Uraga Sutta. "As village boys let go of a crow": Just as village boys, when playing, tie a string to a crow's leg and let it go or toss it, so too, from what do unwholesome thoughts arise and "let go" (disturb) the wholesome mind? Thus he asks.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer those questions, spoke the second verse: "Lust and hatred..." Therein, "from here" (ito) refers to the individual existence (attabhāva). Indeed, lust and hatred have the individual existence as their cause. Discontent, delight, and horripilation are also born from the individual existence. Unwholesome thoughts, such as sensual thoughts, also arise from the individual existence itself and disturb the wholesome mind. Therefore, wishing to reject other causes such as primordial nature (pakati), He said: "They have this individual existence as their cause, they are born from this, they arise from this." The grammatical formation here should be understood in the same way as stated in the previous verse.

275-6. Having thus answered those questions, now, to establish the meaning stated as "having the individual existence as their cause, born from the individual existence, arising from the individual existence" in the words "ito-nidānā" etc., He said: "Born of affection, produced in oneself." For all these, beginning with lust and ending with thoughts, are born from the sap of craving (taṇhā-sneha). While being so born, they are produced in oneself, which is a synonym for the individual existence consisting of the five aggregates of clinging. Therefore, He said: "Born of affection, produced in oneself."

Now, to clarify that meaning, He gives a simile: "Like the aerial roots born from the trunk of a banyan tree." Therein, "born from the trunk" (khandhaja) means born in the trunks; this is a designation for aerial roots (pāroha). What is meant? Just as the aerial roots born from the trunk of a banyan tree arise when there is the sap of water (moisture), and while arising, they are produced in that very banyan tree in various branches, so too, these states such as lust arise when there is the sap of internal craving. While arising, they are produced in that very individual existence, in the various doors, objects, and bases such as the eye. Therefore, it should be understood: "These have the individual existence as their cause, are born from the individual existence, and arise from the individual existence."

Regarding the remaining one and a half verses, this is the comprehensive explanation of the meaning: These defilements, thus produced in oneself, are many and spread among sensual pleasures. Lust spreads by way of the five cords of sensual pleasure; hatred by way of the grounds of malice, etc.; and discontent, etc., by way of their respective divisions. Thus, in every way, all these defilements are numerous and widespread.
41:
Defilements are of various kinds; through the power of bases, doors, and objects, they especially cling, adhere, and remain entangled in those various objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma) in such and such a manner. How? It is like the māluvā creeper that grows extensively in the forest. Just as the māluvā creeper spreading in the forest especially clings, adheres, and remains entangled in the various branches and twigs of a tree, similarly, those who discern the mass of defilements clinging to the extensive objects of sensual desire and know from what cause they arise, they dispel those defilements. Listen, O Yakkha Sūciloma.

In that verse, "yatonidānaṃ" is a term indicating the source. What does it show by this term? Those beings who know that this mass of defilements "arises from this source," knowing that "it arises in the self-identity (attabhāva) moistened by the moisture of craving," they dry up that moisture of craving with the fire of meditative knowledge such as the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā), and thus they dispel, abandon, and eliminate it. Listen to these well-spoken words of ours, O Yakkha. Thus, in this verse, by knowing the self-identity, the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā) is shown; and by dispelling the mass of defilements such as the moisture of craving and lust, the abandoning of the origin (samudaya-pahāna) is shown.

Those who dispel those defilements cross over this flood (ogha) of saṃsāra, which is difficult to cross and has never been crossed before in the past, for the sake of no further rebirth. By this statement, the development of the path (magga-bhāvanā) and the realization of cessation (nirodha-sacchikiriyā) are shown. Indeed, those who dispel that mass of defilements certainly develop the path. Without the development of the path, there is no dispelling of defilements. Those who develop the path cross over the fourfold floods, such as the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), which are difficult to cross, by means of natural wisdom. The development of the path itself is the crossing of the flood. "Atiṇṇapubbaṃ" means not having crossed even in a dream throughout this long duration of saṃsāra. "Apunabbhavāya" means for the sake of Nibbāna. Thus, upon hearing this verse explaining the Four Noble Truths, following in sequence with well-developed wisdom such as "hearing the Dhamma, they retain it; they examine the meaning of the retained teachings," those two yakkha friends established themselves in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) at the very end of the verse. They became pleasing to look at, with a complexion as bright as gold, and adorned with celestial ornaments.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Sūciloma Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
42:
## 6. Explanation of the Kapila Sutta (Dhammacariya Sutta)

The Dhammacariya Sutta is indeed the Kapila Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? Following the method mentioned in the Hemavata Sutta, after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna, two brothers of noble family left the household life and were ordained in the presence of the disciples. The elder brother was named Sodhana, and the younger brother was named Kapila. Their mother was named Sādhanī, and their younger sister was named Tāpanā. They also were ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Then, those two brothers, also following the method mentioned in the Hemavata Sutta, asked, "How many duties (dhura) are there in the Dispensation?" and having heard the answer, the elder brother thought, "I will fulfill the duty of insight (vipassanā-dhura or vāsa-dhura)." After living for five years in the presence of his teachers and preceptors, having reached five years of seniority, he learned the meditation subjects up to Arahantship, entered the forest, and by striving, attained Arahantship. Kapila, however, thought, "I am still young; I will fulfill the duty of insight when I am old," and began the duty of study (gantha-dhura), becoming a master of the Three Piṭakas. Because of his scriptural learning (pariyatti), a following arose for him, and because of that following, gain and honor also arose.

That Kapila, intoxicated with the pride of great learning, considering himself a wise man and imagining he knew even what he did not know, used to say that what was allowable (kappiya) as spoken by others was unallowable (akappiya), and what was unallowable was allowable; what was blameworthy (sāvajja) was blameless (anavajja), and what was blameless was blameworthy. Although he was exhorted by virtuous monks in such ways as, "Friend Kapila, do not speak like this," he went about only insulting and reviling them with words such as, "What do you know, you who are like empty fists?" The monks reported this matter to his brother, the Elder Sodhana. The Elder Sodhana also approached him and said, "Friend Kapila, the life of the Dispensation is the right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) of people like you. Friend Kapila, do not say that what is allowable is unallowable, what is unallowable is allowable, what is blameworthy is blameless, and what is blameless is blameworthy." Kapila did not heed even his brother's words. Then, the Elder Sodhana, having spoken two or three times, said:

"A compassionate person should speak once or twice;
Beyond that, one should not speak, like a servant in the presence of a master."

Having thus avoided him, he said, "Friend, you will be known by your own kamma," and departed. From then on, the virtuous monks abandoned Kapila.
43:
That monk Kapila, being of bad conduct and living surrounded by monks of bad conduct, one day thought, "I will perform the Uposatha." He ascended the high seat, held a decorative fan, and sat down, saying three times, "Venerable sirs, is it proper for the Pātimokkha to be recited to the monks here?" At that time, not even a single monk said, "It is proper for me." Reciting the Pātimokkha was not proper for Kapila nor for those monks. Then Kapila said, "Whether the Pātimokkha is heard or not, there is no such thing as Vinaya," and rose from his seat. In this way, he caused the decline and destruction of the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha. Then, the Elder Sodhana attained Parinibbāna on that very day. As for Kapila, after causing the decline of the Dispensation, he passed away and was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell. His mother and sister also followed his views, and by insulting and threatening the virtuous monks, they passed away and were reborn in hell.

At that same time, five hundred men, who lived by banditry such as destroying villages, were pursued by the people of the countryside. They fled and entered a forest. Finding no thicket or refuge in that forest, they saw a forest-dwelling monk living on a nearby rock. They paid homage to him and said, "Venerable sir, please be our refuge." The Elder said, "There is no refuge for you like virtue (sīla). All of you, undertake the five precepts." They accepted, saying "Sādhu," and undertook the precepts. The Elder said, "Now you are virtuous. Even if others destroy your lives, do not let your minds be corrupted." They accepted, saying "Sādhu." Then the country folk arrived, searched here and there, found the thieves, and took all their lives. After passing away, they were reborn in the celestial realm of the sense sphere (Kāmāvacara Devaloka). Among them, the chief thief became a great deity, and the others became his attendants.

Wandering through the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) in due order, they spent one interval between Buddhas (Budd hantara) in the celestial realm. In the time of our Blessed Buddha, they passed away from the celestial realm. The great deity took rebirth in the womb of the wife of the chief fisherman among five hundred fisherman families in a fishing village near the gate of Sāvatthī. The others took rebirth in the wombs of the wives of the remaining fishermen. Thus, for all of them, conception and birth occurred on the same day. Then the chief fisherman, searching to see if there were other children born in the village that day, saw those children and said, "These will be companions for my son," and provided for the upbringing of all of them. All those children...
44:
Those friends and companions grew up in due course, playing together in the dust. Yasoja was the leader among them.

At that time, Kapila, due to the remainder of his unwholesome kamma from hell, was reborn in the Aciravatī River as a fish with a golden color but with a foul-smelling mouth. One day, all the fisherman youths took their nets, saying, "We will catch fish," went to the river, and cast their nets. That fish entered their net. Seeing that fish, the entire fishing village made a loud noise, saying, "When our sons first went fishing, they caught a golden fish! This will be a prosperous and auspicious sign for these youths. And now the King will give us much wealth." Then the five hundred young friends placed the fish on a boat, lifted the boat, and went to the King. When the King saw it, he asked, "Friends, what is this?" They replied, "Your Majesty, it is a fish." Seeing the golden-colored fish, the King thought, "The Blessed One will know the reason for this fish's color," and had the fish taken to the Blessed One. When the fish's mouth was opened, the Jetavana Monastery became extremely foul-smelling.

The King asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, why is this fish golden in color? And why does a foul odor emanate from its mouth?" "Great King, in the Dispensation of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, this fish was a monk named Kapila. He was very learned and well-versed in the scriptures (Pāḷi and commentaries). He used to insult and threaten virtuous monks who did not follow his words. He was also a destroyer of that Blessed One's Dispensation. Because of the evil kamma of destroying the Blessed One's Dispensation, he was reborn in the Avīci Great Hell. Now, by the remainder of the result, he has become a fish. Because he taught the Buddha's words for a long time and spoke of the Buddha's virtues, he obtained such a color as a result of that merit. Because he insulted and threatened the monks, a foul odor emanates from his mouth."

"Great King, shall I make that fish speak?" the Buddha asked. "Yes, Blessed One, please let it speak," the King replied. Then the Blessed One addressed the fish, "Are you Kapila?" "Yes, Blessed One, I am Kapila," it replied. "Where have you come from?" He asked. "From the Avīci Great Hell, Blessed One," it replied. "Where has Sodhana gone?" He asked. "He has attained Parinibbāna, Blessed One," it replied. "Where has Sādhani gone?" He asked. "She is reborn in the Great Hell, Blessed One," it replied. "Where has Tāpanā gone?" He asked. "She is reborn in the Great Hell, Blessed One," it replied. "Where will you go now?" He asked. "To the Great Hell, Blessed One," it replied. At that very moment, overcome by remorse, the fish struck the boat with its head, died, and was reborn in the Great Hell. The great multitude of people were terrified and their hair stood on end.
45:
Then, the Blessed One, wishing to preach a Dhamma discourse suitable for that moment to the assembly of laypeople and monks gathered there, spoke this Sutta.

277-8. In that Sutta, 'Dhammacariya' means the practice of Dhamma, such as good conduct of the body and so forth. 'Brahmacariya' means the noble practice of the Path. 'Etadāhu vasuttamaṃ' means that the Noble Ones (Ariyas) call these two types of good conduct—mundane and supramundane—'the supreme wealth' because they lead to the happiness of heaven and the bliss of Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. 'Supreme wealth' (vasuttama) means a noble treasure that follows one through Saṃsāra, is under one's own control, and is not shared with others such as kings or thieves.

Having shown with these words that 'right practice is the only refuge for both laypeople and monks,' he now wished to show the worthlessness of a life of renunciation devoid of practice. Rebuking the monk Kapila and others of similar nature, he spoke the words beginning with 'Pabbajitopi ce hoti.'

The explanation of its meaning is as follows: If a person, having cast off the appearance of a layperson and merely approaching the monkhood by shaving their head and wearing saffron robes, etc., has gone forth from the home life to the homeless life for the purpose mentioned before, yet if that monk is of a harsh-tongued nature and uses rough speech, and if he delights in various forms of harassment, he is one who 'delights in harming.' Because of the absence of shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), he is like a wild beast and is called 'maga.' The livelihood of such a person is extremely evil. Why? Because through such wrong practice (micchāpaṭipatti), he increases various dust-like defilements such as lust (rāga) within himself.

It is not only for this reason that his livelihood is evil; rather, such a monk, being harsh-tongued and delighting in quarrels, is covered by the nature of delusion (moha) which obscures the understanding of the meaning of well-spoken words. Even when virtuous monks speak to him, saying, 'Friend Kapila, do not do this; do not say that; try to understand the Dhamma in this way,' he does not understand the Dhamma taught by the Buddha. Even though the Dhamma taught by the Buddha is explained to him in various ways, he does not understand. Because of this lack of understanding, his livelihood is very evil.

Furthermore, such a person, delighting in harming, harasses Khīṇāsava monks (Arahants) who have well-developed selves, such as Elder Sodhana and others, saying, 'You do not know the Vinaya, nor the Sutta, nor the Abhidhamma; you are just those who went forth in old age,' and so forth.
46:
...harasses them. This genitive case (in 'bhāvitattānaṃ') is used in the sense of the accusative case. Alternatively, according to the method mentioned before, the remaining Pali should be understood as "one who harms the virtuous ones who have developed themselves." Thus, the genitive case is established even in its direct sense. 'Avijjāya purakkhato' means being led by ignorance, which covers the seeing of danger in harming those who have developed themselves. Being urged and impelled by it, by harming virtuous ones with developed minds, such as Elder Subhūti, Elder Soṇa, and other monks, he does not know the defilement caused by mental distress even in the present life, nor the path leading to hell that causes one to reach hell in the future.

Being ignorant, he falls into the state of ruin (vinipāta) consisting of the four planes of misery through that path. In that falling, he goes from womb to womb, from darkness to darkness, a hundred times or even a thousand times in each group, from mother's womb to mother's womb, and into the darkness of the Asura realm, which cannot be illuminated even by the moon and the sun. Such a monk, after passing away from this life and going to the next world, suffers various kinds of misery like this Kapila fish.

What is the reason? It is like a cesspool that has been full of excrement for many years and is difficult to clean. For example, a latrine pit or cesspool that has been filled with excrement up to the opening for many years would be difficult to clean because the foul smell and bad color would not disappear even if washed with hundreds or thousands of water pots. In the same way, a monk who has had defiled actions for a long time is like a cesspool; because he is full of the 'excrement' of evil, he is a person with taints (aṅgaṇa) that are difficult to purify. Even though he experiences the results of those taints for a long time, he is not purified. Therefore, for an immeasurable period in terms of the number of years, such a monk truly meets with suffering in the afterlife. Alternatively, this is the connection of this verse: Regarding the statement, "Such a monk truly meets with suffering in the afterlife," the thought might occur to you, "Is it possible to act in such a way that this person does not meet with suffering in the afterlife?" It is not possible. Why? Because the cesspool... is with taints.
47:
283-4. Monks, when you know such conduct that is dependent on the household and dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure, know them as follows: one is called 'evil in desire' (pāpiccha) because of being possessed by evil longing that manifests as a wish for non-existent qualities; one is called 'evil in thought' (pāpasaṅkappa) because of being possessed by thoughts of sensual desire and so forth; one is called 'evil in conduct' (pāpācāra) because of being possessed by evil behavior such as bodily transgression and the corrupt practice of giving bamboo and so forth; one is called 'evil in resort' (pāpagocara) because of having evil haunts such as the houses of prostitutes and so forth. When you know them thus, all being in harmony, you should shun them. In that context, 'abhinibbajjiyātha' means you should avoid them, do not associate with them. And do not remain indifferent merely by shunning them; rather, drive out the chaff, remove the rubbish. Without regard, drive out that person who is like rubbish, just as one would remove rubbish. And remove that person who is like dregs, who has entered into the midst of the assembly of Khattiyas and others, like a leper whose sores are broken and dripping, like an outcast (caṇḍāla); taking him by the arm or by the head, cast him out. It is shown that just as the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna took that person of evil nature by the arm, cast him out beyond the gate-tower, and slid the bolt, in the same way, you should remove them. For what reason? Because the monastery (saṅghārāma) is made for those of virtue, not for those of immoral conduct.

285-6. Therefore, drive away those who are chaff, who are not monks but imagine themselves to be monks. Just as chaff, though devoid of rice grain within, appears like paddy on the outside due to the husks, even so, evil monks, though devoid of virtue and so forth within, appear like monks on the outside due to their requisites such as the saffron-colored robes. Therefore, they are called 'chaff' (palāpa). Drive away those chaff, winnow them, blow them away—those who are not monks in the ultimate sense but imagine themselves to be monks merely by their appearance. Having thus driven them out... remain mindful. In that context, 'kappayavho' means you should conduct (your livelihood). 'Patissatā' means living with mutual respect and deference. Thus being in harmony and being prudent, living together with those who are pure, being in harmony through the equality of view and virtue, being prudent through wisdom that has reached maturity in due course, make an end of all this suffering of the round of rebirth. Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.

At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred sons of fishermen, having been moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and desiring to make an end of suffering, went forth as monks in the Buddha's Dispensation in the presence of the Blessed One, and before long...
48:
Having made an end of suffering, they became those of equal enjoyment with the Blessed One through the enjoyment of the attainment of the imperturbable dwelling (āneñjavihāra-samāpatti). This state of having equal enjoyment with the Blessed One should be understood by way of the Yasojasutta taught in the Udāna.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Kapila Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta. How did it arise? It arose because of this reason stated in the introduction of the sutta by the method beginning with "Atha kho sambahulā". In that context, "sambahulā" means many, numerous. "Kosalakā" means residents of the Kosala country. "Brāhmaṇamahāsālā" means those who are brahmins by birth and are called 'mahāsāla' because of their great wealth (mahāsāratā). It is said that those who have wealth amounting to eighty crores stored and hidden are called 'brāhmaṇamahāsāla'. These brahmins were also of such a nature; therefore, it is said "brāhmaṇamahāsālā". "Jiṇṇā" means decayed, having reached the state of broken teeth and so forth due to old age. "Vuḍḍhā" means those who have reached the limit of growth of their limbs and body. "Mahallakā" means endowed with seniority of birth, meaning those who have lived for a long time. "Addhagatā" means those who have gone a long way in time, meaning those who have passed through two or three reigns of kings. "Vayo anuppattā" means those who have reached the final stage of life.

Alternatively, "jiṇṇā" means ancient, meaning those who have come down through a long-standing family lineage. "Vuḍḍhā" means those endowed with the growth of qualities such as virtue and conduct. "Mahallakā" means those endowed with greatness of wealth, having great riches and great possessions. "Addhagatā" means brahmins who have entered upon the path, living without transgressing the boundaries of the vows and practices of brahmins. "Vayo anuppattā" means those who have reached the final stage of life even in terms of seniority of birth; thus should the connection of meaning be understood here. The remaining words here are quite clear.

"Bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodiṃsu" means that while inquiring about health and so forth, they engaged in mutual friendly conversation. That conversation by which they greeted him, such as "Is the Venerable Gotama well? Is he enduring? Is he free from illness? Is he free from affliction? Is he strong? Is he alert? Does he dwell in comfort?", is called 'sammodanīya' (pleasurable) because it generates joy known as zest and gladness, and it is worthy of being enjoyed by a person who deserves to be pleased. Because of the sweetness of the meaning and the phrasing...
49:
It is called 'sāraṇīya' (memorable) because it is worthy of being remembered for a long time and for its continuous occurrence. It is called 'sammodanīya' (courteous) because of the happiness of hearing it, and 'sāraṇīya' because of the happiness of remembering it. Likewise, it is called 'sammodanīya' due to the purity of its phrasing (byañjana) and 'sāraṇīya' due to the purity of its meaning (attha). Thus, having concluded and finished the courteous and memorable conversation through various methods, they sat to one side, wishing to ask about the purpose for which they had come. Regarding the proper way of sitting to one side:

"Neither behind nor in front,
Neither too close nor too far,
Neither to the side nor against the wind,
Nor in a place too low or too high."

This is just as stated in the commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta.

Sitting thus to one side, those eminent brahmins (brāhmaṇamahāsāla) addressed the Blessed One with the words: "Sandissanti nu kho" (Are they seen?), and so on. All those words have a clear meaning. However, in this context, "brāhmaṇānaṃ brāhmaṇadhamme" refers only to the (true) practice of brahmins, excluding the practices found in other regions and times. "Therefore, O brahmins, since you have requested me, listen, brahmins, pay attention, attend well, attend wisely." He said this. Likewise, "Listen with purity of application (payoga-suddhi), attend well with purity of intention (āsaya-suddhi). Listen without distraction, attend well with exertion (paggaha)." The meaning of these words should be understood in this way, even if not stated previously.

Then, those eminent brahmins, wishing to accept the words spoken by the Blessed One, replied to the Blessed One, "Even so, sir." They listened facing the Blessed One's words. Or, they gave their assent. It means they promised because they wished to fulfill the meaning of the words "Listen, attend well." To those brahmins who had thus assented, the Blessed One said: "Isayo pubbaka" (The sages of old), and so on.

Among those verses, in the first verse, "saññatattā" means they had minds restrained by the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃyama). "Tapassino" means they were endowed with the austerity of sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara). "Attadatthamacārisu" means they performed their own welfare, such as the study of Vedas (mantajjhayana), jhāna, and the development of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra-bhāvanā). The rest is clear.

In the second verse and others, this is the brief explanation: "Na pasū brāhmaṇānāsuṃ" means the ancient brahmins had no cattle; they did not possess animals. "Na hiraññaṃ na dhāniyaṃ" means for the brahmins, there was no gold, nor even a coin made of lac...
50:
...there was none. Likewise, they did not have stored grain of various kinds, such as rice, fine rice, pulses, or wheat. Having abandoned gold and silver and not making any accumulation, they possessed only the wealth and grain of Vedic recitation; they were endowed only with the wealth and grain known as their Vedic study and jhāna. And that living in loving-kindness (mettā) and so on, which is called 'brahmanidhi' (the brahmins' treasure) because of its excellence and its quality of following one (to the next life), they always protected that noble treasure by the constant practice of that meditation on loving-kindness.

For the brahmins who lived in this way, whatever gift was prepared, that gift was prepared specifically for these brahmins. 'Dvārabhattaṃ upaṭṭhitaṃ' refers to the alms-food placed by various donors at their own house doors, having prepared it with the thought, "We shall give to the brahmins." 'Saddhāpakataṃ' means prepared out of faith, an offering given out of faith. 'Esānaṃ' means for those brahmins who are seeking (alms). 'Dātave' means it should be given. 'Tadamanyiṃsu' means the donors considered that the alms-food prepared at the door and given out of faith should be given to those brahmins who came seeking it, and they desired nothing else. The reason is that those brahmins had no desire for other things, being content with merely food and clothing.

'Nānārattehi' means with clothes dyed with various dyes, with beds spread with variegated coverings, and with excellent mansions of one or two stories, etc. 'Āvasathehi' means with such buildings and requisites (they were prosperous). Prosperous provinces and kingdoms, as well as certain parts of provinces and entire kingdoms, worshipped the brahmins like gods in the evening and morning, saying, "Homage to the brahmins."

The brahmins who were thus worshipped by the world were those who should not be killed (avajjha). Not only were they not to be killed, but they were also difficult to conquer (ajeyya) because they could not be oppressed or harmed. For what reason? Because they were protected by Dhamma (dhammarakkhitā). They protected the five excellent virtues (sīla-dhamma). In accordance with the saying, "Dhamma indeed protects the one who practices Dhamma," they were not to be killed and were difficult to conquer because they were protected by Dhamma. "No one barred them" means that because those brahmins were beloved and respected at the doors of families, at all doors, both outside and inside...
51:
People were as intimate with those Brahmins as they were with parents endowed with noble virtue. Therefore, no one ever forbade them, saying, "You must not enter such a place."

Thus, being protected by the Dhamma and wandering without being forbidden at the doors of families, those Brahmins practiced the holy life of youth (komāra-brahmacariya) through virtuous conduct for forty-eight years from their childhood. Even those who were outcaste Brahmins (brāhmaṇa-caṇḍāla) practiced in this way; what then need be said of those who were like Brahma? Thus should the meaning be understood in this context. In former times, Brahmins practiced the search for knowledge (vijjā) and conduct (caraṇa) in this manner; they were not those who did not practice the holy life. In this context, 'the search for knowledge' (vijjā-pariyēṭṭhi) refers to the study of the Vedas. It is also said: "He practices the holy life of youth for forty-eight years, studying the mantras" (as found in the Aṅguttara Nikāya). 'The search for conduct' (caraṇa-pariyēṭṭhi) refers to the guarding of virtue (sīla). There is also a reading "vijjācaraṇapariyēṭṭhuṃ," which means they practiced to seek both knowledge and conduct.

After practicing the holy life for the aforementioned period, even when they established a household thereafter, the Brahmins did not go to other castes such as the Khattiya (warrior) or Vessa (merchant) castes; the meaning is that they took wives only from their own kind, who were like goddesses or within their own boundaries. Furthermore, they did not buy a wife by giving a hundred or a thousand coins, as some do nowadays. They sought a wife only in accordance with the Dhamma. How? After practicing the holy life for forty-eight years, the Brahmins would wander for the 'alms of a maiden' (kaññā-bhikkha), saying, "I am one who has practiced the holy life for forty-eight years; if there is a maiden who has reached the proper age, please give her to me." Then, one who had a daughter of age would deck her with ornaments, bring her out, and while pouring water onto the hands of the Brahmin standing at the door, would give her, saying, "O Brahmin, I give this wife to you for the purpose of maintenance."

Why did they seek a wife even after practicing the holy life for such a long time, and why did they not remain practitioners of the holy life for their entire lives? It was due to the power of wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). They held the view: "One who does not produce a son is one who cuts off the lineage, and consequently, he is reborn in hell." It is said that there are four types of beings who fear what is not to be feared: the earthworm, the kikī bird, the kuntanī bird, and the Brahmin. The earthworms, fearing that the great earth...
52:
...will be exhausted, eat only in moderation; they do not eat too much soil. The female kikī bird, fearing that she might fall from the sky, sleeps on her back with her two legs raised above her eggs. The female kuntanī bird, fearing an earthquake, does not dare to step firmly on the ground with her feet. The Brahmins, fearing the termination of their lineage, seek a wife. Regarding this, it was said:

“The earthworm, the kikī bird, the kuntī, and the righteous Brahmin—these four deluded beings fear what is not to be feared.”

Even after seeking a wife in accordance with the Dhamma, they took delight in union only with mutual affection. They united with one another through love, both in mind and body, becoming mixed, joined, and associated; the meaning is that they did not unite through dislike or coercion.

Even while engaging in union with such affection, the Brahmin would not approach the Brahmin woman except during the fertile period (utu-samaya). Excluding that fertile time, he would not go to his wife during the intervals when she was free from the period, and would observe abstinence from sexual intercourse until that time arrived again. “Methunaṃ dhammaṃ” means for the sake of sexual practice. It is said that here the accusative case carries the meaning of the dative case. “Nāssu gacchanti” means that those Brahmins, who were like gods and kept within boundaries, did not go to their wives for sexual practice (outside the proper time).

In general, however, everyone praised virtues such as the holy life (brahmacariya). Among those virtues, 'brahmacariya' means abstinence from sexual intercourse. 'Sīla' refers to the remaining four precepts. 'Ajjava' means rectitude, which in essence is the absence of crookedness and deceit. 'Maddava' means gentleness, which in essence is the absence of rigidity and pride. 'Tapa' means the restraint of the sense faculties. 'Soracca' means having good habits, a pleasant nature, and conduct that is not offensive. 'Avihiṃsā' means the nature of not harming with hands and so forth, and being compassionate. 'Khanti' means patient endurance. They praised these qualities. Even those who were unable to fully succeed in the practice praised and commended these qualities with their speech, seeing the essence in them.

To those who were thus praising, that supreme Brahma of theirs... who was called Brahmasama, the most excellent...
53:
The first was a Brahmin; because he was endowed with firm effort, he was called Daḷhaparakkama. In the phrase 'sa vā', the word 'vā' is used in the sense of clarification; therefore, it clarifies that such a person was indeed a Brahmin. 'Methunaṃ dhammaṃ' refers to the practice of sexual intercourse. 'Supinantepi nāgamā' means that he did not engage in it even in dreams.

After that, they praised his conduct... Through this verse and the ninth verse, by indicating the virtues already mentioned from beginning to end, he reveals the Brahmins who are like devas (devasama). Indeed, those wise and prudent people follow the conduct of that Brahmin who is like Brahma (brahmasama) through renunciation and the development of jhāna; they also praise these virtues such as celibacy (brahmacariya) through their own practice. All these Brahmins should be understood according to the method stated in the Doṇa Sutta of the Pañcaka Nipāta.

Now, wishing to show the Brahmins who observe boundaries (mariāda), he spoke the verse beginning with 'taṇḍulaṃ sayanaṃ'. The meaning of that verse is: Among them, there were those Brahmins who observed boundaries; if those Brahmins wished to perform a sacrifice, then, because they abstained from receiving raw grain, they would righteously beg for various kinds of rice, beds and chairs, linen and other cloths, and ghee, sesame oil, and other oils, according to the Dhamma expressed as: 'The Noble Ones stand with a purpose (to receive alms); this standing is the begging of the Noble Ones.' Having thus begged according to the Dhamma of standing for a purpose, they would collect and gather whatever someone wished to give, such as the donated rice. There is also a reading 'samudānetvā', which has the same meaning. Then, 'tato yaññamakappayuṃ' means that having taken those items, they performed the act of giving.

Even when the sacrifice, which is called giving, was thus prepared, they did not kill cows. It should be understood that by the word 'cow', all living beings are meant here. Why did they not kill? Because they were endowed with virtues such as celibacy (brahmacariya). Furthermore, especially like a mother... they did not kill cows. In that context, 'yāsu jāyanti osadhā' means that from those cows, the five products of the cow (gorasa), which serve as medicine for bile and so on, are produced.

In the words beginning with 'annadā', because those who consume the five products of the cow find relief from hunger, increase in strength, clarity of complexion, and physical and mental happiness...
54:
...arises, therefore they should be known as givers of food, givers of strength, givers of beauty, and givers of happiness. The remaining words in this context have an obvious meaning.

Thus, those Brahmins, not killing cows in their sacrifices, had bodies sustained by the power of merit and were delicate... This generation of beings, being happy and free from danger, attained various forms of happiness. In that verse, they are called 'sukhumāla' because their hands and feet were soft and tender. They are called 'mahākāya' (great-bodied) because they were endowed with stature and proportion. They are called 'vaṇṇavanta' (beautiful) because they were lovely like the color of gold and well-proportioned. They are called 'yasassī' (famous) because they were endowed with gain and followers. 'By their own practices' means by their own conduct. 'Zealous in duties' means they were those who applied themselves to duties, thinking 'this should be done,' and to non-duties, thinking 'this should not be done.' Thus, those ancient Brahmins, being of such a nature, were pleasant to behold and inspiring to the world, and were the supreme recipients of offerings. As long as they remained in the world with this practice, they were free from the dangers of calamities and attained various forms of happiness, or they attained the growth of happiness. The term 'this generation' refers to the world of sentient beings.

302-3. However, with the passage of time, a perversion (vipallāsa) arose in those who wished to break the established boundaries... measured by portions. In that verse, 'vipallāsa' means a distorted perception. 'From small to small' means seeing sensual pleasure as small—which, when compared to the happiness of jhāna, the commonality of the path, and Nibbāna, or compared to supramundane happiness, is so minute it cannot even be counted—and seeing even the mundane attainment (samāpatti) happiness they had acquired as small compared to the small sensual pleasure. 'And of the king' means belonging to the king. 'Byākāra' means prosperity or wealth. 'Yoked with thoroughbreds' means a chariot yoked with thoroughbred horses. 'Well-made' means well-finished through woodwork and metalwork. 'Artistically stitched' means artistically stitched by way of decoration with lion skins and so on. 'Dwellings' means house sites. 'Houses' means the houses established there. 'Divided' means divided according to length and breadth. 'Measured by portions' means measured by dividing into sections such as courtyards, doors, palaces, and pinnacled houses. What is meant? When those Brahmins saw the sensual pleasure perceived as small, the king's prosperity, the decorated women, and the chariots, dwellings, and houses of the aforementioned types, they applied the thought of 'happiness' to these very things which are actually suffering. Thus, a distorted perception (vipallāsa), characterized by the perversion of the previously existing perception of renunciation (nekkhamma-saññā), arose.
55:
Those Brahmins, having such perverted perceptions, saw the wealth surrounded by herds of cattle and became greedy. In that Pali, 'gomandala-paribyūḷhaṃ' means being crowded with (surrounded by) herds of cattle. 'Nārīvaragaṇāyutaṃ' means being associated with groups of excellent women. 'Uḷāraṃ' means grand (vast). 'Mānusaṃ bhogaṃ' means human possessions and objects of use, such as houses. 'Abhijjhāyiṃsu' means they coveted and planned, increasing their greed and thinking, 'If only this wealth were ours!'

While thinking thus, they reflected: 'These people are well-bathed, well-anointed, with trimmed hair and beards, adorned with jewel ornaments, and they enjoy themselves with the five strands of sensual pleasure. We, however, even though we are worshipped by them, have bodies soiled with sweat and dirt, with long hair in armpits, long nails, and body hair; we are devoid of wealth and have reached a most pitiable state. They travel by elephant-back, horse-back, palanquins, and golden chariots; we travel on foot. They live in palaces with two or more stories; we live at the foot of forest trees. They sleep on excellent beds spread with carpets and such; we sleep on the ground after spreading mats or pieces of hide. They eat food of various flavors; we subsist by wandering for alms. How can we also become like them?'

Having thought thus, they decided, 'Wealth must be sought; this prosperity cannot be attained without wealth.' They then corrupted the Vedas, destroyed the righteous ancient mantras, and composed unrighteous, deceitful mantras (kūṭamanta). Desiring wealth, those Brahmins approached King Okkāka, and after uttering words of blessing (sotthivacana), they said, 'Great King, in our Brahmin lineage, there are ancient mantras handed down by tradition. Because our teachers held them back (ācariyamuṭṭhi), we have never spoken them to anyone. Only you, Great King, are worthy to hear them.' Thus, they praised the performance of sacrifices such as the Assamedha. After praising them, they urged the King, saying, 'Sacrifice, Great King! You are thus endowed with much wealth and grain; you have no lack of sacrificial requisites. If you sacrifice in this way, your lineage for seven generations will be reborn in heaven.' To show this matter, the Blessed One said: 'Te tattha mante... pe... bahu te dhanaṃ.'

In that Pali, 'tattha' means 'on account of that wealth which they coveted.' Here, the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimittattha). 'Tadupāgamuṃ' means they approached at that time. 'Pahūtadhanadhaññosi' means 'you will be endowed with much wealth and grain in the future.' Although it refers to the future, those skilled in grammar allow the use of the present tense when there is great expectation (āsaṃsā).
56:
'Yajassu' means 'perform the sacrifice.' In the phrase 'vittaṃ dhanaṃ,' it is said that jewels such as gold and silver are called 'vitta' because they are the cause of joy (vitti), and they are called 'dhana' because they are the cause of prosperity (samiddhi). Alternatively, 'vitta' refers to utensils such as ornaments that are causes of joy, as found in passages like 'pahūtavittūpakaraṇo' (D. i. 331). 'Dhana' refers to gold, silver, and so on. What is meant? Those Brahmins, having composed the mantras, then approached Okkāka. How? 'Great King, you have much equipment and wealth; sacrifice! In the future also, you will be endowed with much wealth and grain.'

Having thus explained the reason and made him understand, from then on, the King... pe... gave wealth. In that context, 'saññatto' means 'informed' or 'urged.' 'Rathesabho' means a king who is like a bull among the Khattiyas who possess great chariots, in the sense of being unshakable. Among the terms 'Assamedha' and so on: 'Assamedha' is so called because a horse (assa) is sacrificed (medhanti) therein. It is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with two cycles of offerings, having twenty-one sacrificial posts, where all possessions except land and people are given as dakṣiṇā. 'Purisamedha' is so called because a man (purisa) is sacrificed therein. It is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with four cycles of offerings, where the wealth mentioned in the Assamedha is given along with the land. 'Sammāpāsa' is so called because a peg (samma) is thrown (pāsanti) and the sacrifice is performed. It is the name of a Satra sacrifice to be performed by going upstream from the place where the Sarasvatī river disappears, throwing a peg every day and making an altar at the place where it falls, using portable sacrificial posts and so on. 'Vājapeyya' is so called because they drink (pivanti) strength (vāja). It is the name of a sacrifice to be performed with one cycle of offerings, sacrificing seventeen animals, having a post made of bael wood (beluva), and giving seventeen-fold gifts. 'Niraggala' is so called because there is no obstruction or bolt (aggaḷa). It is a specific type of Assamedha, also known as Sabbamedha, to be performed with nine cycles of offerings, where all wealth mentioned in the Assamedha is given along with land and people. The rest of the words are clear here.

307-8. Now, to show what was said as 'he gave wealth to the Brahmins,' he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Gāvo sayanañcā.' That King thought, 'These Brahmins have been weary for a long time with coarse food; let them enjoy the five products of the cow,' and he gave them herds of cattle along with bulls. Likewise, 'Because they slept on the bare ground for a long time...'
57:
The Brahmins, who were weary from wearing thick garments, sleeping in one place, walking on foot, and living at the foot of trees, were given costly beds and seats by the King, who said, "May they enjoy comfort in noble beds and seats spread with carpets and such." In this way, the King gave various other riches such as gold and silver. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Cows, beds, clothing... he gave wealth to the Brahmins."

309-10. Thus, having received wealth from the King at those sacrifices, those Brahmins sought their livelihood daily for a long time and accumulated various objects of sensual desire. Then, being overcome by greed and having their minds descend into the craving for tastes through the enjoyment of the five products of the cow, such as milk, they thought: "Milk and such are already delicious from cows; surely the meat of these cows will be even more delicious." Thus, craving increased further regarding the meat. Then they thought: "If we kill and eat them, we will be blamed. What if we were to compose new Vedas?" Then, having corrupted the Vedas and composed mantras suitable to their desires at that time, those Brahmins, for the sake of that craving for meat, composed fraudulent mantras and approached King Okkāka again. Desiring to explain this meaning, they spoke the verse: "Just as water... your wealth is great," and so on.

What is meant is: "Great King, this is what has come down in our mantras. For example, just as water is used by beings for all purposes such as washing hands, and there is no evil resulting from that use—why? Because it is a requisite for beings, arisen for the purpose of utility. And just as this great earth is used for all purposes such as traveling, and wealth consisting of coins, gold, silver, and so on, and grains such as barley and wheat are used for all purposes such as trade, so too cows have arisen for the purpose of being used in all the affairs of humans. Therefore, having killed these cows, perform various sacrifices. Much wealth will accrue to you, Great King; perform sacrifices, and your wealth will be great."

311-12. Thus, when they petitioned in the same manner as before, King Okkāka then had [cows] killed. Although he had never killed any being in the past, he now had them killed. At that time, it is said, the Brahmins filled the sacrificial pit with cows, bound a festive bull, and brought it to the King, saying: "Great King, perform the cow-sacrifice (Gomadha). By sacrificing in this way, the path to the Brahma-world will be purified for you."
58:
"The path to the Brahma-world will be especially purified," they said. The King, having performed the auspicious rites, took a sword and killed many hundreds of thousands of cows along with the festive bull. The Brahmins cut and cooked the meat in the sacrificial pit and ate it. People killed the cows while wearing blankets of yellow, white, and red colors. It is said that since then, cows become terrified when they see someone wearing a blanket. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Neither with their feet... they killed [them]."

"Then the gods" means that when the King began to kill the cows, immediately after seeing that slaughter of cows, the gods of the Cātumahārājikā realm and others, the Brahmas who are called "fathers" by the Brahmins, Sakka the lord of gods, and the Dānavas, Yakkhas, Asuras, and Rakkhasas living at the foot of the mountains, cried out, "Injustice! Injustice!" and "Woe to humanity! Woe to humanity!" as they wept. Thus, starting from the earth, that sound reached the Brahma-world in an instant, and the whole world was filled with a single cry of condemnation. For what reason? Because the weapon fell upon the cow. It means that because the weapon fell upon the cow, [the world was filled with condemnation].

Not only did the gods and others weep, but this other misfortune also arose in the world. In the past, there were only three diseases: desire (icchā), hunger (anasana), and decay (jarā). It means these were just a slight longing or craving, hunger, and the decay of maturation. Due to the slaughter of animals, those diseases increased to ninety-eight. It means they reached the state of ninety-eight varieties, such as eye diseases and so on.

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to censure that slaughter of animals, said: "This is injustice." The meaning of that verse is: Among the three kinds of punishment (daṇḍa) such as the punishment of the body (kāyadaṇḍa) involved in the harming of these animals, because it is devoid of righteousness, injustice (adhamma) descended and prevailed. And because it has prevailed since then, it is called "ancient" (purāṇa). Since the descent of that injustice, cows, which are innocent because they do not harm anyone even with their feet, are killed. Those sacrificers who kill those cows fall away from, deviate from, and decline from righteousness (dhamma).

"Thus, this is a minor practice (aṇudhamma)" means that this is a low practice, a base practice, an injustice. Or else, because the practice of giving (dānadhamma) in this sacrifice is also small...
59:
The name 'Aṇudhamma' exists; therefore, referring to the gift suitable for that Dhamma, He said 'Aṇudhamma'. 'Porāṇa' means ancient, as it has existed since long ago. It should be understood as 'Viññūgarahita' (censured by the wise) because it is censured by the wise. Since it is censured by the wise, whenever people see such a sacrifice, they censure the sacrificer. How do they censure? They say, 'The Brahmins have created an evil; they kill cows and eat meat,' and so on; this is the tradition in this context.

'Evaṃ dhamme viyāpanne' means when the ancient Brahmin Dhamma was thus destroyed. There is also a reading 'viyāvaṭṭe', which means when it became perverted and changed. 'Vibhinnā suddavessikā' means that the Sudras (Sudda) and Vaisyas (Vessa), who previously lived in harmony, became divided. Many Khattiyas (kings) also became divided among themselves. 'Patiṃ bhariyāvamanyatha' means that wives, having been placed in the position of authority over household affairs and being endowed with the strength of children and so on, despised their husbands; they looked down on and disparaged them, and did not serve them respectfully.

When they were thus divided among themselves, the Khattiyas and the Brahmins... (etc.) ...followed the power of sensual pleasures. To prevent the Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vaisyas, and Sudras from falling into confusion (intermixing), they were called 'Gottarakkhitā' (protectors of lineage) because they protected their respective lineages. All of them, having discarded that doctrine of birth and destroying all such perceptions as 'I am a Khattiya' or 'I am a Brahmin', followed the power of sensual pleasures known as the five strands of sensual pleasure and reached a state of attachment. It means that for the sake of sensual pleasures, they did nothing that they would not do.

Thus, in this Sutta, the Blessed One, having spoken of the virtues of the ancient Brahmins with the nine verses beginning with 'Isayo pubbakā', concluded the teaching by showing their likeness to Brahma with the verse 'Yo nesaṃ paramo', their likeness to Devas with the verse 'Tassa vattamanusikkhantā', the boundaries of conduct with the four verses beginning with 'Taṇḍulaṃ sayanaṃ', the breaking of boundaries with the seventeen verses beginning with 'Tesaṃ āsi vipallāso', and the lamentation of Devas and others due to that wrong practice. However, the 'Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla' (outcaste Brahmin) is not mentioned here. Why? Because it is not the cause of the ruin. Indeed, only through being endowed with the Brahmin Dhamma are the likeness to Brahma, the likeness to Devas, and the boundaries of conduct...
60: The Brahmins' possession of Dhamma, which makes them like Brahmā, like gods, and their adherence to the boundaries of virtue, are the causes [for the stability of the holy life]. The cause of decline, however, is the breaking of those boundaries (the mixing of castes). This Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla of the type mentioned in the Doṇa Sutta is not the cause of the decline of the Brahmins' Dhamma. Why? Because he came into existence after the Dhamma had already declined. Therefore, without showing that Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla, the Buddha concluded the teaching. Nowadays, even such a Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla is hard to find. Thus, this Dhamma of the Brahmins is lost. For that very reason, Doṇa the Brahmin said: "Venerable Gotama, if this is so, we cannot even fulfill the status of a Brāhmaṇacaṇḍāla." The rest of the matter here is just as previously stated. ## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Khuddaka Commentary, ## the Commentary on the Brāhmaṇadhammika Sutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished. ## 8. Dhamma Sutta (Nāvā Sutta) Vaṇṇanā This sutta, beginning with "Yasmā hi dhammaṃ," is called the Dhamma Sutta and also the Nāvā Sutta. What is its origin? This sutta was spoken concerning the Venerable Sāriputta Thera. This is just a summary; the details should be understood starting from the origins of the two chief disciples. To explain: before the Blessed One appeared, it is said that the two chief disciples fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons (kappas) and were reborn in the deva world. The first of them, having passed away, took conception in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Rūpasārī, the wife of a Brahmin village headman who possessed wealth of five hundred and sixty million, in the Brahmin village of Upatissa, not far from Rājagaha. The second also took conception on that very same day in the womb of a Brahmin woman named Moggallānī, the wife of a Brahmin village headman of similar wealth, in the Brahmin village of Kolita, not far from that same village. Thus, their conception and their birth from the womb occurred on the very same day. On that same day, they were named: one as Upatissa because he was born in Upatissa village, and the other as Kolita because he was born in Kolita village.
61:
Those two friends, who used to play together in the dust, gradually reached adulthood. Each had a retinue of five hundred youths. Whenever they went to a park or a riverbank, they went only with their retinues. One went with five hundred golden palanquins, and the second with five hundred chariots drawn by thoroughbred horses.

At that time, there was a festival called Giraggasamajja held periodically in the city of Rājagaha. In the evening, in the center of the city, famous young princes and others from all over the Aṅga and Magadha regions would gather and, sitting on well-prepared couches and benches, watch the splendor of the festival. Then, those two friends went to that festival with their retinues and sat in the prepared seats. While Upatissa was watching the splendor of the festival, he saw the gathered crowd and thought, "This entire multitude of people will die before reaching a hundred years." The thought of death seemed to come and settle upon his forehead. It was the same for Kolita. Although various dancers were performing, their minds were not inclined even to look; instead, spiritual urgency (saṃvega) truly arose.

When the festival ended and the crowd departed, as those two friends were leaving with their retinues, Kolita asked Upatissa, "Friend, did you not feel even a little joy from watching the dancers and such?" Upatissa told him what had happened and asked Kolita the same question. Kolita also told him his own experience and said, "Come, friend, let us go forth as monks and seek the Deathless (Amata)." Upatissa agreed, saying, "Very well, friend."

Then those two men abandoned their wealth and returned once more to the city of Rājagaha. At that time, a wanderer named Sañjaya lived in Rājagaha. They went forth as monks under Sañjaya along with their five hundred youths, and within a few days, they mastered the three Vedas and the entire doctrine of the wanderers. Although they scrutinized the beginning, middle, and end of those scriptures, they did not see the end, so they asked their teacher, "We see the beginning and middle of these scriptures, but we do not see the end. We do not see the conclusion, such as 'By these scriptures, one shall attain this benefit; there is no higher Dhamma to be attained beyond this.'" The teacher also said, "I too do not see such an end to those scriptures." They said, "In that case, we shall seek the end of these scriptures." The teacher said, "Seek as you wish." Having thus received the teacher's permission, they wandered in search of the Deathless and became famous throughout the island of Jambudīpa. When they asked questions to wise kings and others, those people were unable to answer them step by step.
62:
When the names "Upatissa" and "Kolita" were mentioned, there was almost no one who said, "Who are these? We do not know them"; they were that famous. While they were thus wandering in search of the Deathless (Amata), our Blessed One appeared in the world, set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and gradually arrived at the city of Rājagaha. Those wanderers, having traveled throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, let alone the Deathless, did not find anyone who could even answer a final question, so they returned once more to Rājagaha. At that time, the Venerable Assaji, having dressed in the morning, and so on—all the details until their ordination should be understood in detail as they appear in the Mahāvagga, Pabbajjākhandhaka.

After these two friends had thus gone forth, the Venerable Sāriputta realized the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) within half a month. When the Venerable Sāriputta lived in the same monastery as the Elder Assaji, after serving the Blessed One, he would go to serve the Elder out of respect, thinking, "This venerable one is my first teacher; depending on him, I came to know the Blessed One's Dispensation."
