However, when he did not live in the same monastery as the Elder Assaji, he would look toward the direction where the Elder resided, prostrate with the five-point prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita), and pay homage with joined palms. Seeing this behavior, some monks spoke disparagingly, saying, "Sāriputta, despite being a Chief Disciple, is worshipping the directions; I think even now he has not been able to abandon the Brahmin view (brāhmaṇa-diṭṭhi)."

Then the Blessed One, hearing that conversation with his divine ear, while remaining seated on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, manifested himself and addressed the monks, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" The monks reported the matter to him. Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Sāriputta is not worshipping the directions. He is paying homage to, honoring, and respecting his own teacher, depending on whom he came to know the Dispensation. Monks, Sāriputta is one who honors his teacher." Having said this, he spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those gathered there.

In that sutta, "Yasmā hi dhammaṃ puriso vijaññā" means: from whichever person a man should learn the Pariyatti Dhamma consisting of the three Piṭakas, or the Paṭivedha Dhamma consisting of the nine supramundane states to be attained after hearing the Pariyatti. There is also a variant reading "Yassā", but the meaning is the same. "Indaṃva naṃ devatā pūjayeyya" means: just as the deities in the two deva worlds worship Sakka, the lord of the devas, so should the one who knows thus [worship] that teacher, rising early and performing all major and minor duties such as removing his sandals...
63:
When [the student] performs [his duties], he should honor, respect, and revere [the teacher]. For what reason? Because that teacher, being honored... reveals the Dhamma. When the teacher is thus honored, being of a confident mind towards that student, and being learned by way of scriptural mastery (pariyatti) and realization (paṭivedha), he reveals and teaches the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti-dhamma) by way of instruction, and the Dhamma of realization (paṭivedha-dhamma) which is to be attained through practice according to the instruction after hearing the teaching. Or, he reveals the scriptural Dhamma through teaching, and reveals the Dhamma of realization attained by himself through the use of similes.

'Having made that his goal and having listened, the wise man' (tad-aṭṭhikatvāna nisamma dhīro) means that because he is capable of attending to and listening with respect to the Dhamma revealed by the teacher who is thus confident, he is a wise man. 'Practicing the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma' (dhammānudhammaṃ paṭipajjāmāno) means developing insight (vipassanā) which is the 'subsequent Dhamma' (anudhamma) because it is in conformity with the supramundane Dhamma. 'He is wise, clear-sighted, and subtle' (viññū vibhāvī nipuṇo ca hoti) means: he is 'wise' (viññū) due to the attainment of wisdom known as sagacity; he is 'clear-sighted' (vibhāvī) because he is capable of making known and clear to others what he himself knows; and he is 'subtle' (nipuṇo) because of his penetration into the most profound and subtle meanings. 'He who heedfully associates with such a one' (yo tādisaṃ bhajati appamatto) refers to one who, being heedful and intent on pleasing that teacher, associates with such a learned person as described before.

Having thus praised the association with a wise teacher, he now speaks this verse beginning with 'The low and the foolish' (khuddañca bālaṃ) in order to censure the association with a foolish teacher. Therein, 'low' (khuddaṃ) refers to one endowed with low bodily actions and so forth; he is 'foolish' (bālaṃ) because of the absence of wisdom. 'One who has not attained the goal' (anāgatatthaṃ) means one who has not yet attained the benefits of scriptural learning and realization. 'Envious' (usūyakaṃ) means one who, due to an envious mind, cannot endure the progress of the student. The meaning of the remaining words is clear. In terms of the sense, it means that even if a teacher receives many requisites such as robes, he is unable to give them to his students; and in giving the gift of Dhamma, he cannot even speak the mere words of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. Because he is endowed with such low qualities, one who associates with such a low, foolish, ignorant, and envious teacher becomes a fool himself, according to the method stated: 'Like rotting fish wrapped in kusa grass' (pūtimacchaṃ kusaggena). Therefore, in this Dispensation, if one has doubt regarding the teachings without having clarified or understood even a small portion of the scriptural Dhamma or the Dhamma of realization, he meets death without having crossed over that doubt. This is how the meaning should be understood.

## 322-3. Now, to make that same meaning clear, he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Just as a man' (yathā naro). Therein, 'river' (āpagaṃ) means a stream. 'Great water' (mahodakaṃ) means much water. 'Salilaṃ' means...
64:
'Gone here and there' (itō citō ca gataṃ) means flowing here and there, signifying 'extensive.' There is also a reading 'saritaṃ,' which has the same meaning. 'Swift current' (sīghasotaṃ) means having a current that carries things away, signifying 'forceful.' In the phrase 'kiṃ so,' the syllable 'so' is a mere particle (nipāta), as the person is already indicated by the phrase 'he being carried away' (so vuyhamāno). The meaning is 'kiṃ sū,' as in the expressions 'I shall not be that' or 'I shall perish.' 'Dhamma' (dhammaṃ) refers to the two kinds of Dhamma mentioned previously. 'Without having grasped the meaning' (anisāmayatthaṃ) means without having investigated the meaning. The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

In terms of the sense: Just as any man who, having descended into such a river as described and being carried away by that river, following the current, how can he, while following the current himself, be able to take others who wish to reach the far shore to that shore? (There is also a reading 'sakkati'.) In the same way, one who cannot clarify the two kinds of Dhamma with his own wisdom, and has not investigated the meaning in the presence of the learned—being himself one who has not clarified or understood, and thus has not crossed over doubt—how can he be able to make others contemplate or perceive the Dhamma? This is how the meaning should be seen here. In this context, the scriptural passage beginning with 'Indeed, Cunda, that one who is himself sinking in the mud...' (so vata, cunda, attanā palipapalipanno) should be recollected.

324-5. Having thus stated a simile to clarify the inability of a fool to make others perceive [the truth] through associating with fools, he now spoke the two verses beginning with 'Just as a boat' (yathāpi nāvaṃ) to clarify the ability of the wise man, mentioned in the phrase 'he who heedfully associates with such a one,' to make others perceive [the truth]. Therein, 'with a rudder' (phiyena) means with a ladle-like steering oar. 'With a pole' (rittena) means with a bamboo pole. 'Therein' (tatra) means in that boat. 'Knowing the means therein' (tatrūpayaññū) means one who knows the means by knowing how to move that boat forward and backward, and by knowing the route. He is 'skillful' (kusalo) because of having learned the craft and having a very dexterous hand. He is 'intelligent' (mutīmā) because of being capable of remedying dangers that arise. 'One who has reached the end of knowledge' (vedagū) means one who has gone [to Nibbāna] by means of the four path-knowledges known as 'veda.' 'One of developed self' (bhāvitatto) means one whose mind is developed by that same path-cultivation. 'Learned' (bahussuto) is as explained previously. 'One of unshakable nature' (avedhadhammo) means one whose nature is unshakeable by the eight worldly conditions. 'Endowed with attentive listening and the support' (sotāvadhānūpanisūpapanne) means in one who is endowed with the act of listening and with the sufficing condition (upanissaya) for the paths and fruits. The rest consists of words with plain meanings. The connection of the sense can also be understood by the previous method, so it is not elaborated.
65:
Thus, having spoken this illustration to make clear the ability of a wise person to make others contemplate and reflect, and wishing to urge the association with such a wise person, the Teacher spoke this concluding verse beginning with "Tasmā have". The summary of its meaning is: Since those endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya) attain distinction by associating with the wise, therefore, one should indeed associate with a virtuous person (sappurisa). What kind of virtuous person should one associate with? One who is both intelligent (medhāvī) and learned (bahussuta). One is intelligent due to the perfection of wisdom, and learned due to the two kinds of learning mentioned above. A person associating with such a person, having understood the meaning of the Dhamma taught by him, and practicing according to the instruction, becomes one who has understood the Dhamma through the power of penetration (paṭivedha) by that practice. Thus, he would obtain, reach, and attain supramundane happiness consisting of the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. Thus, the Teacher concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## The Commentary on the Dhammasutta of the Sutta Nipāta is finished.
## 9. Commentary on the Kiṃsīla Sutta

"Kiṃsīlo" refers to the Kiṃsīla Sutta. What is the occasion of its origin? A son of a Brahmin who was a friend of Ven. Sāriputta’s father, the Brahmin Vanganta, and who was also a friend of the Elder during his lay life, renounced five hundred and sixty crores of wealth and ordained under the Elder Sāriputta, and learned the entire word of the Buddha. Although the Elder gave him meditation subjects and exhorted him many times, that monk could not attain any distinction through that meditation. Then, the Elder, realizing "This person is one who should be tamed by the Buddha," took him to the Blessed One and, on account of that monk but without specifying the individual, asked the question beginning with "Kiṃsīlo". Then, the Blessed One spoke the following words.

In that sutta, "Kiṃsīlo" means: endowed with what kind of virtue of avoidance (vārittasīla), or of what nature? "Kiṃsamācāro" means: endowed with what kind of conduct (cāritta)? "Kāni kammāni brūhayanti" means: cultivating what kind of bodily actions and so forth? "Naro sammā niviṭṭhassa" means: how would a person be well-established and delighted in the Dispensation? "Uttamathañca pāpuṇe" means: how would one reach the Fruit of Arahantship, which is the highest of all goals? This is the intended meaning.
66:
Then the Blessed One reflected: "Ven. Sāriputta has been ordained for only half a month, yet he has reached the perfection of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramī). Why then does he ask a question concerning a beginner worldling (ādikammika-puthujjana)?" Then, realizing "He asks on account of his resident pupil (saddhivihārika)," the Blessed One, without elaborating on the virtue of conduct (cārittasīla) mentioned in the question, spoke the words beginning with "Vuḍḍhāpacāyī" (one who respects elders), wishing to teach the Dhamma according to what was suitable for that pupil.

In that context, there are four kinds of elders (vuḍḍhā): an elder in wisdom (paññā-vuḍḍha), an elder in virtue (guṇa-vuḍḍha), an elder in birth (jāti-vuḍḍha), and an elder in age (vayo-vuḍḍha). A monk who is young in birth but of great learning is called an elder in wisdom because he is superior in learning and wisdom among elderly monks of little learning. Indeed, even elderly monks learn the word of the Buddha from him and look forward to his exhortations, decisions, and answers to questions. Likewise, even a young monk, if he is endowed with spiritual attainment (adhigama), is called an elder in virtue. Indeed, even elderly monks, established in his exhortation, take up the practice of insight (vipassanā) and reach the Fruit of Arahantship. Likewise, a young king, a consecrated noble (khattiya), or a Brahmin is called an elder in birth because he is worthy of the respect of other people. However, everyone who is born earlier is called an elder in age.

Among those four types, if the Blessed One is excluded, there is no one equal to the Elder Sāriputta in wisdom. Likewise, in virtue, he had already penetrated all the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple within half a month. In birth also, he was born into a wealthy Brahmin family (brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla). Therefore, although he was of the same age as that monk, Ven. Sāriputta was an elder by these three reasons. In this context, however, the Blessed One said "Vuḍḍhāpacāyī" referring only to his being an elder in wisdom and virtue. Therefore, one is "Vuḍḍhāpacāyī" by paying respect to such elders. One should also be "Anusūyako" (not envious) by being free from envy regarding the gains and so forth of those very elders. This is the meaning of the first line of the verse.

In the phrase "Kālaññū cassa", one who goes to see his teachers to dispel lust (rāga) when it arises is called "one who knows the right time" (kālaññū). One who goes to see his teachers to dispel anger (dosa), delusion (moha), or laziness (kosajja) when they arise is also called "one who knows the right time". Thus, one should be a knower of the right time to see one's teachers. "Dhammiṃ kathaṃ" refers to talk associated with tranquillity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). "Khaṇaññū" means one who knows the right moment for that talk, or one who knows that the opportunity to hear such talk is rare. "Suṇeyya sakkaccaṃ" means one should listen to that talk respectfully. The meaning is that one should respectfully listen not only to that talk but also to other well-spoken words (subhāsita) related to the qualities of the Buddha and so forth.

In the phrase "Kālaññū cassa gurūnaṃ dassanāya", as previously mentioned, knowing the time to dispel lust and so forth that have arisen in oneself, one should go to the presence of one's teachers at the proper time...
67:
One should approach the teachers for the purpose of inquiry when seeing them anywhere—at the place of stupa worship, the Bodhi-tree terrace, the alms-round path, or at midday—thinking, "I am a monk who practices meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) and observes the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)." However, at their own dwelling, one should approach for the purpose of asking about meditation methods and so forth, having noted that the teacher is seated in their own place and is at peace. When approaching in this manner, one should discard stubbornness and be humble, destroying the pride that causes stiffness. One should approach like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, or like a snake with its fangs extracted. Then, one should practice the meaning and the Dhamma taught by that teacher... "Attha" means the meaning of what was spoken. "Dhamma" means the Pali text. "Saṃyama" means virtue (sīla). "Brahmacariya" means the remaining noble practice of the Dispensation. "Anussare ceva samācare ca" means one should repeatedly reflect when the meaning is taught, and one should repeatedly reflect when the Pali, virtue, and noble practice are taught. Not being satisfied with mere reflection, one should practice all of it; one should undertake and practice it. It means one should strive to apply those teachings to oneself. One who does so is called one who performs their duty.

Thereafter, one should be one who delights in the Dhamma, rejoices in the Dhamma, stands in the Dhamma, and is skilled in discerning the Dhamma. Here, in all these terms, "Dhamma" refers to serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). "Ārāma" (delight) and "rati" (rejoicing) have the same meaning. One is called "dhammārāma" because of delighting in the Dhamma. One is "dhammarata" because of rejoicing in the Dhamma and not longing for any other thing. One is "dhamme ṭhita" because of standing in and practicing the Dhamma. One is "dhammavinicchayaññū" because of knowing the discernment of the Dhamma, such as "This is the knowledge of arising (udaya-ñāṇa), this is the knowledge of passing away (vaya-ñāṇa)." One should be of such a nature. At that time, "animal talk" (tiracchāna-kathā) such as talk about kings, which causes a person with immature insight to take great delight in external forms and so forth, corrupts the Dhamma of serenity and insight; therefore, it is called "dhamma-sandosa-vāda" (talk that corrupts the Dhamma). One should not practice such talk that corrupts the Dhamma. Instead, while resorting to suitable dwellings (āvāsa-sappāya) and suitable resorts (gocara-sappāya), one should spend time only with truthful and well-spoken words connected with serenity and insight.

Now, wishing to make clear the defilement of a monk engaged in serenity and insight, which was mentioned very briefly in the phrase "dhamma-sandosa-vāda," the Blessed One spoke this verse beginning with "Hassaṃ jappaṃ" along with other defilements. There is also a variant reading "hāsaṃ."
68:
A monk practicing insight should only smile at a laughable object. He should not engage in useless talk. He should not weep over the loss of relatives and so forth. He should not give rise to resentment in his heart toward stumps, thorns, and the like. Deceit (māyā), the three kinds of scheming (kuhana), greed for requisites (giddhi), pride regarding birth and so forth (māna), aggressive rivalry (sārambha) characterized by delighting in opposition, harshness (kakkasa) characterized by harsh speech, the "stains" (kasāva) such as lust, and infatuation (mucchā) characterized by excessive craving—these faults should be abandoned by one who desires happiness, just as one avoids a pit of glowing coals; by one who desires purity, just as one avoids a place of excrement; and by one who desires life, just as one avoids vipers and cobras. One should practice with a mind free from intoxication, being devoid of pride and the like, and with a steady nature due to the absence of mental distraction. One who practices in this way, through meditation purified from all defilements, will before long reach Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Hassaṃ jappaṃ... ṭhitatto."

Now, a monk possessed of the defilements (upakkilesa) described by the method beginning with "Hassaṃ jappaṃ" is one who acts hastily and without reflection. He proceeds being infatuated by the power of lust or being corrupted by the power of anger. He is negligent in developing wholesome states and does not practice continuously. For such a person, the advice given in the method beginning with "One should respectfully listen to well-spoken words" is useless. Therefore, wishing to show that for such a defiled person, this is an obstacle to the growth of learning and so forth through a teaching based on individuals, He spoke this verse: "Viññātasārāni."

The meaning of that verse is: Knowing the well-spoken teachings connected with serenity and insight is the essence. If one understands them, it is good; if one only grasps the sound, it achieves nothing. That by which one understands these teachings through knowledge consisting of what is heard is called "learning" (suta). This knowledge consisting of what is heard has the essence of understood concentration. In those understood teachings, the concentration which is the non-distraction of the mind and the practice for the sake of suchness—this is its essence. Success in any purpose is not achieved by mere understanding alone. However, a person who acts hastily due to the power of lust and so forth, and who is negligent because of not practicing wholesome states continuously, is one who only grasps the sound. For him, because there is no understanding of the meaning, the wisdom that understands those well-spoken teachings does not increase, nor does learning (suta), because there is no practice for the sake of suchness.
69:
Having shown the loss of wisdom and the loss of learning (suta) for those beings who are thus heedless, the Buddha now spoke the verse beginning with "Dhamme ca ye... sāramajjhagū" wishing to show the attainment of the essence of both for those who are heedful. In that verse, what is called the Dhamma known by the Noble Ones is indeed the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā. Indeed, there is no Buddha who has attained Parinibbāna without having taught the Dhamma of Samatha and Vipassanā. Therefore, those persons who delight in this Dhamma known by the Noble Ones, who are heedful and constantly endowed with effort, are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and action. Because they are endowed with the fourfold good conduct of speech, the threefold good conduct of mind, and the threefold good conduct of body, they are unsurpassed in speech, mind, and action; they are unlike other beings, being supreme and distinguished. By this much, the Buddha shows the virtue (sīla) associated with the Noble Path along with the preliminary virtue.

Those persons of such pure virtue, because they are established in peace (santi), gentleness (soracca), and concentration (samādhi), reach the essence of learning and wisdom. Those who delight in the Dhamma known by the Noble Ones are not only unsurpassed in speech and so on, but should be known as those who, being well-established in peace, gentleness, and concentration, have attained the essence of learning and wisdom. The phrase "āsaṃsāyaṃ bhūtavacanaṃ" is a statement of what is manifest. Therein, "santi" means Nibbāna. "Soracca" is the wisdom that penetrates things as they really are through the state of delighting in what is good. The "soracca" of "santi" is "santi-soracca"; this is a designation for the Path Wisdom that has Nibbāna as its object. "Samādhi" is the Path Concentration associated with that Path Wisdom. "Saṇṭhitā" means being firmly established in both (wisdom and concentration). The essence of learning and wisdom is the liberation (vimutti) which is the Fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala). Indeed, this holy life (brahmacariya) has liberation as its essence.

Thus, in this verse, the Blessed One shows the preliminary practice by the word "dhamme"; the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) by the words "anuttarā vacasā" and so on; and the aggregate of wisdom and the aggregate of concentration by the words "santi-soracca-samādhi". By these three trainings, He shows the subsequent practice. Showing the unshakable liberation (akuppa-vimutti) through the essence of learning and wisdom, He concluded the teaching with the Fruit of Arahantship as the pinnacle. At the end of the teaching, that monk attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and, before long, was established in the highest Fruit of Arahantship.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary known as Paramatthajotikā,
## the explanation of the Kiṃsīla Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
70:
## 10. Uṭṭhānasutta-vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Uṭṭhahatha" is the Uṭṭhāna Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? Once, while the Blessed One was staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, having stayed at Jetavana during the night, He entered Sāvatthī for alms in the morning surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. Leaving the city by the eastern gate, He went to the Migāramātupāsāda (the Palace of Migāra’s Mother) for the day-rest.

It is said that it was the Blessed One's constant habit to stay at Jetavana at night and go to Migāramātupāsāda for the day-rest, or to stay at Migāramātupāsāda at night and go to Jetavana for the day-rest. Why did He do so? It was to favor the two families (of Anāthapiṇḍika and Visākhā) and to demonstrate the quality of great generosity. On the ground floor of Migāramātupāsāda, there were five hundred gabled chambers, in which five hundred monks resided. When the Blessed One stayed on the ground floor of that monastery, the monks would not ascend to the upper floor out of respect for the Blessed One.

On that day, however, the Blessed One entered a gabled chamber on the upper floor. Therefore, the five hundred monks entered the five hundred chambers on the ground floor. All those monks were newly ordained, recently come to this Dhamma-Vinaya, and were restless, haughty, and of frivolous faculties. Having entered the chambers, they slept during the day, and upon waking in the evening, they gathered on the great terrace and asked, "What kind of food did you have at the refectory today? Where did you go?" One said, "Friend, I went to the house of King Kosala." Another said, "I went to Anāthapiṇḍika’s house. There, such and such an arrangement of food was provided." Thus, as they spoke various kinds of talk concerning material things (āmisakathā), their voices became very loud and noisy.

Hearing that sound, the Blessed One thought, "Even though these monks live with me, they are so heedless; they are acting very improperly." He then considered the arrival of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. At that very moment, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing the Blessed One’s thought, arrived by psychic power and stood worshipping at His feet. Then the Blessed One addressed him: "Moggallāna, these fellow practitioners of yours are heedless. Please stir them up well (with a sense of spiritual urgency)."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Yes, Bhante," and having accepted the command, he immediately entered the water-kasina meditative attainment (āpo-kasiṇa-samāpatti). He then shook that great palace, which stood on a cesspool, with his big toe, along with the ground it rested on, just as a great wind shakes a boat. Then those monks, crying out in fear, abandoned their robes and fled through the four doors. The Blessed One, wishing to show Himself to them, appeared as if He were entering the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) through another door. Seeing the Blessed One, those monks worshipped Him and...
71:
The monks stood there [in fear]. The Blessed One asked, "Monks, why are you afraid?" Those monks replied, "Venerable Sir, this Migāramātupāsāda palace is shaking." The Buddha asked again, "Monks, do you know by whom it is shaken?" "We do not know, Venerable Sir," they replied. Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, it was shaken by Moggallāna to instill spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in those like you who are unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, and living in negligence." Having said this, he spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to those monks.

In that sutta, "uṭṭhahatha" means: arise from your seats, strive, exert yourselves, and do not be lazy. "Nisīdatha" means: sit down in a cross-legged posture for the purpose of devoting yourselves to meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). "Ko attho supitena vo" means: what benefit is there in sleeping for you who have gone forth to attain Nibbāna without any clinging? It is indeed true that one who is asleep cannot achieve any benefit. "Āturānañhi kā niddā, sallaviddhāna ruppataṃ" means: there is no sleep for those afflicted by diseases such as eye ailments even in a small part of the body, nor for those who are distressed by being pierced by an iron dart, a bone dart, a tooth dart, a horn dart, or a wooden dart that has entered even an inch or two. This being so, what benefit is there in sleeping for you who are afflicted by various diseases of defilements (kilesa) that have arisen by destroying the entire continuity of mind and body? Are you not distressed like those pierced by darts, because the five darts such as the dart of lust (rāga) have pierced and entered into the heart?

After saying this, the Blessed One spoke the verses beginning with "Uṭṭhahatha... vasānuge" again to further encourage and inspire spiritual urgency in those monks. The explanation of the meaning and connection of those verses is as follows: Monks, for you who are thus pierced by the darts of defilements, it is indeed the time to wake up. Why is that? Monks, this holy life (brahmacariya) is as precious as a choice drink; the Teacher is present before you. In the past, however, because you did not see the Noble Truths (Ariyasacca), you slept for a long time on mountains, by rivers, in level places, in uneven places, and even on the tops of trees. Therefore, to make an end of that sleep, arise, sit down, and train firmly for the sake of peace (Nibbāna).

The meaning of the first line of that verse is as already stated. In the second line, "santi" (peace) is of three kinds: absolute peace (accanta-santi), peace of substitution (tadaṅga-santi), and conventional peace (sammuti-santi); these are names for Nibbāna, insight (vipassanā), and right view (sammādiṭṭhi). Here, however, absolute peace, which is Nibbāna, is intended. Therefore, it means: train firmly for Nibbāna, train with unshaken effort. Why is that? Because if the King of Death (Maccu-rāja) knows you are negligent, he will deceive you.
72:
Lest the King of Death, named Māra, knowing you to be negligent, saying "These are negligent," should deceive you who are under his control; lest he should deceive you while making you fall under his power in such a way that you go under his control.

Those devas and humans who do not follow the realm of that King of Death are satisfied and delighted by whatever craving; by whatever craving devas and humans desire forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; they remain attached, clinging, and adhering to those forms and so forth. Cross over, transcend that craving (taṇhā) for existence and wealth, called "visattikā" because it is widespread, extensive, and vast among various objects. May the moment (khaṇa) not pass you by; may this moment for you to perform the recluse's duties (samaṇa-dhamma) not pass away. For those to whom such a moment passes by, and those who let this moment pass, they, having missed the moment, grieve when they are consigned to hell. In the four states of misery (apāya) designated as "hell" (niraya) because of the sense of having no enjoyment, they grieve, saying, "Alas, we did not perform any good deeds," and so on.

Thus, the Blessed One, having encouraged and inspired spiritual urgency in those monks, now censuring their living in negligence and wishing to urge all those monks toward heedfulness (appamāda), spoke this verse: "Pamādo rajo" (Negligence is dust). In that verse, "pamāda" briefly means the absence of mindfulness (sati); that absence of mindfulness is called "dust" (raja) because it defiles the mind. Falling into that negligence is called "pamādānupatita"; because of falling into negligence, the negligence that arises repeatedly is itself dust. Indeed, there is never a time when negligence is not dust. What is shown by this? Do not fall into the confidence of thinking, "We are still young, we will realize it later." Even in youth, negligence is dust; in the middle age and in the age of a senior monk, because of falling into negligence, it becomes a great dust, like a heap of refuse. For example, dust that has been in a house for a day or two is just dust, but when it increases, it becomes a heap of refuse that has lasted for many years. Even so, a monk who learns the Buddha's word in the first stage of life and performs the recluse's duties in the remaining stages, or one who learns in the first stage, listens in the middle stage, and performs the recluse's duties in the last stage, is not one who lives in negligence because he has practiced the path in accordance with heedfulness. But one who lives in negligence in all stages of life, devoted to daytime sleep and talk about material things—just like you—for him, negligence in the first stage is dust, and the great negligence of falling into negligence in the other stages is indeed great dust (mahāraja).
73:
In this way, having reproached their negligent living and wishing to urge them toward diligence (appamāda), he said: “Through diligence and through wisdom (vijjā), one should pluck out one's own thorn.” The meaning of that verse is: Since this negligence is always like dust, therefore, through diligence, which is the non-distraction of mindfulness, and through wisdom, which is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavas), a wise son of good family should pluck out the fivefold thorn, such as lust (rāga) and so on, which resides in his own heart. Thus, he concluded the teaching by making Arahantship the climax. At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred monks, having reached a state of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and reflecting upon that very Dhamma teaching, began to practice insight (vipassanā) and were established in Arahantship.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the Commentary on the Uṭṭhāna Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 11. Commentary on the Rāhula Sutta

The sutta beginning with “Kacci abhiṇhasamvāsā” is the Rāhula Sutta. What is the reason for its arising? After the Blessed One had fully realized the Omniscient Wisdom and traveled in due course from the Bodhi tree to Kapilavatthu, he was asked for an inheritance by Prince Rāhula, who said, “O Ascetic, give me my inheritance.” Thereupon, he commanded the Elder Sāriputta, “Ordain Prince Rāhula as a novice.” All that should be understood in the manner already stated in the Khandhaka Commentary. When Prince Rāhula, who had been thus ordained, reached the proper age, the Elder Sāriputta himself gave him the higher ordination (upasampadā), and the Elder Mahāmoggallāna became his teacher of the formal act (kammavācācariya). The Blessed One thought, “This prince is endowed with noble birth and so on; let him not develop pride (māna) or intoxication (mada) based on his birth, lineage, family, or physical beauty.” Thus, from his youth until he reached the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi), he constantly taught this sutta as an advice. Therefore, it is also stated at the end of this sutta: “In this way, the Blessed One constantly advised the Venerable Rāhula with these verses.”

In that sutta, the summary of the first verse is: “Rāhula, do you not despise the wise one because of the reason of constant association, or because of any other reason such as birth? He is a torch-bearer because he bears the lamp of knowledge and the lamp of the Dhamma teaching...”
74:
“...Are you respected by people? Are you always honored by them?” He spoke this referring to the Venerable Sāriputta.

When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula, wishing to show, “Venerable Sir, I do not act with pride or intoxication due to constant association like a low-born man,” spoke this response verse: “Nāhaṃ abhiṇhasamvāsā.” Its meaning is quite clear.

Thereafter, the Blessed One, wishing to advise him further, spoke the remaining verses beginning with “Pañca kāmaguṇe.” In those verses, the five cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa) are dear and pleasing in nature to beings; they are greatly desired and longed for, and they delight the mind. The Venerable Rāhula, having abandoned those sensual pleasures, left the home life out of faith (saddhā). He did not leave because he was driven out by a king, nor by thieves, nor because he was oppressed by debt, nor by fear, nor because of a loss of livelihood. Therefore, the Blessed One, encouraging him by saying, “Having abandoned the five cords of sensual pleasure, which are dear and delightful to the mind, and having left the home life out of faith,” and wishing to engage him in the practice suitable for this renunciation (nekkhamma), said: “Become one who makes an end of suffering.”

In that regard, it might be asked: “Was not the Venerable Rāhula ordained by force because he asked for an inheritance? Why then does the Blessed One say, ‘having left the home life out of faith’?” The answer is: Because he was inclined toward renunciation (nekkhamma-adhimuttattā). For this venerable one had been inclined toward renunciation for a long time. Having seen a novice named Uparevata, the son of the Padumuttara Buddha, when he was a Naga King named Saṅkha, he gave alms for seven days and aspired to become such a son of a Buddha. From then on, being endowed with that aspiration and resolve (abhinīhāra), he fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons and reached his final birth. The Blessed One knew that Rāhula was thus inclined toward renunciation. This knowledge is one of the powers of a Tathāgata. Therefore, he said, “having left the home life out of faith.” Alternatively, the meaning is: “Having left the home life out of faith for a long time, now become one who makes an end of suffering.”

Now, wishing to show him the practice for making an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) from the very beginning, he spoke the verse beginning with “Mitte bhajassu kalyāṇe.” In that verse, those who are superior in virtue (sīla) and so on are called good friends (kalyāṇamitta). One who associates with such good friends grows in virtue and so on, just as the great Sal trees grow in roots and so on by depending on the Himalayas. Therefore, he said, “Associate with good friends.” And secluded lodgings (pantāni sayanāsanāni), which are remote, quiet, and free from noise—that is, a lodging that is distant, secluded, uncrowded, and free from noise, where the sounds of deer, wild boars, and so on...
75:
The perception of the forest arises; also frequent such lodgings. 'Be one who knows moderation in eating' means be one who knows the measure; it means know the measure in receiving and the measure in consuming. In this context, one who knows the measure in receiving (paṭiggahaṇamattaññū), if the gift is small and the donor wishes to give a small amount, should receive only a small amount. Even if the gift is small but the donor wishes to give a lot, one should receive only a small amount. Even if the gift is very large but the donor wishes to give a small amount, one should receive only a small amount. If the gift is very large and the donor wishes to give a lot, one should receive it after knowing one's own capacity. Indeed, the Blessed One praised only moderation. One who knows the measure in consuming (paribhogamattaññū) should consume food with wise reflection, like [eating] the flesh of one's own son or like [applying] grease to an axle.

Thus, with this verse, having exhorted him to associate with good friends who are helpful to the holy life, and having established him in the purity of virtue regarding the use of requisites through the means of lodging and food, now, because wrong livelihood can occur through craving for requisites such as robes, the Blessed One spoke this verse beginning with 'In robes and in almsfood' to prohibit that craving and to establish him in the purity of virtue regarding livelihood. In that verse, 'requisite' (paccaya) refers to medicinal requisites as support during illness. 'In these' refers to these four requisites such as robes, which are the objects for the arising of craving for monks. 'Do not have craving' means one who sees the danger in the following way: 'These four requisites are for the purpose of covering shame and so on; they support this extremely weak body, which is like a decaying house, just as medicine supports those who are constantly afflicted by illness.' Thus, it means 'do not let craving arise; dwell without producing it.' For what reason? 'Do not come back to the world.' For one who has craving for these requisites, being pulled by craving, comes back to this world again. You, do not have craving for these requisites; if it is so, you will not come back to this world again.

When this was said, the Venerable Rāhula, reflecting, 'The Blessed One told me not to have craving for robes,' undertook the two ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) related to robes: the refuse-rag-robe practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga) and the triple-robe practice (tecīvarikaṅga). Reflecting, 'The Blessed One told me not to have craving for almsfood,' he undertook the five ascetic practices related to almsfood: the alms-round practice (piṇḍapātikaṅga), the house-to-house practice (sapadānacārikaṅga), the one-session practice (ekāsanikaṅga), the bowl-food practice (pattapiṇḍikaṅga), and the practice of refusing later food (khalupacchābhattikaṅga). Reflecting, 'The Blessed One told me not to have craving for lodging,' [he undertook the practices] related to lodging...
76:
Venerable Rāhula undertook the six ascetic practices related to lodging: the forest-dweller's practice (āraññikaṅga), the open-air practice (abbhokāsikaṅga), the tree-root practice (rukkhamūlikaṅga), the any-assigned-seat practice (yathāsanthatikaṅga), the charnel-ground practice (sosānikaṅga), and the sitter's practice (nesajjikaṅga). Reflecting, 'The Blessed One told me not to have craving for medicinal requisites,' he became one who is content with all requisites through the three kinds of contentment: as obtained (yathālābha), according to one's strength (yathābala), and as appropriate (yathāsāruppa). That Venerable Rāhula was like a well-bred son who is easy to admonish and who accepts instructions respectfully. Thus, the Blessed One, having established the Venerable Rāhula in the purity of virtue regarding livelihood, now spoke [the verse] beginning with 'Restrained in the Pātimokkha' to establish him in the remaining virtues and in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). In that verse, in the phrase 'restrained in the Pātimokkha' (saṃvuto pātimokkhasmiṃ), the remaining Pali word 'bhavassu' (be) should be added and understood. Or it should be understood by connecting it with the final word 'bhavā' or with the second word. Thus, with these two statements, he established him in the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) and the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriya-saṃvara-sīla). Although the five sense faculties are mentioned here explicitly, it should be understood that the sixth is also mentioned by implication. 'May mindfulness of the body be yours' means for you who are established in the fourfold purity of virtue, may there be mindfulness of the body in its various forms such as the analysis of the four elements, the four types of clear comprehension (sampajañña), mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), and the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhārepaṭikūlasaññā); it means 'develop that meditation subject.' 'Be one who is full of disenchantment' means be one who is full of weariness towards the round of rebirths (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), and one who has the perception of non-delight in the whole world.

Having thus shown the stage of access (upacāra-bhūmi) which is a part of penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), he now spoke [the verse] beginning with 'Avoid the sign' to show the stage of absorption (appanā-bhūmi). In that statement, 'sign' (nimitta) refers to the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta) which is the basis for lust (rāga). Therefore, he further qualified that sign later by saying, 'the beautiful [sign] associated with lust.' 'Avoid' means abandon it by not giving it attention (amanasikāra). 'Develop the mind through foulness' means develop the mind in such a way that the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) is perfected, whether in a conscious body or an unconscious body. 'One-pointed, well-concentrated' means one-pointed through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and well-concentrated through absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). It means 'develop the mind so that such a state of mind arises for you.' Having thus shown the stage of absorption to the Venerable Rāhula, he spoke [the verse] beginning with 'Signless' (animitta) to show insight (vipassanā). In that statement, 'develop also the signless' means that one whose mind is concentrated through the concentration that is a part of penetration should develop insight. For insight is called 'signless' (animitta) because the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā-ñāṇa) is liberated from the sign of permanence (nicca-nimitta)...
77:
Through the method beginning with "Vimokkha," the name "Animitta" (Signless) is obtained because of not grasping the signs of lust (rāga-nimitta) and so forth. As it was said: "Friends, I, by not attending to any signs, enter and dwell in the signless concentration of mind (animitta cetosamādhi). Friends, for me dwelling in this way, there is consciousness that follows the signs" (SN 4.340).

"Abandon the underlying tendency to conceit" means that after obtaining the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) through this signless meditation (animitta-bhāvanā), one should abandon it in due order as stated: "Meghiya, for one who perceives impermanence, the perception of non-self (anattasaññā) is well-established; one who perceives non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna)" (AN 9.3, Ud 31). This means to give up, abandon, and relinquish the underlying tendency to conceit. Thereafter, through the realization of conceit by the Noble Path—meaning its destruction, passing away, abandonment, and relinquishment—one becomes peaceful, quenched, cooled, and free from all distress and fever. Until attaining Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue remaining (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), one will dwell in the attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) of either the Void (suññata), the Signless (animitta), or the Undirected (appaṇihita). Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.

Thereafter, the words beginning with "Itthaṃ sudaṃ bhagavā" are the words of the Reciters (Saṅgītikārakas). It means "Thus indeed the Blessed One said." The remaining words have clear meanings. Having been thus exhorted, when the qualities that ripen toward liberation (vimuttipari pācanīya-dhamma) had matured, the Venerable Rāhula attained Arahantship at the end of the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, together with many thousands of deities.

## The Explanation of the Rāhula Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## 12. Explanation of the Nigrodhakappa Sutta (Vangīsa Sutta)

The Nigrodhakappa Sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," is also called the "Vangīsa Sutta." How did it arise? Its origin is exactly as stated in its introduction (nidāna). In that sutta, the words beginning with "Evaṃ me" have the meanings already described.
78:
Omitting those words and others of a similar nature, I shall explain only the methods not yet mentioned. "Aggāḷave cetiye" means at the Aggāḷava Shrine in the city of Āḷavī. Before the Blessed One appeared, there were many shrines such as Aggāḷava and Gotamaka, which were the dwellings of yakkhas, nāgas, and so forth. When the Blessed One appeared, people destroyed those places and built monasteries, yet continued to call them by their old names. Therefore, it means he was dwelling in the monastery known as the Aggāḷava Shrine. In the phrase "āyasmato vaṅgīsassa," "āyasmā" is a term of endearment, and "Vaṅgīsa" is the name of that Elder. He should be known from his birth as follows: He was reportedly the son of a wanderer (paribbājaka), born from the womb of a female wanderer, and he mastered a certain science. By the power of that science, he could know the destination (gati) of beings by tapping on the skulls of the dead. People would bring the skulls of their deceased relatives from the cemetery and ask him about their destination. He would say, "He is reborn in such-and-such a hell," or "in such-and-such a human world." People were amazed by that skill and gave him much wealth. Thus, the youth Vangīsa became famous throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for a hundred thousand aeons and being endowed with his past aspirations, he traveled through villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals accompanied by five thousand men, eventually arriving at Sāvatthī. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling in Sāvatthī. The residents of Sāvatthī, after giving alms in the morning, would dress properly in the afternoon and go to Jetavana to hear the Dhamma, carrying flowers, perfumes, and so forth. Seeing that great crowd, he asked, "Where is this great crowd going?" Then the people told him, "A Buddha has appeared in the world; he teaches the Dhamma for the benefit of many, and we are going there." He also went with his retinue, exchanged pleasantries with the Blessed One, and sat at a respectful distance. Then the Blessed One addressed him: "Vangīsa, is it true that you know such a science by which you can declare the destination of beings by tapping on the skulls of the dead?" "Yes, Master Gotama, I know it," he replied. The Blessed One had the skull of one reborn in hell brought and shown to him. He tapped it with his fingernail and said, "Master Gotama, this is the skull of one reborn in hell." In this way, the Blessed One showed him the skulls of those reborn in all the destinations, and he knew and declared them accordingly. Then the Blessed One showed him the skull of an Arahant (khīṇāsava). Although he tapped it again and again, he did not know. Then the Blessed One...
79:
The Blessed One said, "Vaṅgīsa, this is not within your range; this is within my range alone, for this is the head of an Arahant," and he spoke this verse:

"The destination of deer is the forest,
The destination of birds is the sky;
The destination of [wholesome and unwholesome] states is a new existence,
The destination of an Arahant is Nibbāna."

Upon hearing the verse, Vaṅgīsa said, "Venerable Gotama, please give me this science." The Blessed One replied, "This science cannot be accomplished by those who have not gone forth as monks." He then said, "Venerable Gotama, please give me this science, whether by ordaining me or by doing whatever you wish." At that time, the Elder Nigrodhakappa was near the Blessed One, so the Blessed One commanded him, "Nigrodhakappa, ordain this man." That Elder ordained Vaṅgīsa and taught him the meditation on the fivefold skin-parts (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna). In due course, Vaṅgīsa became an Arahant who attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). The Blessed One also appointed him to the foremost position, saying, "Monks, among my monk disciples who possess poetic wit, Vaṅgīsa is the foremost."

The preceptor of the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who attained such special benefits, was named Elder Nigrodhakappa because he was always observant and corrective regarding faults and merits. "Kappa" was the Elder's original name, but because he attained Arahantship at the foot of a banyan tree (nigrodha), the Blessed One called him "Nigrodhakappa." From then on, the monks also called him by that name. He is called an "Elder" (thera) because he reached a state of firmness in the Dispensation. His final passing (parinibbāna) at the Aggāḷava Shrine had occurred recently. "Gone into seclusion and dwelling in retirement" means he went into physical seclusion away from the group and remained mentally still, having withdrawn the mind from various sense objects. Thus, a thought arose in his mind. Why did it arise? It was because the teacher was not present and because of past familiarity. Venerable Vaṅgīsa was not present when that Elder passed away. Based on the knowledge of what he had seen before, such as the Elder's past habits like washing his hands, this thought arose. Such occurrences happen not only to those who are not Arahants but also to Arahants due to past habitual tendencies (vāsanā).

Indeed, the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja used to go only to King Udena’s garden for his afternoon rest because of the habit of having enjoyed himself there when he was a king in a past life. The Elder Gavampati used to go to a quiet celestial mansion in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven because of the habit of having enjoyed himself there when he was a celestial being in the past. The Venerable Pilindavaccha used to address monks with the word "outcast" (vasala) because for five hundred births...
80:
...he had been a brahmin and had used that harsh word "outcast" due to past habitual tendencies. Therefore, because of the teacher's absence and past familiarity, this thought arose in his mind: "Has my preceptor attained Parinibbāna, or has he not?" The meaning of what follows is clear. In the phrase "ekāṃsaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā," it is said thus because of re-arranging the robe properly. The word "ekāṃsaṃ" is a term for the robe placed covering the left shoulder. The meaning should be understood as arranging the robe in such a way that it rests on the left shoulder. The rest is plain. In the word "anomapañña," a small or inferior thing is called "oma"; thus, "anomapañña" means one with wisdom that is not inferior, i.e., supreme wisdom. "Diṭṭheve dhamme" means in the present moment or in this very life. "Vicikicchānaṃ" refers to thoughts of this nature. "Ñāto" means it is clear. "Yasassī" means one endowed with gain and followers. "Abhinibbutatto" means one whose mind is quenched of defilements or one whose mind is not distressed.

"Tayā kataṃ" (made by you) refers to the name given by you, calling him "Nigrodhakappa" because he stayed at the foot of a banyan tree; he spoke according to what he remembered. However, the Blessed One did not call him so merely because he stayed at the foot of a banyan tree, but rather because he attained Arahantship there. He said "brāhmaṇassa" (of the brahmin) with reference to his birth. That Elder was said to have gone forth from a wealthy brahmin family. "Namassaṃ acari" means he lived paying homage. "Muṭyapekkho" means one looking for liberation known as Nibbāna, or one desiring Nibbāna. The Blessed One is addressed as "daḷhadhammadassī." Nibbāna is called "daḷhadhamma" (firm Dhamma) because of its unshakeable nature, and the Blessed One shows that Nibbāna. Therefore, he called the Blessed One "daḷhadhammadassī." He also addressed the Blessed One by his clan name as "Sakya." "Mayampi sabbe" (all of us) is said by including the entire assembly and showing himself. He also addressed the Blessed One as "samantacakkhu" (the All-Seeing One) because of his omniscience. "Samavaṭṭhitā" refers to the assembly that is well-established and attentive. "No" means our. "Savanāya" means for the purpose of hearing the answer to this question. "Sotā" refers to the faculties of hearing. "Tuvaṃ no satthā tvam-anuttarosi" (You are our teacher, you are supreme) is merely a word of praise.
81:
Regarding the words "Cut off our doubts," although that Elder was already free from unwholesome doubt, he made this request with reference to a thought that resembled doubt. "Tell me this" means "O Sakyan Buddha, we all wish to know about that disciple concerning whom I have entreated You." O Buddha of vast wisdom like the earth, please speak in our midst about that Brahmin Elder who has attained Parinibbāna, so that all of us may know. The phrase "Like Sakka, the thousand-eyed lord of devas" is merely a word of praise. Its meaning is: Just as the thousand-eyed Sakka speaks in the midst of the devas and his words are respectfully accepted by them, so too, may You speak in our midst words that are respectfully accepted by us.

He also spoke the verse beginning with "Whatever greed, etc.," praising the Blessed One to inspire Him to speak. Its meaning is: As long as the bonds such as greed (abhijjhā) and so forth are not abandoned, because delusion and doubt cannot be abandoned, they are called "paths of delusion," "groups of ignorance," and "bases of doubt." All these unwholesome states, upon reaching the Tathāgata, are destroyed and vanish through the power of the Buddha's teaching. Why is this? Because this wisdom of the Buddha is the supreme eye for humans. It is said to be the supreme eye of humans because the Tathāgata generates the eye of wisdom that destroys all bonds.

He also spoke the verse beginning with "If indeed..." while praising Him to inspire Him to speak. In that verse, "jātu" means "certainly." "Purisa" (Person) refers to the Blessed One. "Jotimanto" (Luminous ones) refers to those such as the Venerable Sāriputta who are endowed with the lamp of wisdom. The meaning is: Just as the wind, such as the east wind, destroys a mass of clouds, if the Blessed One did not destroy the defilements with the force of His teaching, then just as the world covered by a mass of clouds would be in total darkness, so too the world covered by ignorance would remain in total darkness. Even those persons such as the Venerable Sāriputta who now shine with the lamp of wisdom would not be able to shine among men.

He also spoke the verse beginning with "The wise also..." in the same manner as before. Its meaning is: Wise and learned persons are those who provide light because they produce the lamp of wisdom. Therefore, I regard the Blessed One, who is a Hero (Vīra) endowed with supreme energy, as such a wise person.
82:
I regard the Blessed One only as the Great One who creates the light of wisdom. We approached the Blessed One knowing Him to be the Seer (Vipassī) who sees all things as they truly are. Therefore, reveal him to us in the assembly; tell us and make known the matter of Nigrodhakappa.

He also spoke the verse beginning with "Khippaṃ" (Quickly) in the same manner as before. The meaning of that verse is: O Blessed One, quickly utter Your voice; speak Your pleasant and delightful words without delay. For example, when a golden swan returns from its feeding ground and sees a forest grove by a lake, it raises its neck and with its red beak, slowly and without haste, utters a sweet song. In the same way, may You also slowly utter Your voice, which is endowed with the marks of a Great Man, well-composed, and melodious (bindussara). All of us, being upright and with undistracted minds, will listen to Your utterance.

He also spoke the verse beginning with "Pahīnajātīmaraṇaṃ" (One who has abandoned birth and death) in the same manner as before. In that verse, "na seseti" means without remainder (asesa). It means having abandoned birth and death without even a slight remainder, unlike those such as Stream-enterers. "Niggayha" means entreating well and persistently. "Dhona" refers to one who has shaken off all evil. "Vadessāmi" means "I will have the Dhamma preached." Worldlings (puthujjana) do not have the power to act according to their will (kāmakāra). Whether they wish to know or wish to speak, they cannot do so according to their own will. However, the Tathāgatas possess the power of deliberate investigation (saṅkheyyakāra), which is an action preceded by wisdom. This means that whether they wish to know or wish to speak, they are able to do so.

Now, wishing to show that power of deliberate investigation, he spoke the verse "Sampannaveyyākaraṇaṃ" (The perfect explanation). The meaning of that verse is: O Blessed One, Your word, which is spoken and set forth here and there with such upright wisdom, is a perfect explanation (answer). It is seen that Your declarations—such as "The minister Santati will fly seven palm-lengths into the sky and attain Parinibbāna," and "Suppabuddha the Sakyan will be swallowed by the earth on the seventh day"—are true and unerring. Then, raising his hands in most respectful salutation, he said: This salutation is my final and well-performed one; this is another salutation even better performed than others. Do not leave us in confusion by not speaking; knowing the destination (gati) of the Elder Kappa, do not let us remain bewildered. Thus he addressed the Blessed One as "Anomapañña" (One of supreme wisdom) and made his request.
83:
He speaks this verse starting with 'Parovaraṃ' by another method as well, wishing to request what he desires to know without confusion. In that verse, 'Parovaraṃ' means the good and the bad, or the distant and the near, by way of the mundane and the supramundane. 'Ariyadhammaṃ' refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. 'Viditvā' means having penetrated. 'Jānanti' is said because He knows all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma). 'Vācābhikaṅkhāmi' means: just as a man in the summer, scorched by the heat, exhausted and thirsty, greatly desires water, so too do I greatly desire your words. 'Sutaṃ pavassa' means: please rain down, let flow, release, and bring forth the rain of the sense-object of sound known as 'suta' (the heard Dhamma). There is also a variant reading 'sutassa vassa', which means: rain down the rain of the aforementioned sense-object of sound.

Now, wishing to reveal what kind of words he desires, he spoke the verse:

"For what purpose did Kappāyana (Venerable Kappa) practice the holy life? Was that practice of his not in vain? Did he attain Nibbāna (without residue), or is there residue remaining? We wish to hear how he was liberated."

In that verse, 'Kappāyana' is a way of addressing Venerable Kappa out of reverence. 'Yathā vimutto' is a question: "Was he liberated as the Asekhas are liberated by the Nibbāna-element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), or was he liberated as the Sekhas are liberated by the Nibbāna-element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu)?" The remaining words here are clear.

Being thus requested with twelve verses, the Blessed One, wishing to answer that matter, spoke the verse:

"He has cut off craving for name-and-form here," (said the Blessed One), "the stream of Kaṇha (Māra) that has lain latent for a long time. He has crossed over birth and death entirely," so said the Blessed One, the foremost among the five.

In that verse, first, the meaning of the initial phrase is: craving, distinguished as sensual craving and so forth, which has lain latent in this name-and-form for a long time because it has not been abandoned, is also called the 'stream' of the one named Kaṇha (Māra). Kappāyana cut off that craving in name-and-form, which is the stream of Kaṇha and has lain latent for a long time. The words 'Iti bhagavā' (Thus the Blessed One said) are the words of the redactors (saṅgītikāras) here. 'Crossed over birth and death entirely' means...
84:
He showed that Venerable Kappa, having cut off that craving, crossed over birth and death without remainder and attained Nibbāna by the Nibbāna-element without residue of the karma-born material body (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

'Iccabravī bhagavā pañcaseṭṭho' means: the Blessed One, being questioned by Venerable Vangīsa, spoke these words. He is 'foremost among the five' because He is more excellent than the five initial disciples, the Pañcavaggiyas; or because He is supreme through the five faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) and so forth; or through the aggregates of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha) such as virtue (sīla) and so forth; or through His exceedingly extraordinary eyes. These are the words of the redactors (saṅgītikāras).

When this was said, Venerable Vangīsa, with a mind greatly rejoicing in the Blessed One's words, addressed the verses starting with 'Esa sutvā'. Among those verses, in the first verse, 'Isisattama' means: the Blessed One is called an 'Isi' (Sage) because of His noble meaning, and He is the seventh Buddha. He is called 'Isi-sattama' because He appeared making Himself the seventh along with the six Sages (Buddhas) named Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa. This is addressed to the Blessed One. 'Na maṃ vañcesi' means: since Venerable Nigrodhakappa has attained Nibbāna, therefore You did not deceive me, who wished to know the fact of his attainment of Nibbāna; You did not mislead me. The remaining words here are clear.

In the second verse, because Venerable Nigrodhakappa lived looking towards Nibbāna, he said, referring to that state: "The disciple of the Buddha was one who acted as he spoke." 'Maccuno jālaṃ tataṃ' refers to the net of craving of Māra, which is spread throughout the round of existence in the three realms. 'Māyāvino' means of the deceitful Māra. Some also read 'tathā māyāvino'; according to those teachers, it means the deceitfulness of that Māra who approached the Blessed One many times with many deceits.

In the third verse, 'ādi' means the cause. 'Upādānassa' means of the round of existence (vaṭṭa). Here, the round of existence is called 'upādāna' in the sense of that which should be clung to. He says this with the intention that it is proper to say: "Kappa saw the cause, such as ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā), which is the beginning of that very clinging (the round)." 'Accagā vata' means he has indeed crossed over. 'Maccudheyya' is so called because death (maccu) is established (dhīyati) therein; it is a designation for the round of existence in the three realms. He speaks with joy: "He has indeed crossed over that Maccudheyya (the round), which is so difficult to cross." The remaining words here are clear.

## The explanation of the Nigrodhakappa Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary,
## of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, is finished.
85:
## 13. Commentary on the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (Mahāsamaya Sutta)

The Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta, which begins with "Pucchāmi muniṃ pahūtapaññaṃ," is also called the "Mahāsamaya Sutta" because it was preached on the day of the Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). How did it originate? It originated according to the requirement of a question. Indeed, the Blessed One preached this sutta because he was questioned by a created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha); thus, together with that question, this sutta is called the "Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta." This is merely a summary of this sutta; in detail, however, ancient teachers have commented on it starting from the origin of the Sakyans and the Koliyans.

In that context, this is the explanation pointing out the origin—among the first people of the world-cycle, King Mahāsammata had a son named Roja. The son of King Roja was Vararoja; the son of King Vararoja was Kalyāṇa; the son of King Kalyāṇa was Varakalyāṇa; the son of King Varakalyāṇa was Mandhātu; the son of King Mandhātu was Varamandhātu; the son of King Varamandhātu was Uposatha; the son of King Uposatha was Vara; the son of King Vara was Upavara; the son of King Upavara was Maghadeva. From King Maghadeva, there were eighty-four thousand kings in succession. After those kings, there were three lineages of the Okkāka dynasty. Among those kings, the third Okkāka king had five chief queens: Hatthā, Cittā, Jantu, Jālinī, and Visākhā. Each queen had five hundred female attendants. The eldest queen had four sons—Okkāmukha, Karakaṇḍu, Hatthinika, and Sinipura—and five daughters—Piyā, Suppiyā, Ānandā, Vijitā, and Vijitaseṇā. Thus, after having these nine children, that queen passed away.

Then the King brought another young and beautiful princess and established her in the position of chief queen. That chief queen also gave birth to a son named Jantu. On the fifth day, having adorned the prince Jantu, she presented him to the King. The King was pleased and granted the queen a boon. After consulting with her relatives, the queen requested the kingdom for her son. The King refused, saying, "Perish, you wretched woman! Do you wish harm upon my sons?" That queen repeatedly pleased the King in private and continued to request, saying, "Great King, falsehood is not fitting [for a king]," and so forth. Then the King summoned his sons and said, "Dear sons, upon seeing your younger brother, Prince Jantu, I rashly granted a boon to his mother."
86:
"She wishes to transfer the kingdom to her son. You, my sons, should return and rule the kingdom after my passing." Thus, he sent them away along with eight ministers. Those princes took their sisters and departed from the city with a fourfold army. Thinking, "The princes will return and rule the kingdom after their father's passing; let us go and serve those princes," many people followed them. On the first day, the army was one league in extent; on the second day, two leagues; and on the third day, three leagues in extent.

The princes thought, "This army is very large. If we were to oppress any neighboring king and seize a territory, that territory would not be sufficient for us. What is the use of a kingdom obtained by oppressing others? The island of Jambudīpa is vast; let us establish a city in the forest." Thus, they headed toward the Himalayas.

While searching for a place to establish a city in that forest, they arrived at the dwelling place of a hermit named Kapila, who practiced fierce austerities in a large Sāla grove (Sākasanda) by the side of a pond in the Himalayas. When the hermit saw those princes and questioned them, hearing the whole account, he felt compassion for them. That hermit, it is said, knew the science called Bhūmmijāla, by which he could see the advantages and disadvantages of the ground eighty cubits above in the sky and below in the earth. At that time, in one particular spot, hares and deer would frighten and chase away lions, tigers, and so forth; frogs and mice would terrify snakes. Seeing those creatures, the hermit knew, "This piece of ground is the best of the earth," and he built a hermitage on that spot.

Then the hermit said to the princes, "If you establish a city in my name, I will give this place to you." The princes agreed accordingly. The hermit, saying, "Standing on this spot, even the son of an outcaste (caṇḍāla) can surpass a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) in power," gave them the place, saying, "Build the royal palace on the site of the hermitage and establish the city." He himself then lived in a hermitage he built at the foot of a nearby mountain. Thereafter, the princes established a city on that spot. Because it was built on the site where the hermit Kapila had lived, they named it "Kapilavatthu" and took up residence there.

Then the ministers thought, "These princes have reached the age of maturity. If their father were nearby, he would arrange their marriages. Now, however, it is our responsibility alone." Thus, they consulted with the princes. The princes said, "We do not see any princesses equal to us, nor any princes equal to our sisters..."
87:
"We do not dare to cause a confusion of lineage," they said. Fearing the destruction of their lineage, those princes placed their eldest sister in the position of a mother and cohabited with the remaining sisters. When their father, King Okkāka, heard of this, he uttered an inspired solemn utterance: "Capable indeed, sirs, are the princes! Extremely capable indeed, sirs, are the princes!" This is the origin of the Sakyans. This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One:

"Ambaṭṭha, then King Okkāka addressed his ministers and attendants: 'Sirs, where are the princes living now?' 'Great King, there is a large grove of teak trees (sāka) on the banks of a lotus pond on the slopes of the Himalayas; the princes are living there now. Fearing the destruction of their lineage, they are cohabiting with their own sisters.' Then, Ambaṭṭha, King Okkāka uttered an inspired solemn utterance: 'Capable indeed, sirs, are the princes! Extremely capable indeed, sirs, are the princes!' From that time on, Ambaṭṭha, they have been known as the Sakyans, and that king is the forefather of the Sakyans" (DN 1.267).

While living there, the eldest sister of those princes developed leprosy; her limbs became the color of kovilāra flowers. The princes thought, "If we sit or eat in the same place as this princess, this disease will spread to us as well." Pretending to go for a stroll in the park, they placed the princess on a carriage, entered the forest, dug a pit, placed her inside along with food and snacks, covered it with a wooden plank, spread earth over it, and departed.

At that time, a king named Rāma also suffered from leprosy and was loathed by his harem and dancers. Out of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he handed over the kingdom to his eldest son and entered the forest. While consuming leaves, roots, and fruits in that forest, before long he became free of the disease and his skin became golden in color. While wandering here and there, he saw a large hollow tree. He cleared the hollow space inside, which was about sixteen cubits in size, made a door and a window, attached a ladder, and made his dwelling there. He would place fire in a brazier and sleep at night while listening to pleasant and unpleasant sounds. He would note, "A lion roared in such a place; a tiger roared in such a place," and at dawn, he would go there, take the leftover meat from the animals, cook it, and eat it.

Then one day, at the time of dawn, the king lit a fire and sat down. At that time, a tiger, smelling the scent of the princess...
88:
(The princess) scratched at the pit and made a hole in the wooden planks. Seeing the tiger through that hole, she was terrified and screamed. King Rāma heard that sound and noted, "This is the voice of a woman." He went there early in the morning and asked, "Who is here?" When she replied, "A woman, lord," he said, "Come out." When she said, "I do not dare to come out," he asked, "Why?" She replied, "Because I am a kshatriya maiden." Thus, even though she was buried in a pit, she still maintained her pride. After asking everything, the king revealed his own lineage, saying, "I too am a kshatriya," and added, "Now (our lineages) have become like ghee poured into milk; come out." The princess said, "Lord, I am afflicted with leprosy; it is not proper for me to come out." The king thought, "I have now learned how to treat it; I can cure her." He provided a ladder, brought her out, and took her to his dwelling. By giving her the same medicines he himself had used, she soon became free of the disease and her skin became golden in color. The king lived together with that princess. From their very first union, she became pregnant and gave birth to two sons. In this way, she gave birth to twins sixteen times, resulting in thirty-two brothers. When those sons gradually reached maturity, the father taught them all the arts.

Then one day, a resident of King Rāma's city, while searching for jewels on the mountain, came to that place and recognized the king. "Great King, I recognize you," he said. When the king asked, "Where have you come from?" he replied, "From the city, lord." Then the king asked about all the news. While they were conversing, the youths arrived. Seeing the youths, the man asked, "Great King, who are these?" When the king said, "Friend, they are my sons," the man said, "Great King, what are you doing in the forest now, surrounded by these thirty-two princes? Please come and rule the kingdom." The king replied, "Friend, enough; I am very happy right here." The man thought, "Now I have a gift of news," and went to the city to inform the king's son. The prince thought, "I will bring my father back," and went there with a fourfold army, pleading with his father in various ways. The king also said, "Dear son, enough; I am very happy right here," and had no desire to follow. Then the prince thought, "Now the king has no desire to return; I will build a city for him right here." He cleared those kola trees, built houses, and established a city. Because it was built after removing kola trees, it was named "Kolanagara," and because it was built on a path of tigers, it was named "Vyagghapajja." Having given these two names, he departed.
89:
Thereafter, when the princes reached the age of maturity, their mother commanded them, "Dear sons, the Sakyans residing in the city of Kapilavatthu are your maternal uncles; take their daughters in marriage." On the day the Sakyan princesses went to play in the river, the Koliya princes went there, blocked the river landing, announced their names, and took away the royal daughters they desired. When the Sakyan kings heard of this, they remained silent, saying, "Friends, let it be; they are indeed our own relatives." This is the origin of the Koliyas.

In this manner, as the Sakyans and Koliyas continued to intermarry, the royal lineage descended down to King Sīhahanu, which should be understood in detail. It is said that King Sīhahanu had five sons: Suddhodana, Amitodana, Dhotodana, Sakkodana, and Sukkodana. Among them, while King Suddhodana was reigning, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), who had fulfilled the perfections, passed away from the Tusita heaven and took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā, the daughter of King Añjana and the consort of King Suddhodana, as described in the Jātakanidāna. In due course, he made the Great Renunciation, attained the Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi), and turned the Noble Wheel of Dhamma. Gradually, he traveled to the city of Kapilavatthu, established King Suddhodana and other royalty in the Noble Fruits (ariya-phala), and then departed for a walking tour of the countryside. Later, at another time, he returned and resided at the Nigrodhārāma monastery in Kapilavatthu together with fifteen hundred monks.

While the Blessed One was residing at that monastery, a dispute arose between the Sakyans and the Koliyas concerning water. How did it happen? Between the two cities of Kapilavatthu and Koliya, there flows a river named Rohiṇī. At times, its water is low, and at other times, it is abundant. During the time of low water, both the Sakyans and the Koliyas would construct a dam to bring water for the purpose of irrigating their respective crops. One day, while they were constructing the dam, they began to quarrel with one another, reviling each other based on their birth, saying, "Hey, your royal family lives in cohabitation with their own sisters like animals such as chickens, dogs, and foxes!" and "Your royal family lives in the hollows of trees like demons and vultures!" Thus, they reported the matter to their respective kings. Those kings, becoming enraged and preparing for war, arrived at the banks of the Rohiṇī River. Thus, an army like a vast ocean stood there.
90:
Then the Blessed One, thinking, "My relatives are quarreling; I shall now restrain them," traveled through the air and stood in the midst of the two armies. Some teachers say that, having reflected on that matter, he came from Sāvatthī. While standing thus in the air, he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. Upon hearing that discourse, all the kings were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega); they discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood there. They also prepared a costly seat. The Blessed One descended and sat upon the prepared seat, and then preached the Phandana Jātaka, beginning with "A man with an axe in hand," and the Laṭukika Jātaka, beginning with "I salute you, O elephant."

"The birds fly away happily, carrying the net;
When they shall fall into dispute, then they shall come under my power."

Having preached this Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, and wishing to show their long-standing kinship, he preached this Mahāvaṃsa (Great Lineage). The kings were greatly inspired, thinking, "It is said that we were indeed relatives in the past." Then, the Sakyan kings gave two hundred and fifty princes, and the Koliya kings gave two hundred and fifty princes—five hundred princes in total—to the Blessed One to be his attendants. The Blessed One, seeing the past merits (upaniṣsaya) of those princes, said, "Come, bhikkhus (Etha bhikkhavo)." All those princes, being endowed with the eight requisites that appeared by psychic power, flew up into the air, came and paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood there.

The Blessed One took those princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. Their wives sent messengers, and when those princes were tempted by those women in various ways, they became dissatisfied with the monk's life. The Blessed One, knowing their state of dissatisfaction, showed them the Himālayas. Wishing to dispel their discontent with the story of the Kuṇāla Jātaka in that forest, he asked, "Bhikkhus, have you seen the Himālayas before?"
