When they replied, "No, Venerable Sir," he said, "Come, bhikkhus, look," and taking them through the air by his psychic power, he showed them various mountains, saying, "This is the Golden Mountain, this is the Silver Mountain, this is the Ruby Mountain." He then stopped on the Manosilā plateau by Lake Kuṇāla. Then he made a formal resolve (adhiṭṭhāna): "Let all the animals in the Himālayas, including four-footed and many-footed creatures, come here, and let the Kuṇāla bird come behind them all." As they arrived, he described them according to their species, names, and sounds, showing them to the monks: "Bhikkhus, these are swans (haṃsa), these are cranes (koñca), these are ruddy geese (cakkavāka), cuckoos (karavīka), elephant-trunk birds (hatthisoṇḍaka), and pokkharasātaka birds."
91:
Those monks, with hearts full of wonder, while watching, saw Kunāla, the king of the birds, who came last of all the birds, seated in the middle of a piece of wood held in the beaks of two bird maidens, and surrounded by a thousand bird maidens. Filled with a sense of extraordinary awe, they asked the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, was the Blessed One also Kunāla the king in the past?" "Monks, it is so; I myself established that lineage of Kunāla. In the past, the four of us lived in this place: the sages Nārada and Devila, Ānanda the king of vultures, Puṇṇamukha the cuckoo, and I was Kunāla the bird." Thus, He preached the entire Mahākunāla Jātaka. Upon hearing that Jātaka, the dissatisfaction (anabhirati) that had arisen in those monks regarding their former wives was calmed. Thereafter, the Blessed One preached a discourse connected with the Four Noble Truths to those monks. At the conclusion of the discourse, the lowest among them became a Sotāpanna, and the highest became an Anāgāmī; not a single monk remained as a worldling (puthujjana), nor did any reach Arahatship yet. Then, the Blessed One took those monks and descended again to the Mahāvana forest. Those monks, as they returned, traveled by their own psychic power.

Then, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma again to those monks for the sake of attaining the higher paths and fruits. Those five hundred monks, having undertaken insight meditation (vipassanā), were established in Arahatship. The monk who first attained Arahatship came first, thinking, "I will inform the Blessed One," and having arrived, he said, "Venerable Sir, I find delight in the Dispensation; I am no longer weary," and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat in a suitable place. In this manner, all those monks came in succession and sat surrounding the Blessed One on the evening of the Uposatha day of the full moon of Jeṭṭha. At that time, except for the Asaññasatta Brahmas and the Arūpa Brahmas, the assembly of devas and Brahmas from the ten thousand world systems, as described in the commentary to the Maṅgala Sutta, created subtle bodies and gathered around the Blessed One, who sat upon the noble Buddha-seat surrounded by five hundred Arahants, thinking, "We shall listen to the Dhamma teaching of diverse and brilliant wisdom." Then, four Arahant Brahmas from the Suddhāvāsa realm, having emerged from their meditative attainment and not seeing the host of Brahmas, reflected, "Where have they gone?" Realizing the reason, they followed, but finding no space, they stood at the edge of the world system and each recited a verse. It was said thus:

"Then, this thought occurred to four devas of the Suddhāvāsa host: 'This Blessed One is staying among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Mahāvana forest together with a great community of monks, about five hundred monks, all of whom are Arahants. And devas from the ten world-elements have mostly assembled to see the Blessed One...'"
92:
...and the community of monks. (They have assembled to see). 'What if we too were to approach the Blessed One, and having approached, each of us were to recite a verse in the presence of the Blessed One?'

Everything should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Sagāthāvagga. Having gone there, one Brahma among those four found an opening at the summit of the eastern world-system mountain and, standing there, recited this verse:

"A great assembly is in the forest...
Look at the unconquered Saṅgha."

The second Brahma, standing at the summit of the western world-system mountain, heard the voice of that Brahma who was reciting this verse. The second Brahma, having found an opening at the summit of the western world-system mountain and standing there, heard that verse and recited this verse:

"There the monks have well-concentrated (their minds)...
The wise guard their sense faculties."

The third Brahma, having found an opening at the summit of the southern world-system mountain and standing there, heard that verse and recited this verse:

"Having cut the stake, having cut the bolt...
Like young elephants (they are free from defilements)."

The fourth Brahma, having found an opening at the summit of the northern world-system mountain and standing there, heard that verse and recited this verse:

"Whoever have gone to the Buddha for refuge...
They will fill the host of devas."

The third Brahma, standing at the summit of the southern world-system mountain, also heard the voice of that fourth Brahma. Thus, at that time, these four Brahmas stood praising the assembly; the Great Brahmas stood covering the entire world system.

Then the Blessed One, looking at the assembly of devas, addressed the monks: "Monks, to those Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas who appeared in the past, just such a great number of devas and Brahmas assembled in the presence of those Blessed Ones. For example..."
93:
“Monks, just as deities have assembled in my presence now, so too will deities of such measure assemble in the presence of the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, who will arise in the future.” Thereafter, he divided that assembly of deities into two groups based on those who were capable (bhabba) and those who were incapable (abhabba) of liberation. He distinguished them, thinking, ‘This many are capable, and this many are incapable.’ Among those two groups, he understood that the incapable assembly would not understand the Dhamma even if a hundred Buddhas were to preach it, whereas the capable assembly could be led to enlightenment. He then further divided the capable individuals into six categories according to their temperaments (carita): ‘This many are of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita), and this many are of temperaments of hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), discursive thought (vitakka), faith (saddhā), and intelligence (buddhi).’ Having thus categorized them by temperament, he considered, ‘What kind of Dhamma teaching would be suitable for this assembly?’ and selected a discourse. He then reflected on that assembly: ‘Should I make them understand by my own will, or by the will of others, or by way of a specific occurrence (atthuppatti), or by way of questions and answers?’

Then, knowing, ‘I shall make them understand by way of questions and answers,’ he surveyed the entire assembly to see if there was anyone capable of asking questions, and he realized there was no one. He thought, ‘If I myself were to ask and I myself were to answer, it would not be suitable for this assembly. It would be better if I were to create a Created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha).’ Having so resolved, he entered the foundation jhana (pādakajjhāna), and emerging from it, he fashioned a Created Buddha by the power of his mind. With a mind of determination, the Created Buddha appeared, complete in all limbs and parts, endowed with the marks of a Great Man, bearing the bowl and robes, and perfect in his manner of looking ahead and looking aside.

That Created Buddha came from the eastern world-system and sat upon a seat equal to that of the Blessed One. Having arrived in this manner, there were six suttas preached by the Blessed One in this assembly according to the temperaments of the listeners. They are: the Purābheda Sutta, the Kalahavivāda Sutta, the Cūḷabyūha Sutta, the Mahābyūha Sutta, the Tuvaṭaka Sutta, and this very Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta. Among these suttas, for the purpose of initiating this discourse which was suitable for the deities of lustful temperament, the Created Buddha, wishing to ask a question, spoke this verse: ‘I ask the Sage of great wisdom (pahūtapanna)...’

In that verse, ‘pahūtapanna’ means having great wisdom. ‘Tiṇṇa’ means having crossed over the four floods (ogha). ‘Pāraṅgata’ means having reached Nibbāna. ‘Parinibbuta’ means having extinguished defilements by way of Nibbāna with the fuel remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna). ‘Ṭhitatta’ means having a mind that is unshakable by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). ‘Nikkhamma gharā panujja kāme’ means having left the household life and dispelled the objects of sensual desire. ‘Kathaṃ bhikkhu sammā so loke paribbajeyya’ means how would that monk rightly live and practice in the world, being unstained by the world and transcending the world? The remaining meanings are as previously explained.
94:
Then, because there is no such thing as one who truly wanders rightly (sammāparibbājaka) in the world without reaching the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya), the Blessed One—wishing to dispel the habitual faults of those various groups of deities who shared similar defects and who were categorized by lustful temperament and so on—began with the verse ‘Yassa maṅgalā’ and spoke fifteen verses. In these verses, he proclaimed the practice of the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), placing the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala) as the pinnacle.

Among those verses, in the first verse, the name ‘maṅgalā’ refers to the omens seen (diṭṭhamaṅgala) and so forth as mentioned in the Maṅgala Sutta. ‘Samūhatā’ means well-uprooted and cut off by the weapon of wisdom. ‘Uppātā’ refers to the obsession with portents such as, ‘The falling of meteors and the burning of the quarters will have such and such results.’ ‘Supinā’ refers to the obsession with dreams such as, ‘If one sees a dream in the morning, such a thing happens; if at noon, this happens; if seen while sleeping on the left side, this happens; if on the right side, this happens; if one sees the moon in a dream, this happens; if the sun, this happens.’ ‘Lakkhaṇā’ refers to the obsession with marks after reading texts on the marks of sticks, the marks of clothes, and so on, thinking, ‘By this sign, such a thing happens.’ All these should be understood according to the method explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta.

‘So maṅgaladosavippahīno’ means that, setting aside the thirty-eight great blessings (mahāmaṅgala), the remaining omens are called faulty omens (maṅgaladosa). He for whom these omens and so forth are well-uprooted is one who has abandoned the faults of omens. Alternatively, he is one who has abandoned the faults of omens because he has given up both omens and the defects of portents and so on; he does not rely on omens for purification because he has attained the Noble Path (ariyamagga). Therefore, that Arahant should rightly wander in the world without being stained by the world.

In the second verse, ‘rāgaṃ vinayetha mānusesu, dibbesu kāmesu cāpi bhikkhū’ means that a monk should dispel lust for the sensual pleasures of both humans and devas, bringing it to a state where it cannot arise again by means of the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). ‘Atikkamma bhavaṃ samecca dhammaṃ’ means that after dispelling lust in this way, and thereafter completing full understanding (pariññā) and so forth in every way by the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga), and having penetrated the four Noble Truths, he transcends the three types of existence through this practice. ‘Sammā so’ means that monk also should rightly wander in the world.

In the third verse, ‘anurodhavirodhavippahīno’ means one who has abandoned lust (rāga) and hatred (dosa) toward all objects. The remaining words in all the verses are as previously explained. ‘Sopi bhikkhu...’
95:
The phrase "He should wander rightly in the world" (sammā loke paribbajeyya) should be connected. From here on, I will not explain the grammatical connections (yojanā) but will only clarify the methods not yet mentioned.

In the fourth verse, it should be understood that there are two types: the pleasant and the unpleasant, by way of beings and formations. In those two, having abandoned them by giving up desire-lust (chandarāga) and aversion (paṭigha). "Anupādāya" means without grasping any phenomenon by way of the four types of clinging (upādāna). "Anissito kuhiñci" means not being dependent on any phenomena such as form (rūpa) or on existence (bhava) through the 108-fold dependence of craving (taṇhā) and the 62-fold dependence of views (diṭṭhi). "Saṃyojaniyehi vippamutto" means that all phenomena occurring in the three realms are called "fetter-forming" (saṃyojaniya) because they are the objects of the ten fetters; it means being liberated from those phenomena in every way because they have been fully understood through the development of the Path. In this verse, the first line teaches the abandonment of lust and hatred. The second line teaches the absence of dependence on clinging. The third line teaches liberation from the remaining unwholesome states and unwholesome objects. Alternatively, it should be understood that the first line is the abandonment of lust and hatred, the second line is the means for that abandonment, and the third line is the liberation from fetter-forming things because those defilements have been abandoned.

In the fifth verse, "upadhīsu" refers to the acquisitions of the aggregates (khandhupadhi). "Ādāna" also refers to those same acquisitions in the sense of being grasped. "Ananya-neyyo" means that because one has clearly seen impermanence (anicca) and so on, one cannot be led by another to think "This is superior." The remaining words have clear meanings. This is the meaning: That monk, having entirely removed desire-lust for the things to be grasped by means of the Path of Arahatship, and having thus removed desire-lust, does not take those acquisitions to be the essence, but sees all acquisitions as being without essence. Therefore, not depending on those acquisitions through the two types of dependence (craving and views), that monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who cannot be led by another to think "This is superior," should wander rightly in the world.

In the sixth verse, "aviruddho" means not being in opposition to wholesome states because these three types of misconduct (duccarita) have been abandoned. "Viditvā dhammaṃ" means knowing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by means of the Path. "Nibbānapadābhipatthayāno" means longing for the state of Nibbāna, which is the final passing away of the aggregates without remainder (anupādisesa-khandhaparinibbāna). The remaining words have clear meanings.

In the seventh verse, "akkuṭṭho" means being reviled by the ten grounds for abuse. "Na sandhiyetha" means one should not bear a grudge or get angry. Having received...
96:
...food from others (parabhojanaṃ) given out of faith (saddhādeyya), one should not be intoxicated thinking, "I am well-known, famous, and one who receives many gains." The remaining words have clear meanings.

In the eighth verse, "lobha" refers to uneven greed (visamalobha). "Bhava" refers to the realm of sensual existence (kāmabhava) and so on. Thus, by these two words, craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) and craving for wealth (bhogataṇhā) are mentioned. Alternatively, the first word refers to all craving, and the latter word refers to kamma-existence (kammabhava). "Virato chedanabandhanā ca" means being free from killing and binding others because such kamma-defilements (kammakilesa) have been abandoned. The remaining words are as previously explained.

In the ninth verse, "sāruppaṃ attano viditvā" means knowing by being firmly established in the purity of livelihood (ājīvasuddhi) such as right seeking, having abandoned wrong seeking (anesanā) which is unsuitable for one's state as a monk, and in other forms of right practice (sammāpaṭipatti). Indeed, nothing is accomplished by mere knowing. "Yathātathiyaṃ" means according to the truth (yathābhūta). "Dhammaṃ" means knowing the phenomena such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana) with the knowledge of things as they really are, or knowing the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths by means of the Path. The remaining words have clear meanings.

In the tenth verse, "so nirāso anāsisāno" means that for the person whose latent tendencies (anusaya) no longer exist because they have been destroyed by the Noble Path, and whose unwholesome roots (akusalamūla) have been uprooted, that person is without hope (nirāsa), meaning free from craving. Therefore, due to the absence of longing, he does not long for any phenomena such as forms (rūpa). Thus, it is said, "nirāso anāsisāno." The remaining words are as previously explained.

In the eleventh verse, "āsavakhīṇo" means one whose four taints (āsava) are destroyed. "Pahīnamāno" means one who has abandoned the nine types of conceit (māna). "Rāgapathaṃ" means the collection of phenomena in the three realms which are the objects of lust (rāga). "Upātivatto" means one who has transcended through the three full understandings (pariññā) and abandonment (pahāna). "Danto" means one who has reached the stage of being tamed through the Noble discipline, having given up indulging in all sense doors. "Parinibbuto" means one who has become cooled through the subsiding of the fires of defilements. The remaining words are as previously explained.

In the twelfth verse, "saddho" means one endowed with unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) that is complete in every way, because one no longer needs to rely on others regarding the qualities of the Buddha and so on; it is not a matter of following the practice through the faith of another. Therefore, it was said, "Venerable Sir, I do not go by faith in the Blessed One in this matter..."
97:
"I approach with faith" is stated (in Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.34). 'Sutavā' means having completed the task of hearing, thus possessing hearing endowed with the ultimate meaning. 'Niyāmadassī' means one who sees the Path (Magga) which is the Righteous Certainty (Sammattaniyāma), the way to the Deathless City in the world lost in the forest of Saṃsāra; it means one who has seen the Path. 'Vaggagatesu na vaggasārī': those with the sixty-two types of views, being mutually contradictory, are called factions (vagga); among beings who have gone into such factions of views, he does not follow them through the power of views such as "this will be annihilated" or "this will remain so." 'Paṭigha' means that which destroys the mind, which is a specific name for anger (dosa). 'Vineyya' means having removed. The rest is as previously explained.

In the 13th verse, 'Saṃsuddhajino' means one who has conquered defilements with the pure Path of Arahatship. 'Vivaṭṭacchado' means one who has opened the veil of lust, hatred, and delusion. 'Dhammesu vasī' means one who has attained mastery (vasīpatta) in the Four Noble Truths. Since no one can change the truths known by that Arahat into something else, the Arahat is called 'Dhammesu vasī'. 'Pāragū' means one who has reached the further shore called Nibbāna, specifically attained through the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa). 'Anejo' means one free from the agitation of craving (taṇhā). 'Saṅkhāranirodhañāṇakusalo' means one who is skilled in the knowledge of Nibbāna, the cessation of formations, through the wisdom of the Noble Path; it means being expert because of having developed it four times.

In the 14th verse, 'Atītesu' refers to the five aggregates that have occurred and passed away. 'Anāgatesu' refers to the five aggregates that have not yet reached occurrence. 'Kappātīto' means one who has transcended the conceptualization (kappana) of "I" and "mine" or all conceptualizations of craving and views. 'Aticca suddhipañño' means one with exceedingly pure wisdom or one with pure wisdom through transcending. Transcending what? Transcending the three periods of time (addhattaya). For the Arahat stands having reached the most pure wisdom, having transcended all three periods—the past period known as ignorance and formations, the future period known as birth, aging, and death, and the present period from consciousness to the end of existence—and having crossed over doubt. Therefore, he is called 'Aticca suddhipañño'. 'Sabbāyatanehi' refers to the twelve bases. For the Arahat is thus one who has transcended conceptualizations. Because of transcending conceptualizations and having exceedingly pure wisdom, he does not approach any base in the future. Therefore, it is said, "One who is liberated from all bases."
98:
In the 15th verse, "aññāya padaṃ" means having known each of the steps/states among the Four Noble Truths, which are called the "four steps of the truths," through the wisdom of defining the truths in the preliminary stage. "Samecca dhammaṃ" means penetrating the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths through the other four Noble Paths. "Vivaṭaṃ disvāna pahānamāsavānaṃ" means subsequently seeing Nibbāna—which is called the destruction of the taints, and is open, manifest, and unclouded—through the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). "Sabbupadhīnaṃ parikkhayā" means that because all acquisitions (upadhi)—consisting of the aggregates (khandha), sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa), defilements (kilesa), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra)—have been exhausted, the monk who does not cling to any acquisition should wander rightly in the world; he should travel without being attached to the world. Thus, He concluded the teaching.

Then, that created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha), wishing to praise the Dhamma teaching, spoke this verse beginning with "Addhā hi Bhagavā." In that verse, "yo so evaṃ vihārī" refers to the monk who dwells having uprooted omens and the like, and having abandoned all the faults of omens; it also refers to the monk who dwells having removed lust for celestial and human sensual pleasures, having transcended existence, and having realized the Dhamma. This was said to show the monk indicated by those respective verses. The remaining words are clear. This is the grammatical connection (yojanā): "O Blessed One, it is certainly true as You said, 'For whom omens are uprooted,' and so on, and at the end of each verse, 'He would wander rightly in the world.' Why is that? Because the monk who dwells in such a way is tamed with the highest taming, and has transcended all ten fetters (saṃyojana) and the four yokes (yoga). Therefore, he would wander rightly in the world; I have no doubt in this matter." Having spoken this verse in praise of the teaching, He concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the Sutta, a hundred thousand crores of deities attained the highest fruit (Arahantship). Those who attained the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, and Non-returning were innumerable.

## The explanation of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
99:
## 14. Commentary on the Dhammika Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Dhammika Sutta. What is the reason for its arising? It is said that while the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, was still alive, there was a lay follower named Dhammika, both by name and by practice. That lay follower was endowed with the refuges, endowed with virtue, of great learning, a bearer of the three Piṭakas, an Anāgāmī (Non-returner), a possessor of direct knowledge (abhiññā), and one who could travel through the air. His retinue of five hundred lay followers were also just like him. One day, while observing the Uposatha and dwelling in seclusion, at the end of the middle watch, the thought arose in him: "What if I were to ask about the practice of householders and those who have gone forth?"

Surrounded by his five hundred lay followers, he approached the Blessed One and asked about that matter, and the Blessed One answered him. In that sutta, the terms previously explained should be understood in the same manner as already stated; I shall only explain the new terms.

In the first verse of that sutta, "kathaṃkaro" means what kind of person acting in what way, or practicing in what way. "Sādhu hoti" means how does one become excellent, faultless, and one who achieves the goal. "Upāsakāse" means simply the lay followers (upāsakā). The remaining meanings are clear. The connection of the meaning is: among these two types of disciples—those who go forth from the home to the homeless life, or those who are householder lay followers—what kind of disciple is excellent?

380-1. Now, wishing to show the Blessed One's ability to answer when thus questioned, he spoke two verses beginning with "Tuvañhi." In those verses, "gati" means the destination of one's disposition (ajjhāsaya). "Parāyaṇa" means the fulfillment. Alternatively, "gati" refers to the five realms such as hell, etc.; "parāyaṇa" means the liberation from those realms, which is Parinibbāna. "Na catthi tulyo" means there is no one equal to you. "Sabbaṃ tuvaṃ ñāṇamavecca dhammaṃ, pကာသေသိ သတ္တေ အနုကမ္ပမာနော" means: O Blessed One, having thoroughly penetrated and realized all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) without remainder, you have clearly revealed all knowledge and the Dhamma out of compassion for beings. Whatever was beneficial to whoever it might be, that you revealed and taught to them; it means you have no "teacher's fist" (ācariyamuṭṭhi). "Virocasi vimalo" means you shine beautifully, being free from stains such as lust, like the moon free from smoke, dust, and clouds. The remaining meanings here are self-evident.

Now, praising the devas who listened to the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One at that time, and in honor of the Blessed One, he spoke two verses beginning with "Āgañchi te santike."
100:
In that context, "the king of devas named Erāvaṇa" refers to this deva named Erāvaṇa, who can assume any form at will and dwells in a divine mansion. When Sakka goes out to play in the park, Erāvaṇa creates a body one hundred and fifty leagues (yojana) in size and, manifesting thirty-three frontal globes (kumbha), becomes the elephant named Erāvaṇa. On each of those globes, there are two tusks. On each tusk, there are seven lotus ponds; in each lotus pond, seven lotus clusters; in each lotus cluster, seven lotus flowers; in each lotus flower, seven petals; and on each petal, seven celestial maidens dance. These are Sakka's dancing women, known as the 'Lotus-nymphs' (Padumaccharā), as mentioned in the Vimānavatthu: "Trained maidens dance upon the lotuses."

In the middle of those thirty-three frontal globes, there is the globe named Sudassana, which is about thirty leagues in size. There, within a flower pavilion three leagues high, a jeweled throne one league in size is spread out. In that place, Sakka, the lord of devas, enjoys divine bliss surrounded by a host of celestial maidens. When Sakka, the lord of devas, returns from playing in the park, Erāvaṇa withdraws that form and becomes a deva again. Referring to this, it is said: "The king of devas named Erāvaṇa came into your presence."

"Having heard 'Jina' (Conqueror)" means having heard that "this Blessed One has conquered all evil states." "Having consulted with you" means having discussed with you, with the intention of asking a question. "Ajjhagamā" means arrived or reached. "Having heard 'Sādhu,' he was of a pleased nature" means that having heard the answer to that question, he rejoiced saying, "Excellent, Bhante," and departed with a joyful appearance.

In the phrase "King Vessavaṇa Kuvera," that yakkha is called "Rājā" in the sense of pleasing beings. He is called "Vessavaṇa" because he rules in the royal city named Visāṇā. He should be known by his former name as "Kuvera." It is said that when he was a wealthy brahmin named Kuvera, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and was reborn as the chief of the royal city of Visāṇā. Therefore, he is called "Kuvera Vessavaṇa." And this is stated in the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta: "Friends, the royal city of the Great King Kuvera is named Visāṇā; therefore the Great King Kuvera is called 'Vessavaṇa'." The rest of the words here are quite clear.
101:
In this passage, a question may arise: Why did the deva Erāvaṇa, who dwells in the very distant Tāvatiṃsa heaven, arrive first? Why did the Great King Vessavaṇa arrive later? And why did this lay follower, who lives in the same city, arrive last of all? How did that donor know of the arrival of those devas and speak thus?

The answer is as follows: At that time, the Great King Vessavaṇa was traveling in a twelve-yojana vehicle carried by women, seated on a coral throne of many thousands. Carrying a coral spear and surrounded by ten billion yakkhas, he thought, "I will ask the Blessed One a question." Avoiding the celestial mansions in the sky and traveling stage by stage, he reached the space above the house of the female lay follower Nandamātā in the city of Veḷukaṇḍaka. The spiritual power of that lay follower was such: she possessed pure virtue, constantly abstained from eating at improper times, was a bearer of the Tipitaka, and was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala).

At that time, she had opened the lion-supported casement window and, standing in a place where the breeze blew to take in the season, she was reciting the Aṭṭhakavagga and the Pārāyanavagga with sweet tones and perfect articulation of syllables and phrases. The Great King Vessavaṇa stopped his vehicles right there and listened to everything until the lay follower recited the conclusion: "The Blessed One, while dwelling at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine in the Magadha country, taught this Dhamma to the sixteen brahmin attendants." At the end of the section, he raised his great neck, which was like a golden drum, and gave a cry of appreciation: "Excellent, excellent, sister!"

She asked, "Who is there?" He replied, "Sister, I am the Great King Vessavaṇa." It is said that the lay follower became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) first, and Vessavaṇa became one later. In accordance with the Dhamma, Vessavaṇa addressed her as "sister," regarding her as a sibling. The lay follower said, "Fair-faced brother, it is now past noon; you should consider it time to depart." He replied, "Sister, I am so inspired by you that I will perform an act of devotion."

"If so, brother, the workers are unable to carry the hill paddy harvested from my fields. Please command your retinue to perform that task." Vessavaṇa said, "Very well, sister," and commanded the yakkhas. They filled one thousand two hundred and fifty granaries. From then on, the granaries never became empty, and it became a proverb in the world: "Like the granary of Nandamātā."

After filling the granaries, Vessavaṇa approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "You have arrived after noon." Then he reported everything to the Blessed One. For this reason, although he dwells in the Cātumahārājika heaven which is very near, Vessavaṇa arrived later. As for the deva Erāvaṇa, because he had no business to attend to in between, he arrived earlier.
102:
As for this lay follower Dhammika, although he was an Anāgāmī and normally ate only one meal a day, because that day was an Uposatha day, he undertook the Uposatha precepts. In the evening, well-dressed and properly robed, he went to the Jetavana monastery surrounded by five hundred lay followers. After listening to the Dhamma, he returned to his home. He taught the Dhamma of a lay follower—consisting of the benefits of the Refuges, the Precepts, and the Uposatha—to those lay followers and then dismissed them. For those lay followers, five hundred allowable couches with legs the size of a fist were prepared in individual rooms in his house. They entered their respective rooms and sat down, attaining meditative absorption (samāpatti). The lay follower did the same.

At that time, five million seven hundred thousand families lived in the city of Sāvatthī, with a population of one hundred and eighty million people. Therefore, in the first watch of the night, the city of Sāvatthī was filled with a single roar like the great ocean, from the sounds of elephants, horses, people, and drums. Immediately after the middle watch, that sound subsided. At that time, the lay follower emerged from absorption and reflected on his own virtues: "I dwell happily through the bliss of the Path and the bliss of the Fruit. Depending on whom did I obtain this happiness?" Thinking, "I obtained it depending on the Blessed One," he felt great devotion toward the Blessed One. While reflecting, "In what manner is the Blessed One dwelling now?" he saw the devas Erāvaṇa and Vessavaṇa with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). With his divine ear (dibba-sota), he heard the Dhamma teaching. Knowing their devoted minds through the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa), he thought, "It would be good if I too were to ask the Blessed One about the practice that leads to welfare in both this life and the next." Therefore, although he lived in the same city, he arrived last of all. Thus it was said: "The king of the nāgas came into your presence... and he too, having heard, was delighted in appearance."

Now, wishing to praise the Blessed One as being superior to the recluses and brahmins esteemed by the world outside this Dispensation, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Ye kecime." In those verses, "titthiyā" (sectarians) refers to the six teachers, such as Pūraṇa Kassapa, who were ordained in the teachings of the three original individuals like Nandavaccha and Saṅkicca, and who were born into the "ford" of wrong views created by those "ford-makers" (titthakara). Among them, Nātaputta was a Nigaṇṭha (Jain), and the rest were Ājīvakas. To show all of them, he said: "Ye kecime titthiyā vādasīlā" (Whatever sectarians there are who are prone to disputation). They wander about the world stabbing with the weapons of their mouths, saying, "We alone have practiced rightly; others have practiced wrongly." The phrase "Ājīvakā vā" (or Ājīvakas) distinguishes them from the collective group. "Nātitaranti" means they cannot transcend. "Sabbe" means others as well...
103:
Wishing to include those such as the disciples of other sectarians, the Blessed One said, "As one standing does not reach one running." Just as a person standing, lacking movement, cannot overtake a fast-moving man, so too, these people, due to the absence of the movement of wisdom, are unable to understand various specific meanings and remain stationary; they cannot overtake the Blessed One, who possesses extremely swift wisdom.

With the words "Brahmins, fond of debate, and elders," he points to Cankī, Tārukkha, Pokkharasāti, Jāṇussoṇi, and others. With "even some Brahmins exist," he shows that there are all kinds of Brahmins, middle-aged and young, specifically pointing to Assalāyana, Vāseṭṭha, Ambaṭṭha, Uttara, and others. "Atthabaddhā" means those who are bound to the meaning, thinking, "Indeed, he might answer this question, he might cut this doubt." "Ye cāpi aññe" refers to the countless wise Khattiyas, Brahmins, Brahmas, Devas, Yakkhas, and others who wander about thinking, "We are debaters." He shows that all of them are also bound to the meaning regarding the Blessed One.

386-7. Having thus praised the Blessed One in various ways, now, wishing to praise him through the Dhamma alone and requesting a Dhamma talk, he spoke these two verses beginning with "Ayañhi dhammo." There, "Ayañhi dhammo" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). "Nipuṇo" means subtle and difficult to penetrate. "Sukho" means that when penetrated, it brings about supramundane happiness; because it brings such happiness, it is called "sukho." "Suppavutto" means well-expounded. "Sussūsamānā" means "we desire to hear." "Taṃ no vada" means "preach that Dhamma to us." There is also a variant reading "tvaṃ no," meaning "You, preach to us." "Sabbepi me bhikkhavo" refers to the five hundred monks sitting there at that moment, making the request by pointing to them. "Upāsakā cāpi" shows his own followers and others. The rest is clear here.

Then the Blessed One, wishing first to show the practice of a monk (anagāriya-paṭipadā), addressed the monks and spoke the words beginning with "Suṇātha me bhikkhavo." There, "dhammaṃ dhutaṃ tañca carātha sabbe": it is called "dhuta" because it shakes off (dhunāti) defilements. It means: "I shall proclaim to you such a practice of Dhamma that shakes off defilements; all of you practice that which I have proclaimed, do not be negligent." "Iriyāpathaṃ" refers to the four postures, such as walking. "Pabbajitanulomikaṃ" means the practice endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension, suitable for a recluse. Other teachers say it is the practice that proceeds by way of devotion to meditation subjects in the forest. "Sevetha naṃ" means one should cultivate that posture...
104:
...should cultivate (that posture). "Atthadasa" means one who habitually sees the benefit (hitānupassī). "Mutīmā" means one who is wise (buddhimā). The rest of the verse is clear here.

"No ve vikāle" means that a monk cultivating such a posture suitable for recluses should not wander at the wrong time (vikāla), starting from the passing of midday; but rather, a monk should wander into the village for alms only at the proper time. What is the reason? For attachments (saṅga) cling to a person who wanders at the wrong time; many attachments such as the attachment of lust (rāga-saṅga) cling to, embrace, envelop, and adhere to the person who wanders at the wrong time. Therefore, the Buddhas do not wander at the wrong time; thus, the Noble Ones (ariyapuggala) who have realized the Four Noble Truths do not wander for alms at the wrong time. At that time, the training rule against eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana-sikkhāpada) had not yet been prescribed; therefore, in this discourse, wishing to show the danger to worldlings (puthujjana) by the power of the Dhamma teaching, he spoke this verse. As for the Noble Ones, they abstain from entering the village at the wrong time immediately upon attaining the Path; this is the natural law (dhammatā).

Having thus forbidden wandering at the wrong time, wishing to show that "one wandering at the proper time should also practice in this way," he spoke the verse beginning with "Rūpā ca saddā ca." The meaning is: in those forms and so on which intoxicate beings by generating various kinds of intoxication, one should dispel sensual desire (kāmachanda) according to the method stated in the Piṇḍapātapārisuddhi Sutta and others, and enter for the morning meal (alms) only at the proper time. Here, "pātarāsa" is so called because it is eaten in the morning; it is a name for alms-food (piṇḍapāta). The place where one obtains alms is also called "pātarāsa" here in connection with it. It should be understood that the meaning here is: one should go to the place where one obtains alms-food.

A monk who has thus entered—
"Having obtained alms-food at the proper time,
One should return alone and sit in seclusion;
Contemplating internally, not letting the mind go outward,
With a restrained self, he should not let (the mind) wander out."

In that verse, "piṇḍa" refers to mixed alms-food; for it is called "piṇḍa" in the sense of being gathered and balled together from here and there. "Samayena" means within the time before midday. "Eko paṭikkamma" means returning alone without a companion, fulfilling physical seclusion (kāyaviveka). "Ajjhattacintī" means contemplating one's own continuity of aggregates by applying the three characteristics. The mind...
105:
"Bahiddhā nicchāraye" means that one should not let the mind go out to external objects such as forms, etc., through the power of lust. "Suggahitattabhāvo" means being one whose mind is well-restrained.

A monk living in this way—
"If he should speak with a disciple, or with anyone else, or with another monk, he should speak only the sublime Dhamma; he should not speak slanderous speech, nor speech disparaging others."

What does this mean? If that practitioner (yogāvacara) speaks with a disciple who has approached wishing to hear some Dhamma, or with any other person such as a sectarian or a householder, or with a monk ordained in this Dispensation, he should speak only the sublime Dhamma—which is associated with the Paths and Fruits, etc., or consists of the ten subjects of talk (dasakathāvatthu), and is sublime because it is free from the heat of defilements. He should not utter even a small amount of other speech, such as slander or disparagement of others.

Now, wishing to show the fault in such disparagement of others, he said "Vādañhi eke," etc. The meaning is: In this Dispensation, some empty men (mogha-purisā) engage in and oppose others with various kinds of contentious talk (viggāhikakathā) involving disparagement. They are like those who go to face an army, wishing to fight. We do not praise those of such inferior wisdom. Why? Because from various [kinds of speech], attachments (saṅgā) cling to them. For they cause such individuals to be entangled in the attachments of dispute arising from various paths of speech. Why do they get entangled? Because while opposing others, they let their minds go into that [dispute], far away [from the Dhamma]. A mind that has gone there is far from tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

394-5. Having thus shown the conduct of those of little wisdom, he now said "Piṇḍaṃ vihāraṃ...pe... sāvako," wishing to show the conduct of those of great wisdom. There, by the word "vihāra," a dwelling place is meant; by the word "sayanāsana," a couch and a bench are meant; thus, by all three words, only lodgings (senāsana) are intended. "Āpa" means water. "Saṅghāṭirajūpavāhanaṃ" means the washing of dust and dirt from the outer robe (saṅghāṭi). "Sutvāna dhammaṃ sugatena desitaṃ" means having heard the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such discourses as the Sabbāsava Sutta, in the manner of: "Reflecting wisely, he resorts to the robe for the purpose of warding off cold," etc. Reflecting...
106:
## Seve varapaññasāvako

In the phrase "The disciple of excellent wisdom should resort to," in this Dispensation, the word "piṇḍa" refers to almsfood. By the words "vihāra," etc., lodgings are meant. By the term "āpa," medicinal requisites are shown. By the word "saṅghāṭi," the robe is meant. Thus, having reflected on the fourfold requisites in the manner of "Only for the sake of the stability of this body," etc., the disciple of excellent wisdom should resort to them. A trainee (sekha), an ordinary person (puthujjana), or, in the ultimate sense, an Arahant, who is a disciple of the Tathāgata of excellent wisdom, is able to resort to them. Such a monk is said to be one who possesses the fourfold reflections. It is said: "Reflecting, he resorts to one; reflecting, he endures one; reflecting, he avoids one; reflecting, he removes one." It should be understood that because the disciple of excellent wisdom resorts to them after such reflection, he remains [unstained] by almsfood, etc., like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.

Thus, showing the practice of the Arahants and concluding the practice for monks by crowning it with Arahantship, he now said "Gahaṭṭhavattaṃ pana vo," etc., wishing to show the practice for householders. Among those verses, in the first verse, "sāvaka" refers to a lay disciple (upāsaka) living in the household life. The rest of the meaning is clear. The connection of the meaning is: Previously, I have taught the practice for monks, which is exclusive, unmixed, and entirely complete. That practice for monks cannot be touched or attained by householders who are encumbered with possessions such as fields and property.

Thus, having set aside the practice of monks for that lay disciple and wishing to show only the Dhamma for householders, he said "One should not kill a living being," etc. In that verse, by the first half, he stated the abstinence from taking life, which is pure in three ways (ti-koṭi-parisuddha); by the latter half, he stated the practice of welfare toward beings. In this verse, the third line is fully described in the Khaggavisāṇa Sutta, and the distinction between stable (thāvara) and trembling (tasa) beings in the fourth line is fully described in the commentary on the Metta Sutta. The rest of the meaning is clear. Regarding the connection of the meaning, it should be arranged as: "Having laid down the stick (weapon) toward all beings, whether trembling or stable, one should not kill, nor cause to kill, nor sanction killing." After the words "Having laid down the stick," the remaining verb "one should practice" (vatteyya) must be brought in. Otherwise, there would be no connection between the preceding and following words.

Having thus shown the first precept, he now said "Then, what is not given," etc., wishing to show the second precept. In that verse, "anything" (kiñci) means whether it be a little or a lot.
107:
"Kvacī" means in a village or in a forest. "Sāvaka" means a disciple of the Buddha living in the household life. "Bujjhamāna" means one who knows, "This property belongs to another." "He should avoid all that is not given" means that only one who practices in this way avoids all that is not given, and not otherwise. The rest here is as previously stated and is quite clear.

Having thus shown the second training rule to be pure in three aspects (tikoṭiparisuddha), he said "Abrahmacariya" and so on, intending to show the third training rule starting from the highest limit. There, "asambhuṇanta" means one who is unable.

Now, intending to show the fourth training rule, he said "Sabhaggato vā" and so on. There, "sabhaggata" means one who has gone to a rest house (santhāgāra) and so forth. "Parisaggata" means one who has gone into the midst of a group. The rest here is as previously stated and is clear.

Having thus shown the fourth training rule to be pure in three aspects, he said "Majjañca pānaṃ" and so on, intending to show the fifth. There, "majjañca pānaṃ" is stated thus for the sake of ease in verse composition. The meaning of this is: "One should not practice the drinking of intoxicants." "This Dhamma" (dhammaṃ imaṃ) refers to this Dhamma of abstaining from drinking intoxicants. "Ending in madness" (ummādanantaṃ) means having madness as its conclusion. For even the lightest result of drinking intoxicants, when one becomes a human, leads to madness. "Knowing thus that drinking of intoxicants" (iti naṃ viditvā) means knowing the fault of that drinking of intoxicants. The rest here is as previously stated and is clear.

Having thus shown the fifth training rule to be pure in three aspects, now, to show that drinking intoxicants alone causes defilement and breakage of the previous training rules, and to urge more firmly the abstinence therefrom, he said "Madā hi pāpāni karonti" and so on. There, "madā" means because of the cause of negligence. The word "hi" is a mere particle for completing the verse. "They commit evil deeds" means they commit all unwholesome deeds such as killing living beings. "Causing madness, causing delusion" means causing madness in the next world and causing delusion in this world. The rest has an obvious meaning.

403-4. Having thus shown the constant virtue (niccasīla) of the lay disciple, now, intending to show the factors of the Uposatha, he spoke two verses beginning with "Pāṇaṃ na hane." There, "abrahmacariya" is conduct that is not noble. "Methunā" means from engaging in sexual intercourse. "One should not eat food at the wrong time at night" means one should not eat at night, and during the day...
108:
...one should not eat food that has passed the [proper] time (vikālabhojana). In the phrase "na ca gandhaṃ," by the mention of "perfume," it should be understood that scented powders, ointments, and so forth are also included. "Mañce" means on an allowable bed. "Santhate" means on a covering spread with allowable mats and so forth. On the ground, however, it is allowable to sleep by spreading a woolen coverlet (gonaka) and so forth. "Aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ" (eightfold) is like a musical ensemble with five factors; it is not something separate from its factors. "Dukkhantagunā" means [taught] by the [Buddha] who has reached the end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). The rest here is clear. Some say that the latter half was spoken by the redactors of the Council (saṅgītikārakas).

Having thus shown the factors of the Uposatha, now, intending to show the time for the Uposatha, he said "Tato ca pakkhassa" and so on. There, the word "tato" is a mere particle for completing the verse. The word "pakkhassupavassuposathaṃ" should be connected with the following words thus: "Having observed the Uposatha on these three days—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—and having approached and dwelt in this eightfold Uposatha." In the phrase "pāṭihāriyapakkhañca," these five months—the month of Āsāḷha, the three months of the rains-residence, and the month of Kattika—are called the "extraordinary fortnight" (pāṭihāriyapakkh). Others say it is only the three months of Āsāḷha, Kattika, and Phagguna. Others say the "extraordinary fortnight" refers to the four days each—the 13th, 1st, 7th, and 9th—which are the days before and after the Uposatha days of the fortnight. One may accept whichever view one likes. Or rather, for those desiring merit, all days are taught. Thus, it should be connected: "A person with a confident mind should observe the eightfold Uposatha even for a single day without giving it up, in that extraordinary fortnight, which is of a well-perfected and complete nature."

Having thus shown the time for the Uposatha, now, intending to show what should be done after observing the Uposatha during those times, he said "Tato ca pāto" and so on. Here too, "tato" is either a particle for completing the verse or means "thereafter"; it means "at that time." "Pāto" means the morning of the following day. "Upavutthuposatho" means one who has observed the Uposatha. "Annena" means with gruel, rice, and so forth. "Pānena" means with the eight kinds of drinks. "Anumodamāno" means rejoicing repeatedly, rejoicing continuously. "Yathārahaṃ" means as is suitable for oneself, according to one's ability and strength. "Saṃvibhajetha" means one should distribute or share. The rest is clear.
109:
Having spoken thus about the duties of one who has observed the Uposatha, [the Teacher] now speaks of the grave duty to be practiced for life and the purity of livelihood, and showing the place to be attained by that practice, he said: "Dhammena mātāpitaro" and so forth. In that verse, "dhammena" means with wealth acquired righteously. "Bhareyya" means he should support. "Dhammikaṃ so vaṇijjaṃ" refers to righteous trade, excluding these five types of unrighteous trade: trade in humans, trade in weapons, trade in poisons, trade in meat, and trade in intoxicants. By the term "trade," other righteous means of livelihood such as farming and cattle-breeding are also included. The rest of the words are clear in meaning.

The connection of meaning here is: that noble disciple, endowed with the practice of constant virtue (nicca-sīla), Uposatha virtue, and the practice of giving (dāna), should engage in righteous trade; and with the wealth righteously obtained therefrom, without departing from the Dhamma, he should support his parents. Then, if that householder, being thus diligent, practices this duty mentioned from the beginning, after the breaking up of the body, because he dispels darkness and creates light with his own radiance, he reaches and associates with the six classes of devas of the sense sphere known as "Sayampabha" (self-luminous), being reborn in their place of rebirth.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha,
## the explanation of the Dhammika Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## The second chapter, known by the name Cūḷavagga, is also finished according to the method of explaining the meaning.
110:
## 3. Mahāvagga
## 1. Pabbajjāsutta-vaṇṇanā
It is called the Pabbajjāsutta because it begins with the words 'Pabbajjaṃ kittayissāmi' (I shall praise the going forth). What was the occasion for its origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, a reflection arose in the Venerable Ānanda: 'The going forth of the great disciples such as the Venerable Sāriputta has been praised, and the monks and lay followers know of it. However, the Blessed One's going forth has not yet been praised. What if I were to praise it?' Then, while sitting in his place at the Jetavana monastery, holding an ornate fan, the Venerable Ānanda spoke this sutta to the monks, wishing to praise the Blessed One's going forth.

In that verse, one who praises the going forth should praise how he went forth. In praising how he went forth, one should also praise how he reflected and took delight in the state of renunciation. Therefore, after saying 'Pabbajjaṃ kittayissāmi', he spoke the words beginning with 'Yathā pabbaji' (How he went forth). 'Cakkhumā' (The One with Vision) means the Blessed One who is endowed with the five types of eyes. The remaining words in the opening verse are clear.

Now, wishing to clarify the meaning of the phrase 'Yathā vīmaṃsamāno' (How he was reflecting), he spoke the words beginning with 'Sambādho'yaṃ'. In that context, 'Sambādho' (confined) means that living in a household is narrow and lacks the opportunity to perform wholesome deeds because of the oppression of wife and children, and the oppression of defilements. 'Rajassāyatanaṃ' (abode of dust) means it is the place where the dust of passion (rāga) and other defilements arise, just as places like Kamboja are the origin of horses and such. 'Abbhokāsa' (open air) means the state of a monk which is like the open sky, being the opposite of the aforementioned confinement. Thus, having reflected on the faults and benefits of household life and renunciation, with a heart greatly urged by the states of disease, old age, and death, he departed in the Great Renunciation. On the banks of the Anomā River, he cut his hair with a sword. At that very moment, his hair and beard became two finger-breadths long, suitable for a recluse. Taking the eight requisites offered by Ghaṭīkāra Brahma, he went forth, practicing by the very habit of renunciation developed over many thousands of births, without being taught by anyone, 'This is how to dress, this is how to robe.' It means he established the appearance of a monk by wearing one robe as a lower garment, one as an upper garment, placing one robe on his shoulder, and carrying a clay bowl on his shoulder. The remaining words here are clear.

Having thus praised the Blessed One's going forth, in order to show the practice of the monk and his departure from the banks of the Anomā River to strive for meditation, he said 'Pabbajitvāna'...
111:
He spoke the entire verse beginning with 'Kāyena'. In that verse, 'Kāyena pāpakammaṃ vivajjayī' means he avoided the three types of bodily misconduct. 'Vacīduccaritaṃ' means (he avoided) the four types of verbal misconduct. 'Ājīvaṃ parisodhayī' means he abandoned wrong livelihood and maintained only right livelihood.

Having thus purified his morality with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla), the Buddha-to-be traveled the thirty-yojana journey from the banks of the Anomā River to the city of Rājagaha in seven days. At the time he went to Rājagaha, although he was not yet a Buddha, it is appropriate to say 'The Buddha went' because it was the preliminary practice (pubbacariyā) of the Buddha, similar to the worldly conventional expression, 'The King was born here' or 'He took the kingship here'. 'Magadhānaṃ' means the city of the Magadha country. 'Giribbaja' is also the name of that city. It is called 'Giribbaja' (Mountain Fold) because it is situated like a cattle-pen in the midst of five mountains named Paṇḍava, Gijjhakūṭa, Vebhāra, Isigili, and Vepulla.

'Piṇḍāya abhihāresi' means he wandered in that city for the sake of alms. The Bodhisatta stood at the city gate and thought: 'If I inform King Bimbisāra of my arrival, he will bring many requisites, saying "Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana, has arrived." However, for me who has already gone forth, it is not proper to receive requisites by informing him. Now, I shall wander for alms.' Then, robing himself in the rag-robes offered by the devas and holding a clay bowl, he entered the city through the East gate and wandered for alms from house to house. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said, 'Piṇḍāya abhihāresi'. 'Ākiṇṇavaralakkhaṇo' means one who has excellent marks that appear as if they were scattered over the body, or one who has abundant excellent marks. The word 'ākiṇṇā' also means abundant (vipula). As in the verse, 'Ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticeḷaṃva makkhito', it means 'a man of abundant evil'.

'Tamaddasā' means that for seven days prior to his entry into the city, a festival had been proclaimed in the city. On that day, however, the drum was beaten to announce, 'The festival is over, let work be resumed.' Then, a great multitude of people gathered at the royal courtyard. King Bimbisāra, intending to manage the affairs of work, opened the lion-window and, while looking at the host of troops, saw the Great Being (Mahāsatta) wandering for alms. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said, 'Tamaddasā Bimbisāro, pāsādasmiṃ patiṭṭhito' (Bimbisāra, standing in his palace, saw him). 'Imamatthāṃ abhāsathā' means he spoke of this matter to his ministers.
112:
Now, wishing to show the meaning of what was said to those ministers, King Bimbisāra said: "Friends, (look at) this person." In that verse, by the word "imam" (this), the King points to the Bodhisatta; by the word "bhonto" (friends), he addresses the ministers. "Nisāmetha" means "look/observe." "Abhirūpa" means being endowed with beautiful major and minor limbs. "Brahmā" means being endowed with [perfect] stature and circumference. "Suci" means having a pure complexion. "Caraṇena" means being endowed with [graceful] gait.

414-5. "Nīcakulāmiva" means he is not like one who has gone forth from a low family. The letter "ma" is inserted for euphonic junction (padasandhi). "Where will this monk go?" means the King spoke with the intention: "Where will this monk go? Where will he stay today? Let the royal messengers go quickly to find out, for we wish to see him." He has guarded doors (senses) because of his downcast eyes; he is well-restrained through mindfulness. Alternatively, he has guarded doors through mindfulness and is well-restrained by the graceful wearing of the double robe (saṅghāṭi).

"He quickly filled the bowl" means that because of his clear comprehension and mindfulness, he did not accept more than necessary, and thinking "this is enough," he quickly filled his bowl according to his intention. "Muni" means that although he had not yet reached the state of a Muni (omniscience/mona), he is called a Muni because he is practicing for it; or it is a term used by worldly convention. Worldly people call even a monk who has not yet attained the state of a Muni a "Muni." "He went towards Mount Paṇḍava" means he climbed that mountain. The Bodhisatta had asked people, "Where do the renunciants live in this city?" Then the people informed him, "They live in the cave facing east on the upper part of Mount Paṇḍava." Therefore, thinking "this will be the place to stay," he went towards that very Mount Paṇḍava.

419-23. "Like a tiger, a bull, or a lion in a mountain cave" means he sat in the mountain cave like a tiger, like a bull, and like a lion. These three noble creatures usually stay in mountain caves without fear or dread; therefore, this comparison was made. "By a noble vehicle" means by a noble vehicle such as an elephant, horse, chariot, or palanquin. "Having gone as far as the ground allowed for the vehicle" means going as far as the ground where vehicles like elephants and horses could travel. "Āsajja" means having reached or having gone near the Bodhisatta. "Upāvisi" means he sat down. "Yuvā" means being endowed with youth. "Dahara" means being young by birth. "Paṭhamuppattiko susu" is a qualification of both those terms. "Yuvā susu" means very young. "Paṭhamuppattiko" means appearing in the first stage of youth. "Daharo ca asi" means although he is young, he appears like a tender child.
113:
424-5. "Anīkaggaṃ" means the host of troops, the front of the army. In the phrase "I give wealth, enjoy it," the connection should be understood as: "I give you as much wealth as you desire in the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha. Enjoy it, beautifying it, being at the head of the host of troops surrounded by elephant forces."

When it was said, "I give wealth, enjoy it; when asked, please tell your lineage," the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) thought: "If I desired kingship, even the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) would invite me to their own kingdoms, or remaining at home, I could exercise the rule of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). However, this king speaks thus out of ignorance. I shall let him know." Thinking thus, he raised his arm, pointed to the direction from which he came, and spoke the verse beginning with "Uzūṃ janapado rājā."

In that verse, by saying "Facing the Himālaya," he shows the abundance of crops and the absence of want. Indeed, even the great Sāla trees growing in the rock crevices depending on the Himālaya mountains grow with the five kinds of growth; what need is there to mention the growth of crops sown in the fields? By saying "Endowed with wealth and energy," he shows the completeness of the seven treasures and the constant presence of heroes whom other kings cannot challenge. By saying "Dwellers among the Kosalans," he rejects the status of being a new or minor king. A new king is not called a "Niketī." Only one who has resided in that very country by lineage from the beginning is called a "Niketī." King Suddhodana is a king of such nature; it is in reference to him that he said "Dwellers among the Kosalans." By that, he also shows the abundance of wealth descended through lineage.

Having shown his abundance of wealth with these words, and having declared his perfect lineage with the words "By clan Ādicca, by birth Sākiya," he spoke to reject the King's offer of "I give wealth, enjoy it," saying: "I have gone forth from that royal family; I do not long for sensual pleasures." The meaning here is: "If I longed for sensual pleasures, I would not have gone forth, abandoning a family so endowed with wealth and energy and filled with eighty-two thousand heroes."

Having thus rejected the King's words, he spoke to show the reason for his renunciation: "Having seen the danger in sensual pleasures, and seeing renunciation (nekkhamma) as safety." This should be understood in connection with the phrase "I have gone forth." In that verse, "datthu" means...
114:
In the verse beginning with "Having seen (the danger in sensual pleasures)," whatever words in this verse and the preceding verses have not been analyzed (commented upon) should be understood as not analyzed simply because their meanings are clear. Having thus stated the reason for his own renunciation, and wishing to go for the sake of striving, he addressed King Bimbisāra, saying: "I shall go for the sake of striving; in this my mind delights." The meaning of that statement is: "Great King, because I have seen renunciation (nekkhamma) as safe from the household life, I have gone forth. Therefore, desiring that supreme renunciation called Nibbāna, which is 'striving' (padhāna) in the sense of being the foremost among all dhammas, I shall go for the sake of striving. In this striving alone my mind delights, not in sensual pleasures." When this was said, it is said that the King told the Bodhisatta: "Venerable Sir, I have heard before that 'Prince Siddhattha, the son of King Suddhodana, having seen the four omens, will go forth and become a Buddha.' Having seen your resolve, Venerable Sir, I am thus inspired with faith: 'Surely you will attain Buddhahood.' It is well, Venerable Sir; having attained Buddhahood, may you first visit my kingdom."

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Pabbajjā Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Padhāna Sutta
This sutta, beginning with "Taṃ maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ," is called the Padhāna Sutta. How did it arise (the occasion)? The Venerable Ānanda concluded the Pabbajjā Sutta with the words: "I shall go for the sake of striving; in this my mind delights." While the Blessed One was staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he thought: "For six years, desiring striving, I performed austere practices (dukkharacariya) that are difficult for others to do. Today, I shall preach that matter to the monks." Then, coming out of the Fragrant Chamber and sitting on the Buddha's seat, he began this sutta with "Taṃ maṃ padhānapahitattaṃ."

In that sutta, with the two words "Taṃ maṃ," he refers only to himself. "Padhānapahitattaṃ" means having a mind sent forth for the sake of Nibbāna, or having a body that has been sacrificed. With the phrase "Nadiṃ Nerañjaraṃ pati," he indicates the landmark. This is because the Nerañjarā River was the landmark for his striving. For this reason, the accusative case (upayogavacana) is used here. The meaning of this is "at the river named Nerañjarā," which means on the bank of the Nerañjarā River. "Viparakkamma" means having exerted great effort. "Jhāyantaṃ" means contemplating while constantly engaged in the breathless (appāṇaka) jhāna...
115:
...meditating continuously on the breathless (appāṇaka) jhāna. "Yogakkhemassa pattiyā" means for the sake of attaining Nibbāna, which is security from the four bondages (yoga), such as the bondage of sensuality (kāmayoga).

Namuci is Māra. He is called "Namuci" because he does not release (na muñcati) the devas and humans who wish to escape from his realm, but instead creates obstacles for them. "Karuṇāṃ vācaṃ" means words associated with compassion. "Bhāsamāno upāgamī" (approached while speaking) is obvious in meaning. Why did Māra approach? It is said that one day the Great Being (the Bodhisatta) thought: "If one is always seeking food, one remains attached to life. One who is attached to life cannot attain the Deathless (Nibbāna)." Then, he practiced by cutting off food, and because of that practice, his body became emaciated and discolored. Then Māra, fearing "This person is practicing extremely severe austerities without knowing whether this is the right path to enlightenment or not; he might someday transcend my realm," approached thinking "I will prevent him by saying such and such words." Therefore, he said: "You are emaciated and discolored; death is near to you."

After saying this, wishing to make known the proximity of death, he said: "There are a thousand parts for death, and only one part for your life." The meaning of that statement is: because there are a thousand parts, it is called "sahasabhāga". What are those parts? The remaining text should be filled as "the causes of death". "Ekaṃsa" means one single part. This is what is meant: "These thousand parts, such as the breathless jhāna, are the causes of your death. Among those parts, only one part remains for you to live. Thus, death is near to you." Having thus made known the proximity of death, wishing to encourage him to live, he said: "O Sir, live! Life is better." If asked why it is better, it means "Only if you live can you perform meritorious deeds (puñña)."

Then, wishing to show the merits he approved of, Māra said: "You are practicing the holy life (brahmacariya)", etc. In that context, "brahmacariya" refers to the occasional abstinence from sexual intercourse that ascetics (tāpasa) usually practice. "Jūhato" means to one who offers sacrifices. The rest of the words here are quite clear.

"Duggo maggo" (a difficult path): this half-verse was spoken to create a loss of desire for striving. In that context, because it involves undertaking difficult practices like the breathless jhāna, it must be traveled with suffering, thus it is called "duggo" (a path difficult to travel).
116: It should be understood that 'dukkara' (difficult to do) means it is performed with a suffering body and mind, and 'durabhisambhava' (difficult to master) means it is impossible to achieve while being so close to death. From here on, the half-verse "Māro aṭṭhā Buddhassa santike" was inserted by the Reciters (Sangītikāras). Some teachers say the entire verse was spoken by the Reciters. Our preferred view is that the Blessed One himself spoke all such matters, referring to himself in the third person as if referring to another. In that verse, 'aṭṭhā' means 'stood'. The rest of the words are clear in meaning. In the word 'yenatthena' in the sixth verse, the meaning is: "Evil Mara, you have come to me with your own purpose of wanting to harm the welfare of others." The rest of the words are clear in meaning. Desiring to reject the words (of Mara), "Live and perform merits," he spoke this verse beginning with "Anumattopi." In that verse, 'puñña' (merit) refers to the merit that leads to the round of rebirths as spoken by Mara. The rest is clear. Now, on account of the words "Your life is certain," desiring to threaten Mara, he spoke this verse beginning with "Atthi saddhā." The meaning in that verse is: "Hey Mara, it would be appropriate for you to ask about life to one who has no faith in the supreme and noble state of peace (Nibbāna), or who is lazy despite having faith, or who lacks wisdom despite having faith and exerting effort. But I have faith that is convinced of the supreme and noble state of peace. Furthermore, I possess energy (viriya) consisting of unflagging physical and mental effort, and wisdom like a thunderbolt. Why do you ask about life to me, who has a mind directed towards Nibbāna and has such noble intention? Why do you ask about life?" In the phrase "paññā ca mama," the word 'ca' (and) also includes mindfulness (sati) and concentration (samādhi). This being so, why do you ask about life to me who is thus directed towards Nibbāna and is not lacking even one of the five faculties (indriya) by which people reach Nibbāna? Is it not true that even one day of life is noble for one who exerts firm effort, is wise, burns away defilements, and sees arising and passing away? 436-8. Having thus threatened Mara, desiring to show the process of his own body and mind, he spoke the three verses beginning with "Nadīnamapi." These are clear in meaning. This is...
117: Explanation: The wind produced by the force of energy in my non-breathing meditation (appāṇakajjhāna) in my body could dry up even the currents of rivers like the Ganges and Yamuna in the world. Why then would the four measures of blood in me, whose mind is so directed, not dry up? Not only does my blood dry up, but as that blood dries, the localized bile (baddha-pitta), non-localized bile (abaddha-pitta), and the four measures of phlegm (semha) that cover food and drink, as well as the same amount of urine and nutritive essence (ojā), also dry up. As that urine and nutritive essence dry up, the flesh also wastes away. Even as the flesh wastes away gradually in this manner, my mind becomes even more clear; it does not decline because of that. You, not knowing such a state of mind and seeing only the body, say 'You are thin, of bad color, death is near you.' Not only does my mind become clear, but my mindfulness, wisdom, and concentration stand even firmer. There is not even a tiny bit of negligence, delusion, or mental distraction. For me living thus, whatever painful feelings produced by others that ascetics and Brahmins experience in the past, future, or present, the supreme feeling I have reached is the pinnacle of them. Just as others touched by suffering long for heat when cold, cold when hot, food when hungry, and water when thirsty, my mind does not long for even one of the five strands of sensual pleasure. The thought 'It would be good if I could eat good food and sleep comfortably' has not arisen in my mind in this manner. Mara, behold the purity of a being! 439-41. Having thus shown his purity, to destroy the desire of Mara who came saying 'I will prevent you,' he spoke six verses beginning with 'Kāmā te paṭhamā senā' (Sensual pleasures are your first army), describing Mara's armies and showing his own invincibility. In those verses, first, defilement-based sensuality (kilesakāma) deludes beings living in the household life regarding objective sensuality (vatthukāma). For those who overcome those defilements and become monks, discontent (arati) arises in secluded dwellings or in other higher wholesome states. This was said: 'Friend, for a monk, delight is difficult to achieve.' Then, because they live dependent on others, hunger and thirst oppress them. Through that hunger...
118:
For those who are oppressed, the craving for seeking (pariyesanatanhā) fatigues the mind; then, for those with fatigued minds, sloth and torpor (thīnamiddha) descend. Furthermore, for those who do not attain any distinction and dwell in forest thickets and lodgings that are difficult to endure, fear arises due to the perception of dread. For those who dwell thus with doubt, not enjoying the taste of seclusion for a long time, doubt (vicikicchā) regarding the practice arises: "Could this not be the path?" For those who dwell having dispelled that doubt, due to attaining some slight distinction, conceit (māna), denigrating (makkha), and obstinacy (thambha) arise. For those who dwell having dispelled those states, based on attaining a higher distinction, gain, honor, and fame (lābha-sakkāra-siloka) arise. Being infatuated with gain and so on, they display counterfeits of the Dhamma, acquire false fame, and staying in that fame, they exalt themselves and disparage others based on birth and so on. Therefore, sensual desires and so on should be known as the first army and so forth.

## 442-3. Having thus pointed out the ten-fold army, because that army is endowed with dark, unwholesome states and serves the interest of Namuci Māra, who is called Kaṇha (the Dark One), he said, pointing it out: "Namuci, this is your army, the attacking army of Kaṇha." In that verse, "abhippahārinī" means that which kills, crushes, and creates obstacles for recluses and brahmins. As it is said, "One who is not a hero cannot defeat that army, nor can one obtain happiness by defeating it," so one who is concerned for his body and life cannot defeat your army; only a hero can defeat it, and after defeating it, he attains the happiness of the Path and the happiness of the Fruit. And because he obtains happiness, I too, desiring happiness, shall carry this muñja grass. Men who frequent the battlefield and do not retreat bind muñja grass on their heads, banners, or weapons to make known their non-retreating nature; likewise, regard me as one who carries muñja grass. My life, defeated by your army, is contemptible; therefore, regard it thus: "Death in battle is better for me than that I should live defeated." The meaning is: rather than living defeated by such a life, death in battle against that which creates obstacles for those who practice rightly along with you is better for me.

Why is death better? Because, according to the verse "Plunged herein... those of good vows," some recluses and brahmins who are plunged, submerged, and entered into your army, which ends in exalting oneself and disparaging others through sensual desires and so on, are not seen; they cannot shine with virtues such as morality (sīla); they become as if they have entered darkness. Those thus plunged...
119:
...Even if they occasionally emerge like a man who surfaces and then sinks back into the water, appearing with the thought "Faith is good" and so forth, nevertheless, because they are overwhelmed by that army, they do not know that path to the secure Nibbāna, the way by which all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and others of good conduct travel. Having heard this verse, Māra said nothing further and departed.

445-6. When he had departed, the Great Being (Mahāsatta), the Bodhisatta, having attained no special distinction by practicing those difficult austerities (dukkara-kāriya), reflected in sequence, "Could there be another path to enlightenment?" and so forth. He then partook of gross food and regained his strength. Early on the full-moon day of Vesākha, he partook of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā and spent the day in the Bhadravana grove. Having spent the day there attaining the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti), he proceeded towards the Mahābodhi-maṇḍa in the evening. He scattered the eight handfuls of grass given by the brahmin Sotthiya at the foot of the Bodhi tree, and being honored and revered by the deities of the ten thousand world-systems, he made the fourfold resolution of effort:

"Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain;
let the flesh and blood in my body dry up completely."

Having made the vow, "I shall not break this sitting posture until I have attained Buddhahood (Omniscience)," he sat upon the Unconquered Seat (Aparājita-pallaṅka). The Evil Māra, knowing this, thought, "Today Prince Siddhattha sits having made a vow; this very day I must thwart his vow." He raised the army of Māra, which was twelve leagues wide, extending to the edge of the universe, and nine leagues high. Mounting the elephant king Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty leagues in size, he created a thousand arms, seized various weapons, and saying, "Seize him! Kill him! Strike him!" he caused the various kinds of rain described in the Āḷavaka Sutta to fall. When those rains reached the Great Man, they turned into the forms described in that Sutta. Then, striking the elephant's frontal globes with a vajra-goad, he brought it near the Great Man and said, "Rise, O Siddhattha, from this seat!" The Great Man replied, "Māra, I shall not rise," and looking around at that entire army, he recited these verses beginning with "Samantā dhajiniṃ."
120:
In that verse, ‘dhajiniṃ’ means the army. ‘Yuttaṃ’ means exerting (striving). ‘Savāhanaṃ’ means the army together with the elephant-king Girimekhala. ‘Paccuggacchāmi’ means “I shall go forward and upward”; such going is only by psychic power, not by the physical body. Why? It was said with the intention: “May Māra not move me from this Unconquered Seat (Aparājita-pallaṅka).” ‘Nappasahati’ means cannot endure or cannot overcome. ‘Āmaṃ pattaṃ’ means a clay pot that is freshly baked in a raw state (or not yet fully fired). ‘Asmanā’ means (striking) with a stone. The remaining words are clear.

447-8. Now, wishing to show, “Having destroyed that army of Māra, and thereafter being one who has won the battle and attained the consecration of the King of Dhamma, I shall do this,” he spoke the verse beginning with ‘vasīkaritvā’. In that verse, ‘vasīkaritvā saṅkappaṃ’ means having mastered one’s thoughts by abandoning all wrong thoughts (micchā-saṅkappa) through the development of the Path and maintaining only right thoughts (sammā-saṅkappa). ‘Satiñca sūpatiṭṭhitaṃ’ means well-establishing one’s right mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness, such as mindfulness of the body.
