Being one who has thus mastered his thoughts and has well-established mindfulness, I shall wander from kingdom to kingdom, disciplining many disciples among the host of devas and humans. Then, those who are disciplined by me, being diligent and following my instruction, will reach that Nibbāna where they shall not sorrow. That state of being without sorrow is the Deathless (amata) which is Nibbāna itself.

449-51. Then, having heard these verses, Māra asked, “O monk, do you not fear seeing such a group?” “Yes, Māra, I do not fear,” he replied. When asked, “Why do you not fear?” he replied, “I do not fear because I have performed the meritorious deeds of the perfections (pāramīs) such as giving (dāna).” When asked again, “You say you have performed deeds such as giving, but who knows of this?” he replied, “O Evil One, what is the use of a witness here? Indeed, this Great Earth (Mahāpathavī) itself is the witness, which quaked seven times in six different ways by the power of the dāna I gave while being King Vessantara in just one lifetime.” When this was said, the Great Earth quaked up to the edge of the waters, emitting a terrifying sound. Hearing that sound, Māra was terrified as if struck by lightning, and lowering his banner, he fled along with his retinue. Then the Great Man realized the three knowledges (tevijjā) during the three watches of the night, and at dawn, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna): “Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ... taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā.” Hearing the sound of the inspired utterance, Māra came and thought, “This person is claiming, ‘I have become a Buddha.’ Now I shall follow him to observe his conduct. If there is any slip in his body or speech, I shall harass him.” Thus, he had followed the Bodhisatta for six years previously, and he followed the Blessed One for another year after he attained Buddhahood. Even though he followed him thus, he did not see even a single slip of the Blessed One, and so he recited the verses of disenchantment (nibbajanīya-gāthā) beginning with “Satta vassāni.” In those verses, ‘otāraṃ’ means opportunity. ‘Nādhigacchissaṃ’ means could not find. ‘Medavaṇṇaṃ’ means (a stone) resembling a lump of fat. ‘Anupariyāgā’ means followed all around. ‘Muduṃ’ means a soft manner. ‘Vindema’ means might find. ‘Asmanā’ means...
121:
Māra followed the Bodhisatta for six years, and after he attained Buddhahood, he followed him for another year. While following thus, he did not see even a single slip of the Blessed One, and so he recited these verses of disenchantment (nibbajanīya-gāthā) beginning with “Satta vassāni.”

In those verses, “otāraṃ” means an opportunity (an opening). “Nādhigacchissaṃ” means I can no longer find it. “Medavaṇṇaṃ” means (a stone) resembling a lump of fat. “Anupariyagā” means went around or wandered all around. “Muduṃ” means something soft. “Vindema” means might find. “Assādanā” means having a pleasant and tender taste. “Vāyasetto” means in this context, the crow should depart from here. The remaining words are clear.

This is the connection of meaning (yojanā): For seven years, Māra followed the Blessed One, seeking an opportunity to find fault, never leaving his side even for a step. Even though he followed him thus, he did not find an opportunity to blame him. That Māra is like a crow who, perceiving a stone resembling fat to be actual fat, pecks at it from one side with its beak but finds no taste, and thinking, “Might I find something soft here? Or might there be some sweetness from this?” pecks and goes around it in the same way, but finding no taste at all, becomes weary and departs, thinking, “This is just a stone.” Similarly, I have been pecking and testing the Blessed One’s bodily actions and so on with my beak of meager wisdom, and have gone all around him. I thought, “Might I find something soft, such as impure bodily conduct, in some place? Might there be some sweetness from somewhere?” Now, we who find no sweetness, like the crow that approached the stone and became weary, shall approach Gotama and, becoming weary, depart from him.

It is said that as Māra was speaking thus, great sorrow arose in him due to his seven years of fruitless exertion. Because of that sorrow, as his limbs became weary, the lute named Beluvapaṇḍu fell from his armpit. That lute, when played once by a skilled person, could emit a sweet sound for four months. Sakka took that lute and gave it to the deva Pañcasikha. Māra did not even realize that the lute had fallen. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“The lute of that Māra, who was overcome by sorrow, fell from his armpit;
Then that dejected Yakkha disappeared right there.”

Some say that the reciters of the council (saṅgītikārakas) spoke this verse, but that statement is not pleasing to us.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## The explanation of the Padhāna Sutta of the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
122:
## 3. Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta

This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," is the Subhāsita Sutta. Its origin is through the Blessed One's own intention. For the Blessed One delights in well-spoken words; by manifesting his own practice of well-spoken speech, he spoke this sutta desiring to prevent beings from the practice of ill-spoken speech. In this sutta, the words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" are the words of the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgītikāras). In this sutta, the passage "Tatra kho bhagavā... pe... bhadante'ti te bhikkhū" consists of new terms; the remaining words follow the method already described.

Therefore, to explain the new terms, it is said: The word "tatra" indicates the place and time. This is because it shows that he was staying at a certain time, and in a certain monastery. Alternatively, it indicates the place and time suitable for speaking. This is because the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma at an unsuitable place or time. The words "Bāhiya, now is not the time," etc., serve as evidence in this matter. "Kho" is a particle used merely for completing the sentence or in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), etc. "Bhagavā" indicates his status as the Teacher of the world. "Bhikkhū" indicates the persons suitable for listening to the discourse. "Āmantesi" means he called, he spoke, or he made them understand.

"Bhikkhavo" indicates the manner of addressing. This word is used because it is established through qualities such as the habit of seeking alms. By saying this, he manifests their livelihood as one practiced by both the lowly and the noble, and he suppresses states such as agitation and misery. With this word "Bhikkhavo," preceded by a look from eyes and a heart clear with the expansion of compassion, he causes those monks to face him; and with that very word which indicates the desire to speak, he generates in those monks the desire to listen; and with that very word which has the meaning of making them understand, he urges those monks toward listening well and proper attention. This is because the perfection of the Dispensation (Sāsana) depends on listening well and proper attention.

If it is asked why he addressed only the monks when other devas and humans were present, it is because of their seniority, excellence, proximity, and constant presence. This is because this Dhamma teaching is common to the entire assembly, not just for a single individual. Among the assembly, the monks are senior because they were the first to appear; they are excellent because, starting from their renunciation of the household life, they follow the Teacher's conduct and are the recipients who uphold the entire Dispensation. They are called "āsanna" (near ones) because they were sitting in the presence of the Teacher, and they are called "constantly present" because they move about in the vicinity of the Teacher. Therefore, the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma common to the entire assembly, addressed only the monks. Furthermore, those monks are like vessels for this discourse because of the existence of their practice according to the instruction...
123:
...he addressed in this way. "Bhadante" is a term of address showing respect. "Te bhikkhū" means those monks whom the Blessed One addressed, replied to the Blessed One while speaking in this manner with respect.

"Catūhi aṅgehi" means by four reasons or by four factors. Indeed, the four such as abstaining from false speech are the reasons for well-spoken speech. The four such as speaking the truth are the factors, and the word "aṅga" is also used in the sense of reason. The word "catūhi" is in the ablative case (nissakka) in the sense of reason, and in the instrumental case (karaṇa) in the sense of factor.

"Samannāgatā" means well-attained, arisen, or endowed with. "Vācā" means well-spoken speech. This is the kind of speech that appears in passages such as "Vācā girā byappatho" and "Nelā kaṇṇasukhā." However, although communication (viññatti) in the passage "Vācāya ce kataṃ kammaṃ," abstinence (virati) in the passage "Yā catūhi vacīduccaritehi ārati virati... ayaṃ vuccati sammāvācā," and volition (cetanā) in the passage "Pharusavācā... nirayasaṃvattanikā hoti" are also called "vācā," such communication, abstinence, and volition are not intended here. Why? Because harsh speech and so forth should not be spoken.

"Subhāsitā hoti" means it is well-spoken. By saying this, he shows its quality of bringing benefit. "Na dubbhāsitā" means it is not ill-spoken. By saying this, he shows its quality of not bringing harm. "Anavajjā" means speech free from the faults known as lust (rāga) and so forth. By saying this, he shows the purity of its cause and the absence of the aforementioned faults. "Ananuvajjā ca" means speech free from the censure of others. By saying this, he shows its perfection in all aspects. "Viññūnaṃ" refers to the wise. By saying this, he shows that fools are not the standard in matters of blame and praise.

"Katamehi catūhi" is a question asked with the desire to explain (kathatukamyatā-pucchā). "Idha" means in this Dispensation. "Bhikkhave" is the address to the monks whom he wishes to teach. "Bhikkhū" refers to the persons who speak the speech of the described variety. "Subhāsitaṃyeva bhāsati" is a statement that singles out one of the four factors of speech by way of a teaching based on a person (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). "No dubbhāsitaṃ" is the prohibition of speaking the opposite of that well-spoken factor. By saying this, he refutes the view that "false speech and so forth should also be spoken sometimes." By the words "no dubbhāsitaṃ," he shows the abandoning of wrong speech (micchā-vācā), and by the words "subhāsitaṃ," he shows the characteristic of speech that should be spoken by the virtuous who have abandoned wrong speech. Likewise, not doing evil unwholesome deeds, being endowed with merit...
124:
It refers to the perfection of merit. Regarding the explanation of the factors, it is said that what was not spoken before is now spoken for the sake of showing the benefit. This same method should be understood in the phrases beginning with 'Dhammaṃyeva' (only Dhamma). In this Sutta, by the passage 'He speaks only what is well-spoken, not what is ill-spoken,' speech that is free from the fault of slander and promotes harmony is meant. By the phrase 'He speaks only Dhamma, not non-Dhamma,' speech that is free from the fault of frivolous talk and is consistent with the Dhamma, being counsel, is meant. By the remaining two phrases, endearing speech free from harshness and truthful speech are meant. With the phrase 'Imehi kho' (By these...), he concludes the discourse, wishing to show those factors of speech directly. Specifically, here, by saying 'Monks, speech endowed with these four factors is well-spoken,' the Blessed One refutes the view of other teachers who consider speech 'well-spoken' (subhāsita) if it is endowed with components such as pledges, or words like nouns, or perfections of gender, number, case, tense, and instrument. For even if speech is endowed with such components, if it is accompanied by slander and so on, it is indeed ill-spoken because it brings harm to oneself and others. However, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it belongs to the Milakkha (barbarian) language or is contained in the song of a servant girl fetching water, is still well-spoken because it brings about mundane and supramundane welfare and happiness. An example is the sixty monks practicing insight who, while traveling along a road in Sri Lanka, heard a Sinhalese servant girl guarding crops singing a song in the Sinhalese language about birth, aging, and death, and attained Arahantship right there. Similarly, a monk named Tissa, who was practicing insight, while walking near a lotus pond, heard a servant girl plucking lotuses and singing:

'The red lotus that blooms in the morning is withered by the light of the sun; likewise, beings who have attained human state are withered (oppressed) by the momentum of aging.'

Hearing this song, he attained Arahantship. Also, in the interval between two Buddhas, a certain man came from the forest with his seven sons and heard a woman pounding rice with a pestle...
125:
'This body is oppressed by aging; it stands depending on the withered thick and thin skin. This body is liable to be destroyed by death; it is merely bait (prey) to be swallowed by the King of Death.

'This body is the abode of worms; it is filled with various kinds of impurities. This body is like a pot of excrement; it is a thing without essence, like the trunk of a banana tree.'

Hearing this song, he attained Paccekabodhi along with his sons. Others reaching the Noble stage through such means is also evidence. It is not surprising that five hundred monks attained Arahantship upon hearing the verses spoken by the Blessed One, who is skilled in the underlying tendencies (āsayānusaya), in the manner beginning with 'All formations are impermanent' (Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā), and many other devas and humans attained it upon hearing discourses related to the aggregates (khandha) and sense bases (āyatana). Thus, speech endowed with these four factors, even if it belongs to the Milakkha language or the song of a water-carrying servant girl, should be known as 'well-spoken' (subhāsita). Precisely because it is well-spoken, it is a faultless and blameless refuge for sons of good family who are wise, who desire the meaning, and who rely on the meaning rather than the phrasing.

'The Blessed One said this' means the Blessed One spoke this characteristic of well-spoken speech. 'Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this' means after speaking this characteristic, the Teacher spoke this other word as well. Wishing to show the verses to be spoken now, the reciters of the Council (Saṅgītikārakas) said all these words. There, 'aparaṃ' (further/another) is said with reference to the words composed in verse. That is of two kinds: it is a further explanation of the same meaning for the sake of those in the audience who arrived later and have not heard it, so they may hear it well, retain it, and be firm in it. Or, it is an explanation of a specific meaning by clarifying a meaning that was omitted earlier for some reason, as in the passage beginning with 'When a man is born, an axe is born in his mouth.' Here, however, it is a further explanation of the same meaning.

In that verse, 'santo' (the peaceful ones) refers to the virtuous ones such as the Buddhas. Those virtuous ones praise well-spoken speech as 'the highest, the best.' The words 'second, third, fourth' are spoken following the order previously indicated. At the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Vangīsa gained confidence in the well-spoken words of the Blessed One.

To show the manner in which the Elder expressed his confidence and the words spoken by the Blessed One, the reciters of the Council said the words beginning with 'Atha kho āyasmā' (Then the venerable...).
126:
In that verse, 'paṭibhāti maṃ' means 'it appears to my intellect' (it shines for me). 'Paṭibhātu taṃ' means 'let it appear to your intellect' (let it shine for you). 'Sāruppāhi' means 'with suitable words'. 'Abhitthavi' means 'he praised'.

'Na tāpaye' means one should not cause burning through remorse. 'Na vihiṃseyya' means one should not harm by causing division among one another. 'Sā ve vācā' means that speech is indeed well-spoken. With this much, he praises the Blessed One for speaking words free from slander.

'Paṭinanditā' means welcomed and cherished by going forward with a joyful heart. 'Yaṃ anādāya pāpāni, pareaṃ bhāsate piyaṃ' means that a person, when speaking, does not take up the unpleasant, disgusting, or harsh words of others, but speaks only pleasant words that are sweet in meaning and phrasing; it means one should speak only such pleasant speech. With this verse, he praises the Blessed One for speaking pleasant words.

'Amatā' means it is like the deathless ambrosia because of its sweetness. It is also said, "Truth is indeed the sweetest of all tastes." Alternatively, it is called 'amatā' because it is a cause for the deathless Nibbāna. 'Esa dhammo sanantano' means that which is called truthful speech is an ancient nature, practice, and lineage. This is indeed the habit of the ancients; they did not speak untruths. Therefore, it was said: "The virtuous are established in truth, in welfare, and in the Dhamma." In that statement, because they are established in truth, they are those who are established in the welfare of themselves and others. It should be understood that because they are established in welfare, they are those who are established in the Dhamma. Alternatively, the latter two terms should be understood merely as qualifiers of truth. They are established in truth. What kind of truth? Truth that is established in welfare and the Dhamma. It means speech that does not conflict with welfare because it is not divorced from the welfare of others. Even if it is non-conflicting, it means speech that accomplishes welfare in accordance with the Dhamma because it is not divorced from the Dhamma. With this verse, he praises the Blessed One for speaking truthful words.

'Khemaṃ' means secure and free from affliction. For what reason is it free from affliction? It is because of the attainment of Nibbāna and the making an end of suffering. It means that it leads to the quenching of defilements and to the making an end of the suffering of the round of rebirths. Alternatively, because the Buddha declares the secure path for the sake of the two Nibbāna elements—the attainment of Nibbāna and the making an end of suffering—he speaks secure speech. That speech is indeed the most excellent of all speeches.
127:
It should be understood that 'seṭṭhā' (most excellent) is the meaning in this context. While praising the Blessed One with this verse regarding truthful speech, he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship; this is the new word-commentary in this sutta. The rest should be understood according to the method already mentioned.

## The Commentary on the Subhāsita Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary,
## of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, is finished.
## 4. Commentary on the Pūraḷāsa Sutta (Sundarikabhāradvāja Sutta)

What is the origin (uppatti) of the Pūraḷāsa Sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ"? When the Blessed One was surveying the world with the Buddha-eye at the conclusion of his duties after the meal, he saw that the Brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for Arahantship. Knowing that "If I go there, a conversation will take place; then, at the end of the conversation, having heard the Dhamma teaching, this Brahmin will go forth and reach Arahantship," he went there, initiated a conversation, and spoke this sutta.

In that sutta, "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth are the words of the reciters (saṅgītikārakas). "Kiṃjacco bhavaṃ" and so forth are the words of that Brahmin. "Na brāhmaṇo nomhi" (I am not a Brahmin) and so forth are the words of the Blessed One. Combining all of these, it is called the "Pūraḷāsa Sutta." In this sutta, what is similar to what has been said before should be understood by the method already mentioned. I shall comment on what has not yet been said. In doing so, I will explain without touching upon words whose meanings are already clear.

"Kosalesu" refers to the princes who reside in the country named Kosala. A single district that is the dwelling place of those princes is also called "Kosala" by way of conventional designation (ruḷhī). It means in that Kosala country. Some teachers, however, explain it thus: "In the past, the King, having heard that Prince Mahāpanāda did not even smile upon seeing various dancers and performers, issued a decree: 'Whoever can make my son laugh, I shall adorn him with all manner of ornaments.' Then, a great multitude of people abandoned their plows and gathered together. Although those people showed various games and performances for over seven years, they were unable to make the prince laugh. Then, Sakka, the King of Gods, sent a celestial dancer. That celestial dancer showed a divine dance and made him laugh. Then, those people departed toward their respective dwellings. When they met friends and relatives on the way, they exchanged greetings: 'Friends, is it well? Friends...'"
128:
He commanded, saying, "I will adorn the celestial dancer." At that time, the people left their plows and gathered together. Although those people performed various types of entertainment for seven years, they were unable to make the prince laugh. Then, Sakka, the King of Devas, sent a celestial dancer, and that celestial dancer performed a divine dance and made him laugh. At that time, the people returned to their respective places. When they met their friends on the way, they spoke pleasant words, saying, "Friends, are you well (safe)? Are you free from illness?" Based on the sound of this word 'Kusala' (meaning safety or wellness), that region is called 'Kosala'—so it is explained.

'On the banks of the Sundarikā River' means on the bank of the river named Sundarikā.

'At that time' (Tena kho pana) refers to the time when the Blessed One, wishing to discipline that Brahmin, went and sat at the foot of a tree on the bank of that river, in a posture of sitting with his head covered.

'Sundarika Bhāradvāja' means that the Brahmin lived on the bank of that river and offered sacrifices to the fire; 'Bhāradvāja' was his clan (gotta), and therefore he was called so. 'He offers to the fire' (aggiṃ juhati) means he makes the fire blaze by throwing in oblations. 'He tends the sacred fire' (aggihuttaṃ paricarati) means he serves and attends to the fire-chamber by sweeping, plastering with clay, making offerings (bali), and so forth.

"Who shall eat these remains of the oblation?" means that after the Brahmin had offered to the fire, he saw the remaining milk-rice and thought: "The milk-rice first thrown into the fire has been consumed by the Great Brahmā, but these remains still exist. If I could offer these remains of the oblation only to a Brahmin born from the mouth of Brahmā, then by this offering, my ancestors as well as my son would be satisfied, and the path leading to the Brahma-world would be well-cleared. Now, I shall search for a Brahmin." Then, wishing to find a Brahmin, he rose from his seat and looked around the four directions, thinking, "Who shall eat these remains of the oblation?"

'At the foot of a certain tree' means at the foot of a noble tree in that forest grove. 'Covered including the head' means having the body wrapped together with the head. Why did the Blessed One do this? Was it because, despite having the strength known as Nārāyaṇa, he was unable to withstand the falling snow and the cold wind? There is a reason for doing this. Indeed, the Buddhas do not always attend to the grooming of their bodies. Rather, the Blessed One did this for the purpose of initiating a conversation, thinking, "When the Brahmin arrives, I will uncover my head. Upon seeing me, the Brahmin will start a conversation; then, following the course of his words, I will preach the Dhamma."

It is said that when the Brahmin saw the Blessed One, he approached with the perception that he was a Brahmin, thinking, "This person, having wrapped himself including his head, must be a Brahmin who has been practicing meditation all night; I shall give the libation water to this Brahmin and offer him these remains of the oblation." As soon as the Blessed One uncovered his head and the Brahmin saw the edge of the hair, he said, "This venerable one is shaven-headed; this venerable one is a mere shaven-headed one." Then, looking more closely and not seeing even a small top-knot (sikhā), he said, "Vile shaven-headed one..."
129:
Not seeing (a top-knot) and wishing to revile him, the Brahmin said, "Shaven-headed one." Such was the view of those Brahmins. "Or from there" (Tato vā) means from the place where he stood and saw; for some reason, there are also those with shaven heads.

In the phrase "Na brāhmaṇo nomhi," the letter "na" is in the sense of negation, and the word "no" is in the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), as in "na no samaṃ" and so forth. Therefore, he shows, "I am certainly not a Brahmin." "I am not a prince" means he is not a Khattiya. "I am not a merchant" means he is not a Vessa. "I am not anyone else" means he is not a Sudda, a Caṇḍāla, or anyone else; in this way, he definitively rejects the discourse on birth (caste). Why? Just as rivers that reach the great ocean give up their former names and clans, so too do clansmen who have gone forth into homelessness give up their former names and clans. The Pahārāda Sutta is the evidence in this matter. Having thus rejected the discourse on birth and wishing to reveal himself as he truly is, he said: "Having understood the lineage of worldlings, I wander the world with wisdom, without possessions."

How did he understand the lineage? The Blessed One understood the five aggregates through the three types of full understanding (pariññā); when those aggregates are fully understood, the lineage is already fully understood. Due to the absence of possessions such as lust (rāga), the Blessed One is called "akiñcana" (one without possessions). Having known with wisdom, he conducts himself with bodily actions and so forth that follow knowledge. Therefore, he said: "Having understood the lineage... in the world." What is called "mantā" is indeed wisdom; he conducts himself with that wisdom. For that reason, making it short (rassam) by the power of meter, he said: "Mantā carāmi loke" (I wander the world with wisdom).

459-60. Having thus revealed himself, now wishing to bring a rebuke upon the Brahmin, thinking, "Do you not know what should and should not be asked even after seeing such a clear appearance?", he said: "Wearing the outer robe... (why do you ask) the question of lineage?" Here, because of the sense of being cut and sewn together, all three robes are intended by the word "saṅghāṭi"; because he wears those robes, he is called "saṅghāṭivāsī." "Agaha" means being without a house, meaning being without craving. As for the Blessed One's dwelling places, there were many in Jeta's Grove, such as the Mahāgandhakuṭi, Karerimaṇḍalamāḷa, Kosambakuṭi, Candanamālā, and so forth; it is not appropriate to say "without a house" with reference to those dwellings. "Nivuttakeso" means having the hair and beard removed. "Abhinibbutatto" means having a mind that is exceedingly tranquil or a mind that is well-guarded. "Alippamāno idha māṇavehi" means being unattached to requisites and thus not mixing with people, being absolutely secluded. The Blessed One said: "Brahmin, while I am one who wears the robes... and is unattached (not mixing), why do you ask a question about name and lineage which is unsuitable for one who is a monk?"
130:
## 
"While I live thus, wearing the saṅghāṭi, with hair removed, with a very peaceful mind, not mixing with youths in this world, O Brahmin... why do you ask me, who have gone forth, an improper question of lineage and ordinary names and clans?" When this was said, the Brahmin, wishing to free himself from the reproach, said: "Venerable sir, when Brahmins meet with other Brahmins, they are accustomed to ask, 'Is the venerable one a Brahmin? Is the venerable one of the Bhāradvāja clan?' Thus they ask about both birth and clan."

461-2. When this was said, the Blessed One, in order to soften the Brahmin's heart and to demonstrate his own expertise in the Vedas, said: "If you say, 'I am a Brahmin,' and you say of me that I am not a Brahmin, then I ask you about the Sāvittī which has three lines and twenty-four syllables; tell that Sāvittī to me." In this context, the Blessed One is asking with reference to the Noble Sāvittī, which is the beginning of the three Piṭakas—the ultimate Vedas—proclaimed by all the Buddhas who are the ultimate Brahmins, and which is perfect in meaning and phrasing: "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, Saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." Even if the Brahmin had spoken of something else, the Blessed One would have shown the worthlessness of that Veda by saying, "Brahmin, this is not called the Sāvittī in the Noble Discipline," and would have established him in this Dispensation. However, the Brahmin, upon hearing the words uttered with a Brahma-voice, which indicated the characteristics of the Sāvittī established in his own tradition—"I ask about the Sāvittī of three lines and twenty-four syllables"—concluded: "Surely this ascetic has reached the goal in the Brahmin tradition. Out of ignorance, I looked down on him, thinking 'This man is not a Brahmin.' This is indeed a true Brahmin of good nature who has reached the end of the Vedas." Having reached this conclusion, he thought, "Now I shall ask him about the procedure of sacrifice and the procedure regarding those worthy of offerings." Wishing to ask about that matter, he spoke this verse: "Depending on what, desiring what, longing for what, do sages, kings, Brahmins, and other men in this world prepare many sacrifices for the sake of the gods?"

The meaning of that verse is: For what benefit do sages, kings, Brahmins, and other men perform sacrifices for the gods? 'Akappayiṃsu' means they prepared or performed. 'Puthū' means many, in various ways such as giving food, drink, and so on. Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer that matter, spoke the remaining two lines of the verse. In that verse, in the word 'yedantagū', it should be split as 'ye antagū'. Here, the letter 'd' is inserted for euphonic junction. The meaning is: That person is called 'antagū' because he has reached the end of suffering. He is called 'vedagū' because he has known and transcended the defilements through the Vedas, which are the path-knowledges. Such a person, at the time of sacrifice of any sage, man, king, or Brahmin...
131:
## 
"Depending on what did they prepare the sacrifice? How does that action of theirs succeed?"—he asks with this intention.

Then the Blessed One, answering that matter, spoke these remaining two lines: "At the time of sacrifice, if an antagū and vedagū should receive someone's offering, I say that his sacrifice succeeds." Among those words, "yadantagū" should be analyzed as "ye antagū"; the letter 'e' is changed to 'a', and the letter 'd' is merely a euphonic junction, like the letter 'm' in passages such as "asādhāraṇamaññesaṃ". This is the meaning: He is an "antagū" because he has reached the end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) through the three full understandings (pariññā). He is a "vedagū" because he has gone having pierced the defilements with the four Vedas of path-knowledge (magganyāṇa). If such a person, at the time of sacrifice of any sage, man, king, or Brahmin, when any food is present, should receive an offering even of forest leaves, roots, or fruits—if he should receive any gift—then that sacrificial act of his would succeed, it would be successful, it would be of great fruit; so I say.

Then the Brahmin, having heard that teaching of the Blessed One which was profound regarding the ultimate union, and endowed with an extremely sweet and unchanging voice, and appreciating the perfection of all virtues indicated by the perfection of his physical body, became filled with joy and happiness and spoke the verse beginning with "Addhā hi tassa". In that verse, the words "iti brāhmaṇo" are the words of the redactors (saṅgītikāras), and the rest are the words of the Brahmin. The meaning is: "Indeed, that offering of mine will succeed; today this gift will succeed, it will be fully successful and of great fruit, because I have seen such a vedagū, because I have seen a vedagū of such a nature as the venerable one. For you alone are that vedagū, no one else. Previously, however, not seeing such vedagūs and antagūs like you, other people alone ate the milk-rice, cooked rice, and cakes prepared for the sacrifices of people like us."

Then the Blessed One, knowing the Brahmin to be confident in him and ready to receive his words, and wishing to reveal the ones worthy of offerings in various ways so that they would be clearly manifest to him, spoke the verse beginning with "Tasmātiha tvaṃ". The meaning is: "Because you have faith in me, therefore, Brahmin, approach and ask here," he said, indicating himself. Now, from here on, the word "atthika" (seeker) should be connected with the word "attha" (benefit) and the subsequent words. You, who are a seeker of benefit, in a manner appropriate to that state of seeking benefit, [approach the one who is] peaceful (santa) through the quenching of the fire of defilements, and smokeless (vidhūma) through the disappearance of the smoke of anger...
132:
Because of the absence of suffering, he is called 'Anīgha' (free from suffering); because of the absence of various kinds of longing, he is called 'Nirāsa' (free from desire). Indeed, whether staying in this place or within this Dispensation, one will obtain, find, and attain the one of noble wisdom, whose taints are destroyed, and who is worthy of offerings. Alternatively, [the Buddha] spoke showing himself, saying: 'Brahmin, since you have faith in me, being one who desires benefit, approach and ask me—the one who is peaceful, smokeless, free from suffering, and free from desire.' It should be understood that the connection (yojanā) here is: 'By asking thus, one will indeed find in this Dispensation the one of noble wisdom, whose taints are destroyed, and who is worthy of offerings.'

Then the Brahmin, practicing according to the instruction, addressed the Blessed One: 'I delight in sacrifice... tell this to me.' In this context, sacrifice (yañña), offering (yāga), and giving (dāna) are identical in meaning. Therefore, [he meant]: 'I delight in giving; because of that delight in giving, I wish to give, but I do not know [how]. Please, Bhante, instruct me who does not know. And while instructing, tell me in a clear manner in whom an offering becomes successful.' Thus the connection of meaning should be understood here. There is also a variant reading 'yathāhutaṃ'.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to speak to that Brahmin, said: 'In that case... I shall preach.' For the benefit of instructing that Brahmin who was ready to listen, he first spoke the verse: 'Do not ask about birth.' In that context, 'Do not ask about birth' means: if you desire the fulfillment of the sacrifice and the great fruit of the gift, do not ask about birth. For birth is not the cause for investigating one worthy of offerings. 'Ask about conduct' (caraṇa) means: rather, ask about conduct characterized by virtues such as morality (sīla). This conduct alone is the cause for investigating one worthy of offerings.

Now, wishing to clarify that matter, he spoke the illustration beginning with: 'Fire is indeed born from wood.' The meaning there is: in this world, fire is born from wood. That fire does not perform the function of fire only when born from wood such as Sal; nor does it fail to do so when born from wood such as a water-ladle. Rather, it performs the function of fire simply because it is endowed with qualities such as flames. Similarly, one does not become worthy of offerings merely by being born in a Brahmin family and so forth; nor does one fail to be so by being born in a Caṇḍāla family and so forth. Rather, whether of low birth or high birth, a sage (muni) whose taints are destroyed, who is steadfast (dhiti) and who restrains [evil] through shame (hiri), is a person of noble breeding (ājāniya). Being endowed with such qualities as steadfastness and shame, he is one of noble birth and a supreme person worthy of offerings. He maintains virtues through steadfastness and restrains faults through shame. It is also said: 'The virtuous do not commit evil because of shame.' Therefore, I say to you—
133:
“Do not ask about birth, but ask about conduct. Just as fire is truly produced from wood, so a sage, though of low birth, who is steadfast and restrains [evil] through shame, is a person of noble breeding.” This is the summary; the detail should be understood according to the Assalāyana Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya).

Thus, the Blessed One, having instructed on the purity of the four castes, now spoke the verse beginning with 'Saccena danto' (tamed by truth) to show in whom an offering becomes successful and how it becomes successful. In that verse, 'Saccena' means by the ultimate truth (paramattha-sacca). One who has reached that ultimate truth is tamed. Therefore, he said: 'Saccena danto'. 'Damasā upeto' means endowed with the restraint of the senses. 'Vedantagū' means one who has reached the end of defilements through the Vedas (knowledges), or one who has reached the fourth path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), which is the end of the Vedas. 'Vūsita-brahmacariyo' means one who has lived the holy life of the path, because there is nothing further to be lived. 'Kālena tamhi habyaṃ pavecche' means, having noted the time when one's gift is ready and the time when the recipient is present, at that time one should offer, present, or provide the gift to such a person worthy of offerings.

469-71. 'Kāme' refers to both the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and the defilement of sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'Susamāhitindriyā' means those with well-composed faculties, meaning undistracted faculties. 'Candova rāhuggahaṇā pamuttā' means those who, like the moon released from the grasp of Rahu, are liberated from the grasp of defilements and shine and glow exceedingly. 'Satā' means those endowed with mindfulness. 'Mamāyitāni' refers to things possessed as 'mine' through craving and views.

From the phrase 'Yo kāme hitvā' onwards, the Blessed One speaks referring to himself. There, 'kāme hitvā' means having abandoned the defilements of sensuality. 'Abhibhuyyacārī' means, because of having abandoned those defilements, he lives having overcome the objects of sensuality. The end of birth and death is called Nibbāna, and he has known that through the power of his own wisdom. 'Udakarahado vā' refers to the seven great lakes in the Himalayas: Lake Anotatta, Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Lake Rathakāra, Lake Chaddanta, Lake Kuṇāla, Lake Mandākinī, and Lake Sīhappapāta, which [are not dried up] by the heat of fire and the sun...
134:
The seven great lakes in the Himavant are always cool because they are not touched by the heat of the sun or fire. Just as any one of those lakes is cool, the Blessed One is also cool (tranquil), as the fever of defilements has been extinguished. 'Sammo' means being equal. 'Samehi' means being equal to Buddhas such as Vipassī. These Buddhas are called 'Samā' (equals) because they are equal in their penetration (paṭivedha). There is no difference among those Buddhas in the qualities to be attained through penetration, nor in the faults to be abandoned. However, there is variation among those Buddhas in terms of duration, lifespan, clan, physical stature, renunciation, exertion, the tree of enlightenment, and radiance.

Indeed, at the lower limit, those Buddhas fulfill the perfections for four incalculable periods (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappa). At the upper limit, they fulfill the perfections for sixteen incalculable periods and a hundred thousand aeons. This is their variation in duration (addhāna-vemattatā). At the lower limit, they are born during a time when the human lifespan is one hundred years. At the upper limit, they are born during a time when the human lifespan is one hundred thousand years. This is their variation in lifespan (āyu-vemattatā). They are born either in the Khattiya clan or the Brāhmaṇa clan. This is their variation in clan (kula-vemattatā). Those Buddhas who are tall are eighty-eight cubits in stature. Those who are short are fifteen or eighteen cubits in stature. This is their variation in physical stature (pamāṇa-vemattatā).

They renounce the world by means of elephants, horses, chariots, palanquins, and so forth, or through the air. Indeed, the Buddhas Vipassī and Kakusandha renounced the world by horse-chariot. The Buddhas Sikhī and Koṇāgamana renounced on the back of an elephant. The Buddha Vessabhū renounced by palanquin. The Buddha Kassapa renounced through the air. The Buddha Sakyamuni renounced on horseback. This is their variation in renunciation (nekkhamma-vemattatā). They practice exertion for seven days, or for half a month, one month, two months, three months, four months, five months, six months, one year, or for two, three, four, five, or six years. This is their variation in exertion (padhāna-vemattatā). The tree of enlightenment is either the Assattha tree or one of the other trees such as the Nigrodha. This is their variation in the tree of enlightenment (bodhi-vemattatā).

They are endowed with a radiance of one fathom, a radiance of eighty cubits, or infinite radiance. Among these, the radiance of one fathom or the radiance of eighty cubits is common to all Buddhas. However, the infinite radiance goes to a far distance or a near distance—one gāvuta, two gāvutas, one league (yojana), many leagues, or even to the edge of the world system. The bodily radiance of the Buddha Maṅgala spread throughout ten thousand world systems. Even so, for all Buddhas, it depends only on the thought of the mind. Whatever extent a Buddha desires, his radiance goes to that extent. This is their variation in radiance (rasmi-vemattatā). Except for these eight variations, there is no difference among those Buddhas in the remaining qualities to be attained through penetration or in the faults to be abandoned. Therefore, they are called 'Samā' (equals). Thus, he is equal to those who are equal.
135:
'He is far from those who are unequal' means those who are not equal, namely, Paccekabuddhas and all other remaining beings. He is far from those unequal ones by way of being dissimilar. Even if Paccekabuddhas, sitting cross-legged and touching knee to knee, were to fill the entire Jambudīpa, they would not be worth a sixteenth part of the qualities of a single Fully Enlightened Buddha; what then to say of disciples and others? Therefore, it is said, 'Far from those who are unequal.' The term 'Tathāgato' should be connected with the term 'is far' in both instances. 'Anantapañño' means having infinite wisdom. For, in comparison to the wisdom of worldly people, the wisdom of one on the path (maggaṭṭhāna) is superior; in comparison to his wisdom, the wisdom of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is superior. In this way, up to the wisdom of an Arahant, the wisdom of a Paccekabuddha is superior. However, it should not be said that the wisdom of the Tathāgata is superior in comparison to the wisdom of a Paccekabuddha; rather, it should simply be said that it is infinite. Therefore, it is said, 'Anantapañño.' 'Anūpalitto' means being unstained by the stains of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). 'Idha vā huraṃ vā' means in this world or in the next world. The connection (yojanā) here is: The Tathāgata is equal to the Buddhas who are equal and is far from those who are unequal. Why? Because the Buddha who possesses infinite wisdom and is unstained by craving and views exists in this world or in the next world; therefore, the Tathāgata deserves the sacrificial offering (pūraḷāsa).

This verse beginning with 'Yamhi na māyā' and other similar verses should be understood as spoken to remove the perception of being 'worthy of offerings' in Brahmins who are possessed of faults such as deceit (māyā). In that verse, 'amamo' means the state of having abandoned the sense of 'this is mine' regarding beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra). 'Nivesanaṃ' means the settling of the mind through craving and views. For by those two, the mind settles firmly in the three realms of existence; therefore, that settling is called 'the dwelling place of the mind.' Or, it settles firmly in those three realms because of the inability to leave that existence; for that reason also, it is called 'nivesanaṃ.' 'Pariggahā' are simply craving and views, or the things grasped by those two. 'Keci' means there are not even a few such things. 'Anupādiyāno' means not clinging to any phenomenon because of the absence of those dwellings and attachments. He is well-concentrated by means of the Path-concentration (magga-samādhi). 'Udatārī' means he has crossed over. 'Dhammaṃ caññāsī' means he has known all knowable things (ñeyya-dhamma). 'Paramāya diṭṭhiyā' means by means of the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).
136:
"Bhavāsava" refers to the craving for existence (bhavataṇhā), the attachment to jhāna (nikanti), and the lust (rāga) that is accompanied by the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). "Vacī" means speech. "Kharā" refers to harsh and rough speech (pharusavācā). "Vidhūpita" means burnt or destroyed. "Atthagata" means gone to cessation. Because they are burnt and have gone to cessation, they no longer exist. Both terms should be applied to both meanings. "Sabbadhī" means in all aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and so forth.

"Mānasattesu" means among beings who are stuck due to conceit (māna). "Dukkhaṃ pariññāya" means having fully understood the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭadukkha) through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). "Sakhettavatthu" means together with causes and conditions, along with kamma and defilements (kilesa).

"Āsaṃ anissāya" means without relying on or clinging to craving (taṇhā). "Vivekadassī" means one who is accustomed to seeing Nibbāna (seclusion). "Paravediyaṃ" means that which is to be made known by others. "Diṭṭhimupātivatto" means one who has transcended all sixty-two types of wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). "Ārammaṇa" means causes, specifically the causes for renewed existence.

"Paroparā" refers to noble and ignoble states, or good and bad states. Alternatively, "parā" refers to external states and "aparā" refers to internal states. "Samecca" means having penetrated with knowledge (ñāṇa). "Dhamma" refers to phenomena such as the aggregates and sense bases. "Upādānakhaye vimutto" means one who is liberated from defilements in Nibbāna by taking Nibbāna as the object; it means one who has attained the liberation that has Nibbāna as its object.

"Saṃyojanañjātikhayantadassī" means one who sees the end of the destruction of fetters and the end of the destruction of birth. In this context, the "end of the destruction of fetters" refers to the Nibbāna element with residue (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu), and the "end of the destruction of birth" refers to the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). "Khayanta" is a designation for absolute destruction, which is abandonment by eradication (samucchedappahāna). Here, the elision of the nasal (anunāsikalopa) is not performed as it is in phrases like "vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ." "Yopānudī" means he who has dispelled. "Rāgapatha" refers to the object of lust or lust itself. Lust is also called "rāgapatha" because it is a path to woeful states, similar to "kammapatha" (path of action). "Suddho, nidoso, vimalo, akāco": He is "suddho" (pure) because he is endowed with pure bodily conduct and so forth. Beings are called "those with the fault of lust, the fault of hatred, and the fault of delusion" because of certain faults; because he lacks those faults, he is "nidoso" (faultless). He is "vimalo" (stainless) because he is free from the stains of the eight types of noble persons. He is "akāco" (flawless) because of the absence of corruptions (upakkilesa). Indeed, one who is corrupted is called "sakāca" (flawed) due to corruptions. Alternatively, he is "suddho" because he is faultless; being faultless, he is "vimalo" (stainless); being stainless due to the absence of external stains, he is "akāco" (flawless). One who has stains (samalo)...
137:
...a person with stains is called 'sakāca'. Alternatively, because he is stainless, he does not commit evil, and thus he is 'akāca'. The act of committing evil is called 'kāca' because it causes harm (upaghāta).

'Does not see a self in himself' means that a person practicing insight (vipassanā) with a mind associated with knowledge does not see any other thing called a 'self' within his own aggregates; he sees only the aggregates. The view 'I know myself by myself' might arise as if it were true and stable; because of the absence of that view, he does not see a self in himself, but rather sees the aggregates with wisdom. He is concentrated by path-concentration (magga-samādhi). He has reached uprightness (ujjugato) because of the absence of crookedness of body, etc. He is steadfast (ṭhitatto) because he is unshakable by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). He is 'anejo' (unshaken), 'akhilo' (free from barrenness), and 'akankho' (free from doubt) because of the absence of the shaking called craving (taṇhā), the five mental barrennesses (cetokhila), and the eight types of doubt.

'Mohandharā' means because of delusion, or having delusion as a condition; it is a term for all defilements. 'Knower and seer of all things' means one who has realized Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). That knowledge exists regarding all things, and the Blessed One saw that knowledge and lived having realized it, thinking 'I have attained it.' Thus, he is called 'knower and seer of all things.' 'Sambodhi' refers to the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). 'Anuttaraṃ' (unsurpassed) means it is not shared with Paccekabuddhas or disciples. 'Sivaṃ' means peaceful, free from danger, or auspicious. 'Yakkhassa' means of the man (the person). 'Suddhī' means the state of purity. Here, the absence of the darkness of delusion means the absence of all faults; thereby, the cause of Saṃsāra is cut off, and he bears his final body. Because of being a knower and seer, he is endowed with all virtues. Thus, he has attained the unsurpassed Enlightenment, and there is no further dhamma to be abandoned or realized. Therefore, it is said: 'To this extent is the purity of the Yakkha (the person).'

When this was said, the Brahmin was exceedingly pleased with the Blessed One. Wanting to show his devotion, he said: 'Hutañca mayhaṃ' (And my sacrifice...). The meaning of that verse is: 'I do not know whether the sacrifices I made in the past to the Brahmās in the fire were true or false. But now, let this sacrifice of mine be true; let it be a true sacrifice,' he says as a request. 'I have found such a Knower of the Vedas (vedagū); staying right here, I have found a Knower of the Vedas like you. You are indeed Brahmā in person; therefore, let the Blessed One accept my milk-rice; accept and consume it,' he said, wishing to offer it. Then, the Blessed One taught the verses in the manner described in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Then the Brahmin thought, 'This Venerable Gotama does not desire it, neither this milk-rice nor for the sake of another person, among all those worthy of offerings, he who has virtues such as being a Great Sage (Mahesi)...'
138:
Offering the remains of the sacrificial oblation, he said, "May the Blessed One accept and partake of my sacrificial offering."

Then the Blessed One spoke two verses in the same manner as taught in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta. Then the brahmin, not grasping the meaning of the verses, thought: "This Venerable Gotama does not desire [the food] for himself, but referring to someone else, he says, 'Serve with food and drink one who is perfect in all qualities, a great seer, one whose taints are destroyed, and whose remorse is stilled.'" Desiring to know the reason, he said, "It is well, Blessed One."

In that context, 'Sādhu' is a particle in the sense of request. 'Tathā' means in that manner, as you have said. 'Vijaññaṃ' means I would like to know. 'Yaṃ' implies the remaining words: "whom should I seek out and serve as a recipient of offerings at the time of sacrifice?" 'Pappuyya' means having reached. 'Tava sāsanaṃ' means your instruction. This is what is meant: "It is well, Blessed One; relying on your instruction, I would like to know such a recipient of offerings; please tell me who that perfect one is." He means: "If you do not partake, then point out to me such a worthy recipient who should partake of the offering of one like me, whom I should seek out and serve at the time of sacrifice."

488-90. Then the Blessed One, wishing to point out such a worthy recipient in a clear manner, spoke the three verses beginning with "Sārambhā yassa." In those verses, 'sīmantānaṃ vinetāraṃ' means: 'sīmā' is the boundary of the conduct of virtuous people; the end or subsequent part of that boundary is called 'sīmanta,' which refers to the defilements; thus it means one who removes those defilements. Some say 'sīmanta' refers to those to be trained by the Buddha, both trainees (sekhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas), and it means one who trains them. 'Jātimaraṇakovidaṃ' means one who is skilled in [understanding] "such is birth, such is death." 'Moneyyasampannaṃ' means one endowed with wisdom, or one endowed with the 'sagehood' of body, etc. 'Bhakuṭiṃ vinayitvāna' means that some unwise people frown when they see a seeker; having removed that frowning and having a clear face is the meaning. 'Pañjalikā' means those who have raised their hands in salutation.

Then the brahmin, wishing to praise the Blessed One, spoke the verse beginning with "Buddho bhavaṃ." In that verse, 'āyāgo' means one who should be repeatedly worshipped, or it is called 'āyāga' because one comes from various places to worship this Blessed One; it means one who is the basis for gifts. Words not explained in this sutta or in the preceding verses are not explained because their meaning is clear and can be easily understood. From here on, it should be understood in the same way as stated in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

The explanation of the Puraḷāsa Sutta in the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha and Suttanipāta, is finished.

Māgha Sutta. This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Māgha Sutta. The origin is the same as stated in this prologue. Specifically, the youth named Māgha was a donor who loved to give. To those guests, travelers, etc., who came to him...
139:
(It means one who should be repeatedly worshipped, or one who should be worshipped here by those coming from various places; thus he is called 'āyāga' because he is the basis for gifts.) In this sutta and in the verses prior to this, whatever words were not explained were left unexplained because their meaning is obvious and can be understood even without explanation. From here on, it should be understood in the same way as stated in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta.

## The Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha named Paramatthajotikā
## The Explanation of the Puraḷāsa Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Māgha Sutta
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" etc. is the Māgha Sutta. What is its origin? It is exactly as stated in the prologue of this sutta. This youth named Māgha was a donor, a master of giving. The thought occurred to him: "Is the gift given to those who have arrived, such as the poor, travelers, etc., of great fruit or not? I will ask the ascetic Gotama about this matter, for it is said that the ascetic Gotama knows the past, future, and present." He approached the Blessed One and asked. And the Blessed One answered him according to his question. This sutta is called the "Māgha Sutta," combining the words of the reciters, the brahmin youth, and the Blessed One.

In that sutta, "Rājagahe" refers to the city of that name. It is called "Rājagaha" because it was possessed and ruled by kings such as Mandhātu and Mahāgovinda. Other teachers explain it in various other ways. What is the use of those [explanations]? It is simply the name of that city. This city exists as a city during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch); at other times, it is empty, possessed by yakkhas, and remains as their forest dwelling. Having thus shown the resort village (gocara-gāma), he stated the place of residence: "Gijjhakūṭe pabbate" (on the Vulture Peak Mountain). It should be known that it is called "Gijjhakūṭa" because vultures lived on its peaks, or because its peaks are like vultures.

In the words beginning with "Atha kho," "Māgha" is the name of that brahmin. He is called "māṇavo" (youth) because he has not yet passed the stage of living as a resident pupil, though by birth he was elderly. Some say that, like the youth Piṅgiya, he was called "māṇavo" by force of old habit. Indeed, even though Piṅgiya was a hundred and twenty years old, he was known as "Piṅgiya Māṇava" by force of old habit. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
140:
“Venerable Gotama, I... produce [merit].” In this context, “dāyaka dānapati” means both a donor and a lord of alms. This is because one who gives another's property by their command is also called a dāyaka (donor), but since they lack ownership over that gift, they are not a dānapati (lord of alms). This Māgha the young man, however, gives only his own property. Therefore, he says, “Venerable Gotama, I am a donor and a lord of alms.” This is the only correct meaning here. In other contexts, however, one who is occasionally overcome by stinginess is called a dāyaka, while one who is not overcome by stinginess is called a dānapati; it is also appropriate to speak in this manner.

“Vadanyū” means knowing the words of petitioners, or it means being charitable by discerning specific individuals, such as “This person deserves this, that person deserves that,” or by grasping the state of being of great benefit. “Yācayoga” means being fit to be asked. One who, upon seeing petitioners, frowns and speaks harsh words, etc., is not yācayoga. He shows that he himself is not such a person. “Dhammena” (righteously) means seeking through begging, like collecting alms-food, while avoiding taking what is not given, deceit, and fraud. For Brahmins, begging is the righteous way (dhamma) of seeking wealth. The wealth given to those begging Brahmins by others who wish to support them is called “righteously obtained” (dhammaladdha) and “righteously acquired” (dhammādhigata). That Māgha the young man also sought and obtained wealth in that way. Therefore, it is said, “I seek wealth righteously... with wealth righteously acquired.” “Bhiyyopi dadāmi” means I give even more than that, without limit; here it shows that he gives according to the amount of wealth he has obtained.

“Taggha” is an indeclinable particle meaning “certainly.” Indeed, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples certainly praise a gift given even to animals. It has been said, “Giving is praised everywhere; giving is never blamed anywhere.” Therefore, the Blessed One also, wishing to certainly praise that gift, said, “Young man, you certainly... produce [merit].” The remaining words have clear meanings. Although the Blessed One said, “He produces much merit,” the Brahmin Māgha, wishing to hear about the purity of the offering through the power of the recipient (dakkhiṇeyya), asked the Blessed One further. Therefore, the Reciters (Saṅgītikāras) said, “Then Māgha the young man addressed the Blessed One with a verse.” Its meaning is the same as the method already mentioned.

In the verses beginning with “Pucchāmahaṃ,” “vadanyū” means one who knows words, meaning one who knows the intentions of the words spoken by beings in every way. “Sujjhe” means it would be pure or of great fruit through the power of the recipient. The construction (yojanā) in this verse is: One who is fit to be asked...
141:
A householder who is a lord of alms, being one who desires merit, gives and sacrifices food, drink, and refreshments to others, not merely by throwing offerings into the fire. Such a sacrifice is made by looking only to merit, without looking for reciprocal favors, good reputation, fame, and so on. For such a person who sacrifices, how can the sacrifice (offering) be purified (be of great fruit)? “Ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyyebhi tādī” means such a donor who is accessible to petitioners should honor the noble recipients (dakkhiṇeyya); they should fulfill and purify (that gift). They should make that sacrifice one of great fruit, and not otherwise. By this, the question of Māgha the young man, “How is the sacrifice purified for the one who sacrifices?” is answered. In the phrase “Akkhāhi me bhagavā dakkhiṇeyye,” the construction should be understood as: “Venerable Sir, tell me of the noble recipients for me, who gives and sacrifices to others.”

Then the Blessed One, wishing to reveal the noble recipients through various methods, spoke the verses beginning with “Ye ve asattā.” In those verses, “asattā” means those who are not attached by way of attachments such as passion (rāga). “Kevalino” means those who have completed their task (Arahants). “Yatattā” means those with guarded minds.

496-7. Those who are tamed (dantā) by the supreme taming, those who are liberated (vimuttā) by the liberation of wisdom and mind, those who are painless (anīghā) due to the absence of suffering in the future rounds of rebirth, and those who are desireless (nirāsā) due to the absence of defilements at present. The second verse of this stanza should be understood as being spoken by way of revealing the power of meditative development (bhāvanā). “Monks, for a monk who dwells devoted to meditative development, even if such a wish does not arise: ‘O, may my mind be liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging,’ yet his mind is liberated from the taints without clinging.” This Sutta is the evidence here.

498-502. “Rāgañca... yesu na māyā... na taṇhāsu upātipannā” refers to those who have no involvement or clinging to sensual craving and so on. “Vitareyya” means having crossed over. “Taṇhā” (craving) is of six kinds, such as craving for forms. “Bhavābhavāya” means for eternalism or for annihilationism, or otherwise, for the non-existence of becoming, or for the sake of rebirth in a new existence. The phrase “idha vā huraṃ vā” (here or elsewhere) is an elaboration of the term “kuhiñci loke” (anywhere in the world).
142:
"Ye vītarāgā... pe... samitāvino" means those whose defilements are stilled, or those who are habituated to stilling defilements. Because their defilements are stilled, those who are free from lust (vītarāga) are without anger. "Idha vippahāya" means having abandoned the aggregates (khandhas) currently existing in this world, there is no going elsewhere from there. After this verse, some teachers also recite this verse: "Those who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, wander homeless, being well-restrained in body, are as straight as a shuttle."

506-8. "Jahitvā" means having abandoned. There is also a reading "jahitvānā," which has the same meaning of abandoning. "Attadīpā" refers to the Arahants who wander making their own virtues their island (refuge). In the phrase "ye hettha," the letter "ha" is a particle (nipāta) used merely to complete the verse. The meaning here is: those who know the nature of these aggregates, sense bases (āyatanas), etc., as they truly are; knowing them through the power of impermanence (anicca), etc., they truly understand their nature. "This is our final birth; now there is no more rebirth"—thus they know.

"Yo vedagū": The Blessed One now spoke this verse referring to himself. In that verse, "satimā" means one endowed with constant mindfulness (chasatata-vihāra-sati). "Sambodhipatto" means one who has reached omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). "Saraṇaṃ bahūnaṃ" means one who is the refuge for many devas and humans by dispelling dangers and harms.

Hearing about the worthy recipients (dakkhiṇeyya) in this way, the young Brahmin Māgha, being delighted, said: "Indeed, Your words are not in vain." In that statement, "You know everything in this world that should be known (ñeyya-dhamma) as it truly is" means that whatever the nature of a phenomenon is, You know it exactly as it is. This is because the Dhamma-element (dhamma-dhātu) is well-penetrated by You. Because it is well-penetrated, whatever Dhamma You wish to know, You know that knowable thing.

Thus, having praised the Blessed One and knowing the perfection of the sacrifice through the perfection of the recipient, the Brahmin, wishing to hear about the perfection of the sacrifice consisting of six factors through the perfection of the donor (dāyaka-sampadā), asked the further question starting with "Yo yācayogo." The connection in that verse is: "The donor who gives an offering worthy of those fit to be asked, gives to others; O Blessed One, please tell me the perfection of that donor's sacrifice."
143:
Then the Blessed One explained to the young man Māgha with two verses. The connection of the meaning in those verses is as follows: Māgha, perform the sacrifice. While sacrificing, make the mind very clear in all three times. Thus, your sacrifice will be: "One should be glad even before giving, one should clarify the mind while giving, and one should be delighted after giving; this is the perfection of the sacrifice." It will be a sacrifice endowed with the perfection of sacrifice as taught.

In that regard, there might be a question: "How should the mind be clarified?" It should be clarified by abandoning faults (dosa). How does the abandonment of faults occur? It occurs by taking the sacrifice as the object (ārammaṇa). For the one performing the sacrifice, this sacrifice is the object, and by being established in that object, one abandons faults. For the one who gives with a mind that has loving-kindness (mettā) foremost towards beings and has the darkness of delusion (moha) dispelled by the lamp of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi), the sacrifice known as the gift (deyya-dhamma) becomes the object. Being established in the occurrence of that object in this sacrifice, one abandons greed (lobha) caused by the gift, anger (kodha) caused by the recipient, and delusion (moha) which is the root of both; thus one abandons the three types of faults.

That person, being thus free from lust for possessions and removing anger towards beings, with the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) abandoned by that very removal of anger, gradually develops boundless loving-kindness (mettā) by pervading immeasurable beings or by pervading a single being without remainder, through the distinctions of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā). Then, for the sake of the abundance of meditation, being diligent in all postures day and night without interruption, he pervades all directions with that very state known as metta-jhāna, [developing] the immeasurable (appamaññā).

Then the Brahmin Māgha, not knowing that this mettā is "the path to the Brahma-world" (brahmaloka-magga), and hearing about the development of mettā which was beyond his own sphere, developed an even greater sense of reverence for the Blessed One's omniscience. Since he himself was inclined towards the Brahma-world and regarded reaching the Brahma-world as purity and liberation, wishing to ask about the path to the Brahma-world, he spoke the verse beginning with "Ko sujjhati" (Who is purified?). In that verse, referring to one who performs merit leading to the Brahma-world, he asked, "Who is purified? Who is released?" and referring to one who does not perform it, "Who is bound?" "Kenattanā" means by what cause. "Sakkhi brahmajja diṭṭho" means today Brahma has been seen face-to-face. "Saccaṃ" is an oath made with great respect, focusing on the Blessed One's Brahma-like qualities. "How does one reach [it]?" he asked again with great respect. "Jutimā" is an address to the Blessed One.

In that context, if a monk, by developing mettā, produces the third or fourth jhāna and, using that metta-jhāna as a basis, develops insight (vipassanā), he reaches the fruit of Arahantship and is thus purified from the stains of defilements and released from coming to the Brahma-world. Such a person no longer goes to the Brahma-world. However, if a monk produces metta-jhāna and finds delight in the peace of that meditative attainment, he is bound by the jhāna. If he does not fall away from that jhāna, he reaches the Brahma-world by that very jhāna. Therefore, the Blessed One, not permitting the journey to the Brahma-world for the monk who is purified from defilements and released from coming to the Brahma-world, but wishing to show how a person bound by delight in jhāna reaches the Brahma-world by that jhāna, spoke this verse beginning with "Ko sujjhati" in a manner suitable for the Brahmin Māgha. In that verse, "tividhaṃ" (threefold) is spoken in reference to the clarity in the three times. By that Pali text, the endowment of the donor with three factors is shown.
144:
In this context, whichever monk, having produced the third and fourth jhanas through the development of loving-kindness (metta), and making that very jhana the basis, develops insight (vipassana) and reaches the fruit of Arahatship, he is purified and liberated (from samsara). Such a person does not go to the Brahma world. However, whichever monk, having produced the third and fourth jhanas through the development of loving-kindness, finds delight in that jhana, thinking, 'This attainment is indeed peaceful,' and so forth, he is bound (to it). That monk, not having fallen away from the jhana, goes to the Brahma world by means of that very jhana. Therefore, the Blessed One, not permitting the going to the Brahma world for one who is purified and liberated, but wishing to show the going to the Brahma world by means of that jhana for the person who is attached to it, spoke this verse beginning with 'Yo yajati' (He who sacrifices) in a manner suitable for the brahmin Māgha.

In that verse, 'tividhaṃ' (threefold) refers to devotion in the three times. By this, he shows the three factors on the part of the donor. 'Ārādhaye dakkhiṇeyyebhi tādī' means that such a person, who accomplishes the three types of fulfillment, should accomplish or complete the fulfillment of the threefold sacrifice through the Arahants, who are the noble recipients of offerings. By this, he shows the three factors on the part of the recipients. 'Evaṃ yajitvā sammā yācayogo' means that having properly offered the sacrifice endowed with the six factors, which is the proximate cause of the metta-jhana, that person, who is devoted to giving to those who ask, reaches the Brahma world through the metta-jhana supported by that six-factored sacrifice. Saying 'Brahmalokanti brūmi' (I say, to the Brahma world), he concluded the teaching while encouraging the brahmin Māgha. In all the remaining verses, the meaning is clear. From this point onwards, it should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Māgha Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Sabhiya Sutta
'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' (Thus have I heard) and so forth is the Sabhiya Sutta. What is the origin? It is exactly as stated in the prologue (nidāna) of this sutta. The sequence of the explanation of the meaning should also be understood in the same way as before. We shall explain only the new terms, omitting those whose meanings are already clear. 'Veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe' (In the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Ground) is the name of that park. It is said that the park was surrounded by bamboo clumps and an eighteen-cubit wall.
145:
Because it was endowed with gateways, watchtowers, and battlements, had a dark green hue, and was delightful to the heart, it is called 'Veḷuvana' (Bamboo Grove). Because they used to give food to the squirrels there, it is called 'Kalandakanivāpa' (Squirrels' Feeding Ground). 'Kalandaka' refers to black squirrels. It is said that in the past, a certain king came to that park for recreation and, being intoxicated with liquor, fell asleep during the day. His attendants, thinking 'The king is asleep,' wandered here and there, enticed by flowers, fruits, and so on. Then, attracted by the smell of the liquor, a cobra came out from a hollow tree and approached the king. Seeing this, a tree deity, thinking 'I will save the king's life,' came in the form of a black squirrel and made a sound near the king's ear. The king woke up, and the cobra turned back. Seeing this occurrence, the king thought, 'This black squirrel has given me my life,' and established a feeding ground for squirrels in that park and had a proclamation of sanctuary announced. Therefore, from that time on, it became known as 'Kalandakanivāpa'.

In the phrase 'Sabhiyassa paribbājakassa', 'Sabhiya' is the name of that person, and 'paribbājaka' (wanderer) is said in reference to his state as an ascetic outside the [Buddhist] dispensation. 'Purāṇasālohitā devatā' (a deity who was a former blood-relative) means that although not his mother or father, that young deity is called 'a deity who was a former blood-relative' because of having a beneficial intention towards Sabhiya, like a mother or a father. It is said that after the Blessed One Kassapa had attained Parinibbāna and the golden stupa had been established, three young men of good family went forth as monks in the presence of the contemporary disciples. Taking up meditation subjects suitable for their conduct, they went to the border regions and practiced the Dhamma of a recluse in a forest haunt. From time to time, they would go to the city to worship the stupa and listen to the Dhamma. At a later time, not desiring to live away from the forest even for that long, they dwelt there diligently. Even though they dwelt in this way, they did not attain any distinction (spiritual attainment). Then it occurred to them: 'While we are going for alms, we are concerned for our lives. As long as one is concerned for life, it is not possible to attain the supramundane Dhamma. Dying as a worldling (puthujjana) is also very painful. Come, let us build a ladder, climb the mountain, and practice the Dhamma of a recluse without regard for body or life.' They did as they had planned.

Then, among those monks, the elder monk, being possessed of the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), realized Arahatship together with the six higher powers (abhiññā) on that very day. That elder monk went to the Himalayas by psychic power, washed his face at Lake Anotatta, wandered for alms in Uttarakuru, and after finishing his meal, went to another place, filled his bowl, and [brought] Anotatta water and Nāgalatā tooth-sticks...
146:
That Arahant elder, having taken food and water, approached those monks and said, "Friends, behold my psychic power. This alms-food was brought from Uttarakuru. This water for washing the face and this tooth-stick were brought from the Himavanta. Partake of this food and tooth-stick and practice the recluse's Dhamma. If you practice thus, I will attend to you at all times." Upon hearing these words, those monks said, "Venerable sir, you have completed your task. For us, even the mere act of conversing with you is a hindrance (to our practice). From now on, do not come to us again." That elder, being unable to make those monks accept by any means, departed.

Then, after two or three days had passed, one of those monks became an Anāgāmī (Non-returner) endowed with the five supernormal powers. That Anāgāmī elder also did the same, but being rejected by the other monk, he departed just as before. That third monk, having rejected the words of the second elder and practicing, died on the seventh day from the day he climbed the mountain without attaining any special distinction of the Path or Fruit, and was reborn in the deva world. The Great Arahant elder also attained Parinibbāna on that very day. The Anāgāmī elder was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). The young deva, after enjoying divine bliss in the six sensual-sphere deva worlds in forward and reverse order, passed away from the deva world during the time of our Buddha and took conception in the womb of a certain female wanderer (paribbājikā). That female wanderer was said to be the daughter of a certain khattiya (warrior-noble). Her parents, saying, "Let our daughter learn other doctrines," had entrusted her to a certain wanderer. A certain wanderer who was a student of that teacher committed misconduct with that princess, and she became pregnant. Seeing her pregnant, the fellow female wanderers expelled her. While she was going elsewhere, she gave birth to a son in a rest-house along the way, and thus she named the boy "Sabhiya." That Sabhiya, when he grew up, went forth as a wanderer, studied various scriptures, and became a great debater. Because he was capable of refuting others with his doctrine, he traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Finding no debater equal to himself, he had a hermitage built at the city gate and lived there, teaching arts and sciences to khattiya princes and others.

At that time, the Blessed One, having set in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma, arrived in due course at the city of Rājagaha and was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the Kalandakanivāpa. Sabhiya, however, did not yet know of the Buddha's arising. Then, that Suddhāvāsa Brahma, having emerged from meditative attainment, reflected, "By whose power did I attain this special distinction?" Remembering his practice of the recluse's Dhamma in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa and those companions, he looked and reflected, "Who among them has attained Parinibbāna?"
147:
Reflecting, "One has attained Parinibbāna; where is the other one now?" he realized, "Having passed away from the deva world, he is born in Jambudīpa and does not even know of the Buddha's arising." Thinking, "Come, I shall urge him to attend upon the Buddha," he prepared twenty questions. In the night, he came to Sabhiya’s hermitage, stood in the air, and called out, "Sabhiya, Sabhiya!" Sabhiya, who was sleeping, heard the voice three times, came out, and seeing the radiance, stood with palms joined. Then that Brahma said to him, "Sabhiya, I have brought twenty questions for your benefit; learn these questions. Whichever recluse or brahmin, when asked these questions, can answer them, you should lead the holy life in his presence." It was in reference to this young deva that it was said, "Questions were pointed out by a deity who was a former kinsman." "Pointed out" means they were spoken only as an outline, not with detailed analysis.

When this was said, Sabhiya learned those questions in the order of the words with just a single hearing. Then that Brahma, although he knew, did not tell Sabhiya of the Buddha's arising. With the intention, "The wanderer who is searching for the meaning will find the Teacher by himself, and he will also know the emptiness of the recluses and brahmins outside this Dispensation," he said, "Sabhiya, whoever...
