(etc.) ...lead the holy life." However, the commentators who explain the Apadāna of Sabhiya Thera in the Catukkanipāta of the Theragāthā say, "His mother, reflecting on her own misconduct and being disgusted by it, developed jhāna and was reborn in the Brahma world; it was that Brahma deity, who had been his mother, who pointed out those questions."

"Ye te" is a reference again to the words that are about to be spoken. "Samaṇabrāhmaṇā" means those who are recluses and brahmins either by having gone forth or by worldly designation. "Saṅghino" means those who have a community (saṅgha). "Gaṇino" means teachers who claim, "We are omniscient." "Gaṇācariyā" means teachers of a group of monks or laypeople through instruction and inquiry. "Ñātā" means well-known, famous, and prominent. "Yasassino" means those endowed with gain and a large following. "Titthakarā" means those who create the "fords" of wrong views, which are to be descended into and entered by those who follow their doctrines. "Sādhusammatā bahujanassa" means those who are regarded by many people as "these are of good nature, peaceful, and virtuous men."
148:
## 
"Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle used in the sense of "Who are they?". Pūraṇa is the name, and Kassapa is the clan (gotta). It is said that Pūraṇa Kassapa was a slave by birth, born to complete a hundred slaves. Therefore, they named him "Pūraṇa" (The Completer). He ran away and was ordained among the naked ascetics (Acelakas); he pointed to his clan, saying, "I am of the Kassapa clan," and also claimed omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Makkhali is the name, and because he was born in a cowshed, he is also called Gosāla. He too was a slave by birth, ran away, was ordained, and claimed omniscience. Ajita is the name. Because he had few wishes, he used to wear a blanket made of human hair, and thus he is also called "Kesakambala." He too claimed omniscience. Pakudha is the name, and Kaccāyana is the clan. Because of his fewness of wishes and his perception of life in water, he abstained from bathing, washing his face, and so on. He too claimed omniscience. Sañjaya is the name, and Belaṭṭha was his father; therefore, he is called "Belaṭṭhaputta." He too claimed omniscience. He is called Nigaṇṭha by his ascetic name and Nātaputta by his father's name. It is said that Nāta was his father's name, and being the son of Nāta, he is called Nātaputta. He too claimed omniscience. All those teachers had five hundred disciples each as their retinue. "Te" refers to those six teachers. "Te pañhe" refers to those twenty questions. "Te" refers to those six teachers who "na sampāyanti," meaning they could not provide complete answers (to the questions). "Kopaṃ" refers to the turbid state of the mind and mental factors. "Dosaṃ" refers to the state of a corrupt mind. Both of these are synonyms for anger (kodha), distinguished by being slow or quick. "Appaccayaṃ" refers to displeasure or dejection (domanassa). "Pātukaronti" means they manifest through bodily and vocal changes; they make it evident.

"Hīnāya" refers to the state of a householder. The state of a householder, when compared to monkhood, is called a "lowly state" because it is deficient in virtues such as morality (sīla), or because it involves indulgence in low sensual pleasures. Monkhood is indeed a noble state. "Āvattitvā" means turning back (from monkhood). "Kāme paribhuñjeyyaṃ" means one should indulge in sensual pleasures. Thus, for Sabhiya, such a thought occurred upon seeing the claim of omniscience (by others) and the emptiness of those ordained. Coming by the power of the thought that had arisen and repeatedly investigating, the wandering ascetic Sabhiya had this thought: "This recluse also..." and "Even those venerable ones..." and "A recluse should not be despised even if he is young," and so forth. In that passage, the words beginning with "jiṇṇa" are just as previously explained. "Therā" refers to those who have reached a state of firmness in their own recluse-dharma. "Rattaññū" means one who knows the jewel (ratanaññū), meaning those who are designated by the world according to their own claim, "We know the jewel of Nibbāna." Alternatively, it means those who know many nights (long-standing). Because they have been ordained for a long time, they are called "cirapabbajitā." "Na uññātabbo" means he should not be looked down upon; he should not be regarded as being in a low position.
149:
## 
The meaning is: "Na paribhotabbo" means he should not be mistreated; it means one should not hold the view, "What can this person know?".

"Kaṅkhī vecikicchī": Sabhiya, while conversing joyfully with the Blessed One, praising the omniscience indicated by the Blessed One's physical perfection and tranquility, became free from agitation and said, "Kaṅkhī vecikicchī." In that context, he is "kaṅkhī" (doubting) due to the doubt regarding the answering of the questions, thinking, "Will I obtain the answers to these questions?". He is "vecikicchī" (wavering) because of the doubt, "What is the meaning of this and that question?". Alternatively, he is "kaṅkhī" because of doubting the meaning of those questions with weak doubt; and he is "vecikicchī" because when investigating with strong doubt, he only becomes exhausted and is unable to reach a conclusion. "Abhikaṅkhamāno" means greatly desiring. "Tesantakaro" means one who makes an end to those questions. Wishing to indicate that "The Venerable One is indeed such a person," he said the words, "Pañhe me puṭṭho... vyākarohi me" (The questions asked by me... explain to me). In that passage, "pañhe me" means the questions by me. "Puṭṭho" means having been asked. "Anupubbaṃ" means according to the order of the questions. "Anudhammaṃ" means presenting the Pali text in accordance with the meaning. "Vyākarohi me" means please explain to me.

"Dūrato": It is said that Sabhiya, while wandering here and there, came from a journey of seven hundred yojanas. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Dūrato āgatosi" (You have come from afar). Alternatively, he said to Sabhiya, "Dūrato āgatosi," because he came from the dispensation (sāsana) of Kassapa Buddha.

With this verse, "Puccha maṃ" (Ask me), He invited Sabhiya with the invitation of an Omniscient One (sabbaññu-pavāraṇā). In that verse, "manasicchasi" means you desire with your mind.

"Yaṃ vatahaṃ" means in whatever way I (shall be). "Attamano" means having a mind filled with satisfaction, joy, and happiness. "Udaggo" means being greatly uplifted in both body and mind. However, this word "udaggo" is not present in all versions of the text. Now, wishing to show the states by which he is satisfied, He said, "Pamudito pītisomanassajāto" (Delighted, born of joy and happiness).

"Kiṃ pattinaṃ" means what has been reached? What has been attained? "Sorataṃ" means well-calmed. There is also a reading "surataṃ," which means well-ceased. "Dantaṃ" means one who is tamed. "Buddho" means one who is fully awakened, or a person who knows what is to be known. Thus, Sabhiya asked twenty questions using five verses, making four questions in each verse. The Blessed One, however, to that Sabhiya...
150:
The Blessed One answered each question with a single verse, concluding with the fruit of Arahantship, using twenty verses in total.

In those verses, because a monk in the ultimate sense (paramattha-bhikkhu) who has abandoned defilements is one who has reached Nibbāna, [the Buddha] wishing to answer the question "How is one reached? How is one attained? Who is called a monk?" spoke the verse beginning with "Pajjena". The meaning of that verse is: That monk who, through the Path (magga) he has developed, has reached the cessation of defilements, and because of reaching that cessation, has crossed over doubt (vicikicchā). Having abandoned failure and success, loss and gain, the views of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) and eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi), the distinctions of merit and demerit, and the low and the high; having lived the life of the Path and ended rebirth—such a person, worthy of these words of praise, is called a "monk" (bhikkhu).

Because he is well-withdrawn from wrong practice and because of the stilling of various defilements, he is "gentle" (sorata). Therefore, to show this, [the Buddha] spoke the answer to the second question in the manner beginning with "Sabbattha upekkhako". The meaning of that verse is: He who is equanimous through the six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā), not being pleased or displeased upon seeing a form with the eye among all objects such as forms, etc. He possesses extensive mindfulness. He does not harm any being in the whole world, whether trembling or firm. He is called "crossed over" (tiṇṇa) because he has crossed the four floods (ogha); a "recluse" (samaṇa) because evil is stilled; and "undisturbed" (anāvila) because he has abandoned turbid thoughts. For him, the seven obsessions (ussada) known as lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, views, defilements, and misconduct—whether gross or subtle—do not exist at all. That monk is called "gentle" (sorata) because of this living in equanimity, extensiveness of mindfulness, non-violence, withdrawal from wrong practice, and the stilling of defilements such as the floods.

Also, because he has developed faculties (indriya), is fearless, unchanging, and tamed, [the Buddha] answered the third question with the verse beginning with "Yassindriyāni". The meaning of that verse is: For that monk, the six faculties such as the eye, etc., have been developed by applying the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) such as impermanence to the objects and by taking up the scent of mindfulness and wisdom through the practice of cultivation. Those faculties are developed both internally and externally in the whole world. Wherever there is a deficiency of faculties or the possibility of deficiency, he does not let [defilements] grow by the power of greed (abhijjhā), etc. Knowing thus, penetrating this world and the next, his own continuity and that of others, and desiring Nibbāna which is deathless, he awaits the time when life will end.
151:
"Have been developed" means having thus penetrated and known, having realized this world and the next, the world of aggregates (khandha) within one's own continuity and the world of aggregates in another's continuity, he awaits the time of death without wavering. He waits for and anticipates the time of the end of life; he does not fear death. As the Elder said:

"I have no fear of death, nor have I a longing for life."

"I do not long for death, I do not long for life. I await the time just as a laborer awaits his wages."

"That developed one is tamed" means that one who has such developed faculties is tamed.

Furthermore, a "Buddha" is so called because he is endowed with wisdom (buddhi) and is awakened from the sleep of defilements. To show this meaning, [the Buddha] answered the fourth question with the verse beginning with "Kappāni". In that verse, "kappāni" refers to craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). They are called "kappāni" because they conceptualize in various ways. "Viceyya" means having investigated through characteristics such as impermanence. "Kevalāni" means all. "Saṃsāra" means:

"The succession of aggregates, elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana), proceeding without interruption, is called Saṃsāra."

Thus, having investigated the entire Saṃsāra, which is the succession of aggregates, etc. By this much, he spoke of insight (vipassanā) into the three rounds (vaṭṭa) regarding the karma and defilements which are the roots of the aggregates, and regarding the aggregates themselves. "Dubhayaṃ cutūpapātaṃ" means investigating and knowing both the passing away and the rebirth of beings. By this, he spoke of the knowledge of passing away and rebirth (cutūpapāta-ñāṇa). He is called "one whose dust is gone, without blemish, pure" (vigataraja manaṅgaṇa visuddha) because of the departure of the dust of lust, etc., the absence of blemishes, and the departure of stains. "Attained the end of birth" (pattāṃ jātikhayaṃ) means reaching Nibbāna. He is called "Buddha" because he is endowed with the wisdom of supramundane insight and the various types of knowledge of passing away and rebirth, because he is awakened from the sleep of defilements by being free from dust, etc., and because he has reached the end of birth through that practice.

Alternatively, "having investigated all kappāni" means having investigated in the manner: "In many aeons of contraction and expansion (saṃvaṭṭa-vivaṭṭa-kappa), I was in such a place," etc. By this, he spoke of the first knowledge (vijjā). "Saṃsāra and both passing away and rebirth" means both the passing away and rebirth of beings...
152:
It means investigating and contemplating saṃsāra in the manner of "These beings pass away and are reborn," and so forth. By this term [cutūpapāta], the second knowledge, the Divine Eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa), is spoken of. By the remaining words, the third knowledge, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa), is spoken of. Through the knowledge of the destruction of the taints, the state of being free from the dust of defilements and the attainment of Nibbāna occur. "He is called a Buddha" means that one who is endowed with such knowledge consisting of the three types of higher knowledge (vijjā) is called a Buddha.

Having thus answered the question asked in the first verse, regarding the questions asked in the second verse, since a true Brahmin who has reached the supreme state has warded off all evil, [the Buddha] answered the first question with the verse beginning with "Bāhitvā" to show that meaning. The meaning of that verse is: One who has warded off all evils by the Path of Arahantship and remains so is called "one who stands firm" (ṭhitatto). Because he has warded off evil, he is stainless (vimala); having reached the stainless supreme state, he is well-composed (sādhusamāhito) with the concentration of the fruit of Arahantship, which is free from the dust of defilements that disturb the calmed concentration. Because he has crossed over saṃsāra by transcending the causes of saṃsāra and has completed his task, he is called Kevalī. Because he is unattached (asita) to craving and views, and because he is unshakeable by the worldly conditions, he is also called "Tādī" (the Such). Such a person, worthy of praise, is called a Brahma and a Brāhmaṇa.

Because he is a Samaṇa by having calmed evil, a Nhātaka by having washed away evil, and a Nāga by not committing any sin (āgu), [the Buddha] answered the three questions with the next three verses to show that meaning. Therein, "samitāvī" refers to one who stands having calmed the defilements by the Noble Path. Because of such a nature, he is called a Samaṇa. With this, the question is answered; the remaining words are words of praise to inspire great respect in Sabhiya for that Samaṇa (monk). One who has calmed the defilements, having abandoned merit and evil (puññapāpa) by not creating further rebirth, is called "viraja" (stainless) because of the departure of the dust of defilements. Knowing through the lens of impermanence and so forth, he is a Tādī person who has transcended this world, the next world, birth, and death.

In this verse "ninhāya... nhātako", one who has washed away (ninhāya) with the knowledge of the Path all evils that are liable to arise based on internal and external objects within the entire world of sense bases (āyatana-loka), both internal and external, and because of that state of having washed away evil, he no longer enters into the conceptions (kappa) of gods and humans who conceive through craving and views; such a person is called a Nhātaka. This is how the meaning should be understood.

In the fourth verse as well, "āguṃ na karoti kiñci loke" means one who does not commit even the slightest sin (āgu) known as evil in the world; such a person is called a Nāga.
153:
By the word "tathattā", the question is answered to this extent. The remaining words are merely words of praise as in the previous method. One who does not commit sin because he has abandoned sin through the Path, having released and abandoned all bonds such as the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga) and all fetters consisting of the ten types of fetters (saṃyojana), no longer clings to anything such as the aggregates (khandha) with any attachment, is liberated through the two types of liberation (vimutti), and is a Tādī person.

Having thus answered the questions asked in the second verse, regarding the questions asked in the third verse, since the sense bases (āyatana) are called "fields" (khetta), [the Buddha answered]. As it is said: "The eye is a field, the eye-base is a field... the base is a field." According to this teaching, having thoroughly investigated and contemplated those sense bases such as the eye in terms of impermanence and so forth, and specifically [investigating] the celestial field, the human field, and the Brahma field which are causes of attachment—alternatively, the twelve types of celestial sense bases, the twelve types of human sense bases, and the six types of Brahma sense bases—having conquered or investigated all of them. Since ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth are the root-bonds of all these fields, he is liberated from the root-bonds of all fields. Thus, because he has conquered or investigated these fields, he is called a "Conqueror of Fields" (khettajina). Therefore, [the Buddha] answered the first question with this verse "khettāni". In that word "khettāni", some teachers say that "Kamma is the field, consciousness is the seed, and craving is the moisture," and thus they call kammas "fields". They explain that kamma leading to the celestial realm is the celestial field (dibba-khetta), kamma leading to the human realm is the human field (mānusaka-khetta), and kamma leading to the Brahma realm is the Brahma field (brahma-khetta). The remaining words are as previously explained.

Furthermore, because kammas are like scabbards (kosa) by their own nature, they are called "kosas". Because he is skilled in cutting (lunana) and completely uprooting those kammas, he is called "kusala". Therefore, to show that meaning, [the Buddha] answered the second question with the verse "kosāni". The meaning of that verse is: One should investigate all "kosas" known as wholesome and unwholesome kammas in terms of impermanence and so forth, both by way of object and by way of function of mundane and supramundane insight (vipassanā). Specifically, having investigated the celestial kosa and human kosa consisting of the eight types of wholesome volitions of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala-cetanā), and the Brahma kosa consisting of the nine types of wholesome volitions of the sublime sphere (mahaggata-kusala-cetanā), which are causes of attachment, and having investigated them, he is liberated from the root-bonds of all kosas consisting of ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth through the development of this Path. Thus, because of the cutting of those kosas, he is called "kusala" (skilled/cutter). Because of being so, he is also a Tādī person. Alternatively, of beings...
154:
The three realms of existence and the twelve sense bases (āyatana) should be known as 'kosa' (sheaths/receptacles) because they are the dwelling places of beings and phenomena (dhammas), similar to a scabbard for a sword. This is how the connection of meaning should be made here.

In fact, one is not called a 'paṇḍita' (wise person) merely by the word 'paṇḍati' (one who knows). Rather, one is called a 'paṇḍita' because one approaches pure dhammas and because one is attached to investigative wisdom. Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, the Buddha answered the third question with the verse beginning with 'Dubhayāni'. The meaning of that verse is: One should distinguish the two types of dhammas—internal and external—by their nature of impermanence and so forth. 'Paṇḍarāni' refers to the sense bases (āyatanas). These are so called because they are naturally pure or by way of conventional usage. One who investigates these sense bases and has expelled impurities through this practice is called a 'paṇḍita' because of having pure wisdom. This is so because of that truth and because one knows those sense bases called 'paṇḍara' through wisdom. The remaining words are merely words of praise for that person. That person is thus praised because he has transcended the 'black and white' dhammas, known as evil and merit, and has become a 'tādī' (equanimous) person.

Because one is endowed with 'mona'—which refers to knowledge, wisdom, and right view—one is called a 'muni' (sage). Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, the Buddha answered the fourth question with the verse beginning with 'Asatañca'. The meaning of that verse is: Having known the dhammas of the wicked and the virtuous, which are distinguished as unwholesome and wholesome, in this entire world through investigative knowledge, and because of that knowledge, one stands having transcended the sevenfold bonds (saṅga) such as lust, and the twofold net (jāla) of craving and views. That person is a 'muni' because of being endowed with that investigative knowledge called 'mona'. The phrase 'worshipped by gods and humans' is a word of praise for that muni. Because that person is a muni who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), he is worthy of worship by gods and humans. Therefore, he is thus praised.

Having thus answered the question asked in the third verse, regarding the questions asked in the fourth verse: the muni who reaches the destruction of defilements through the knowledge of the four paths (magga-ñāṇa) is called a 'vedagū' in the ultimate sense. Also, one who investigates all the 'vedas'—which are designated as scriptures by all recluses and brahmins—through the development of that path, by way of its function and by way of impermanence and so forth. In those known dhammas, by abandoning desire and lust...
155:
Having transcended all those known dhammas (veda), one becomes dispassionate (vītarāga) towards all feelings (vedanā) that arise either because of that knowledge or through other causes. Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, the Buddha answered the first question with the verse beginning with 'Vedāni' instead of saying 'This person is a wise one'. Alternatively, whoever investigates the 'vedas' (known dhammas) with investigative wisdom and stands transcending all veda by abandoning desire and lust therein, that person is one who has reached, known, and transcended the vedas designated as scriptures. Whoever is dispassionate towards feelings is also one who has reached and transcended the vedas designated as feelings. Because one has reached the vedas, one is called a 'vedagū'. Therefore, wishing to show that meaning as well, the Buddha answered the first question with this verse instead of saying 'This person is one who has attained the goal'.

Furthermore, in the second question, 'anuvidito' refers to one who has understood (anubuddha). That person, having investigated and understood the proliferation (papañca) of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) which is internal to his own continuity—namely the proliferation consisting of craving, conceit, and views, and the name-and-form caused by them—through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth; and not only internally, but also externally, having investigated the root of disease, which is the root of this disease of name-and-form in the continuity of others, such as ignorance and craving for existence; or having investigated that very proliferation, through that meditation, he becomes liberated from the root-bond of all diseases, or from all diseases distinguished as ignorance, craving for existence, and so forth, or from that very proliferation. Therefore, showing this, the Buddha answered the second question with the verse beginning with 'Anuvicca'.

Regarding the question 'How is one energetic (vīriyavā)?', whoever is abstinent (virata) from all evil dhammas through the Noble Path, and because of such abstinence, stands having transcended the suffering of hell by not taking rebirth in the future, that Arahant, who is the abode or dwelling of energy, deserves to be called 'vīriyavā'. Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, the Buddha answered the third question with the verse beginning with 'Virato'. 'Padhānavā' (striving), 'dhīro' (wise), and 'tādī' (equanimous) are words of praise for him. He is 'padhānavā' because of his striving in path-meditation, 'dhīro' because of his ability to destroy the enemy of defilements, and 'tādī' because of his immutability. Thus he is praised. The rest should be connected and spoken accordingly.

Regarding the question 'What is a thoroughbred (ājāniya)?', in the world, a horse or an elephant that has abandoned all faults of crookedness and knows what is a cause and what is not is called an 'ājāniya'.
156:
In the world, although elephants and horses are called 'thoroughbreds' (ājāniya), those elephants and horses have not completely abandoned all faults. Only in the Arahant are those faults abandoned. Therefore, wishing to show that only the Arahant deserves to be called 'thoroughbred' in the ultimate sense, He answered the fourth question with the verse beginning with 'Yassa'.

The meaning of that verse is: For that Noble One, the bonds known as internal and external fetters (saṃyojana) have been cut and destroyed by the weapon of path-wisdom (magga-paññā). 'Saṅgamūlaṃ' refers to the root cause of the inability to overcome attachment to various objects; or, for that person, the bonds such as lust (rāga) and so on, which are the root of internal and external attachment, have been cut. Because he is liberated from the bonds that are the root of all attachments, he is called a 'thoroughbred' (ājāniya). He is also one of such nature (tādi).

Having thus answered the question posed in the fourth verse, regarding the questions in the fifth verse: Scholars who contemplate syllables praise someone as a 'sottiya' (learned/pure) merely by their own desire; such a person is a 'sottiya' only in conventional usage. However, a Noble One is a 'sottiya' in the ultimate sense due to great learning (bāhusacca) and the discarding of evil (nissutapāpatā). Therefore, wishing to show this meaning, instead of saying 'Idaṃ pattinaṃ', He answered the first question with the verse 'Sutvā'.

The meaning of that verse is: In this world, having heard through the function of wisdom based on hearing (sutamaya-paññā) or through the function of what ought to be done, and having known with higher knowledge (abhiññā) all things pertaining to insight (vipassanā) in terms of impermanence (anicca) and so on—whatever is blameworthy or blameless—and having overcome the defilements and the states that are the basis of defilements through this practice, he reaches the designation 'Abhibhū' (Conqueror). One who has thus heard and known all things and can overcome the blameworthy and blameless in the world, being a learned one, is called a 'sottiya'. Furthermore, one who is without doubt, liberated from the bonds of defilements, and free from the distress (īgha) of lust and so on in all things such as the aggregates (khandha) and sense-bases (āyatana), is called a 'sottiya' because he has discarded evil in all things.

Because he is to be approached (araṇīya) by those seeking welfare, he is called 'Ariya' (Noble); this means he has the nature of being one to be approached. Therefore, wishing to show the qualities by which that person is one to be approached, He answered the second question with the verse beginning with 'Chetvā'. The meaning of that verse is: Having cut the four taints (āsava) and the two attachments (ālaya) with the weapon of wisdom, that wise, discerning, and clear-minded one who possesses the four path-knowledges (magga-ñāṇa), does not, by the power of renewed existence...
157:
That person, having cut through defilements with the weapon of wisdom and being one who possesses the fourfold path-knowledge that is wise and skillful, no longer enters into a womb by the power of renewed existence. They do not approach any kind of thinking such as craving and so forth, and having abandoned attachment to the cords of sensual pleasure, they do not approach any of the thoughts among craving and wrong view. Such a person, endowed with qualities such as the destruction of the taints (āsavas), is called a Noble One (ariya).

Alternatively, one is called a Noble One (ariya) because of being far from evil unwholesome states. One is also called a Noble One because of not practicing harmful unwholesome states. Desiring to show this meaning, He answered the second question with this verse. Indeed, evil states such as the taints are known as 'harmful' (anaya). These unwholesome states called 'harmful' have been cut and abandoned by this person. The Noble One is not shaken by those states. Thus, those unwholesome states are far from that person. Because of being far at all times from the three kinds of perceptions such as sensual desire and from unwholesome states that cause harm and destruction, that person is called a Noble One. In this way, the connection of the meaning in this verse should be understood. The phrase "The wise one does not enter into a womb" (vidvā so na upeti gabbhasayyaṃ) is merely a word of praise in this interpretation of meaning.

In this inquiry "How is one endowed with conduct?" (kathaṃ caraṇavā), a person who has reached the fruit of Arahatship, which is to be reached through the practices of conduct (caraṇa), deserves to be called "one endowed with conduct" (caraṇavā). Therefore, desiring to show that person, He answered the third question with the verse beginning with "He who here" (yo idha). In that verse, "He who here" (yo idha) means in this Dispensation (sāsana) of the Buddha. "In conducts" (caraṇesu) means in practices such as virtue (sīla) and so forth, or in the fifteen states mentioned in the Hemavata Sutta. Here, the locative case is used in the sense of cause (nimitta). "Attained the attainment" (pattipatto) means that person has reached the fruit of Arahatship which is to be reached. It means they have reached the fruit of Arahatship to be reached by taking conduct as the sign, the cause, or the condition. "He is endowed with conduct" (caraṇavā so) means that person, through this attainment of what is to be reached by conduct, is endowed with conduct. By this much, the question is answered; the remaining words are merely words of praise for that person. Indeed, the person who has reached the attainment through conduct is skillful and expert, and always knows the state of Nibbāna. Because of having a mind constantly inclined towards Nibbāna, they have no attachment to any states such as the aggregates (khandhas). They are one whose mind is liberated from defilements through the two kinds of liberation (vimutti), and for that person, there is no resentment (paṭigha).

Because of renouncing actions (kamma) such as unwholesome ones, one is called a "wanderer" (paribbājaka). Desiring to show that meaning, He answered the fourth question with the verse "Having suffering as its result" (dukkhavepakkaṃ). Therein, 'vepakka' is the same as 'vipāka' (result). It is called "dukkhavepakka" because the actions (kamma) occurring in the three realms have suffering as their result. Because of producing the suffering of the round of existence (pavatti-dukkha), all actions in the three realms are called "dukkhavepakka". "Above" (uddhaṃ) refers to the past time; "below" (adho) refers to the future time; "across or in the middle" (tiriyaṃ vāpi majjhe) refers to the present time. That present time is neither above (past) nor below (future), but occurs between both; therefore, it is called "in the middle" (majjhe). "Having renounced" (paribbājayitvā) means having expelled or having abandoned. "One who wanders with full understanding" (pariññacārī) means one who practices while knowing with full understanding. This is first the explanation according to the sequence of words. What follows is the connection of the sense: Whatever action (kamma) exists that produces suffering included in the three realms, having abandoned all such actions by drying up the moisture of craving with the Noble Path, and no longer performing the nature that produces rebirth—because of such abandonment, one is called "one who wanders with full understanding" (pariññacārī) because of practicing while knowing that action with full understanding. Indeed, it is not only action that is fully understood; one who practices while fully understanding these states—conceit (māna), deceit (māyā), and greed (lobha)—through the full understanding of abandoning (pahāna-pariññā), makes an end of the round of rebirth. They make an end of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa); they abandon it. In this way, this meaning should be understood. Because of abandoning these actions and so forth, that person is called a "wanderer" (paribbājaka).
158:
Having expelled (niddhametvā). 'Pariññacārī' means one who practices having distinguished with wisdom. This is first the word-by-word explanation (apubbapadavaṇṇanā) that has not been previously explained. This is the connection of the meaning (adhippāyayojanā): whatever action (kamma) exists that produces suffering included within the three realms, drying up the moisture of craving and ignorance through the Noble Path, and having abandoned it (paribbājayitvā) by making it such that it does not produce rebirth; and because of being thus abandoned, one is called 'pariññacārī' because of practicing having fully understood that kamma. Not only kamma is fully understood and practiced, but also deceit (māyā), conceit (māna), as well as greed (lobha) and anger (kodha)—one who practices having fully understood these things through the full understanding of abandonment (pahānapariññā) is a 'pariññacārī'. It means he has made an end of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa), made an end of mind-and-matter, and abandoned it. Because of abandoning these things such as kamma, they call that person a wanderer (paribbājaka). The word 'pattipatta' (attained the attainment) is a word of praise for him.

Thus, Sabhiya, being pleased by the answering of the questions, in the verses of praise beginning with 'Yāni ca tīṇi', 'osaraṇāni' means the views which are landing places (resorts). Those views, when combined with the sixty-two views taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta along with identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), become sixty-three. Those views are depended upon (sitāni) by the power of pointing out the scriptures which are the doctrines of the ascetics of other sects; they are not by the power of actual occurrence. By the power of occurrence, however, there is the mere conventional name which is the marking of the names 'woman' or 'man', and the perverted perception (viparītasaññā) that arises in fools as 'it should be a self (attā) of such a nature' by the power of wrong thoughts, hearsay, etc. Dependent on those two, they arise by the power of those people; they are not things known by personal realization. Having removed those views, the Blessed One has crossed over the darkness of the flood (oghatamaṃ). There is also a reading 'oghantamagā', meaning he has reached the end of the floods. Therefore, he said, 'Yāni ca tīṇi... (pe)... tamagā'.

After that, because of reaching Nibbāna, which is the end of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha) and the far shore, because of the absence of suffering and because of being the opposite of that suffering, referring to that Nibbāna, he said: 'You have reached the end, reached the far shore of suffering' (antagūsi pāragū dukkhassā). Alternatively, the Blessed One is called 'pāragū' because he has gone to Nibbāna; addressing that quality, he said: 'Pāragū antagūsi dukkhassā'—this is the connection here. He knows well (sammā) and he knows by himself (sāmaṃ), therefore he is the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). 'Taṃ maññe' means 'I think only of that Buddha, not another,' spoken with great respect. 'Jutimā' means he is endowed with radiance because he dispels the darkness of others. 'Mutimā' means he is endowed with the wisdom called 'muti' which is capable of knowing the things to be known (ñeyyadhamma) without depending on others. 'Pahūtapañño' means...
159:
...endowed with wisdom. 'Pahūtapañño' means having infinite wisdom. Here, omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is intended. He addresses him saying, 'Dukkhassantakarā' (Ender of suffering). 'Atāresi maṃ' means 'You have crossed me over from doubt.'

546-9. With the verse beginning 'Yaṃ me', he speaks of paying homage. In that verse, the word 'kaṅkhitaṃ' refers to the meaning connected with the twenty questions. That person indeed had doubt regarding those twenty questions. 'Monapathesu' means in the paths of knowledge (matters to be known by wisdom). 'Vinaḷīkatā' means made free like a reed, meaning it has been cut off. 'Nāga nāgassa' is a word of address; one 'nāgassa' should be connected with the words 'bhāsato anumodanti'. 'Dhammadesanaṃ' is the remaining text. 'Sabbe devā' means all the sky-dwelling and earth-dwelling deities. 'Nāradapabbatā' means those two groups of deities are also wise; those deities also rejoice—thus he speaks of paying homage with full devotion.

550-53. Having heard the fulfillment of the answers which are worthy of appreciation, he raised his hands in salutation and said, 'Namo te' (Homage to you). 'Purisājaññā' means a noble thoroughbred among men, endowed with excellent birth. 'Paṭipuggalo' means a peerless person. You are called 'Buddha' because of the penetration of the Four Truths; 'Satthā' (Teacher) because of your instruction and because of being a caravan leader to Nibbāna; 'Mārābhibhū' because of conquering the four Maras; and you are a 'Muni', a Great Sage who is a Buddha. 'Upadhī' refers to the four acquisitions: aggregates (khandha), defilements (kilesa), cords of sensual pleasure (kāmaguṇa), and volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra). 'Vaggū' means having a very beautiful appearance. 'Puññေ ca' means not being stained by mundane merit. This is because of not performing those merits, or because even if performed in the past, there is no experiencing of the result in the future, or because of not being stained by the impurities of craving and views which arise based on that merit. 'Vandati satthuno' means while praising in this way, he clasped the ankles and paid homage with the fivefold prostration.

'Aññatitthiyapubbo' means one who was formerly of another sect. 'Ākaṅkhati' means he desires. 'Āraddhacittā' means having very delighted minds. 'Api ca mettha puggalavemattatā viditā' means: 'I, the Buddha, know the difference among individuals regarding the probationary period (parivāsa) of other sectarians in this case of Sabhiya the Wanderer; not everyone needs to undergo the probation.' Who does not need to undergo the probation? The fire-worshipping ascetics, those of the Sakyan clan, and those who come having abandoned their former appearance (sectarian garb). Even one who comes without abandoning the appearance but is endowed with the causal merit for attaining the paths and fruits does not need to undergo the probation; Sabhiya the Wanderer is such a person. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Sabhiya, for you there is no reason to undergo the probation for the purpose of fulfilling the duties of the sectarians; I know that you are one who desires the benefit and are endowed with the cause for attaining the paths and fruits,' and thus [granted] his monkhood...
160:
The Blessed One, wishing to grant (Sabhiya) the status of a monk, said: "Moreover, in this case, I recognize the distinction of individuals regarding the probationary period for those from other sects." Sabhiya the wanderer, wishing to show his respect, said: "If, Bhante..." and so forth. All these words and other similar ones are not explained here because their meaning is clear and they follow the method already mentioned previously. They should be understood according to the method explained before.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā
## The Commentary on the Sabhiya Sutta of the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## 7. Commentary on the Sela Sutta

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Sela Sutta. What is its origin? It is just as stated in the introduction to this discourse. The sequence of the explanation of the meaning is also just as mentioned before, so it should be understood according to the previous method. However, I shall explain the words not yet explained, omitting those with obvious meanings. "Anguttarāpesu" means that region is indeed the Anga country. However, because it is not far from the waters to the north of the Ganges, it is also called "Uttarāpa." If one asks, "To the north of which Ganges?" it is the waters of the great Mahāmahī Ganges.

In this regard, for the purpose of clarifying that river, the explanation from the beginning is as follows: This island of Jambudīpa is ten thousand leagues (yojanas) in extent. Therein, an area of four thousand leagues is covered by water and is called the "ocean" (samudda). Humans live in an area of three thousand leagues. The Himavanta mountains are situated in an area of three thousand leagues. These mountains are five hundred leagues in height, adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks, and are diversified by five hundred rivers flowing all around. In that Himavanta, there are seven great lakes such as Lake Anotatta, which were mentioned in the commentary on the Pūraḷāsa Sutta, each being fifty leagues in length and breadth, and fifty leagues in depth, with a circumference of one hundred and fifty leagues.

Among those seven great lakes, Lake Anotatta is surrounded by these five mountains: Sudassana Peak, Citrakūṭa Peak, Kāḷakūṭa Peak, Gandhamādana Peak, and Kelāsa Peak. Among those five mountains, Sudassana Peak is made of gold and is two hundred leagues high. Curving inwards and shaped like a crow's beak, it stands overhanging Lake Anotatta itself. Citrakūṭa Peak is made of all kinds of jewels. Kāḷakūṭa Peak is made of antimony. Gandhamādana Mountain is made of a ridge, and inside it has a color like grass (green beans), covered with various medicinal plants. On the new moon Uposatha day, it stands glowing like a heap of burning embers. Kelāsa Peak is made of silver. All these mountains have a height and shape similar to Mount Sudassana. They stand overhanging Lake Anotatta itself. They are inhabited by the power of devas and nāgas. Rivers also flow on those mountains. All that water flows only into Lake Anotatta. When the moon and the sun travel to the south or the north, they illuminate the water of that lake through the gaps between the mountains, but when they travel directly overhead, they do not illuminate it. For that reason, the lake is called "Lake Anotatta." In that Lake Anotatta, the delightful cool waters are always clear like crystal and free from impurities.
161:
(Sudassana Mountain) which stands overhanging Lake Anotatta itself; Citrakūṭa Mountain, made of all kinds of jewels; Kāḷakūṭa Mountain, made of antimony; Gandhamādana Mountain, made of a ridge, having the color of green beans inside and covered with various kinds of medicinal plants, standing as if glowing like a heap of burning embers on the new moon Uposatha day; and Kelāsa Mountain, made of silver. All these mountains have a height and shape similar to Mount Sudassana and stand overhanging that lake itself. All these mountains exist through the power of devas and nāgas; rivers flow on those mountains. All those waters flow only into Lake Anotatta. When the moon and the sun travel by the south or by the north, they illuminate that lake through the mountain passes; but when they travel directly overhead, they do not illuminate it. For that reason, the name 'Anotatta' became well-known for it.

In that Lake Anotatta, there are delightful cool waters, an absence of fish and turtles, and well-prepared bathing places with crystal-clear water free from impurities. At those bathing places, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Arahants, and groups of sages bathe; devas, yakkhas, and others also engage in garden sports.

On the four sides of that lake, there are four outlets: the lion's mouth, the elephant's mouth, the horse's mouth, and the bull's mouth. From these outlets, four rivers flow. On the banks of the river issuing from the lion's mouth, lions are very numerous; at the elephant's mouth and the others, elephants, horses, and bulls are numerous. The river issuing from the eastern direction circles Lake Anotatta three times clockwise and, without approaching the other three rivers, travels through the eastern Himavanta by a path uninhabited by humans and enters the great ocean. The rivers issuing from the western and northern directions likewise circle clockwise and travel through the western and northern Himavanta respectively by paths uninhabited by humans and enter the great ocean.

But the river issuing from the southern direction circles that lake three times clockwise and travels straight south for sixty leagues over a rocky surface. Then, striking a mountain and rising upwards, it becomes a water column about three gāvutas in circumference, travels through the air for sixty leagues, and falls onto a rock named Tiyaggaḷa. That rock was broken by the force of the water column. At that place, a lotus pond named Tiyaggaḷa, fifty leagues in extent, was formed. Breaking through the bank of that pond, it enters the rock and travels for sixty leagues. From there, it breaks through the solid earth and travels for sixty leagues through a tunnel. Then, striking the mountain named Viñjha which stands crosswise, it flows out as five streams like the five fingers on the palm of a hand. In the place where that river travels after circling Lake Anotatta three times, it is called the 'Āvaṭṭaganggā'.
162:
It is called (that river). In the place where it flows straight for sixty yojanas over a stone surface, it is called "Kaṇhagangā." In the place where it flows for sixty yojanas through the sky, it is called "Ākāsagangā." In the place where it occupies a space of fifty yojanas at the Tiyaggala stone, it is called "Tiyaggala-pokkharaṇī." In the place where it breaks the bank, enters into the stone, and flows for sixty yojanas, it is called "Bahalagangā." In the place where it breaks the earth and flows for sixty yojanas through a tunnel, it is called "Umangagangā." In the place where it strikes the transverse mountain named Vinjhā and flows in five streams, it is called by five names: "Gangā, Yamunā, Aciravatī, Sarabhū, and Mahī." Thus, these five great rivers originate from the Himalayas (Himavanta). Among these five rivers, the fifth one named Mahī is intended here as the "Mahāmahīgangā." Because that region is not far from the waters to the north of that Ganges river, it should be known as "Anguttarāpa." In those regions of Anguttarāpa.

"Cārikaṃ caramāno" means performing a long-distance journey. In this regard, the Blessed One has two types of journeys: the swift journey (turitacārika) and the gradual journey (aturitacārika). Among them, seeing individuals capable of realization (babbapuggala) even at a distance and going immediately is called the swift journey. This is to be seen in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. Indeed, the Blessed One, while going to meet him, traveled three gāvutas in just a moment; he traveled thirty yojanas to discipline Āḷavaka, and similarly for Angulimāla. For Pukkusātissa, he traveled forty-five yojanas; for King Mahākappina, one hundred and twenty yojanas; and for Dhaniya, he traveled a distance of seven hundred yojanas. This is called the swift journey. However, the journey of one who favors the world by going in the sequence of villages, market towns, and cities for alms-round and so forth is called the gradual journey. This is what is intended here. Thus, while wandering on a journey. "Mahatā" means great both in terms of number and in terms of spiritual qualities. "Bhikkhusaṅghena" means with the community of monks. "Aḍḍhateḷasehi" means with twelve hundred and fifty (1250) monks, which is half of the thirteenth hundred. "Yena... tadavasari": That market town received the name "Āpaṇa" because of the abundance of shops (āpaṇa). It is heard that there were twenty thousand shop fronts distributed there. By whichever direction or path one should descend to the market town of the Anguttarāpa country, by that path he descended (tadavasari), meaning he went or reached that market town.

"Keṇiyo jaṭilo" refers to one named Keṇiya, who was an ascetic (jaṭila) by practice. It is said that although he was of the wealthy brahmin class (brāhmaṇamahāsāla), he took up the ascetic life to protect his wealth, and after giving a gift to the king and receiving a piece of land, he built a hermitage there and lived as a refuge for a thousand families. In his hermitage...
163:
It is said that there is a palm tree that yields one golden fruit (or fruit of instruction) every day. During the day, he wears saffron-colored clothes and binds his hair in a topknot; at night, however, he enjoys himself as he pleases, fully endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure. "Sakyaputto" indicates his noble lineage. "Sakyakulā pabbajito" indicates the fact of his going forth out of faith; it means he renounced that clan, which was not diminished or overcome by any loss, and went forth out of faith. "Taṃ kho pana" is an accusative expression in the sense of relating a matter; it means "of that Master Gotama." "Kalyāṇo" means endowed with good qualities, meaning "noble." "Kittisaddo" means fame or the sound of praise.

"Itipi so bhagavā" In the phrase beginning with these words, the construction is as follows: That Blessed One is called Arahaṃ for this reason; he is called Sammāsambuddho for this reason... he is called Bhagavā for this reason. It means for such and such reasons. Among those qualities, the Blessed One should be known as "Arahaṃ" for these reasons: because of being remote from defilements, because of having destroyed the enemies and the spokes [of the wheel of saṃsāra], because of being worthy of requisites, etc., and because of the absence of secret evil-doing.

Indeed, he is Arahaṃ because he is remote (ārakattā) from all defilements, having destroyed them along with their traces (vāsanā) by means of the Path. He is also Arahaṃ because those enemies (ari) which are defilements were destroyed (hata) by him through the Path. And there is this wheel of saṃsāra which has existed from time immemorial, with ignorance and craving for existence as its hub, with formations such as merit as its spokes, with aging and death as its rim, pierced by the axle made of the origin of taints (āsava), and well-joined to the chariot of the three worlds. Having stood on the ground of virtue with the feet of energy at the terrace of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and having taken the axe of knowledge that brings about the destruction of kamma with the hand of faith, all the spokes (ara) were destroyed by him; thus he is also Arahaṃ because the spokes were destroyed (arānaṃ hatattā). He is also Arahaṃ because he is worthy (arahati) of the highest offerings, such as robes and other requisites, as well as respect and honor. And just as some fools in the world who consider themselves wise commit evil in secret out of fear of ill-repute, this Blessed One never does so; thus he is also Arahaṃ because of the absence of secret evil-doing (rahābhāvā).

Because he is remote and because he has destroyed
The enemies that are defilements, that Sage is Arahaṃ.
The spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra have been destroyed by him,
And he is worthy of requisites and so on.
He does no evil in secret,
Therefore he is called Arahaṃ.

He is "Sammāsambuddho" because he has perfectly and by himself realized the Four Noble Truths. He is "Vijjācaraṇasampanno" because he is endowed with extremely pure types of clear vision (vijjā) and with most excellent conduct (caraṇa).
164:
He is called Sugato because of His excellent going, because He has gone to an excellent place (Nibbāna), because He has gone well, and because He speaks rightly. He is called Lokavidū because He knows the world in all its aspects. That Blessed One has known the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) in every way—by its nature, its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation—including the aggregates (khandha), bases (āyatana), and so forth.

'One world: all beings subsist on nutriment. Two worlds: mind and matter. Three worlds: the three types of feeling. Four worlds: the four nutriments. Five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging. Six worlds: the six internal bases. Seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness. Eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions. Nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings. Ten worlds: the ten bases. Twelve worlds: the twelve bases. Eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements.' Thus, He has known the world of formations in all its aspects.

He knows the inclinations of beings, their underlying tendencies (anusaya), their characters, and their dispositions (adhimutti). He knows beings as those with little dust in their eyes or much dust, with keen faculties or dull faculties, with good qualities or bad qualities, those easy to teach or difficult to teach, and those capable or incapable of liberation. Thus, He has known the world of beings (sattaloka) in all its aspects. Likewise, a single world-system (cakkavāḷa) measures 1,203,450 yojanas in length and breadth. Its circumference is 3,610,350 yojanas.

In that world-system:
This earth is reckoned to be 240,000 yojanas in thickness.
The water resting on air is 480,000 yojanas in thickness.
The air rising into the sky is 960,000 yojanas. This is the constitution of the world.

In this established world-system:
The most noble Mount Sineru is submerged 84,000 yojanas in the great ocean and rises 84,000 yojanas above it.
165:
From that Mount Sineru, following in order with half the measurement of each preceding one, there are seven great mountain ranges that are submerged in the ocean and rise above it. They are the dwellings of deities, adorned with various jewels:

Yugandhara, Isadhara, Karavīka, Sudassana, Nemindhara, Vinataka, and Assakaṇṇa. These seven great mountains stand around Mount Sineru, serving as the abodes of the Four Great Kings and frequented by devas and yakkhas.

Mount Himavā is 500 yojanas high and 3,000 yojanas in length and breadth.

It is adorned with 84,000 peaks. The Jambu tree (rose-apple), named Naga, has a trunk circumference of fifteen yojanas.

The length of its main branches from the trunk is fifty yojanas. It has a spread of seven yojanas all around and stands fifty yojanas high.

Due to the power of that Jambu tree, this continent is known as Jambudīpa. The Cakkavāḷa mountain is submerged 82,000 yojanas in the great ocean.

It rises to the same height above. That Cakkavāḷa mountain stands encircling all of that, made of the substance of the world-system.

In that world-system, the moon's disk is 49 yojanas and the sun's disk is 50 yojanas. The realm of Tāvatiṃsa is 10,000 yojanas. Likewise, the Asura realm, the Avīci great hell, and Jambudīpa are each 10,000 yojanas. The western continent (Aparagoyāna) is 7,000 yojanas. Likewise, the eastern continent (Pubbavideha) is 7,000 yojanas. The northern continent (Uttarakuru) is 8,000 yojanas. In this world-system, each great continent is surrounded by 500 small islands. All of that together is called one world-system (cakkavāḷa) or one world-element (lokadhātu). Between the world-systems lie the Lokantarika hells. Thus, He has known infinite world-systems and infinite world-elements through His infinite Buddha-knowledge. In this way, He has known the world of space (okāsaloka) in all its aspects. Thus, the Blessed One is to be understood as Lokavidū because He has known the world in every way.

He is called Anuttaro (Unsurpassed) because there is no one superior to Him in His own virtues. He is called Purisadammasārathi (Charioteer of men to be tamed) because He tames those who are fit to be tamed through various wonderful means of discipline.
166:
He is called 'Satthā' (Teacher) because he instructs as appropriate regarding the benefits of the present life, the benefits of the future life, and especially the ultimate goal, and because he delivers [beings from Saṃsāra]. The inclusion of gods and humans [in the phrase 'Teacher of gods and humans'] is done by way of defining the highest and by way of encompassing those capable of liberation. However, he also instructs [beings like] Nagas with regard to worldly benefits. He is called 'Buddha' because he knows all that is to be known (ñeyya) and by virtue of the 'Vimokkhantikāñāṇa' (knowledge at the end of liberation) which occurs at the conclusion of the fruit of Arahantship. Because:

"He is called 'Bhagavā' because he is fortunate, he has broken [defilements], he is endowed with [six] glories, he has analyzed the Dhamma, he has frequented [the Jhanas, Paths, and Fruits], and he has ended wandering in the three realms of existence."

This is just a summary here. These terms are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

'So imaṃ lokaṃ' means that the Blessed One [knows] this world. Now he shows the meaning to be stated. The meaning of terms like 'Sadevakaṃ' is the same as explained in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta and the Āḷavaka Sutta. 'Sayaṃ' means by himself, without being led by another. 'Abhiññā' means having known through higher knowledge. 'Sacchikatvā' means having realized for himself. 'Pavedeti' means he makes known, points out, and clearly reveals.

'So dhammaṃ deseti ... pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ': Out of compassion for beings, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, even having relinquished the unsurpassed bliss of seclusion. When he teaches that Dhamma, whether a little or a lot, he teaches it only in a way that is beautiful in the beginning and so forth. How? Even a single verse is beautiful in the beginning with its first line, beautiful in the middle with its second and third lines, and beautiful in the end with its last line, because the Dhamma is auspicious in every way. A Sutta with a single sequence is beautiful in the beginning with its introduction (nidāna), beautiful in the end with its conclusion (nigamana), and beautiful in the middle with the rest. A Sutta with multiple sequences is beautiful in the beginning with the first sequence, beautiful in the end with the last sequence, and beautiful in the middle with the remaining sequences.

The entire Teaching (Sāsana) is beautiful in the beginning with virtue (sīla) which is its essence, beautiful in the middle with tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala), and beautiful in the end with Nibbāna. Or, it is beautiful in the beginning with virtue and concentration, beautiful in the middle with insight and the Path, and beautiful in the end with the Fruit and Nibbāna. Or, it is beautiful in the beginning due to the Buddha's perfect awakening, beautiful in the middle due to the Dhamma's excellent nature, and beautiful in the end due to the Sangha's good practice. Or, for one who hears that Dhamma and practices accordingly, it is beautiful in the beginning with the Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) to be attained, beautiful in the middle with the Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa, and [beautiful in the end] with the Sāvaka-ñāṇa.
167:
...beautiful in the end. This Dhamma is beautiful in the beginning because even while being heard, it brings benefit just by hearing, as it can suppress hindrances and so forth. It is beautiful in the middle because while being practiced, it brings benefit through the practice itself, as it brings the bliss of tranquility and insight. It is beautiful in the end because when one has practiced and is established in the Fruit of the Path, it brings benefit through the fruit of practice, as it brings the state of 'Tādi' (steadfastness). It is beautiful in the beginning through the purity of origin, as it originates from the Buddha; beautiful in the middle through the purity of meaning; and beautiful in the end through the purity of purpose. Therefore, it should be understood that whether he teaches a little or a lot, he teaches only the Dhamma that is beautiful in the beginning, middle, and end.

In the phrases such as "Sātthaṃ Sabyañjanaṃ" (with meaning and with phrasing), when he teaches this Dhamma, he reveals the noble life of the Dispensation (Sāsana-brahmacariya) and the noble life of the Path (Magga-brahmacariya) through various methods. That teaching is 'Sāttha' due to the fulfillment of meaning, and 'Sabyañjana' due to the fulfillment of phrasing. It is 'Sāttha' because of the proper combination of conciseness, detailed explanation, revelation, analysis, clarification, designation, and meaningful terms. It is 'Sabyañjana' due to the fulfillment of letters, words, phrasing, modes, language, and description. It is 'Sāttha' due to the depth of meaning and the depth of penetration. It is 'Sabyañjana' due to the depth of the Dhamma and the depth of the teaching. It is 'Sāttha' because it is the object of the Attha-paṭisambhidā and Paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā. It is 'Sabyañjana' because it is the object of the Dhamma-paṭisambhidā and Nirutti-paṭisambhidā. It is 'Sāttha' because it is to be known by the wise and thus inspires faith in similar people. It is 'Sabyañjana' because it is to be believed and thus inspires faith in worldly people. It is 'Sāttha' because of its deep intention. It is 'Sabyañjana' because of its clear words. It is 'Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ' (entirely complete) because there is no meaning to be added, being complete in every way. It is 'Parisuddhaṃ' (pure) because there is no fault to be removed, being pure. It is 'Brahmacariya' because it is encompassed by the three trainings, because it is to be practiced by the noble ones, and because it is their way of life. Therefore, it is said, "He reveals the holy life... with meaning and with phrasing."

Alternatively, it is beautiful in the beginning because he teaches it with the introduction and the originating story. It is beautiful in the middle because it is suitable for those to be disciplined, because the meaning is not distorted, and because it is joined with reasons and examples. It is beautiful in the end because the listeners gain faith and because of the conclusion. Teaching in this way, he reveals the holy life. That holy life is 'Sāttha' because of the clear attainment (adhigama) through practice. It is 'Sabyañjana' because of the clear transmission (āgama) through learning (pariyatti). It is 'Kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ' because it is associated with the five groups of Dhamma (Sīla, etc.). It is 'Parisuddhaṃ' because it is free from defilements, because it proceeds for the sake of crossing over [Saṃsāra], and because it is independent of worldly lures. It is called 'Brahmacariya' because it has a noble meaning and is the practice of Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Disciples. Therefore, it is said, "That Blessed One teaches the Dhamma... reveals the holy life."

"Sādhu kho pana" means it brings benefit and happiness. "Dhammiyā kathāyā" means they heard that the Blessed One was coming with a discourse connected with benefit. Desiring to go and see the Blessed One, and thinking that juice is suitable for the Buddhas who abstain from eating after noon, they came bringing well-prepared mangoes in five hundred carts.
168:
That Dispensation is called pure because it is free from the defilements of impurity, it leads to liberation from the round of suffering, and it is devoid of concern for worldly gains. It is called 'Brahmacariya' (the Holy Life) because it is the practice of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who have become like Brahmā in the highest sense. Therefore, it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma... he reveals the Holy Life."

"Sādhu kho pana" means it is truly excellent, beneficial, and brings happiness. "Dhammiyā kathāyā" means (teaching) with a discourse connected to the benefits of beverages. This Keniya the ascetic heard of the Blessed One's arrival in the evening. Thinking, "I would be ashamed to go and see the Blessed One empty-handed; even for those who abstain from eating at the wrong time, beverages are allowable," he had five hundred carrying-poles of well-prepared jujube drink brought and went to him. As stated in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka: "Then this thought occurred to Keniya the ascetic: 'What should I have brought for the ascetic Gotama?'" (Mahāvagga 300), and so all should be understood.

Thereafter, just as the Blessed One showed the benefits of lodgings to the Sakyans in the Sekkha Sutta, the benefits of harmony to the three young men of good family in the Gosingasālavana, and the ten topics of discussion to the monks from the native land in the Rathavinīta Sutta, so too, with a discourse appropriate for that moment and connected to the benefits of beverages, he showed the benefits of the gift of beverages. He encouraged them to perform such meritorious deeds again and established them therein. He inspired them, making them enthusiastic and energetic. He gladdened them with the specific fruits of the present and the future. Therefore, it is said: "With a Dhamma talk... he gladdened them."

That Keniya the ascetic, being exceedingly pleased with the Blessed One, invited the Blessed One. The Blessed One, after declining three times, accepted by remaining silent. Therefore, it is said: "Then Keniya the ascetic... the Blessed One accepted by remaining silent."

Why did the Blessed One decline? It was so that through repeated requesting, the ascetic's merit would increase and he would prepare more offerings. Because of that requesting, he would obtain sixteen (pots of rice) prepared for eight hundred and fifty monks. If it is asked, "From where would the other three hundred monks come?"—even before the meal was prepared, Sela the Brahmin would go forth as a monk along with three hundred young students. Seeing this matter, the Blessed One spoke thus. "Mittāmacce" means friends and workers. "Ñātisālohite" means blood relatives such as sons and daughters, and other kinsmen.
169:
## 
"Yena" means "because of which." "Me" means "my." "Kāyaveyyāvaṭika" means physical service or duties. "Maṇḍalamāḷaṃ paṭiyādeti" means preparing a pavilion with a white canopy.

"Tiṇṇံ vedānaṃ" refers to the three Vedas: the Iruveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda. "Sanighaṇḍukeṭubhānaṃ" refers to being proficient in the texts along with the Nighaṇḍu and Keṭubha. "Nighaṇḍu" is the text that explains synonyms for trees and other things. "Keṭubha" is the text on the science of rituals and poetic composition for the benefit of the wise (poets). "Sakkharappabhedānaṃ" refers to being proficient in the texts along with the analysis of letters. "Akkharappabheda" refers to the Sikkhā (phonetics) and Nirutti (etymology). "Itihāsapañcamānaṃ" means those texts in which the Itihāsa (history/epics), consisting of ancient legends associated with the words "Thus it was, thus it was," is the fifth, with the Atharvaveda being the fourth. He is a "Padaka Veyyākaraṇa" because he is one who studies and knows the words and the remaining grammar of those five texts. He is called "Anavayo" (proficient/complete) in the Lokāyata (casuistry) and the Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa (the science of the marks of a Great Man), which consists of twelve thousand verses for determining the marks of a Great Man, because he is one who practices them fully without deficiency. It means he is not "avaya" (deficient). One is called "avaya" if they are unable to maintain those texts in terms of both meaning and wording (gantha).

Walking that is suitable for the calves is called "jaṅghāvihāra." It refers to walking a distance that is not too long in order to stretch the legs and dispel the fatigue caused by sitting for a long time. "Anucaṅkamamāno" means simply walking up and down. "Anuvicaramāno" means wandering here and there. The hermitage of Keniya the ascetic means Keniya's dwelling place. "Āvāha" means taking a bride. "Vivāha" means giving a bride. "Mahāyañña" means a great sacrifice. "Māgadha" means the ruler of the Magadha kingdom. He is called "Seniya" because he is endowed with a great army. "Bimbi" means gold; therefore, he is called "Bimbisāra" because he has a complexion like excellent gold. "So me nimantito" means "That Buddha has been invited by me."

Then, Sela the Brahmin, because of his previously performed meritorious deeds, upon hearing the word "Buddha," felt as if he were being sprinkled with the Deathless (Nectar) and, in a state of amazement, said: "O Keniya, did you say 'Buddha'?" The other, stating the truth as it was, said: "O Sela, I said 'Buddha'." Then, to make it certain, he asked Keniya the ascetic again, and Keniya informed him in the same way. Then, (considering) the rarity of the sound "Buddha" even in a hundred thousand aeons...
170:
Desiring to show the rarity of the sound 'Buddha', he said: "Even this sound 'Buddha' is rare in the world." In that statement, "yadidaṃ" is a particle, meaning "that which is this sound." Then, upon hearing the sound 'Buddha', the Brahmin Sela, desiring to investigate, thought: "Is he truly a Buddha, or is he a Buddha only by name?" Or he spoke the words: "āgatāni kho pana ... vivaṭṭacchado." In that passage, "mantesu" means in the Vedas. Even before the Buddha appeared, the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, in the guise of Brahmins, inserted the marks into the Vedas and taught them, saying: "According to these marks, beings of great power will recognize the Tathāgata." For that reason, the marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisa) appeared in the Vedas in ancient times. However, after the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, they gradually disappeared; therefore, they no longer exist today. "Mahāpurisassa" refers to a man who is great in qualities such as aspiration, the undertaking of knowledge, and compassion. "Dveva gatiyo" means there are only two destinies (final outcomes). This word 'gati' is used in the sense of realms of rebirth in passages such as "Sāriputta, there are these five destinies"; in the sense of a place in passages such as "The destiny of wild animals is the forest"; in the sense of wisdom in passages such as "Thus, those possessed of superior wisdom (gati)"; and in the sense of pervasiveness in passages such as "reached pervasiveness (gatigata)." Here, however, it should be understood in the sense of a final outcome. In this context, although one who is endowed with these marks becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti), it is not because of those marks alone that he becomes a Buddha. However, because they belong to the same class (jātisaamañña), they are called the same marks. Therefore, it is said: "For one endowed with these marks."

"If he lives the life of a householder" means if he dwells in a home. "He becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti)" means he is called a King (Rājā) because he pleases the world through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu) and the four wonderful qualities. He causes the Wheel-treasure to turn. He exists through the four wheels of prosperity (sampatticakka), and through them, he causes others to prosper. Because the turning of the wheels of his postures (iriyāpathacakka) exists for the benefit of others, he is called a Cakkavatti. In this phrase, "Rājā" is a general term, and "Cakkavatti" is a qualifying term. He is called "dhammika" because he practices according to the Dhamma, meaning he conducts himself justly and fairly. He is called "Dhammarājā" because he becomes a king after obtaining kingship through righteous means. Alternatively, he is "dhammika" by performing deeds for the benefit of others, and "Dhammarājā" by performing deeds for his own benefit. He is called "cāturanto" because he is the lord of the earth bounded by the four oceans; it means he is the lord of the earth adorned with the four great islands and bounded by the four oceans. He is called "vijitāvī" (conqueror) because he has conquered internal enemies such as anger and all external kings. "Janapadatthāvariyappatto" means he has reached a state of stability and permanence in the country, such that no one is able to shake it...
171:
He is called "janapadatthāvariyappatto" (one who has reached the highest stability in the realm) because no one can shake him, or because, due to that Wheel-turning Monarch, the country has reached a state of long-lasting stability where the people, free from envy, are constantly devoted to their own duties and remain unshakable.

"Seyyathidaṃ" is a particle meaning "as follows" or "what are those treasures?" The seven treasures, from the Wheel-treasure to the Counselor-treasure, have been explained in detail in all their aspects in the commentary on the Ratana Sutta. Among those treasures, this Wheel-turning Monarch conquers unconquered enemies with the Wheel-treasure; he travels at will through conquered countries with the Elephant-treasure and Horse-treasure; he protects conquered countries with the Counselor-treasure; and he enjoys the pleasure of use and possession with the remaining treasures. Through the first treasure, he is endowed with the power of effort (ussāha-satti); through the Elephant, Horse, and Householder treasures, he is endowed with the power of authority (pabhu-satti); and through the Counselor-treasure, he is well-endowed with the power of counsel (manta-satti). Through the Woman-treasure and the Gem-treasure, he obtains the fruits of these three powers. The Wheel-turning Monarch enjoys the pleasure of wealth through the Woman-treasure and the Gem-treasure, and the pleasure of sovereignty through the remaining treasures. Specifically, his first three treasures are accomplished through the power of kamma born from the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa); the middle three treasures through the power of kamma born from the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha); and the final one, the Counselor-treasure, should be understood as being accomplished through the power of kamma born from the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha).

"Parosahassa" means a number exceeding one thousand. "Sūrā" refers to those who are brave by nature. "Vīraṅgarūpā" is interpreted by some teachers as those having bodies like celestial beings. In this context, according to their nature, the noble and brave are called "vīrā"; the limb (cause) of the brave is "vīraṅga," which refers to energy (vīriya) as the cause of being brave. They are called "vīraṅgarūpā" because they have bodies as if made of energy. "Parasenappamaddanā" means they are capable of crushing an enemy army if it stands before them. "Dhammena" means by the Dhamma of the Five Precepts, such as "one should not kill living beings."

In the phrase "He is an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One in the world, one who has drawn back the veil (vivaṭṭacchado)," he is called "vivaṭṭacchado" because, while the world was covered in the darkness of defilements by the seven veils of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, views, ignorance, and misconduct, he drew back that veil and remained having produced light all around. In that passage, the first term shows his worthiness of veneration; the second term shows the reason for that worthiness, which is that he is a Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). The third term should be understood as showing the cause of his Buddhahood, which is the removal of the veil. Alternatively, he is "vivaṭṭacchado" because he is free from the round of rebirth (vivaṭṭa) and free from the veil (vicchada). He is called "Arahaṃ" because of the absence of the round of rebirth, and "Sammāsambuddha" because of the absence of the veil; thus, these are the two causes for the previous two terms. Between those two, the first term (Arahaṃ) is accomplished here by the second, the knowledge of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), and the second term (Sammāsambuddha) is accomplished by the first.
172:
The completion of the third term occurs through the third and fourth terms of 'vivaṭṭacchadda'. It should be understood that the first term, 'arahant', accomplishes the Eye of Dhamma (dhamma-cakkhu); the second term, 'sammāsambuddha', accomplishes the Eye of a Buddha (buddha-cakkhu); and the third term, 'vivaṭṭacchadda', accomplishes the All-seeing Eye (samanta-cakkhu).

Now, desiring to go to the presence of the Blessed One, the Brahmin Sela said: "Where, sir... is the Fully Enlightened One?" In the words beginning with "Thus spoken" (evaṃ vutte), "by which way" (yena-esā) means in whichever direction this region lies. "Blue forest range" (nīlavanarājī) refers to a row of blue-colored trees. It is said that the forest resembles a row of dark clouds. Pointing to where the Blessed One was staying at that time, he said: "Where this blue forest range is, O Sela." In that context, the phrase "He dwells there" is an ellipsis, or the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative. "Step by step" (pade padaṃ) means placing a foot near the previous footprint. By this, he forbids hurried walking. "For they are difficult to approach" (durāsadā hi) states the reason. Because those Buddhas are far from being disturbed by sounds and so on, therefore he said: "Sirs, come in this manner."

If it is asked, "For what reason are they difficult to approach?" They wander alone like lions. Just as lions wander alone because they have no need for companions, so too those Buddhas dwell alone because of their love for seclusion. With the words beginning with "And when I..." (yadā cāhaṃ), he teaches those young students the proper conduct in the presence [of the Buddha]. Therein, "Do not interrupt" (mā opātetha) means do not interject or speak. "Let them wait" (āgamentu) means let them be patient; the meaning is to remain silent until the talk reaches its conclusion.

"He sought" (samannesi) means he searched. "For the most part" (yebhuyyena) means he saw many marks and did not see a few. Therefore, pointing out those he did not see, he said: "Except for two." "He doubts" (kaṅkhati) means he gives rise to doubt and produces the longing: "Oh, if only I could see them!" "He is uncertain" (vicikicchati) means that although he investigates those marks here and there, he is unable to see them and becomes weary. "He does not resolve" (nādhimuccati) means he cannot reach a conclusion because of strong doubt. "He is not satisfied" (na sampasīdati) means because of such doubt, he does not attain confidence in the Blessed One, thinking, "This ascetic Gotama possesses the complete marks." Alternatively, "doubt" (kaṅkhā) refers to weak uncertainty, "vacillation" (vicikicchā) to medium uncertainty, and "non-resolution" (anadhimuccanatā) to strong uncertainty. By "lack of satisfaction" (asampasāda), it means the turbidity of the mind caused by those three states.

"Enclosed in a sheath" (kosohita) means covered by a membrane. "Privy member" (vatthaguyha) refers to the male organ. For the Blessed One's privy member, enclosed in a sheath like that of a noble elephant, is golden-colored and resembles the interior of a lotus. Because it was covered by a cloth, he could not see it, and because he did not notice the extensiveness of the tongue within the mouth, he was doubtful regarding those two marks.
173:
He was doubtful and unable to decide. What is the nature of "such a kind" (tathārūpaṃ)? What should we say in this matter? This point was previously answered by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda:

"Venerable Nāgasena, the Blessed One has performed a difficult task." "Great King, what task has he performed?"
