"Venerable sir, the Blessed One showed the privy member, which is a cause for shame among the public, to the Brahmin Brahmāyu, to the student Uttara, to the sixteen Brahmin disciples of Bāvarī, and to the three hundred students of the Brahmin Sela." "Great King, the Blessed One did not show the hidden privy member [directly]; the Blessed One showed it only by way of a sign. Having created it by psychic power, he showed only a shadow-image of himself wearing the undergarment, bound with the waistband, and clad in the robe." "Venerable sir, when the shadow-image is seen, is it not as if he himself is seen?" "Let that be, Great King. If there were a being who could be enlightened only by seeing the heart, the Fully Enlightened One would even take out his heart and show it." "Venerable Nāgasena, your words are most fitting."

"Having extended" (ninnāmetvā) means having taken out. Here, it should be understood that by touching the ear-holes, the length of the tongue was shown; by touching the nostrils, the thinness of the tongue was shown; and by covering the forehead, the breadth of the tongue was shown. "Of teachers and teachers' teachers" (ācariyapācariyānaṃ) means of the teachers and the teachers of the teachers. "In his own praise" (sake vaṇṇe) means his own virtues.

"Complete in body" (paripuṇṇakāyo) means having a body complete due to the perfection of the marks and the lack of deficiency in limbs and parts. "Beautifully radiant" (surucī) means having a beautiful bodily aura. "Well-born" (sujāto) means well-produced with perfection in height, girth, and form. "Lovely to behold" (cārudassano) means having an appearance that is delightful, not repulsive, and which brings no satiation even to those who look for a long time. Some teachers, however, say "lovely to behold" means having beautiful eyes. "Golden-colored" (suvaṇṇavaṇṇo) means having a color like gold. The word "you are" (asi) should be applied to all the preceding terms. "Having very white teeth" (susukkadāṭho) means having extremely white canine teeth. From the Blessed One's canine teeth, rays as white as moonbeams emerge. Therefore, it is said: "You have very white teeth."

"Marks of a Great Man" (mahāpurisalakkhaṇā) is a conclusion using different words for the characteristics mentioned previously.
174:
Now, wishing to praise the Blessed One with the physical characteristics he most admired among those marks, he spoke the words beginning with "He has clear eyes." The Blessed One has clear eyes because he is endowed with the fivefold clarity of vision. He has a beautiful face because his face is like the full orb of the moon. He has a stately body because he is endowed with perfection in height and circumference. He has an upright body because his limbs are straight like those of Mahābrahmā. He is majestic because he possesses a radiant glow. Even the characteristic mentioned previously is stated again here, praising him through this method: "In the midst of the community of monks." For one with such characteristics shines in this way. This same method should be understood for the subsequent verse as well.

## 557-8.
"Uttamavaṇṇino" means one endowed with an excellent complexion. "Jambusaṇḍassa" means of the Rose-apple Island (Jambudīpa). This is said to praise his sovereignty because it is a well-known island. In fact, a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) is the ruler of all four great islands.

"Khattiyā" refers to those who are nobles by birth. "Bhojā" refers to those who are wealthy. "Rājāno" refers to any persons who exercise kingship. "Anuyantā" refers to the followers and servants who constantly attend. "Rājābhirājā" means a king honored by other kings, implying a Universal Monarch. "Manujindo" means being the chief and supreme lord of men.

When this was said, the Blessed One, wishing to fulfill the heart's desire of the brahmin Sela—thinking, "Those Worthy Ones, the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, manifest themselves when their virtues are spoken of"—said, "I am a king." The meaning therein is this: "O Sela, for whatever reason you entreat me, saying 'You deserve to be a king, a Universal Monarch,' be free from concern regarding this kingship; I am indeed a king. While another king, being a king, might rule over a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, or five hundred yojanas, or even a thousand yojanas, or as a Universal Monarch up to the limits of the four great islands, I do not have such a limited domain. I am the incomparable King of Dhamma, and I rule from the pinnacle of existence (Bhavagga) down to the Avīci hell, and horizontally across immeasurable world systems. As far as there are beings—those without feet, those with two feet, and so on—I am the foremost among them. There is no one equal to me in virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), or the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimuttiñāṇadassana). Such as I am, the incomparable King of Dhamma, I set in motion the wheel by means of the Dhamma known as the incomparable factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), such as the four foundations of mindfulness, with instructions such as 'Abandon this, dwell having attained that'—this is the Wheel of Authority (āṇācakka) which is the scriptural Dhamma (pariyatti); or I set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka) itself through the scriptural Dhamma, beginning with 'Now this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering.' The wheel..."
175:
"Appaṭivattiyaṃ" means a wheel that cannot be turned back by a recluse or by anyone else in the world.

561-2. Seeing the Blessed One thus manifesting himself, Sela, filled with joy and happiness, spoke two verses beginning with "You claim to be fully enlightened" for the sake of confirmation. In those verses, he asked, "Who is the general (senāpati) of the Venerable King of Dhamma, the one who follows in turning the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by the Dhamma?"

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting on the right side of the Blessed One, shining with glory like a mass of gold. Pointing to the Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Set in motion by me." In that verse, "anujāto tathāgataṃ" means one who is born following the Tathāgata due to the right cause; the meaning is one born because of the Tathāgata.

Having thus answered the question "Who is the general?", and wishing to remove doubt regarding Sela's statement "You claim to be fully enlightened," the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with "What is to be directly known (abhiññeyyaṃ)" to make him understand: "I do not claim to be a Buddha merely by making a claim; rather, I am a Buddha because of this reason." In that verse, "abhiññeyya" refers to true knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti). Although the Truth of the Path and the Truth of the Origin are things to be developed and abandoned respectively, by mentioning the cause, the results are achieved, and thus the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of Suffering are also effectively stated. Therefore, it is meant in this discourse that what should be realized has been realized, and what should be fully understood has been fully understood. Thus, showing the fruit of developing the Four Noble Truths and true knowledge and liberation, he establishes his Buddhahood with the proper reason: "Having known what is to be known, I have become a Buddha."

565-7. Having thus manifested himself without reservation, and wishing to urge the brahmin to overcome his doubts about him, he spoke three verses beginning with "Subdue [your doubt] (vinayassu)." In those verses, "sallakatto" means a surgeon who has removed the seven darts, such as the dart of lust. "Brahmabhūto" means one who has become supreme. "Atitulo" means one who has transcended comparison or example; the meaning is incomparable. "Mārasenappamaddano" means the crusher of the army of Māra, which is described as the assembly of Māra that disparages others, beginning with "Sensual pleasures are your first army." "Sabbaṃ" (all) refers to bringing all enemies under his control, such as the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), the Māra of death (maccu-māra), and the Māra as a deity (devaputta-māra).
176:
He is the subduer of Māra’s army. 'Sabbāmitte' refers to all enemies, such as the Māra of the aggregates (khandha-māra), the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), the Māra of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra-māra), the Māra of death (maccu-māra), and the Māra as a deity (devaputta-māra). 'Vasīkatvā' means having brought under one's own control. 'Akutobhayo' means one who has no fear from any quarter.

568-70. When this was said, Sela the Brahmin immediately gained faith in the Blessed One and, desiring ordination, being well-urged by his matured merit of supportive conditions (upanissaya-sampatti), spoke the three verses beginning with 'Imaṃ bhavanto'. In those verses, 'Kaṇhābhijātiko' refers to one born in a low caste, such as the Caṇḍālas.

Furthermore, those youths also desired ordination in the same way; being clansmen who had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) together with Sela, they spoke the verse beginning with 'Etañce ruccati bhoto'. Then Sela, with a joyful heart towards those youths, pointing them out and requesting ordination, spoke the verse beginning with 'Brāhmaṇā'.

Then the Blessed One, knowing that in the past, during the dispensation of the Buddha Padumuttara, Sela had been the leader of these same three hundred men, and together with them had built a monastery (pariveṇa) and performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), and consequently enjoyed the bliss of devas and humans, and in this final birth had become their teacher; and knowing that their karma was ripe for liberation from defilements and served as a supportive condition for the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination—therefore, wishing to ordain them all with the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Svākkhātaṃ'. In that verse, 'Sandiṭṭhikaṃ' means directly visible. 'Akālikaṃ' means the fruit is to be attained without delay, as the fruit arises immediately after the path. 'Yattha' means 'due to which cause' (due to the practice of the path). For one who is diligent, not lacking in mindfulness, and trains in the three trainings, ordination is not in vain. Therefore, he said: 'Svākkhātaṃ...pe... sikkhato'.

Having spoken thus, the Blessed One said, 'Come, monks' (Etha bhikkhavo). They all became monks possessed of bowls and robes, and coming through the air, they paid homage to the Blessed One. Thus, referring to their 'Ehi Bhikkhu' status, the reciters of the council (saṅgītikāras) said: 'Alattha kho selo...pe... upasampadaṃ'.
177:
'Bhuttāviṃ' means one who has eaten. 'Onītapattapāṇiṃ' means one who has removed his hand from the bowl, which means one who has washed his hands. In this context, the elided word 'upagantvā' (having approached) should be understood. Otherwise, the statement 'sat down near the Blessed One' would not be appropriate.

'Aggihuttamukhā' was spoken by the Blessed One to please the mind of Keṇiya the ascetic. In that verse, since there is no sacrifice for Brahmins without the fire-offering, it was said: 'Among sacrifices, the fire-offering is the foremost.' It means the fire-offering is the best, the primary. Because it is to be recited first by those reciting the Vedas, the Sāvitrī verse is called 'the foremost of meters'. Because he is the best among men, the king is called 'the foremost'. Because it is the repository and refuge of rivers, the ocean is called 'the foremost'. Because it enables the recognition of 'Today is the Kattikā constellation, today is the Rohiṇī constellation' through its conjunction, and because it provides light and is pleasant, it is said: 'The moon is the foremost of constellations.' Because it is the best among those that burn and shine, the sun is said to be 'the foremost of those that burn'. Because the Saṅgha is the best among those worthy of offerings, especially at that time, referring to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, it was said: 'For those seeking merit, the Saṅgha is indeed the foremost of those to be sacrificed to.' By this, he shows that the Saṅgha is the source (āyamukha) of merit.

Sela the Elder spoke another verse of declaration beginning with 'Yaṃ taṃ saraṇaṃ'. The meaning of that verse is: 'O Blessed One, endowed with the five eyes, we went to you for refuge on the eighth day from today. Therefore, within seven days, we have become tamed by the unsurpassed discipline in your dispensation. Oh, how wonderful is the power of taking refuge in you!'

577-8. After that, having praised the Blessed One with two verses, he requested to pay homage with the third verse:
'These three hundred monks stand with palms joined.
O Hero, stretch out your feet;
Let these noble ones (nāgā) pay homage to the Teacher.'

## The explanation of the Sela Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary
## of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
178:
## 8. Sallasutta-vaṇṇanā

The Salla Sutta begins with 'Animittaṃ'. How did this sutta arise? It is said that a son of a lay follower, who was an attendant of the Blessed One, passed away. Overwhelmed by grief for his son, that lay follower remained without food for seven days. The Blessed One, out of compassion for him, went to his house and taught this Salla Sutta to dispel his grief.

In that sutta, 'animittaṃ' means being devoid of a sign or cause for action. For example, in cases such as 'When I wink my eye or raise my eyebrow, steal that item by that sign,' there is a sign or cause for action; however, there is no such sign in life. Indeed, it is impossible to obtain the right to live by saying, 'Live as long as I am doing this or that; do not die yet.' 'Anaññātaṃ' means that because there is no such sign, it is impossible to know for certain that 'this person must live for this much or that much time,' whether by way of destination (gati) or by way of the limit of lifespan. Just as the lifespan of the devas in the Realm of the Four Great Kings is limited, it is not so for mortals; thus, it is also unknown for certain.

'Kasiraṃ' means difficult and not easily maintained because its existence is dependent on many conditions. Indeed, that life is dependent on the in-breath, dependent on the out-breath, dependent on the great elements (mahābhūta), dependent on physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra), dependent on internal heat (usmā), and dependent on consciousness (viññāṇa). If one does not breathe in, one does not live; if one does not breathe out, one does not live. Among the four elements, like a person bitten by a venomous snake such as the Kaṭṭhamukha, when the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) is disturbed, the body first becomes stiff like a log. Therefore, it is said:

'The body becomes stiff, as if bitten by a Kaṭṭhamukha snake;
Due to the disturbance of the earth element, it becomes just like a Kaṭṭhamukha.'

When the water element (āpo-dhātu) is disturbed, the body reaches a state of putrefaction, with pus and blood flowing out, leaving only bones and skin. Therefore, it is said:

'The body becomes putrid, as if bitten by a Pūtimukha snake;
Due to the disturbance of the water element, it becomes just like a Pūtimukha.'

When the fire element (tejo-dhātu) is disturbed, it burns all around as if placed in a pit of glowing embers. How is it stated?
179:
'The body becomes heated, as if bitten by an Aggimukha snake;
Due to the disturbance of the fire element, it becomes just like an Aggimukha.'

When the air element (vāyo-dhātu) is disturbed, the connections of the joints are severed, and it is as if the bones are being crushed and pulverized with stones. Therefore, it is said:

'The body is severed, as if bitten by a Satthamukha snake;
Due to the disturbance of the air element, it becomes just like a Satthamukha.'

A person whose body is afflicted by the disturbance of the elements also cannot live. However, when those elements carry on equally, performing their mutual functions such as providing a foundation, then life proceeds. Thus, life is dependent on the great elements. In times of famine and the like, the exhaustion of life of beings due to the cutting off of nutriment is indeed evident. Thus, life is dependent on physical nutriment. Likewise, when the kamma-born fire element that digests what is eaten and drunk is exhausted, it is also evident that beings reach the end of life. Thus, life is dependent on heat. Furthermore, from the moment consciousness (viññāṇa) ceases, there is no more life for beings; this is also well-known in the world. Thus, life is dependent on consciousness. In this way, life should be understood as difficult (kasiraṃ) because its existence is dependent on many conditions.

'Parittañca' means brief or trifling. Compared to the life of the devas, it is like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass; or it is brief because it does not exist beyond a single thought-moment (cittakkhaṇa). Even a being with an extremely long lifespan lived with a past thought, but does not live now and will not live later; they will live with a future thought, but do not live now and did not live before; they live with the present thought, but did not live before and will not live later. And this has been said:

'Life, the individual identity (attabhāva), and all pleasures and pains,
Are joined with a single thought; the moment passes quickly.

Even those devas who remain for eighty-four thousand aeons,
Do not live joined with two thoughts.'

'Tañca dukkhena saṃyutaṃ' means that life, although being thus signless, unknown, difficult, and brief, is joined with the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha), the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), and the suffering of pain (dukkha-dukkha) such as the touch of cold, heat, gadflies, and mosquitoes, as well as hunger and thirst. What is meant? Because the life of mortals is of such a nature,
180:
Therefore, as long as that life has not yet expired, cultivate only the practice of Dhamma; do not grieve for your son.

If you should think, "Even though I protected my son with all resources and provisions, my son has died, and therefore I grieve," do not grieve in this way either. There is no such effort by which beings, once born, do not die. It means that it is impossible to protect born beings from death through any kind of effort. Then, because that person thought, "Venerable Sir, death is appropriate only after reaching old age; my son has died while still very young," the Buddha said: "Death comes even after reaching old age; such is the nature of living beings." It means that death occurs whether one has reached old age or not; there is no fixed rule in this matter.

Now, wishing to establish this point with a simile, he spoke the verse beginning with "Phalānamiva pakkānaṃ". The meaning of that verse is: Just as, from sunrise, when the tree becomes heated by the sun's heat, the essence of earth and the essence of water gradually enter the earth from the leaves to the branches, from the branches to the trunk, and from the trunk to the roots; but from sunset, they rise again from the earth to the roots, from the roots to the trunk, and so on to the branches, leaves, and sprouts. Even though they rise in this way, they no longer enter the base of the stalk in a fruit that has reached maturity. Then, due to the sun's heat, a burning sensation arises at the base of the stalk. Therefore, those fruits fall constantly every morning. It means that for those fruits, there is danger because of falling. Likewise, for born mortals, there is always danger because of death. Beings are like ripe fruits.

583-6. Furthermore, there is much more to be said: "Just as a potter's... [pe]... life." Therefore, "Both the young... [pe]... the final goal"—reflect in this way. Having reflected thus, reflect also: "Their death... [pe]... or kinsmen." Because a father cannot save his son, nor kinsmen their kin, he said: "While they are looking on... [pe]... is led away."

The grammatical connection in that verse is: While the kinsmen are looking on and lamenting in many ways, such as "Mother, Father," etc., among mortals...
181:
Just as an ox to be slaughtered is led away, so mortals are led away one by one. Lay devotee, see this world as being so without protection.

In that matter of death, there are those such as Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas who are endowed with fortitude. Because they know, "In this way, the world is afflicted by death and old age; no one is able to provide protection," the wise do not grieve, having understood the nature of the world. It means they do not grieve, knowing this nature of the world.

But you lament the path of one whose [path you do not know]. What does this mean? You do not know the path by which he came to his mother's womb, nor the path by which he went elsewhere after passing away from here. Not seeing these two ends of that person, you lament uselessly. But the wise, seeing them and knowing the nature of the world, do not grieve.

Now, wishing to demonstrate the uselessness of the lamentation mentioned in "You lament uselessly," he spoke the verse beginning with "Paridevayamāno ce". In that verse, "udabbahe" means one should carry or bear; it means one should produce within oneself. "Sammūဠှော hiṃsamattānaṃ" means being deluded and harming oneself. "Kayirā ce naṃ vicakkhaṇo" means if such lamentation could bring any benefit, the wise person would also perform that lamentation.

The connection of the meaning in the phrase "Na hi ruṇṇေန" is: No one at all can reach peace of mind through weeping or through grief. On the contrary, for one who weeps and grieves, suffering only increases further, and the body deteriorates through loss of complexion and so on.

"Na tena petā" means that by such lamentation, those who have passed away cannot be protected or sustained. That lamentation is of no use to them. Therefore, lamentation is useless.

Indeed, it is not only useless but also brings harm. Why? Because it is said: "Not abandoning grief... [pe]... he goes under the sway [of death]." In that verse, "anutthunanto" means grieving repeatedly. "Vasamanvagū" means coming under the power of death.
182:
Having thus shown the futility and the harmfulness of grief, now, wishing to give advice to dispel grief, he spoke the verse beginning with "Look at others as well." In that verse, "gamine" means those who are prepared to go to the next world. "Phandantevidha pāṇino" means beings in this world who are trembling with the fear of death.

"Yena yena" means in whatever way they think: "He will live long, he will be free from disease." It happens only in a way other than what was thought; the person so thought of also dies and also falls ill. Such separation happens contrary to what was thought. "O lay follower, look at the nature of the world"—thus should the connection of the meaning here be understood.

"Arahato sutvā" means having heard such a Dhamma teaching of the Buddha, the Worthy One. "Neso labbhā mayā iti" means that deceased person—realizing "It is not possible for him to live again for me now"—should dispel lamentation; this is the meaning.

What more is there to say? "As one would [extinguish] a burning house... should destroy," he said. In that verse, one should be known as "dhīro" (the steadfast) because of being endowed with fortitude, as "sapanno" (the wise) because of natural wisdom, as "paṇḍito" (the learned) because of wisdom from great learning, and as "kusalo" (the skilful) because of being clever by nature. Or, it should be connected with wisdom resulting from reflection (cintāmaya-paññā), wisdom resulting from hearing (sutamaya-paññā), and wisdom resulting from mental development (bhāvanāmaya-paññā).

598-9. Not only grief, but also lamentation... one's own dart (should be destroyed). In that verse, "pajappaṃ" means craving (taṇhā). "Domanassaṃ" means mental suffering. "Abbahe" means one should pull out. "Sallaṃ" (the dart) means these three things, in the sense of being difficult to extract and in the sense of piercing within. Or, it refers to the seven kinds of darts such as lust, etc., mentioned previously. When that dart is pulled out, the one who has pulled out the dart... is at peace—thus he concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. In that verse, "asito" means one who is not dependent on craving and views. "Pappuyya" means having reached. The remaining words are not explained because their meanings are clear, having been mentioned before this sutta.

## The explanation of the Salla Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary
## of the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
183:
## 9. Vāseṭṭhasutta-vaṇṇanā

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is called the Vāseṭṭha Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? Its origin is exactly as stated in the introduction (nidāna). We shall provide the commentary by avoiding those words whose meanings have already been explained or whose meanings are already clear. Icchānaṅgala is the name of a village. These names of the great wealthy Brahmins—Caṅkī, Tārukkha, and Todeyya—are merely conventional names (vohāra-nāma). The names Pokkharasāti and Jāṇussoṇi are causal names (nemittika). Among them, it is said that one [child] was conceived in a lotus (paduma) in a lotus pond (pokkharaṇī) near the Himalayas; a certain ascetic, seeing the child lying in that lotus, raised him and presented him to the King of Kosala. Because he lay in a lotus (pokkhara), he was named "Pokkharasāti." To another, a causal name was given according to his high position. That person is well-known by that title because he obtained the position of chaplain (purohita) named Jāṇussoṇi.

Why did all of them and other famous great wealthy Brahmins reside in Icchānaṅgala? They resided there for the purpose of reciting and investigating the Vedas. At that time, the Brahmins in the Kosala country who were experts in the Vedas gathered in that very village for the purpose of reciting the Vedas and for the purpose of investigating their meaning. Therefore, they also came from their respective fief-villages (bhoga-gāma) from time to time and resided there.

"Vāseṭṭhabhāradvājānaṃ" means to Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja. "This intermediate talk" (antarākathā) means that while they were wandering about speaking words suitable for their friendship, this other talk arose in the very midst of that conversation. "Saṃsuddhagahaṇiko" means one of pure womb, meaning one born only in the womb of a pure Brahmin woman. For in the passages beginning with "samavepākiniyā gahaṇiyā," the digestive fire (udaraggi) is called "gahaṇီ." But in this sutta, it means the mother's womb. "Up to seven generations" means up to seven generations back, such as the mother's mother and the father's father. Here, the grandfather and grandmother are called "pitāmahā"; likewise, the maternal grandfather and grandmother are called "mātāmahā"; and grandfathers and grandmothers [collectively] are also called "pitāmahā." A pair of grandfathers is called "pitāmahayugaṃ." "Yuga" means the extent of life. Although this word is just a designation, in terms of meaning, the grandfathers themselves are called "pitāmahayugaṃ." "Akkhitto" means not being reproached by anyone regarding birth, such as "Who is he?" ...
184:
Anavaññāto, anupakkuṭṭho means one who has not been previously reproached by way of disparaging their lineage. Vatasampanno means one who is endowed with conduct. Saññāpetunti means for the purpose of making known, making understand, or doing continuously. Āyāmā means "let us go."

Anuññātapatiññātā means those who are acknowledged as disciples, having been authorized by their teachers saying, "You are masters of the three Vedas," and having acknowledged it themselves. Asmā means "we are." Ubho refers to both young men. "I am the senior resident pupil and chief disciple of Pokkharasāti, and this one is the disciple of the Brahmin Tārukkha"—this is said with the intention of showing the excellence of the teacher and one's own attainment.

Tevijjānanti means of those who possess the three Vedas. Kevalino means those who have reached the end (perfection). Asmase means "we are." Now, wishing to elaborate on that state of perfection, he said, "Padakasmā... pe... sādisā," and so on. In that verse, jappe means in the Vedas. Kammunā means by the ten-fold wholesome courses of action. This Brahmin Vāseṭṭha previously referred to the seven-fold bodily and verbal actions with the words "When, sir, one is virtuous (sīlavā)." He referred to the three-fold mental actions with "endowed with practice (vatasampanno)." Because he is endowed with those qualities, he is one endowed with conduct.

## 602-5.
Now, wishing to show that endowment of conduct with other words, he said, "And I speak by action (Ahañca kammunā brūmī)." Khayātītanti means having transcended deficiency, meaning complete or perfect. Peccā means having approached. Namassantī means they perform an act of homage. Cakkhu loke samuppannanti means in the world which is a mass of darkness due to ignorance, having destroyed that darkness and showing the welfare of the present life and so forth, he has arisen as the eye of wisdom.

Having praised him thus, when requested by Vāseṭṭha, the Blessed One, wishing to favor both young men, said, "I will explain them to you (Tesaṃ vo ahaṃ vyakkhissaṃ)," and so on. Therein, vyakkhissanti means "I will answer." Anupubbaṃ means let the considerations of the Brahmins be for now; I will explain to you in due order starting from insects, grass, and trees—this is how the meaning should be understood. These young men were indeed to be disciplined by such an elaborate discourse. Jātivibhaṅganti means the detailed classification of births. Aññamaññā hi jātiyo means the births of various living beings are different and diverse from one another.
185:
Furthermore, when the detailed classification of the births of living beings is to be taught, he began by first teaching things not acquired by kamma (non-sentient), saying, "Know also the grass and trees." For what purpose is it taught thus? It is to make the distinction of births easily understood among sentient beings acquired by kamma. Indeed, if the distinction of births is understood among non-sentient things like grass and trees, that distinction becomes even more evident among sentient beings.

Among those, what is called "grass" (tiṇa) has a pithless interior and a solid exterior. Therefore, trees such as palms and coconuts are also included in the category of grass. What is called a "tree" (rukkha) has a pithless exterior and a solid interior. Both grass and trees are called "grass and trees" (tiṇarukkha). Wishing to show them in the accusative plural, he said, "Know also the grass and trees."

And those grass and trees do not acknowledge, "We are grass, we are trees." Liṅgaṃ jātimayaṃ means that although they do not acknowledge it, the form of those grass and trees, which is produced by their species, is just like their fundamental nature as grass and so forth. Why is that? Because the species are different from one another. For the species of grass is one, and the species of trees is another. Even among grasses, the species of palm is one, and the species of coconut is another; thus it should be elaborated.

What is shown by saying this? That which is different by way of species can be distinguished from other species even without one's own acknowledgment or the instruction of others. If one were a Brahmin by birth, then that Brahmin should also be distinguishable from the warrior caste, the merchant caste, or the menial caste even without his own acknowledgment or the instruction of others. However, he is not so distinguishable. Therefore, it shows that one is not a Brahmin by birth. Later on, with the verse beginning "Just as among these species (Yathā etāsu jātīsu)," he will clarify this meaning through verbal expression.

Having thus shown the distinction of species among non-sentient grass and trees, wishing to show it among sentient beings, he spoke the words beginning with "Then the insects (Tato kīṭe)." In those words, kīṭā means worms and larvae. Paṭaṅgā means insects such as dragonflies. Yāva kunthakipillike means ending with small red ants and black ants.

Khuddake refers to black ants and the like. Mahallake refers to animals such as rabbits and cats. All of them have various colors. Pādūdare means those whose feet are on their bellies, meaning those whose bellies are their feet. Dīghapiṭṭhike means because snakes have only a back from their head to their tail, they are called "long-backed" creatures. Those snakes also have many varieties, such as cobras and so forth.
186:
"Odake" refers to beings born in water. Fish also have many varieties, such as the Rohita fish and others.

"Pakkhi" refers to birds. They are called "pakkhi" because they possess wings (pakkha). They are called "pattayānā" because they travel by means of wings. They are called "vihaṅgamā" because they travel in the sky. These birds also have many varieties, such as crows and others.

Having thus shown the different species of beings that frequent land, water, and sky, and now wishing to clarify the intention for which He showed those species, He spoke the verse beginning with "Yathā etāsu". The meaning of this verse should be understood in brief, solely by way of the explanation of the intention mentioned previously.

614-6. To show in detail what should be said in this regard, He Himself spoke the verse beginning with "Na kesehi". The connection of meaning therein is: "There is no distinction of appearance based on birth among humans"—this statement should be understood as such. The way it does not exist is: just as the appearance of elephants, horses, deer, etc., is determined by birth, there is no such fixed rule like "the hair of Brahmins is like this, the hair of Khattiyas is like this." In this manner, everything should be connected. "There is no appearance based on birth at all, as in other species"—this statement should be understood as the conclusion of the meaning already stated. Its connection is: Since there is no distinction of appearance based on birth among humans regarding these features like hair, etc., it should be understood that "just as in other species the appearance is determined by birth, so too among humans such as Brahmins, etc., there is no appearance based on birth at all."

Now, to show how the distinction of "Brahmin" or "Khattiya" arises even though there is no such distinction of birth, He spoke the verse beginning with "Paccattaṃ". Its meaning is: The distinction of shapes such as hair, etc., which is established solely by birth as in animals, does not exist in the individual bodies of Brahmins and others among humans. Even though it does not exist, the distinction of the five aggregates (vokāra), which is the means for designating "Brahmin" or "Khattiya," is spoken of among humans by way of conventional designation; it is spoken of merely as a conventional term.
187:
619-625. With this sequence of words, the Blessed One refuted the view of the Brahmin Bhāradvāja. Now, if one were a Brahmin by birth, then even a person who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct would be a Brahmin. Since the ancient Brahmins and other wise people in the world do not desire such a person's state as a Brahmin, the Buddha spoke the eight verses beginning with "Yo hi koci manussesu" to support Vāseṭṭha's view. 

In those verses: "Gorakkha" means the protection of fields; "kasikamma" means the work of plowing. The earth is called "go", and the division of that earth is called "khetta" (field). "Puthusippa" refers to various crafts such as weaving and others. "Vohāra" means trade. "Parapessana" means performing services (veyyāvacca) for others. "Issattha" means living by weapons, referring to arrows and spears. "Porohicca" means the work of a chaplain (purohita).

Thus, having established that one who has failed in livelihood, virtue, and conduct is not a Brahmin according to both Brahmin tradition and worldly convention, it follows that one is not a Brahmin by birth, but a Brahmin by qualities. Therefore, whoever is endowed with qualities, regardless of the family they are born into, is a Brahmin. Having established this principle in meaning, and wishing to express that same principle in words, He spoke the verse beginning with "Na cāhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ brūmi".

The meaning of that verse: I do not call one a Brahmin merely because they are born in any of the four types of wombs, or specifically born from a mother designated as a Brahmin, or because they have a pure lineage of birth as described by Brahmins as "well-born on both sides," or because they are "yonija mattisambhava" (born from a mother's womb) due to the mother's perfection. Why? Because if that person has defilements (kiñcana), they are merely called a "Bhovādin" (one who says 'bho, bho') because they are distinguished from others who have defilements only by their manner of address. But whoever is "akiñcana" (without possessions/defilements) because they lack defilements like lust, etc., even if born in any family, and is "anādāna" (without grasping) because they have relinquished all grasping—him I call a Brahmin. Why? Because he has warded off evil (bāhitapāpa).

For this reason, He spoke the twenty-seven verses beginning with "Sabba saṃyojanaṃ chetvā". In that verse, "sabba saṃyojana" refers to the ten fetters.
188:
Furthermore, there are twenty-seven verses beginning with 'Sabba-saṃyojanaṃ chetvā'. In those verses, 'sabba-saṃyojanaṃ' refers to the ten fetters. 'Na paritassati' means not trembling with craving. 'Tamahaṃ' means that I call him a Brāhmaṇa because he has transcended attachments (saṅga) such as lust, thus being 'saṅgātiga', and because of the absence of the four bonds (yoga), thus being 'visamyutta'.

'Naddhiṃ' refers to anger that has arisen in the nature of binding. 'Varattaṃ' refers to craving that has arisen in the nature of binding. 'Sandānaṃ sahanukkamaṃ' refers to the bond of the sixty-two wrong views together with the underlying tendencies (anusaya) in their respective order. Because he stands having cut all these, and because the cross-bar of ignorance (avijjā-paligha) has been lifted, he is called 'ukkhittapaligha'. Because he knows the Four Noble Truths, he is called 'Buddha'. Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Aduṭṭho' refers to one who, with a mind free from anger, endures abuse through the ten grounds of abuse, beating with hands and so on, and binding with stocks, shackles, and so on. Because he is endowed with the strength of patience, he is called 'khantībala'. Because he is endowed with the army of that very strength of patience which has arisen repeatedly, he is called 'balānīka'. Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Vatavantaṃ' refers to one endowed with the ascetic practices (dhuta-vata), one who possesses virtue through the fourfold morality of purification (pārisuddhi-sīla), one who is 'anussada' because of the absence of the abundance of craving, one who is tamed (danta) by the restraint of the six sense faculties, and one who bears the final body (antimasārīra) as he stands in his last existence. Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Yo na limpati' means that in this way, whoever is not smeared by the two kinds of sensual pleasures (kāma) within his internal continuity, and does not stand in those sensual pleasures, that person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Dukkhassa' means of the suffering of the aggregates (khandha-dukkha). 'Pannabhāraṃ' refers to one who has laid down the burden of the aggregates, and who is detached from the four bonds (yoga) or from all defilements (kilesa). Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Gambhīrapaññaṃ' refers to one endowed with wisdom that proceeds into deep matters such as the aggregates, and one who is wise (medhāvī) with wisdom that has the essence of the Dhamma. Because he is skilled in what is the path and what is not the path, thinking, 'This is the cause of a miserable destination, this is the cause of a happy destination, this is the path to Nibbāna, this is not the path'...
189:
...skilled in what is the path and what is not the path, and who has reached the supreme goal known as the fruit of Arahatship—that person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Asaṃsaṭṭha' means not mixing, due to the absence of association through seeing, hearing, conversing, using things together, or physical contact. 'Ubhaya' means not mixing with both householders and those who are homeless (monks). 'Anokasāriṃ' refers to one who practices with a conduct free from attachment. Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Nidhāya' means having laid down or put aside (the rod/weapon). 'Tasesu thāvaresu ca' refers to both 'tasa' beings, who tremble with craving, and 'thāvara' beings, who are firm due to the absence of craving. Whoever, being free from enmity towards all beings in this way, has laid down the rod, and neither kills any being himself nor causes others to kill—that person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Aviruddha' means being non-opposing, due to the absence of enmity, even among the worldly masses who are opposing by way of resentment. Among people who have the rod (weapons) in themselves—who, even if they do not have sticks or swords in their hands, are not free from striking others—he is one who has laid down the rod and is peaceful (nibbuta). Among those called 'sādāna' because they have grasped the five aggregates as 'I' and 'mine', he is called 'anādāna' because of the absence of such grasping. Such a person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Āraggā' means that for such a person, those defilements such as lust, as well as this 'makkha' (denigration) which has the characteristic of smearing the virtues of others, have fallen off like a mustard seed from the point of an awl. Just as a mustard seed does not remain on the point of an awl, likewise they do not remain in his mind. That person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

'Akakkasa' refers to speech that is not harsh. 'Viññāpani' refers to speech that makes the meaning known. 'Sacca' refers to speech that is true. 'Nābhisaje' means that by which speech one should not cause another to be attached by way of making them angry. One who is called an Arahat should speak only such speech. Therefore, that person I call a Brāhmaṇa.

Whether it be long or short in garments and ornaments, whether it be small or large in pearls and gems, whether it be good or bad by way of being high-priced or low-priced, whoever...
190:
It means: 'In this world, he who does not take what is possessed by others, him I call a Brahmin.'

'Nirāsāsa' means one who is without craving. 'Visamyutta' means one who is detached from all defilements. It means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Ālaya' means craving. 'Aññāya akathaṃkathī' means one who, having known the eight bases as they truly are, is free from doubt regarding those eight bases. 'Amatogadhamanuppatta' means one who has entered and reached the deathless Nibbāna. It means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Ubho' means having abandoned both merit and demerit. 'Saṅga' means attachment such as lust. 'Upaccagā' means one who has crossed over. It means: 'Him I call a Brahmin'—one who is 'Asoka' (sorrowless) because there is no sorrow which is the root of the cycle of existence, 'Viraja' (stainless) because of the absence of the dust of lust within, and 'Suddha' (pure) because of being free from corrupting defilements.

'Vimala' means one free from stains like clouds. 'Suddha' means one without corrupting defilements. 'Vippasanna' means one with a clear mind. 'Anāvila' means one free from the turbidity of defilements. 'Nandībhavaparikkhīṇa' means one whose craving for the three realms of existence is exhausted. It means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

The monk who has transcended this obstacle of lust, the difficult path of defilements, the cycle of saṃsāra, and the delusion of not piercing the Four Noble Truths; who, having crossed the four floods, has reached the other shore; who meditates with the two types of jhāna; who is 'Aneja' (unshaken) due to the absence of craving; who is 'Akathaṃkathī' (free from doubt) due to the absence of uncertainty; who, without clinging due to the absence of acquisitions, is extinguished through the extinction of defilements—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

The person who, in this world, gives up both types of sensual pleasures and wanders forth as a homeless one, having exhausted both sensual desire and existence—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'
191:
The person who, in this world, abandons craving for the six doors and, having no desire for household life, becomes a homeless one and wanders forth; because of the exhaustion of both craving and existence, it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin'—one whose craving and existence are exhausted.

'Mānusakaṃ yogaṃ' refers to human life and the five strings of sensual pleasure. The same applies to the divine bond (dibbayoga). 'Upaccagā' means that the person who has abandoned the human bond and transcended the divine bond, being detached from all four bonds—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Rati' refers to delight in the five strings of sensual pleasure. 'Arati' refers to discontent with living in the forest. 'Sītibhūta' means one who is cooled (extinguished). 'Nirupadhi' means one without the baggage of defilements. 'Vīra' means the energetic one who remains having overcome the entire world of the aggregates—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Yo vedī' means the one who clearly knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in every way; called 'Asatta' because of being unattached; called 'Sugata' because of being well-established in practice; called 'Buddha' because of knowing the Four Noble Truths—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Yassa' means the one whose destination gods and others do not know; called 'Khīṇāsava' because of the exhaustion of taints; called 'Arahanta' because of being far from defilements—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

'Pure' refers to past aggregates; 'pacchā' refers to future aggregates; 'majjhe' refers to present aggregates. 'Kiñcana' refers to the impediment known as grasping through craving in those states. Called 'Akiñcana' because of the absence of impediments such as lust; called 'Anādāna' because of the absence of any grasping—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'

Called 'Usabha' because of being like a bull due to fearlessness; called 'Pavara' in the sense of being noble; called 'Vīra' because of being endowed with energy; called 'Mahesi' because of seeking the great aggregate of virtue and so on; called 'Vijitāvin' because of having conquered the three Māras; called 'Nhātaka' because of having washed away defilements; called 'Buddha' because of knowing the Four Noble Truths—it means: 'Such a person I call a Brahmin.'

The one who clearly knows the sequence of past lives (pubbenivāsa); who sees the twenty-six heavenly realms and the four states of misery with the divine eye; and who has reached Arahantship, which is the destruction of birth—it means: 'Him I call a Brahmin.'
192:
Thus, after the Blessed One had spoken of the nature of a Brāhmaṇa in terms of spiritual qualities, he spoke two verses beginning with "Samaññā hesā" to show that "Those who cling to the view 'One is a Brāhmaṇa by birth' do not understand that this is merely a conventional designation, and their view is a wrong view." The meaning of those verses is: This name and lineage called "Brāhmaṇa, Khattiya, Bhāradvāja, Vāseṭṭha" should be understood as a mere worldly designation, a mere conventional term. Why? Because it has come about through common consensus. Indeed, it was devised and established by relatives and kinsmen at the time of birth in various places. If they had not devised and established it so, no one, upon seeing another, would know "This person is a Brāhmaṇa" or "This person is a Bhāradvāja."

This name and lineage, thus devised, has long been a latent tendency of wrong view in those who do not know. In the hearts of beings who do not know that "A name and lineage is merely something devised; this name and lineage is devised only for the purpose of conventional communication," this wrong view has long been latent. Because it is latent, they, not knowing the reality of that name and lineage, say "One is a Brāhmaṇa by birth." It means they say this only because they do not know.

656-7. Thus, having shown that "Those who cling to the view 'One is a Brāhmaṇa by birth' do not understand that this is merely a conventional designation, and their view is a bad view," he now rejects the doctrine of birth in its primary sense and, wishing to establish the doctrine of action (kamma), spoke the verse beginning with "Na jaccā." In that verse, to explain in detail the meaning of this half-verse "By action one is a Brāhmaṇa, by action one is a non-Brāhmaṇa," he spoke the words beginning with "Kassako kammunā." In that context, "kammunā" (by action) refers to the volitional action (cetanā-kamma) that brings about present occupations such as farming. "Paṭiccasamuppādadassā" refers to those who habitually see dependent origination, thinking "Because of this cause, this arises." "Kammavipākakovidā" refers to those who are skilled in the results of kamma, [knowing that] birth in a family worthy of respect or a family that is despised occurs by the power of kamma, and other states of being low or excellent occur when low or excellent kammas bear fruit. In the verse "Kammunā vattati," although the terms "loka" (world), "pajā" (progeny/beings), and "sattā" (beings) are used, the meaning is the same; it is only a difference in terminology. By the first word...
193:
In this (verse), the refutation of the following view should be understood: "Brahma exists, Mahābrahmā... the supreme, the creator, the master, the father of what has been and what will be" (D. i. 42). Indeed, the world (of beings) proceeds because of kamma and arises in various destinations (gati); who then is its creator? By the second phrase, he shows: "Even though it has arisen through kamma, it continues to proceed through kamma alone in the present, just as in the past, undergoing happiness and suffering and reaching states such as low and high." By the third phrase, he concludes that very meaning: "Thus, in every way, beings who have kamma as their bond proceed being bound by kamma alone, and not otherwise." By the fourth phrase, he clarifies that meaning with a simile: "Like the linchpin of a moving chariot" (rathassāṇīva yāyato). Just as the linchpin is the fixed bond for a moving chariot, and without being bound by it, the chariot cannot move, so too kamma is the fixed bond for the world in its arising and proceeding; without being bound by it, the world neither arises nor proceeds.

Now, since the world is thus bound by kamma, wishing to show the state of excellence through excellent kamma, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Tapena." In those verses, "tapena" means by the restraint of the senses (indriyasaṃvara). "Brahmacariyena" means by the remaining excellent conduct based on the training (sikkhā) that was not yet mentioned. "Saṃyamena" means by virtue (sīla). "Damena" means by wisdom (paññā). By this kamma, which is of an excellent nature and has become noble (brahmabhūta), one becomes a Brahmin. Why? Because this kamma is called the supreme Brahmin, or because this kamma is the state of a supreme Brahmin. There is also a variant reading "brahmānaṃ," the meaning of which is: he is "brahmānaṃ" because he brings about (āneti) the noble state (brahma); it means he brings, conveys, or gives the noble state.

In the second verse, "santo" means one whose defilements are stilled. "Brahmā sakko" means Brahma and Sakka. One who is of such a nature is not only a Brahmin, but indeed, in the eyes of the wise (paṇḍita), he is both Brahma and Sakka. "O Vāseṭṭha, know it thus," is the intended meaning. The rest is to be understood in the manner already stated.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Vāseṭṭha Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
194:
## 10. Kokālikasuttavaṇṇanā

This discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Kokālika Sutta. The origin (uppatti) of this sutta will become clear in the commentary on its meaning. The commentary on its meaning also follows the same method as previously stated for "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "Atha kho kokāliko," who is this Kokālika and why did he approach? It is said that this Kokālika was the son of the merchant Kokālika in the city of Kokālika within the Kokālika country. After ordaining, he resided in the very monastery built and donated by his father. He was known by the name "Cūḷakokālika" (Kokālika the Lesser) and was not a disciple of Devadatta. The son of a brahmin who was a disciple of Devadatta was known as "Mahākokālika" (Kokālika the Greater).

While the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, the two Chief Disciples, while wandering through the countryside with about five hundred monks, wished to live in seclusion as the time for the rains retreat (vassa) approached. They sent those monks away, took their own bowls and robes, arrived at that city in that district, and went to that monastery. There, after greeting Kokālika pleasantly, they said to him, "Friend, we shall stay here for the three months of the rains retreat; do not tell anyone."

Although he promised, "Very well," after the three months had passed, on the morning of the following day, he entered the city and said, "Did you not know that the Chief Disciples have been staying here? No one has even invited them or offered them the four requisites."

The townspeople asked, "Venerable sir, why did you not tell us beforehand?" He replied, "What is the use of telling? Did you not see the two monks staying here? Are they not the Chief Disciples?" Then the townspeople quickly assembled, brought ghee, molasses, cloth, and other items, and placed them before Kokālika. 

Kokālika thought, "The Chief Disciples have very few desires. If they know these gains have arisen through intimation by speech (vaci-viññatti), they will not accept them. When they do not accept, they will surely say, 'Give them to the resident monk.' I will wait until they have me take these gains and then I will go." He acted according to his plan, but as soon as the Elders saw the items, they realized they had arisen through intimation by speech. Thinking, "These requisites are not suitable for us, nor are they suitable for Kokālika," they did not say, "Give them to the resident monk," but instead refused them and departed. Because of this, Kokālika became resentful, thinking, "Why did they not let them be given to me when they would not take them themselves?"
195:
Those Elders went to the presence of the Blessed One. It was the custom of the Tathāgatas that after performing the Pavāraṇā ceremony, if the Buddha himself did not go wandering in the countryside, he would send the Chief Disciples, saying, "Monks, wander for the welfare of the many," and so forth. At that time, the Buddha himself did not wish to go. Then he sent these Chief Disciples again, saying, "Monks, go, wander for the sake of wandering."

As those Chief Disciples were wandering with about five hundred monks, they eventually arrived at that same city in that country. The townspeople, recognizing the Elders, prepared offerings along with requisites, built a pavilion in the center of the city, and gave the offerings; they also presented the requisites to the Elders. The Elders accepted them and gave them to the Saṅgha of monks. Seeing this, Kokālika thought: "Formerly these men had few desires, but now they have become possessed of evil desires, overcome by greed. Previously, they only seemed to have few desires, contentment, and seclusion; now these are evil monks who display virtues they do not possess."

He approached the Elders and said, "Friends, formerly you were as if you had few desires, were contented, and secluded, but now you have become evil monks." Having said this, he took his bowl and robes and immediately departed in haste. Thinking, "I will report this matter to the Blessed One," he headed toward Sāvatthī and eventually approached the Blessed One. In this context, this is the reason why Kokālika approached. Therefore, it is said, "Then the monk Kokālika approached where the Blessed One was," and so forth.

The Blessed One, seeing Kokālika coming in great haste, reflected and knew, "He has come wishing to revile the Chief Disciples." When he reflected, "Is it possible to prevent him?" he saw, "It is not possible; he has come after having already offended the Elders; he will certainly be reborn in the Paduma hell." Even though he saw this, in order to free himself from the criticism of others who might say, "He heard them reviling Sāriputta and Moggallāna but did not stop them," and to show the great fault of slandering the Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda), he forbade him three times, saying, "Do not say so," and so forth.

In that passage, 'Mā hevaṃ' means "Do not say this" or "Do not speak thus." 'Pesala' means those who love virtue. 'Saddhāyika' means one who inspires faith or brings about clarity of mind. 'Paccayika' means one who provides a cause for trust, or one who brings about the conclusion that "this is truly so."

'Acirapakkantassa' means that not long after he had departed, his entire body became covered (with sores). Without leaving a space even the size of a hair's tip, his whole body...
196:
Kokālika's body was covered with a mass of boils that erupted, piercing through his bones. Regarding those boils, due to the power of the Buddhas, such karma does not bear fruit in the presence of the Buddhas; it only bears fruit when one has just moved beyond the range of their sight. Therefore, shortly after Kokālika had departed, the boils erupted. For this reason, it was said: "And to Kokālika, who had not long departed" (acirapakkantassa ca kokālikassa). If one asks, "Why did it not happen right there?" the answer is that it was due to the momentum of his karma. Karma that has found its opportunity will inevitably bear fruit; that karma did not allow him to remain in that place. Urged by the power of karma, he rose from his seat and departed.

The boils were the size of chickpeas. Then they became the size of young bael fruits and burst. When they burst, his whole body became like a ripe jackfruit. With his body covered in festering sores, he met with ruin and destruction, and, overcome by suffering, he lay at the gatehouse of Jetavana. Then, people who came to listen to the Dhamma saw him and said, "Shame on you, Kokālika! Shame on you, Kokālika! You have done what is improper; because of your own mouth, you have come to ruin and destruction." Hearing the words of those people, the guardian deities also reviled him. From there, the deities of the sky reviled him in this manner, and a single cry of condemnation arose as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm.

At that time, a monk named Turu, who had been Kokālika's preceptor and had attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) and was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes), arose from his meditative attainment. Hearing that cry of condemnation, he came and advised Kokālika to inspire faith in Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Kokālika, without even listening to his teacher's words, actually offended him as well, and upon passing away, he was reborn in the Paduma Hell. Therefore, it was said: "Then the monk Kokālika, through that very illness... having offended..."

In the phrase "Then Sahampati Brahmā" (atha kho brahmā sahampati), who is this Brahmā, and why did he approach the Blessed One and speak these words? This Brahmā had been a monk named Sahaka during the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa; having become a Non-returner, he was reborn in the Suddhāvāsa realm, where he is known as "Sahampati Brahmā." He approached the Blessed One for this reason: "I shall approach the Blessed One and announce the Paduma Hell. Then the Blessed One will inform the monks. Monks who are skilled in the sequence of discourse will ask about the lifespan there, and the Blessed One, while explaining, will reveal the danger of reviling the Noble Ones (ariyas)." To the Blessed One...
197:
(Sahampati Brahmā) approached and spoke these words. The Blessed One did exactly as (the Brahmā requested). Another monk also asked (about the lifespan). To that monk who asked, the Blessed One spoke the words beginning with, "Monks, it is as if..." In that context, 'vīsati-khārika' means: four patthas by the Magadhan measure equal one pattha in the Kosala country. Four of those (Kosala) patthas make one āḷhaka; four āḷhakas make one doṇa; four doṇas make one mānikā; four mānikās make one khārī. Twenty of such khārīs is what is meant by 'vīsati-khārika'. 'Tilavāha' refers to a cartload of sesame seeds. 'Abbuda Hell' is not a separate hell by the name of Abbuda; rather, a place in Avīci where one suffers for the duration of an abbuda count is called 'Abbuda Hell'. This same principle applies to Nirabbuda and the others.

The count of years in those hells should be understood as follows: just as one hundred hundred-thousands make one koṭi, so one hundred hundred-thousand koṭis is called a pakoṭi; one hundred hundred-thousand pakoṭis is a koṭippakoṭi; one hundred hundred-thousand koṭippakoṭis is a nahuta; one hundred hundred-thousand nahutas is a ninnahuta; one hundred hundred-thousand ninnahutas is one abbuda. Multiplying that abbuda by twenty results in a nirabbuda. This method applies throughout. Some teachers, however, say, "These names are acquired due to the distinctiveness of the wailing or the distinctiveness of the torture in those respective hells." Others say, "These are simply cold hells."

The phrase 'atha aparaṃ' (then further) is said with reference to the verse composition that illustrates the specific meaning of that matter. Among the twenty verses mentioned in the text, only this single verse, "Sataṃ sahassānaṃ," illustrates the meaning already stated; the remaining verses illustrate specific meanings. However, the final two verses are not found in the established text of the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, we said, "among the twenty verses."

In those verses, 'kuṭhārī' (axe) refers to harsh speech which is like an axe in the sense of cutting oneself. 'Chindati' (cuts) means destroying one's own root, known as the root of wholesome merit. 'Nindiyaṃ' refers to one who is blameworthy. 'Yo pasaṃsiyo' refers to a person who is worthy of praise in the highest sense; (the offender) reviles even such a praiseworthy person by accusing them of having evil desires and so on. 'Vicināti' means accumulating. 'Kali' means a fault. 'Ayaṃ kali' means this fault. 'Akkhesu' refers to the dice in gambling. 'Sabbassāpi saha attanā' means (losing) along with all of one's wealth and oneself.
198:
Because he has gone well, and because he has gone to the excellent place of Nibbāna, if one offends with the mind even the Sugatas—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples—it means that this mental offense of his is indeed a very great fault.

Why is that? Because for two hundred thousand [years] one experiences evil results. The period during which one, having established speech and mind with the slander of Noble Ones, reaches an evil hell and is cooked in that hell, is of such duration. This is, in brief, the life-span in the Paduma Hell.

Now, to clarify this meaning in another way—that 'this very act of slandering Noble Ones by offending the mind against the Sugatas is a great fault'—he spoke the verse beginning with 'Abhūtavādī'. In that verse, 'Abhūtavādī' means one who speaks untruth by way of slandering Noble Ones. 'Nirayaṃ' refers to Paduma Hell and so forth. 'Pecca samā bhavanti' means that after passing away from this life, they become equal through rebirth in hell. 'Parattha' means in the next world.

What more need be said? In the phrase 'Yo appaduṭṭhassa', one should be known as 'appaduṭṭha' (unoffending) because of the absence of mental offense, 'suddha' (pure) because of the absence of the stain of ignorance, and 'anaṅgaṇa' (blemishless) because of the absence of evil desires. Alternatively, one is pure because of being unoffending, and blemishless because of being pure; thus it should be applied here.

Having thus established the great fault of mental offense against the Sugatas, he now spoke the fourteen verses known as the 'Vāritavatthu-gāthā'. It is said that these verses were spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna as an instruction to Kokālika while he was dying; some teachers say they were spoken by Mahābrahmā. To collect these verses together with this Sutta, this summary is given: 'Yo lobhaguṇe anuyutto', etc. Among those verses, in the first verse, because it is first pointed out as 'guṇa', or because it occurs many times, greed itself is called 'lobhaguṇa'; this is a designation for craving (taṇhā). 'Avadaññū' means one who does not know the Dhamma of the virtuous because of not following the instruction of the Buddhas. 'Maccharī' means one who is possessed of the five types of stinginess. 'Pesuṇiyaṃ anuyutto' means one who is repeatedly engaged in slander with the desire to divide the Chief Disciples. The rest is clear.

This is the intended meaning: 'Friend Kokālika, a person like you, who has repeatedly engaged in greedy craving and is devoted to the strands of greed, who is faithless, miserly, ignorant of the Dhamma of the virtuous, stingy, and devoted to slander, reviles with speech another person who should not be reviled. Therefore, I call that person "Mukhaduggā" (foul-mouthed),' thus he spoke in three verses.
199:
The remaining words are clear. The meaning is: 'Friend Kokālika, a person like you, having repeatedly engaged in greedy craving, being devoted to repeated attachment, lacking faith, being miserly and stingy, not following the Dhamma of the virtuous, and being repeatedly engaged in slanderous speech—that Kokālika reviles with speech another person who should not be reviled. Therefore, the Buddha spoke of him with the three verses beginning with "Mukhaduggā".'

The meanings of the obscure terms in that verse are as follows: 'Mukhadugga' means one with uneven/foul speech; 'Vibhūta' means one who is devoid of truthful speech; 'Alikavādီ' means one who habitually speaks untruth; 'Anariya' means one who is not a noble person; 'Bhūnahu' means a destroyer of great prosperity or a destroyer of growth; 'Purisanta' means the lowest among men; 'Kali' means one who is deceitful and without glory; 'Avajāta' means a degenerate son (low-born son) of the Buddha.

'Rajamākirasi' means throwing the dust of defilements upon oneself. 'Papatanti' means falling into the abyss of hell. There is also a variant reading 'Papātaṃ', which has the same meaning. There is also a variant reading 'Papadaṃ', which means the Great Hell.

In the phrase 'Eti hataṃ', 'ha' is a particle, and 'taṃ' refers to that wholesome or unwholesome kamma. Alternatively, 'hataṃ' has the meaning of what has been practiced or accumulated. 'Suvāmီ' means being the owner of that kamma because of having performed it. It means that the person certainly receives the result of that kamma, and that kamma does not perish. Because of receiving it, the fool who is habitually cruel sees suffering (in the afterlife).

Now, wishing to reveal the suffering that fools encounter, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Ayosaṅkusamāhataṭṭhānaṃ'. In that verse, first, the meaning of the first half-verse is: The Buddha referred to it when he said, 'Monks, the hell-wardens inflict upon him the torture called the fivefold binding (pañcavidhabandhana)'; he reaches the place where he is constantly struck with iron spikes. When he reaches there, he is made to lie down on the glowing iron ground, and he approaches the iron spikes, which are called hot stakes, having sharp edges, with which he is struck in five places by the hell-wardens. Referring to this, the Buddha said, 'They drive a hot iron stake through the hand,' and so forth.

After that, the next half-verse: For the one who, after being cooked in that hell for many thousands of years, goes gradually to the bank of the Khārodaka River to experience the remaining results, it is said: 'They put a glowing iron ball into the mouth; they pour molten copper into the mouth.' This was said in reference to that meaning. In that context, 'ayo' means iron. 'Gulasannibhaṃ' means having the shape of a wood-apple (beluva) fruit. Here, by the word 'ayo', copper should be understood, and by the other word, the iron ball should be understood. 'Patirūpaṃ' means according to the kamma performed.

In the subsequent verses, 'Na hi vaggū' means that the hell-wardens, who say things like 'Seize him! Strike him!', do not speak pleasant or sweet words. 'Nābhijavanti' means they do not approach with a face turned toward him with a desire for his welfare; they do not approach with a bright face, but they approach bringing only harm and destruction.
200:
The hell wardens do not speak pleasant words. They do not run towards the beings with a friendly face out of a desire for their welfare, nor do they approach with a clear countenance. It means they approach only to bring about ruin and destruction. 'Na tāṇamupenti' means they do not approach to become a shelter, a refuge, or a support; rather, it means they approach only to seize and kill.

'Aṅgāre santhate sayanti' means that, having been placed upon a mountain of embers, they must lie on a spread of glowing coals for many thousands of years. 'Ginisampajjalitaṃ' refers to the fire blazing brightly from all sides and in all directions. 'Pavisanti' means that, having been cast into the Great Hell, they enter it. That hell named Mahāniraya is called 'Catukkaṇṇa' (four-cornered); the eyes of those who look at it even from a hundred yojanas away are shattered.

'Jālena ca onahiyānā' means they are killed like hunters killing deer by ensnaring them with iron nets. This is a form of punishment (kammakāraṇa) not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta. 'Andhaṃva timisamāyanti' means they go like the blind into the hell named Dhūmaroruva, which is designated as 'Timisa' (darkness) because it is extremely dark. In that hell, their eyes are shattered from inhaling the harsh smoke; therefore, it is said 'andhaṃva' (like the blind). 'Taṃ vitatañhi yathā mahikāyo' means that the mass of intense darkness is as vast as a mass of frost or mist. There is also a variant reading 'vitthataṃ'. This too is a punishment not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.

'Atha lohamayaṃ' refers to this Lohakumbhī (copper cauldron) hell, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas deep, reaching down to the edge of the earth, and is filled to the brim with molten copper. 'Paccanti hi tāsu cirarattaṃ' means they are cooked in those cauldrons for a long time. 'Agginisamāsu' means in the cauldrons where the fire burns uniformly. 'Samuppilavāte' means they are cooked amidst rising bubbles, sometimes going up and sometimes going down while floating. This should be understood according to the method described in the Devadūta Sutta.

'Pubbalohitamisse' means in the Lohakumbhī cauldron mixed with pus and blood. 'Tattha' means in that cauldron. 'Yaṃ yaṃ disakaṃ' means towards any direction or intermediate direction. 'Adhiseti' means he goes. There is also a variant reading 'abhiseti', meaning he clings to or leans against whichever part of that cauldron. 'Kilissati' means he is tormented. There is also a variant reading 'kilijjati', meaning it is putrid. 'Samphusamāno' means being touched by that pus and blood. This also is a punishment not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.
201:
'Puḷavāvasatha' refers to the abode of worms. This hell is also a Lohakumbhī cauldron, called 'Gūthaniraya' (Excrement Hell) in the Devadūta Sutta. The worms with needle-like snouts bite through the skin and so forth of those who fall there and eat the bone marrow. 'Gantūṃ na hi tīramapatthī' means they are unable to reach the shore. Although there is a variant reading 'tīravamatthī', the meaning is the same. Here, 'tīram-eva' is expressed as 'tīrava'. Since the upper part of that cauldron is also covered with a lid, it is completely closed all around; therefore, it means there is no shore to escape to.

The description of the Asipattavana (Sword-leaf Forest) hell is just as described in the Devadūta Sutta. That forest appears delightful like a mango grove from afar, so the denizens of hell enter it with a mind of longing. Then, the sword-leaves stirred by the wind fall and sever their major and minor limbs. Therefore, it is said: 'Taṃ pavisanti samucchidagattā' (They enter it and their limbs are severed). In that Asipattavana hell, the hell wardens pull out the tongues of the liars who have fallen there after running swiftly, using fishhooks. Just as people spread wet hide on the ground and strike it with stakes, they split the tongues with adzes and torment them by cutting off each edge. The edges that have been cut off arise again and again. The reading 'āracayāracayā' means pulling and dragging repeatedly. This punishment is also not directly mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta.

'Vetaraṇī' refers to the river called the 'Great Caustic Water River' in the Devadūta Sutta. That river appears to be full of water like the Ganges, so the denizens of hell go down into it to bathe and drink. 'Tiṇhadhārakhuradhāra' means having sharp razor edges. Since sharp razors are placed in rows along the upper and lower parts and on both banks of that river, it is called 'Tiṇhadhārakhuradhāra'. Those fools, longing for water, approach it and, urged by their own evil kamma, fall into that river. The phrase 'sāmā sabalā' should be read in conjunction with the subsequent word 'soṇā'. It means that black dogs and spotted dogs bite and eat them.
202:
"A flock of crows" (kākolagaṇā) refers to a group of black crows. "Extremely greedy" (paṭigiddhā) means having become thoroughly greedy; some teachers say "great vultures" (mahāgijjhā). "Hawks" (kulalā) refers to the hawk species; some teachers say it is a name for "falcons" (senā). "Crows" (vāyasā) refers to crows that are not black. This is also a form of torture (kammakaraṇa) not mentioned in the Devadūta Sutta. Although some matters mentioned in that Devadūta Sutta are not mentioned here, they should be understood as already mentioned because they are parts of the preceding and succeeding sections.

Now, wishing to give advice by showing the entire state of affairs in this hell, he spoke the verse beginning with "Kicchā vatāyaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: Oh, indeed, this existence in hell, characterized by various types of torture, is very painful; a person who habitually commits cruel unwholesome deeds experiences that suffering. Therefore, while life still remains in this world, while the continuity of life exists, one should be a person who performs his duty by practicing wholesome states such as taking refuge (saraṇagamana). Even while performing wholesome deeds, one should do so with constant application and should not be negligent even for a moment. This is the collective explanation here. Since the remaining words are easy to understand due to the method already mentioned and their clear meaning, a word-by-word commentary is not provided.

## In the Minor Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Kokālika Sutta of the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

## 11. Nālaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
"Ānandajāte" and so forth is the Nālaka Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that—having seen a disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara practicing the way of a sage (moneyyapaṭipadā) and greatly desiring such a state, the hermit named Nālaka, the nephew of the hermit Asita, who had fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) for a hundred thousand aeons from that time, asked about the way of a sage with two verses beginning with "Aññātametaṃ" on the seventh day after the day the Blessed One set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion. To him, the Blessed One explained it in the manner beginning with "I will declare the state of a sage to you." After the Blessed One had passed away, while the Venerable Mahākassapa was conducting the Council, the Venerable Ānanda was asked about that same way of a sage, [explaining] by what cause and at what time Nālaka the hermit was inspired to [ask] the Blessed One.
203:
[Nālaka the hermit] asked. Wishing to make all that clear, he spoke the twenty introductory verses (vatthugāthā) beginning with "Ānandajāte." All of that is called the "Nālaka Sutta."

Therein, "ānandajāte" means attained to prosperity, attained to greatness. "Patīte" means satisfied. Alternatively, "ānandajāte" means joyful; "patīte" means gladdened in heart. "Sucivasane" means having garments that are not soiled. Indeed, the garments of the gods produced from the wishing-trees (kapparukkha) do not catch dust or dirt. "Dussaṃ gahetvā" means having lifted up a divine cloth which has received the designation "dussa" because it is similar to cloth in this world. "Asito isi" is the hermit who received this name because of his dark body color. "Divāvihāre" means in the place of the day-abiding. The rest of the words are clear in their sequence.

Regarding the connection: This [Asita] was formerly the chaplain (purohita) of King Sīhahanu, the father of Suddhodana. Before King Suddhodana was consecrated, he was his teacher of arts (sippācariya), and after the consecration, he remained the chaplain. When he came for royal service in the evening and morning, the King did not show him respectful humility as he did when he was young, but merely performed the salutation with joined palms (añjalikamma). This is the natural custom of Sakyan kings who have attained consecration. The chaplain, becoming weary because of that, said, "Great King, I shall go forth [into homelessness]." The King, knowing his determination, requested, "In that case, teacher, you should live in my own garden so that I may see you frequently." He agreed, saying, "So be it," and having gone forth as a hermit, he lived in the garden itself, being attended to by the King. By practicing the kasina preliminary work, he produced the eight attainments (samāpatti) and the five superknowledges (abhiññā). From then on, after taking his meal in the royal palace, he would go to one of the places such as the Himālaya or the realm of the Four Great Kings to spend the day-abiding. Then one day, having gone to the Tāvatiṃsa realm and entered a jewel mansion, he sat on a divine jewel throne and experienced the bliss of concentration. Emerging in the evening, he stood at the door of the mansion and, looking here and there, saw the gods, headed by Sakka, playing and uttering words of praise for the virtues of the Bodhisatta, while waving their cloths on the great street sixty leagues in extent. Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said: "Ānandajāte... etc... divāvihāre."

Then, having seen the gods thus, he [spoke the verse] "deve... etc... kiṃ paṭicca." Therein, "udagge" means having uplifted bodies. "Cittiṃ karitvānā" means having shown respect. "Kalyarūpo" means being of a joyful nature. The remaining meanings are clear.
204:
## 
Now, the verses beginning with "Yadāpi āsi" have a clear connection of meaning. Regarding the word-by-word meaning of the first verse: "Saṅgamo" means battle (saṅgāma). "Jayo surānaṃ" means the victory of the devas.

To clarify this statement, this sequential account should be understood: Sakka, in the kingdom of Magadha, was a young man named Magha, the leader of thirty-three men in Macala village. Having fulfilled the seven vows, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven along with his followers.
