At that time, the old devas said, "Guest devas have arrived; let us pay them honor," and they offered divine lotuses and invited them to share half of the celestial kingdom. Sakka, not being satisfied with half the kingdom, informed his followers, and one day, while those old devas were intoxicated with wine, he seized them by their feet and threw them down to the base of Mount Sineru. For them, the Asura realm, ten thousand yojanas in extent, appeared at the lower level of Mount Sineru. It was adorned with a magnificent Trumpet Flower tree (Cittapāṭalī), which was like the Parichattaka tree.

Later, they regained consciousness and, not seeing the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, said, "O friends, we have been ruined because of the fault of being addicted to drink. Now we shall no longer drink wine (surā); because we do not drink wine, we are no longer Sura devas, but have become Asuras." From then on, the name "Asura" arose. Then, saying, "Come, let us now do battle with the devas," they climbed up Mount Sineru.

Then Sakka fought and subdued the Asuras, throwing them back into the ocean, and created Indra-statues resembling himself at the four gates. Then the Asuras thought, "Indeed, this Sakka is vigilant and always guarding," and they returned to their own Asura realm.

Then the devas, proclaiming their victory and waving their clothes in the main streets, celebrated the festival. At that time, the hermit Asita, having the power to recollect forty aeons of the past and future, reflected, "Have these devas ever played like this before?" While reflecting, he saw the victory of the devas in that Deva-Asura battle and said:

"When there was a battle with the Asuras,
Jayo surānaṃ—the devas were victorious and the Asuras were defeated;
Tadāpi netādiso lomahaṃsano—even then, there was no such joy that makes the hair stand on end."

Even at that time, there was no such joy that causes horripilation. "Kimabbhutaṃ daṭṭhu marū pamoditā" means: what wonder have the devas seen now that they are so joyful?
205:
In the second verse, "seḷenti" means they utter the sound of "Ussḷana" (shouts of Sādhu) with their mouths. They sing various songs, play sixty-eight thousand musical instruments, and "phoṭenti" means they snap their fingers. "Pucchāmi vo" means that although he is capable of knowing by his own reflection, he asks because he wishes to hear their words. "Merumuddhavāsino" refers to those who dwell on the peak of Mount Sineru. Indeed, at the base of Mount Sineru is the Asura realm, ten thousand yojanas wide; in the middle part are the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands; and on the upper surface is the Tāvatiṃsa realm, ten thousand yojanas wide. Therefore, the devas are called "dwellers on the peak of Meru." "Mārisa" is an address to the devas, meaning those who are without suffering and without affliction.

Then, in the third verse spoken by the devas who were reporting that matter, "Bodhisatta" means a being who will realize omniscience, a being worthy of reaching Supreme Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi). "Ratanavara" means one who is like an excellent jewel. For that reason, we are pleased and joyful. The reason is that when that Bodhisatta reaches Buddhahood, he will preach the Dhamma in such a way that we and other groups of devas will reach the stages of Sekha and Asekha. It is said that the intention of those devas is that humans, too, having heard the Dhamma of that Buddha, those who are not yet able to attain Parinibbāna, will perform meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and fill the celestial realms. In that verse, although the two words "tuṭṭhā" and "kalyarūpā" are not different in meaning, it should be understood that they were spoken to answer the two questions: "Why are the hosts of devas so exceedingly pleased and joyful?"

Now, in the fourth verse spoken by the devas to clarify the intention with which they were joyful when the Bodhisatta was born, the word "satta" (beings) includes devas and humans, and the word "pajā" (progeny/beings) includes the remaining realms of existence (gati). Thus, with these two words, he shows the Bodhisatta's supremacy among the five realms of existence. Even among animals, although beings such as lions are endowed with qualities like fearlessness, this Bodhisatta alone excels them. Therefore, he is called "pajānamuttamo" (supreme among beings). Among devas and humans, there are four types of persons, such as those practicing for their own benefit; among them, this Bodhisatta is the supreme person who practices for the benefit of both himself and others. Among men, he is called "narāsabha" because he is like a noble bull (usabha). Therefore, the devas, chanting his praise, spoke these two words as well.
206:
In the fifth verse, 'taṃ saddaṃ' refers to that sound of the words spoken by the devas. 'Avasarī' means descended or entered. 'Tada bhavanaṃ' refers to the entry into King Suddhodana's palace at that time.

In the sixth verse, 'tato' means immediately after the words of the hermit Asita. 'Ukkāmukheva' means in the very mouth of a torch, referring to the mouth of a goldsmith's crucible. 'Sukusalasampahaṭṭhaṃ' means struck by a very skillful goldsmith, and heated while being struck. 'Daddallamānaṃ' means shining brilliantly. 'Asitavhayassa' refers to the hermit named Asita, who is called Kaṇhadevila by his second name.

In the seventh verse, 'tārāsabhaṃ vā' refers to the moon, which is like a bull among the stars. 'Visuddhaṃ' means pure, free from impurities such as clouds. 'Saradariva' means as if in the autumn season (the month of Tazaungmon). 'Ānandajāto' means one who has reached joy because of the rapture (pīti) that arose just by hearing. 'Alattha pītiṃ' means he gained rapture once again upon seeing.

Following that, the eighth verse is spoken to show the constant worship and honor being paid to the Bodhisatta by the devas. In that verse, 'anekasākhaṃ' means having many ribs (spokes of an umbrella). 'Sahassamaṇḍalaṃ' means endowed with a thousand circles made of red gold. 'Chattaṃ' refers to the divine white umbrella. 'Vītipatanti' means they are flying up and down while fanning the body.

In the ninth verse, 'jaṭī' refers to the hermit with matted hair. 'Kaṇhasirivhayo' is one who is called by both the names Kaṇha and Siri. It means that they also address or call that hermit 'Sirikaṇha'. 'Paṇḍukambale' means on a red blanket. Here, according to the sense, the word 'kumāraṃ' (the prince) should be inserted, or it should be understood as an elliptical expression. In the previous verse, the word 'disvā' (having seen) was used with reference to seeing from a distance before reaching the hermit's hands. In this verse, however, 'disvā' is said again because of seeing the prince being brought forward to be received into his hands. Alternatively, 'disvā' in the previous verse refers to the gain of rapture from merely seeing, as stated at the end of the verse: 'vipulamalattha pītiṃ' (he gained abundant rapture); whereas 'disvā' in this verse refers to the act of receiving, as stated at the end: 'sumano paṭiggahe' (with a joyful mind, he received). Furthermore, the term in the previous verse relates only to the prince, while the term in this verse relates to the white umbrella as well. 'Disvā' means seeing the prince, who is as beautiful as pure gold on a red Gandhāra blanket worth a hundred thousand, and seeing the white umbrella, of the kind described in the phrase 'chattaṃ marū', being held over his head. Some teachers, however, say that this refers to a human umbrella. For just like the devas, humans also approach the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) holding umbrellas, yak-tail whisks, peacock-feather whisks, palm-leaf fans, and hair-whisks.
207:
Even so, there is no special excellence in that teacher's words; therefore, the method already stated is indeed excellent. 'Paṭiggahe' means he received with both hands. It is said that they brought the prince near to make him pay homage to the hermit. Then the prince's feet turned over and rested on the hermit's head. Seeing that wonder, the hermit, with a joyful and delighted heart, received him.

## In the tenth verse, 'jigīsako' means one who investigates, searches, or contemplates. 'Lakkhaṇamantapāragū' is one who has reached the far shore (mastered) of both the marks and the Vedas. 'Anuttarāyaṃ' means this prince is the unsurpassed one. That hermit, having seen the wheel-marks on the soles of the Bodhisatta who had come before him, followed those wheel-marks to investigate the remaining marks; seeing the perfection of all the marks, he knew, 'Surely this prince will become a Buddha,' and spoke thus.

## In the eleventh verse, 'athattono gamanaṃ' means going to the formless realm (arūpa-bhūmi) by the power of his own rebirth. 'Akalyarūpo gaḷayati assukāni' means that reflecting on the cause of his future birth in the formless realm, he thought, 'Now I shall not have the opportunity to hear the Dhamma-teaching of this Buddha,' and being displeased, overcome by powerful grief, he became dejected and shed tears; he let them flow. There is also a variant reading 'garayati'. If this hermit were to incline his mind toward the fine-material realm (rūpa-bhūmi), why could he not be born there? Why does he weep so? It is not that he could not be born there; he could. However, because of lack of skill, he did not know the procedure for being born in that fine-material realm. Even so, if it is argued that it is inappropriate for him to feel dejection since his defilements have been suppressed by the attainment of meditative absorptions (samāpatti)—no, it is possible precisely because they are only suppressed.

In truth, defilements that are entirely cut off by the development of the Path (magga-bhāvanā) do not arise again; however, for those who have attained meditative absorptions, defilements can arise due to a powerful cause. If it is asked, 'When defilements arise and the jhana is diminished, how can his going to the formless realm be possible?'—it is because it can be regained without difficulty. Indeed, when defilements arise in those who have attained meditative absorptions, they do not fall into grave transgressions; as soon as the force of the defilement subsides, they regain that special distinction without difficulty. It is difficult to know that such persons have even diminished from their distinction; and this hermit is such a person. 'No ce kumāre bhavissati antarāyo' means that surely no danger will befall this prince.

## In the twelfth verse, 'na orakāyaṃ' means this prince is not an inferior or lowly person. This is said with reference to the state of Buddhahood that will be mentioned in the verse above.
208:
In the thirteenth verse, 'sambodhiyagga' refers to the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññutañāṇa). That Omniscient Knowledge is called 'sambodhi' because it knows rightly and unerringly; it is called 'agga' (supreme) because it is the most excellent of all knowledges, being unobstructed in any matter. 'Phusissati' means he will reach (attain). 'Paramavisuddhadassī' means one who sees Nibbāna. That Nibbāna is called 'paramavisuddha' because it is absolutely pure. 'Vitthārikassa' means that the Buddha's dispensation (sāsana) will be extensive. 'Brahmacariya' refers to the dispensation (sāsana).

In the fourteenth verse, 'athantarā' means that danger (antarāya) will occur only in the interval before reaching the Buddha's Enlightenment (sambodhi). 'Na sossanti' means they will not hear the Dhamma. 'Asamadhurassa' refers to the Buddha who possesses incomparable effort. 'Aṭṭo' means one who is afflicted (due to mental distress). 'Byasanaṃ gato' means one who has reached the destruction of happiness. 'Aghāvī' means one who has reached suffering; this is said with reference to the arising of all mental distress (domanassa). That hermit Asita was afflicted with mental distress. That mental distress is called 'byasana' because it destroys happiness. He is called 'aghāvī' because of that mental suffering.

In the fifteenth verse, 'vipulaṃ janetvāna' means having produced extensively. This is the reading. 'Niggamā' means he departed from home. Having thus departed, that hermit [spoke to] his own nephew Nālaka, meaning his sister's son. 'Samādapesi' means that, knowing his own short life and knowing through his own power that the young Nālaka, his younger sister's son, had accumulated merit, and out of compassion, thinking "When he reaches maturity, he might become negligent," he went to his sister's house and asked, "Where is Nālaka?" When told, "Venerable sir, he is playing outside," he ordered, "Bring him here," and at that very moment, he had him ordained as a hermit, and exhorted, and instructed him. How did he instruct? He spoke the sixteenth verse beginning with 'Buddhoti ghosaṃ'.

In that verse, 'yada parato' means when in the future. 'Dhammagga' means the path to the supreme Dhamma, Nibbāna, or the supreme Nibbāna together with the practice (paṭipadā). 'Tasmiṃ' means in the presence of that Buddha. 'Brahmacariya' means the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma).

In the seventeenth verse, 'tādinā' means by being well-established in that Buddha; it means at that time, when there is the suppression of defilements and the attainment of concentration, with defilements suppressed and with a concentrated mind. 'Anāgate paramavisuddhadassīnā' means "This Nālaka will see the perfectly pure Nibbāna in the presence of the Blessed One in the future..."
209:
"...because of seeing thus, that hermit Asita is called 'one who sees the perfectly pure in the future' by this method. Thus, [he is] one who sees the perfectly pure in the future. 'Upacitapuññasañcayo' means one who has an accumulation of merit performed and gathered starting from the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Expecting the arising of the Buddha, he lived in the guise of a hermit after ordaining. 'Rakkhitindriyo' means living with guarded hearing faculty (sotindriya). It is said that from then on, that Nālaka hermit did not dive into water, thinking, 'If I enter the water, the hearing faculty might be destroyed; if it is destroyed, I would be excluded from hearing the Dhamma.'

In the eighteenth verse, 'sutvāna ghosaṃ' means while the hermit Nālaka was living in this way, the Blessed One gradually attained Enlightenment and turned the Wheel of Dhamma in Bārāṇasī; at that time, he heard the sound of the turning of the Wheel of the Noble Conqueror (Jina) from deities who desired his welfare, who came and informed him, saying, 'The Blessed One has turned the Wheel of Dhamma; the Blessed One has indeed arisen as the Perfectly Enlightened One,' and so on. 'Gantvāna disvā isinisabhaṃ' means that while the deities were making the 'Moneyya-uproar' for seven days, on the seventh day he went to Isipatana and saw the Blessed One, the noble hermit who is like a bull (usabha), sitting on the noble Buddha-seat with the intention, 'Nālaka will come, I will preach the Dhamma to him.' 'Pasanno' means having a devout mind immediately upon seeing. 'Moneyyaseṭṭhaṃ' means the supreme knowledge, the Path Knowledge (maggañāṇa). 'Samāgate asitāvhayaassa sāsane' means the arrival of the time of the hermit Asita's instruction. That hermit Asita had previously instructed: 'When the Blessed One opens the path of Dhamma that leads to Nibbāna, go then and, inquiring about the time, practice the holy life under that Blessed One.' This was that very time. Therefore, it is said, 'samāgate asitāvhayaassa sāsane.' The remaining words in this verse are clear.

## This is the explanation of the introductory verses (vatthugāthā).

In the two questioning verses, 'aññātametaṃ' means 'I have known this meaning.' 'Yathātathaṃ' means as it really is, unerringly. What is the meaning? The hermit Asita, knowing 'This prince will reach the supreme Buddhahood,' had told me, 'When you hear the sound "Buddha" in the future, he will attain Enlightenment and open the path of Dhamma; you will hear that.' Today, having seen the Blessed One face-to-face, I have known that the words of the hermit Asita are 'exactly as they were.' 'Taṃ taṃ' means therefore that word. 'Sabbadhammāna pāraguṃ' means reaching the further shore of all phenomena through the six ways as mentioned in the Hemavata Sutta.
210:
## 
'Anagāriyupetassa' means for the monk who has entered the state of homelessness. 'Bhikkhācariyaṃ jigīsato' means for one who seeks the undefiled practice of alms-gathering as practiced by the Noble Ones. 'Moneyya' is the Dhamma which is the wealth of the Sages (Munis). 'Uttamaṃ padaṃ' is the supreme practice. The rest of the words in this verse are clear.

Then, the Blessed One, being thus asked, answered the practice of Sagehood (Moneyya-paṭipadā) to the hermit Nālaka starting with the words 'Moneyyaṃ te upanyissaṃ' (I shall declare Sagehood to you). In that context, 'upanyissaṃ' means I shall prescribe, reveal, and show. 'Dukkaraṃ durabhisambhavaṃ' means it is difficult to perform, and it is difficult for it to arise or to be endured while being performed. The meaning here is: If it were easy to perform or to penetrate that Moneyya-dhamma, I would prescribe it for you. However, it is difficult to perform and difficult to achieve because it must be practiced without allowing a defiled mind to arise from the time one is a worldling (puthujjana). Indeed, only a single disciple of a single Buddha can perform and sustain it.

Thus, the Blessed One, wishing to show the difficulty and the hard-to-achieve nature of the Moneyya practice, and having inspired Nālaka's effort, said: 'Handa te naṃ pavakkhāmi, santhambhassu daḷho bhava' (Come, I shall tell it to you; steady yourself, be firm), wishing to speak of that Moneyya. In that verse, 'Handa' is a particle in the sense of resolve. 'Te naṃ pavakkhāmi' means I shall tell you that Moneyya practice. 'Santhambhassu' means support yourself with the support of energy (viriya) that is capable of doing what is difficult. 'Daḷho bhava' means be firm with unslackening effort capable of enduring what is hard to achieve. What is meant? Because you have the accumulation of merit (puṇya-sambhāra), I, having absolute resolve, shall tell you this Moneyya practice, though it is difficult to perform and hard to achieve. Steady yourself, be firm.

Wishing to speak of the Moneyya practice, which is the supreme effacement (sallekha), and having exhorted the Elder Nālaka to be steady and firm, He first spoke the half-verse beginning with 'Samānabhāgaṃ' to show the abandonment of defilements associated with the village. In that verse, 'Samānabhāgaṃ' means having an equal share, being identical without any distinction. 'Akkuṭṭhavanditaṃ' refers to abuse and veneration.

Now, wishing to show the method of how to make them equal, He spoke the half-verse beginning with 'Manopadosaṃ.' The meaning of that verse is: When abused, one should guard against mental corruption; when venerated, one should live peacefully without being uplifted. Even when venerated by a king, one should not fall into agitation (uddhacca), thinking 'He venerates me.'
211:
## 
Now, wishing to show the abandonment of defilements associated with the forest, He spoke the verse beginning with 'Uccāvacā.' The meaning of that verse is: Even in the grove known as the forest, various high and low objects arise according to pleasant and unpleasant nature; they come into the range of the eyes and other senses. These objects are like flames because they produce burning (suffering).

For example, just as in a burning forest, various flames arise—whether with smoke or without smoke, blue, yellow, red, small, or large—similarly, in the forest, various high and low objects arise, whether frightening, lust-inducing, anger-inducing, or deluding, due to the sounds of lions, tigers, humans, non-humans, and various birds, and due to flowers, fruits, and shoots. Therefore, He said: 'Various high and low objects arise in the grove, like flames.'

While such various objects arise, women who have gone to play in the garden or forest, or women who naturally frequent the forest such as wood-gatherers, seeing the Sage (muni) in seclusion, might tempt him with laughter, talk, weeping, or improper dress. Let those women not tempt that Sage; let those women not tempt that Sage. The meaning is: 'Act in such a way that they cannot tempt you.'

710-11. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the method of practice in the village and the forest to that monk, now wishing to show the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), spoke the two verses beginning with 'Viraṭo methunā dhammā.' In that verse, 'Hitvā kāme paropare' means having abandoned the five cords of sensual pleasure, whether good or bad, which remain apart from sexual intercourse. By abandoning those sensual pleasures, the refraining from sexual intercourse is well-perfected. Therefore, He said: 'Hitvā kāme paropare.' This is the intended meaning here. The words beginning with 'Aviruddho' (not opposed) are spoken to show the perfection of refraining from taking life (pāṇātipāta-veramaṇī) mentioned in the phrase 'He should not kill, nor cause to kill.'

The brief explanation there is: Not being opposed to beings of another's faction, and not being attached to beings of one's own faction; among all beings, whether trembling or stable, whether with craving or without craving, because of their desire to live, their desire not to die, their desire for happiness, and their loathing of pain, one removes opposition toward those beings by seeing them as equal to oneself, thinking 'As I am, so are these.' Likewise, one removes compliance (attachment) toward oneself by seeing oneself as equal to others, thinking 'As these are, so am I.' Thus, having abandoned both compliance and opposition, and taking oneself as the example (attānaṃ upamaṃ katvā) due to the loathing of death, one should not kill any beings, whether trembling or stable, through efforts such as one's own hand, nor cause others to kill through efforts such as command.
212:
Thus, having briefly stated the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint for that monk by way of abstaining from sexual intercourse and abstaining from taking life, and having shown the virtue of sense restraint with the words beginning with "hitvā kāme" (having abandoned sensual pleasures), he now speaks the verse beginning with "hitvā icchañca" to show the purity of livelihood. The meaning of that verse is: that craving which, having obtained one thing, desires a second; having obtained two, desires a third; and having obtained a hundred thousand, desires even more than that—because of desiring objects not yet obtained, it is called "icchā" (wish). That greed which is attached to objects already obtained is called "lobha" (greed). Having abandoned that wish (icchā) and that greed (lobha), in whatever requisites such as robes a worldling (puthujjana) remains attached and bound by those wishes and greed; having abandoned both in those requisites, without impairing the purity of livelihood for the sake of requisites, and being one with vision through the eye of wisdom, one should practice this practice of sagehood (moneyya-paṭipadā). One who practices thus would cross over this "hell" (naraka)—so called because it is difficult to fill—which is this craving for requisites that is the cause of wrong livelihood. Or, it means one would cross over by means of this practice.

Thus, having shown the purity of livelihood by way of abandoning craving for requisites, he now speaks the verse "ūnūdaro" (one with a light stomach) to show the virtue regarding the use of requisites by way of moderation in eating, and the practice following that purity of livelihood until the attainment of Arahantship. The meaning of that verse is: a monk who consumes nutriment from requisites such as robes, whether inferior or sublime, obtained righteously and fairly—

"When four or five mouthfuls remain to be eaten, one should stop eating and drink water. This is sufficient for the comfortable living of a monk who is resolute (pahitatta)."

By the manner stated, he should be one with a light stomach (ūnūdaro). He should not have a distended stomach like a leather bag filled with air. He should abandon sloth and torpor (thina-middha) caused by the intoxication of food.

Even while being one with a light stomach, he should be one who knows moderation in eating (mattaññū). He should be one who consumes food after defining its benefits and faults through reflection, such as "neva davāya", etc. Even being such a person who is moderate in eating, he should be one with few wishes (appiccho), being endowed with the four kinds of fewness of wishes by way of requisites, ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), scriptural learning (pariyatti), and attainment (adhigama). Indeed, a monk who has definitely undertaken the practice of sagehood should be one with few wishes in this way. Among those four: contentment with the three kinds of satisfaction regarding each requisite is called fewness of wishes regarding requisites (paccaya-appicchatā). Being one who practices asceticism, the lack of desire for others to know "I am an ascetic" is called fewness of wishes regarding ascetic practices (dhutaṅga-appicchatā). Being one who is very learned (bahussuta)...
213:
"Not wishing 'Let others know me as one of great learning' is called fewness of wishes regarding learning (pariyatti-appicchatā), like Elder Majjhantika. Not wishing 'Let others know that I have attained this wholesome state' despite being endowed with high attainment is called fewness of wishes regarding attainment (adhigama-appicchatā). This fewness of wishes should be understood at the levels below the attainment of Arahantship. This is because this practice is for the purpose of attaining Arahantship. Thus, a monk who has few wishes should also be one who is not fickle, having abandoned the fickleness of craving through the Path of Arahantship. Indeed, such a monk who is not fickle is always one without wishes, being free from the hunger of desire, and is quenched (nibbuto). Because of that desire by which beings are hungry and unsatisfied like those afflicted by hunger and thirst, he is one without wishes; and because of being without wishes, he is free from hunger, free from the affliction of defilements, and has reached the highest contentment. Thus, being free from hunger, he is 'quenched' (nibbuto), with the fever of all defilements calmed; in this way, the non-sequential connection (yojanā) should be understood here.

Having thus preached the practice up to the attainment of Arahantship, now, wishing to preach the consummation of the attainment of Arahantship for the monk who practices that path, as well as the undertaking of the ascetic practices (dhutanga) and the duties regarding lodgings, he spoke the two verses beginning with 'Sa piṇḍacāraṃ'. In those verses, 'Sa piṇḍacāraṃ caritvā' means that monk, having wandered for alms or having finished his meal. 'Vanantamabhihāraye' means he should go only to the forest without delay caused by association with laypeople. 'Upaṭṭhito rukkhamūlasmiṃ' means being stayed at the foot of a tree. 'Āsanūpagato' means having approached a seat, which means sitting down. 'Muni' means one who practices the practice of sagehood (moneyya-paṭipada). Here, by the term 'piṇḍacāraṃ caritvā', the alms-food eater's practice (piṇḍapātikanga) is meant. Since an excellent alms-food eater is also one who practices the uninterrupted alms-round (sapadānacārī), the one-sessioner's practice (ekāsanika), the bowl-food eater's practice (pattapiṇḍika), and the practice of refusing later food (khalupacchābhattika), and also undertakes the three-robe wearer's practice (tecīvarika) and the refuse-rag wearer's practice (paṃsukūlikanga), these six practices are also already mentioned. By the term 'vanantamabhihāraye', the forest-dweller's practice (āraññikanga) is meant; by 'upaṭṭhito rukkhamūlasmiṃ', the tree-root-dweller's practice (rukkhamūlikanga) is meant; by 'āsanūpagato', the sitter's practice (nesajjikanga) is meant. Since they are compatible with these in due order, the open-air-dweller's practice (abbhokāsika), the any-bed-user's practice (yathāsanthatika), and the charnel-ground-dweller's practice (sosānikanga) are also already mentioned. Thus, by this verse, he preached the thirteen ascetic practices to Elder Nālaka.

'Sa jhānapasuto dhīro' means that monk is devoted to and engaged in the jhānas, both by producing jhanas not yet arisen and by the reflecting, attaining, resolving, emerging, and reviewing of jhanas already arisen. 'Dhīro' means one endowed with stable wisdom. 'Vanante ramito siyā' means he should delight only in the forest, not in a monastery near a village. 'Jhāyetha rukkhamūlasmiṃ, attānamabhivedayaṃ' means at that time, he should meditate at the foot of that very tree, making himself greatly pleased with the supramundane jhāna associated with the Path of Arahantship. Indeed, having reached the highest contentment, he makes himself greatly pleased only with supramundane jhāna, and not by any other means. Therefore, it was said 'attānamabhivedayaṃ'. Thus, by these two verses, the devotion to jhāna, delighting in forest lodgings, and the Fruit of Arahantship were preached. Now, having heard this Dhamma teaching, Elder Nālaka was one who went directly to the forest, and even without consuming food...
214:
One should delight only in the forest; it means one should not delight in a dwelling near a village. "One should meditate at the foot of a tree, greatly pleasing oneself" means that one should not only be devoted to mundane jhāna (lokiya-jhāna), but also meditate at that very foot of the tree, greatly pleasing oneself with supramundane jhāna (lokuttara-jhāna) associated with the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) and so forth. Indeed, having reached supreme contentment, the mind is greatly pleased only by supramundane jhāna, and not by any other means. Therefore, He said, "greatly pleasing oneself." Thus, by this verse, He spoke of delighting in a forest dwelling through the practice of jhāna, as well as the attainment of Arahantship.

Now, because the Elder Nālaka, having heard this Dhamma teaching, went towards the forest and was extremely diligent in fulfilling the practice even without food; and it is not possible to practice the recluse's Dhamma without food. For one who does so, life cannot continue; food must be sought without giving rise to defilements; this is the proper way in this matter. Therefore, to show the Elder Nālaka that "one should wander for alms on various days, but defilements should not be allowed to arise," the Buddha spoke the six verses beginning with "Tato ratyā vivasāne," which culminate in the attainment of Arahantship and describe the duty of wandering for alms.

In those verses, "Tato" means even beyond the wandering for alms and going to the forest mentioned in the passage: "Having performed the alms-round, he should go to the forest." "Ratyā vivasāne" means at the end of the night, on the second day. "Gāmantamabhihāraye" means having performed the duties of conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta), one should go to the village while contemplating the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) according to the method mentioned in the duties of going and returning, developing seclusion until the time for alms-round. "Avhānaṃ nābhinandeyya" means that a monk fulfilling the practice should not delight in or accept invitations such as "Venerable Sir, please take your meal at our house," nor should he entertain thoughts like "Will they give or not? Will they not give? Will they give something good? Will they give something not good?" or delight in the food itself. If, however, they take the bowl by force, fill it, and offer it, he should consume it and practice the recluse's Dhamma; the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are not broken. However, from that day on, he should not enter that village. "Abhihārañca gāmato" means if they bring food in hundreds of dishes to the monk who has entered the village, he should not delight in it, nor should he accept even a single morsel from it; instead, he should wander for alms from house to house in order.
215:
When a monk called a sage (muni) reaches a village, he should not behave with a joyful and cheerful manner in the houses of the lay devotees. When the sage practicing the Moneyya-practice reaches a village, he should not behave heedlessly in the houses of the lay devotees; it means he should not engage in inappropriate association with laypeople, such as socializing together.

In seeking food, he should be one who has cut off speech; he should not speak words for seeking food that involve hints (obhāsa), roundabout talk (parikathā), signs (nimitta), or intimation (viññatti). If desired, if he is ill, he may speak to remove the illness. Or, except for verbal intimation regarding lodgings, he may speak hints, roundabout talk, or signs; however, for the remaining requisites, a monk who is not ill should not say anything at all.

718-9. "Alatthaṃ yadidaṃ" etc. The meaning of this verse is: when entering a village for alms, if he receives even a little something, he thinks, "This which I have received is good." If he receives nothing, he thinks, "Not receiving is good (wholesome)." In both gain and loss, that monk remains tādī (equanimous), unchanged, and returns just as he came from the tree. For example, just as a man seeking fruit approaches a tree and, whether he gets fruit or not, goes away without delight or dissatisfaction, being merely indifferent; likewise, approaching a lay devotee's house, whether he receives a gain or not, he goes away being merely indifferent. The verse beginning with "Sa pattapāṇီ" has a very clear meaning.

"Uccāvacā" etc. The connection of this verse is: even though one is endowed with the duty of wandering for alms in this way, one should not be satisfied with just that much but should strive to fulfill the practice. This is because the Dispensation (Sāsana) has the practice as its essence. That practice is said as "Uccāvacā...pe... mutaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: the ascetic (samaṇa) who is the Buddha has declared that Path-practice as high and low (uccāvacā) in terms of superior and inferior. The easy practice with quick direct knowledge is called high (uccā). The difficult practice with slow direct knowledge is called low (avacā). The remaining two are high in one factor and low in another. Or, only the first practice is high, and the remaining three are low. By such high or low practice, they do not go to the other shore, which is Nibbāna, twice. There is also a variant reading "duguṇaṃ." It means they do not go to Nibbāna twice with a single Path. Why? Because those defilements that have been abandoned by a certain Path do not need to be abandoned again. By this, it shows the absence of the nature of falling away (parihāna-dhamma). "Nayidaṃ ekaguṇaṃ mutaṃ" means that the other shore, Nibbāna, is not worthy of being reached only once. Why? Because it is not possible to abandon all defilements with a single Path. By this, it shows that Arahantship cannot be reached with only one Path.
216:
Now, wishing to show the benefits of the practice, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with 'Yassa ca visatā'. The meaning of that verse is: For a monk who practices in this way, because of that practice, the 108 types of craving that are widespread no longer exist. For that monk who has cut the stream of defilements, who has completed all that is to be done by abandoning both merit and demerit, there exists not even the slightest feverish heat born of lust or born of hatred.

Now, upon hearing these verses, the thought arose in the mind of the Elder Nālaka: 'This Moneyya practice is easy to perform, not difficult; it can be fulfilled without much hardship.' Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show that 'the Moneyya practice is indeed difficult,' spoke again the verse beginning with 'Moneyyaṃ te upaññissaṃ'. Therein, 'upaññissaṃ' means I shall show, I shall preach. 'Khuradhārūpamo' means one who should have an analogy like a razor's edge. The meaning is: A monk practicing the Moneyya practice should conduct himself regarding the four requisites by using the razor's edge as an analogy. Just as one licking a razor's edge smeared with honey carefully protects the tongue so it is not cut, likewise, when using requisites obtained rightfully, one should protect the mind so that defilements do not arise. Because it is not easy to obtain requisites through pure means and to use them with blameless consumption, the Blessed One spoke extensively on the instructions related to requisites.

'Jivhāya tālumāhacca, udare saññato siyā' means that even by pressing the tongue against the palate to dispel the craving for taste, one should be restrained in the stomach, not indulging in requisites obtained through impure means. 'Alīnacitto ca siyā' means one should have a mind that is not sluggish, being diligent in the constant cultivation of wholesome states. 'Na caāpi bahu cintaye' means one should not think much through the power of thoughts concerning relatives, the country, or celestial beings. 'Nirāmagandho asito, brahmacariyaparāyaṇo' means being free from defilements, not depending on anything in any existence through craving or views, one should be devoted only to the holy life, which consists of the entire Dispensation along with the three trainings.

724-5. 'Ekāsanassa' refers to a monk who has a secluded seat. Here, by the word 'seat' (āsana), all postures are intended. Therefore, it should be understood to mean that one should practice having the nature of being solitary in all postures. The word 'Ekāsanassa' is in the dative case.
217:
'Samaṇūpāsana' refers to a monk who is constantly devoted to the thirty-eight meditation objects which are to be regularly attended to by recluses, or it refers to the state of attending to the various thirty-eight meditation objects of recluses. This word is also in the dative case, meaning 'for the sake of attendance'. In this verse, it should be understood that 'physical seclusion' (kāya-viveka) is expressed by 'living alone' (ekāsana), and 'mental seclusion' (citta-viveka) is expressed by the practice attended to by recluses.

'Ekattaṃ monamakkhātaṃ' means that this state of being solitary through the power of physical and mental seclusion is called the Moneyya practice. The phrase 'Eko ce abhiramissasi' is a phrase that looks forward to the subsequent verse and should be connected with 'Atha bhāhisi dasadisā'.

'Bhāhisi' means you will speak, you will make known. It means that one who cultivates this Moneyya practice will become famous through renown in all directions. The meaning of the four words beginning with 'Sutvā dhīrānaṃ' is: You will become famous in the ten directions with the sound of fame; upon hearing that sound of fame of those wise ones who are meditators and who have abandoned sensual desires, you should not fall into restlessness because of that fame, but should instead increase your sense of shame (hiri) and faith (saddhā). Being modest because of that fame, and producing faith thinking 'This is the practice leading out of suffering,' you should further increase the practice itself. 'Māmako' means that in such a case, one is my disciple (one who is dear to me).

'Taṃ nadīhi' means that when I say 'increase your shame and faith,' I mean that restlessness should not be practiced; understand this through the analogy of these rivers, and understand the opposite of that restlessness in the small channels and rivulets. 'Sobbhesu' means in the channels. 'Padaresu' means in the small streams. How? Small streams go making noise, being turbulent and agitated, while great rivers like the Ganges go silently. Likewise, one who is restless and boastful, saying 'I am fulfilling the Moneyya practice,' is not my dear disciple. But my dear disciple (māmaka) is one who, having produced shame and faith, has only a humble mind.

727-9. What other analogy is there? It refers to the verse beginning with 'Yadūnakaṃ'. In that verse, if a fool is like a half-filled pot because of his noise-making, and a wise man is like a full lake because of his silence, then why does the Buddha-recluse, being thus occupied with preaching the Dhamma, speak so much? In connection with this question, he spoke the verse 'Yaṃ samaṇo'. Its meaning is: The Buddha-recluse speaks much that is endowed with benefit and possessed of reason.
218:
Endowed with benefit, endowed with the Dhamma, and associated with welfare, the Blessed One teaches that Dhamma not out of restlessness, but indeed knowing it; even if he teaches all day long, he does so being free from proliferation (nippapañca). For all his verbal actions follow his knowledge. Even while teaching in this way, he speaks much, knowing in various ways that 'this is for the welfare of this person,' and not merely because of being talkative.

The connection of the final verse is as follows: In this way, first, the Buddha-ascetic, endowed with the knowledge of omniscience, teaches the Dhamma knowing it; he speaks much knowing it. But he who, having known the Dhamma taught by the Buddha with knowledge that partakes of penetration, is self-restrained and does not speak much though he knows—that muni is worthy of sagehood (mona); that muni has attained sagehood. 

The meaning of that verse is: Knowing that Dhamma, being self-restrained and guarded in mind, he does not speak much though he knows what is spoken that does not bring welfare and happiness to beings. Such a muni, who has entered upon the practice for the sake of sagehood, is worthy of the mona called the practice of sagehood (moneyya-paṭipadā). Not only is he worthy, but it should be understood that the muni has attained the mona called the knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahatship as the climax.

Having heard that, the Elder Nālaka became one of few desires (appiccha) in three matters: in seeing, in hearing, and in questioning. For at the conclusion of the teaching, with a confident mind, he paid homage to the Blessed One and entered the forest; he did not give rise to the restlessness of thinking, 'Oh, if only I could see the Blessed One again.' This was his fewness of desire in seeing. Likewise, he did not give rise to the restlessness of thinking, 'Oh, if only I could hear the Dhamma teaching again.' This was his fewness of desire in hearing. Likewise, he did not give rise to the restlessness of thinking, 'Oh, if only I could ask about the practice of sagehood again.' This was his fewness of desire in questioning.

Being thus of few desires, he entered the foot of a mountain and did not stay in one forest grove for two days, did not sit at the foot of one tree for two days, and did not enter one village for alms for two days. Thus wandering from forest to forest, from tree to tree, and from village to village, practicing the practice suitable for the supramundane Dhamma, he became established in the supreme fruit (Arahatship). Then, because a monk who fulfills the practice of sagehood by making it supreme (ukaṭṭha) lives for only seven months; one who fulfills it by making it medium (majjhima) lives for seven years; and one who fulfills it by making it mild (manda) lives for sixteen years. Since this Elder Nālaka fulfilled it by making it supreme, he remained for seven months, and knowing the exhaustion of his life-span, he bathed, dressed in his inner robe, fastened his girdle, put on his double outer robe, and facing the direction of the One Tenfold Powerful, paid homage with the fivefold prostration.
219:
While standing and leaning against Mount Hiṅgulaka with hands joined in salutation, he attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Knowing that the Elder had attained Parinibbāna, the Blessed One went there together with the Saṅgha of monks, performed the funeral rites, had the relics collected, and after having a cetiya built, he departed.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the Explanation of the Nālaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 12. Explanation of the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta. How did it arise? This sutta arose by the Blessed One's own inclination (attajjhāsaya). For the Blessed One taught this sutta by his own inclination. This is the summary; the details will become clear in the word-by-word explanation itself. Therein, the words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" are just as previously explained. "Pubbārāme" means in the monastery located in the eastern direction of the city of Sāvatthī. "Migāramātu pāsāde": here, the laywoman Visākhā is called "Migāramātā" (Migāra's mother) because she was placed in the position of a mother by her father-in-law, the merchant Migāra. The palace-monastery built by that Migāramātā by selling the Mahālatā ornament worth nine crores is called "Migāramātu-pāsāda" because it has a thousand rooms, with five hundred rooms on the lower floor and five hundred rooms on the upper floor, having a thousand gabled chambers. In that Migāramātu-pāsāda.

"Tena kho pana samayena Bhagavā" means at that time when the Blessed One was dwelling in the Migāramātu-pāsāda in the Eastern Monastery (Pubbārāma) near Sāvatthī. "Tadahu-posathe" means on that day which was the Uposatha; this is what is meant by "on the Uposatha day." "Pannarase": this word, by specifying the Uposatha, excludes other Uposatha days that had arrived. "Puṇṇāya puṇṇamāya rattiyā": it is called "puṇṇāya" (full) because it was the fifteenth day by day-count, and because it was free from defilements such as clouds, and because it was endowed with the qualities of the night. It means on the night of the full moon (puṇṇamāya) because the moon was entirely full. "Bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto" means surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks. "Abbhokāse nisinno hoti" means he was sitting on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the open space (abbhokāse) that was not covered above, within the precinct of the Migāramātu Ratana Palace. "Tuṇhībhūtaṃ tuṇhībhūtaṃ" means being very silent, or from whichever [direction]...
220:
The Blessed One was staying in an open space, on a noble Buddha-seat prepared in a place without overhead covering. While staying there, he surveyed the assembly of monks who were profoundly silent, remaining quiet in both speech and body. "Bhikkhu saṅghaṃ anuviloketvā" means that he looked here and there at the assembly of monks, numbering more than a thousand, who sat surrounding him in great silence, in order to discern the appropriate Dhamma teaching, thinking: "In this assembly, there are this many Sotāpanna monks, this many Sakadāgāmi monks, this many Anāgāmi monks, and this many kalyāṇa-puthujjanas (virtuous worldlings) who are currently practicing insight (vipassanā). What kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable for this assembly of monks?"

"Ye te bhikkhave kusalā dhammā" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), which are called wholesome (kusala) because they are free from disease, faultless, yield desired results, and are born of wisdom; or it refers to the scriptural teachings (pariyatti) that illuminate those factors. They are called "Ariya" (noble) because they are to be approached. They are called "Niyyānika" (emancipating) because they lead out from the three worlds. They are called "Sambodhagāmino" (leading to enlightenment) because they lead to Arahatship, which is known as Sambodhi. "Tေသံ ဝေါ ဘိက္ခဝေ ... သဝနာယ" means: "Monks, what is the reason for your listening to these teachings that are noble, that lead out to Nibbāna, that lead to the attainment of Arahatship, and that yield good results? For what purpose do you listen to these teachings?"

In the phrase "Yāvad-eva dvayatānaṃ dhammānaṃ yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya," the word "yāvad-eva" is a term denoting delimitation and emphasis. It is called "dvaya" because it has two parts; the collection of those two is called "dvayatā." There is also a variant reading "dvayānaṃ." "Yathābhūtaṃ ñāṇāya" means for the sake of knowledge that sees things as they truly are, without distortion. The meaning is: it is for the sake of the true knowledge known as insight (vipassanā) to perceive the states that are established in two parts, such as mundane and supramundane, and not for any purpose beyond this. Through listening, only this much can be achieved; however, the attainment of higher distinction beyond that is possible only through the development of meditation (bhāvanā). In the passage "Kiñca dvayataṃ vadethā," the intention is: "Monks, if the desire to know should arise in you, 'Venerable Sir, what kind of dyad (dvayata) of states do you speak of?'" The literal meaning of the words is: "What kind of state of being a dyad do you speak of?"

(1) After asking this, the Blessed One, wishing to show the dyad, spoke the words beginning with "Idaṃ dukkhaṃ." In that context, among the four noble truths which constitute the dyad, the first contemplation (anupassanā) is the seeing of the mundane truth of suffering as one part, together with its cause, as in "This is suffering, this is the origin of suffering." The second contemplation is the seeing of the supramundane truth of cessation as the second part, together with its means (the path). Here, the first contemplation occurs through the third and fourth purifications (visuddhi), and the second contemplation occurs through the fifth purification. In this way, for one who rightly contemplates the dyad of states according to the method described as "rightly contemplating the dyad..."
221:
For a monk who is diligent (appamatta) by not being devoid of mindfulness, who is ardent (ātāpī) by the heat of physical and mental energy that burns away defilements, and who is dedicated (pahitatta) by having a mind directed toward Nibbāna without regard for body or life. "Pāṭikaṅkhā" means it is to be expected (or desired). "Aññā in this very life" means the attainment of Arahatship in this very existence. In the phrase "if there is a residue (upādisesa), the state of Non-returning (Anāgāmitā)," "upādisesa" refers to the remainder of the aggregates of clinging that are to be grasped for a future birth. It shows that if such a residue exists, the state of a Non-returner is to be expected. In this matter, although the lower fruits also result from such contemplation of the dyad, this was said to generate effort for the higher fruits.

"He said this," etc., are the words of the Reciters (Saṅgītikāras). In that context, "idaṃ" refers to the preceding words beginning with "Monks, those..." "Etaṃ" refers to the verse composition that is about to be spoken, beginning with "Whatever suffering..." Since these verses illuminate the Four Noble Truths, they merely clarify the meaning already stated. Nevertheless, they were spoken for the benefit of those who delight in verses, those who arrived later, those who could not remember the previously spoken words, and those with distracted minds, who might think, "It would be good if he spoke now." Alternatively, they were spoken to show the distinction by illustrating those who do not practice insight and those who do, and by demonstrating the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). In the subsequent verses, the method should be understood in this same way.

In that verse, the word "yattha ca" indicates Nibbāna. For in Nibbāna, suffering ceases in every way, in all aspects, along with its cause, and without remainder. "Tañca maggaṃ" refers to the path endowed with the eight factors.

731-3. In the phrase "cetovimuttihīnā te, atho paññāvimuttiyā," it should be understood that the concentration in the fruit of Arahatship is called deliverance of mind (cetovimutti) due to the fading of lust (rāga-virāga). The wisdom in the fruit of Arahatship is called deliverance by wisdom (paññāvimutti) due to the fading of ignorance (avijjā-virāga). Alternatively, for one of a craving temperament, the fruit of Arahatship attained by suppressing defilements through the power of absorption (appanā-jhāna) is called cetovimutti due to the fading of lust; for one of a view-inclined temperament, the fruit of Arahatship attained by practicing insight after developing only access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) is called paññāvimutti due to the fading of ignorance. Or, cetovimutti refers to the fruit of Non-returning which is free from sensual lust, and paññāvimutti refers to the fruit of Arahatship which is free from ignorance in every way. "Antakiriyāya" means for the sake of making an end to the suffering of the round. "Jātijarūpagā" should be understood as those who have come to birth and aging, or those who are approached by birth and aging, and thus cannot escape those dangers. The rest of the words from the beginning are quite clear. At the conclusion of the verses, sixty monks...
222:
Having learned this teaching and developed insight, they reached the state of Arahantship right in that very seat. Just as in this instance, so too in all the sections (vāra), the monks attained Arahantship.

(2) For that very reason, the Blessed One taught the contemplation of dualities (dvayatānupassanā) in various ways, starting with the method: "It might also be in another way."
In that second section, "upadhi-paccayā" (conditioned by acquisitions) means having kamma accompanied by taints (sāsava-kamma) as its condition. In this context, kamma accompanied by taints is intended by the term "upadhi" (acquisition). "Asesavirāganirodhā" (through the total fading away and cessation) means either through cessation by the total fading away of lust, or the cessation known as the total fading away of lust.

"Upadhinidānā" (having acquisitions as their source) means having kamma as their condition. "Dukkha-ssa jātippabhavānupassī" (observing the source and birth of suffering) means repeatedly observing "upadhi" as the cause of the birth of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). The remaining words here are clear. Thus, this section is also taught with the Four Noble Truths, culminating in the peak of Arahantship. Just as this section is understood, so should all sections be understood.

(3) In that third section, "avijjā-paccayā" (conditioned by ignorance) means conditioned by ignorance associated with the accumulation of kamma that leads to existence (bhava). As for "dukkha" (suffering), in all places, it refers only to the suffering of the round.

"Jātimaraṇasaṃsāraṃ" (the round of birth and death) refers to birth (jāti) as the arising of the aggregates (khandha), death (maraṇa) as the breaking up of the aggregates, and the round (saṃsāra) as the succession of the aggregates. "Vajanti" means they go or they arrive. "Itthabhāvaññathābhāvaṃ" (this state and the other state) refers to this human state and the states of other remaining classes of beings. "Gati" (destination/course) refers to the state of being a condition (paccaya-bhāva).

"Avijjā hāyanti" (ignorance is abandoned) refers to this very ignorance. "Vijja-gatā ca ye sattā" (those beings who have attained knowledge) refers to those beings whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who have gone through and pierced the defilements with the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. The remaining words have a clear meaning.

(4) In the fourth section, "saṅkhāra-paccayā" (conditioned by volitional formations) means conditioned by meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations (puññā-apuññā-āneñjābhisaṅkhāra).

738-9. "Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā" (knowing this danger) means knowing this suffering caused by volitional formations as "this is a danger." "Sabbasaṅkhārasamathā" (the calming of all formations) means the calming of all types of volitional formations mentioned through Path-knowledge; it means being endowed with the fruit because the defilements have been destroyed. "Saññānaṃ" (of perceptions) refers to the cessation of sensual perceptions (kāma-saññā) and so on, by the Path alone. "Etaṃ ñatvā yathātathaṃ" (knowing this as it really is) means knowing this cessation of suffering (Nibbāna) without distortion. "Sammaddasā" means seeing rightly. "Sammadaññāya" (having known rightly) means having known the conditioned (saṅkhata) as impermanent and so on, and the unconditioned (asaṅkhata) as permanent and so on. "Mārasaṃyogaṃ" (the bond of Māra) refers to the round of rebirth in the three planes of existence. The remaining words have a clear meaning.
223:
(5) In the fifth section, "viññāṇa-paccayā" (conditioned by consciousness) means conditioned by volitional consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa) co-arisen with kamma. "Nicchāto" means a person without craving. "Parinibbuto" means one who is cooled through the extinguishing of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna). The rest is clear.

(6) In the sixth section, "phassa-paccayā" (conditioned by contact) means conditioned by contact associated with volitional consciousness. Thus, in this context, contact (phassa) is mentioned without mentioning mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) and the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) which are usually stated in sequence. The reason is that those—mind-and-matter and the six sense bases—are mixed with materiality and thus are not exclusively associated with kamma. This suffering of the round can arise either from kamma or from states associated with kamma (therefore, only contact associated with kamma is mentioned).

742-3. "Bhavasotānusārinaṃ" (those who follow the stream of existence) refers to those who follow the stream of craving. "Pariññāya" (having fully understood) means having distinguished with the three types of full understanding (pariññā). "Aññāya" (having known) means having known with the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship. "Upasame ratā" (delighting in peace) refers to those who delight in Nibbāna by the power of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). "Phassābhisamayā" (through the realization of contact) means through the cessation of contact. The rest is clear.

(7) In the seventh section, "vedanā-paccayā" (conditioned by feeling) means conditioned by feeling associated with kamma.

744-5. "Adukkhamasukhaṃ saha" (together with neither-painful-nor-pleasant) means together with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. "Etaṃ dukkha-nti ñatvāna" (knowing this as suffering) means either knowing all this that is felt as the "cause of suffering," or knowing it as suffering through the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-dukkha), the suffering of states (ṭhiti-dukkha), and the suffering of ignorance (aññāṇa-dukkha). "Mosadhammaṃ" (of a nature to deceive) refers to things that have the nature to perish. "Palokinaṃ" (subject to disintegration) refers to things that have the nature to disintegrate through aging and death. "Phussa phussa" (having touched repeatedly) means having known repeatedly with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). "Vayaṃ passaṃ" (seeing the passing away) means being one who sees only the destruction at the end. Thus, one knows those feelings, or one knows the state of suffering in those feelings—this is the meaning of "evaṃ tattha vijānati." "Vedanānaṃ khayā" (through the destruction of feelings) means through the destruction of feelings associated with kamma by Path-knowledge thereafter. The rest is clear.

(8) In the eighth section, "taṇhā-paccayā" (conditioned by craving) means conditioned by craving which is the constituent of kamma (kamma-sambhāra-taṇhā). "Etamādīnavaṃ ñatvā, taṇhaṃ dukkhassa sambhavaṃ" (knowing this danger, craving as the origin of suffering) means knowing the danger of craving which is the cause of the arising of this suffering. The rest is clear.

(9) In the ninth section, "upādāna-paccayā" (conditioned by clinging) means conditioned by clinging which is the constituent of kamma (kamma-sambhāra-upādāna).
224:
748-9. 'Existence' (bhava) refers to resultant existence (vipākabhava), the manifestation of the aggregates. 'The one who has come to be is suffering' means that the one who has come to be reaches the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). Although fools think, 'The one who has come to be reaches happiness,' [the Buddha] said, 'Everyone born must die,' showing only suffering even in that existence. The meaning of the second verse is: The wise, who thoroughly know through [the characteristics of] impermanence and so forth, realize through higher knowledge Nibbāna—the end of birth—due to the destruction of clinging, and they no longer go to a new existence.

(10) In the tenth turn, 'due to the cause of effort' (ārambhapaccayā) means due to the cause of energy associated with kamma. 'Liberated in the effortless' (anārambhe vimuttino) refers to one whose mind is liberated in Nibbāna, where there is no effort to be made. The remaining words are clear in meaning.

(11) In the eleventh turn, 'due to the cause of nutriment' (āhārapapaccayā) means due to the cause of nutriment associated with kamma. Alternatively, there are four types of beings: those who approach form, those who approach feeling, those who approach perception, and those who approach formations. Among these four, beings in the eleven realms of the sense sphere (kāmadhātu) are called 'approachers of form' (rūpūpaga) because they consume edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra). In the fine-material sphere (rūpadhātu), excluding the non-percipient beings, the remaining beings are called 'approachers of feeling' (vedanူpaga) because they consume contact-nutriment (phassāhāra). In the lower three immaterial spheres (arūpadhātu), beings are called 'approachers of perception' (saññūpaga) because they consume mental volition-nutriment (manosañcetanāhāra) produced by perception. In the highest existence (bhavagga), beings are called 'approachers of formations' (saṅkhārūpaga) because they consume consciousness-nutriment (viññāṇāhāra) produced by formations. Thus, it should be understood that whatever suffering arises, it all arises due to the cause of nutriment.

'Health' (ārogya) refers to Nibbāna. 'One who uses after reflection' (saṅkhāya sevī) refers to one who uses the four requisites after reflecting on them, or one who reflects on the world as 'the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements' and uses them with the knowledge of 'impermanence, suffering, and non-self.' 'Established in the Dhamma' (dhammaṭṭha) refers to one who stands in the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. 'Does not fall into designations' (saṅkhyaṃ nopeti) means they no longer fall into designations or categories such as 'deva' or 'human' and so forth. The remaining words are clear in meaning.

(12) In the twelfth turn, 'due to the cause of shaking' (iñjitapaccayā) means due to the cause of the shaking of kamma-accumulation from among any of the shakings of craving, conceit, views, kamma, and defilements. 'Relinquishing shaking' (ejaṃ vossajja) means abandoning craving. 'Having suppressed formations' (saṅkhāre uparundhiya) means causing the cessation of kamma and the formations associated with kamma. The remaining words are clear in meaning.
225:
(13) In the thirteenth turn, 'shaking occurs to the one who relies' means that for one who relies on the five aggregates through craving, or through craving, views, and conceit, shaking occurs due to fear, like the devas in the Sīha Sutta. The remaining words are clear.

(14) In the fourteenth turn, 'by forms' refers to fine-material existences or fine-material attainments. 'Formless things' refers to immaterial existences or immaterial attainments. 'Cessation' refers to Nibbāna.
'Those who abandon death' refers to those who abandon death as mortality (maraṇa-maccu), death as defilements (kilesa-maccu), and death as the deity Mara (devaputta-maccu); it means those who go having abandoned these three kinds of death. The remaining words are clear.

(15) In the fifteenth turn, 'which thing' is said in reference to mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). For that mind-and-matter is closely observed by the world as 'this is the truth' by way of being permanent, beautiful, and pleasant. In the phrase 'that is for the Noble Ones' (tadamariyānaṃ), it is said by eliding the nasal and the 'i' sound from 'taṃ idaṃ ariyānaṃ.' 'This is false' means that even if it is taken by way of permanence and so forth, it is false; it is not like that. Again, 'which thing' is said in reference to Nibbāna. For that Nibbāna is closely observed by the world as 'this is false, there is nothing' because of the absence of form, feeling, and so forth. 'That is the truth for the Noble Ones' means that Nibbāna is clearly seen with right wisdom as it really is, as 'truth' in the ultimate sense, because it is beautiful due to being free from defilements, pleasant due to being the opposite of the suffering of the process of existence, and permanent due to being ultimate peace.

762-3. 'Thinking of self in what is non-self' means thinking of self in mind-and-matter, which is non-self. 'Thinks this is truth' means thinking of this mind-and-matter as 'truth' by way of permanence and so forth. 'In whatever way' means they think in whatever way such as 'my form, my feeling' regarding form or feeling. 'Otherwise than that' means that mind-and-matter becomes otherwise than the way they thought. What is the reason? Because that thinking is false for them. Since the way they thought is false, it becomes otherwise; this is the meaning. Why is it false? For that which is deceptive is brief. Whatever is brief and appears only for a moment is of a deceptive nature, of a vanishing nature; and mind-and-matter is of such a nature. 'Due to the realization of truth' means due to the penetration of the Four Noble Truths. The remaining words are clear.

(16) In the sixteenth turn, 'which thing' is said in reference to the six kinds of desirable objects (iṭṭhārammaṇa). For the world [sees] those desirable objects like moths, fish, and monkeys [see] lamps, hooks, and resin...
226:
The multitude (those who are not Noble Ones) closely contemplate sensual pleasures as happiness. The Noble Ones (Ariyas), however, clearly see these very things as suffering (dukkha) according to reality with right wisdom, in the manner: "Sensual pleasures are variegated, sweet, and delightful; they churn the mind in various forms" (Sn. 50; Cnd. 136). Again, with the word "yaṃ", He refers to Nibbāna itself. The multitude closely contemplates Nibbāna as suffering because of the absence of sensual pleasures. The Noble Ones, however, clearly see this Nibbāna as happiness according to reality with right wisdom, because it is the ultimate happiness (paramattha-sukha).

765-6. "Kevalā" means without remainder. "Iṭṭhā" means desired or longed for. "Kantā" means beloved. "Manāpā" means objects that expand or please the mind. "Yāvatatthīti vuccati" means as many as these six objects are said to exist. Here, a grammatical variation (vacanabyattaya) should be understood. In the phrase "ete vo", the word "vo" is a mere particle (nipāta).

767-8. "Sukhanti diṭṭhamariyēhi, sakkāyassuparodhanaṃ" means that the Noble Ones see the cessation of the five aggregates, which is Nibbāna, as happiness; it refers to Nibbāna. This view is contrary to the view of worldlings. "Passataṃ" means for those who see (the wise). In this context, the word "yaṃ" in "yaṃ pare" refers to the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma). Again, the word "yaṃ" in "yaṃ pare" refers to Nibbāna.

769-71. "Passa" is an address to the listener. "Dhammaṃ" refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna. "Sampamūḷhetthaviddasū" means that in this Nibbāna, the fools (the ignorant) are greatly deluded. Why are they greatly deluded? For those obstructed by ignorance and unable to see, there is darkness that causes blindness; because of that darkness, they cannot see the Dhamma of Nibbāna. For the virtuous, however, Nibbāna is open like light, seen with the eye of wisdom. "Santike na vijānanti, magā dhammassa kovidā" means that although Nibbāna is near—because it can be attained immediately by discerning the five components ending in skin (taca-pañcaka: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, and skin) within one's own body, or because it is merely the cessation of one's own aggregates—those who are like animals or those who are unskilled in the Truth (Dhamma) do not know it at all. ... "Māradheyyānupannehi" means by those who do not follow the cycle of the three realms (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa).
227:
The connection of the final verse is as follows: "Who else besides the Noble Ones (Ariyas) can know Nibbāna, which is so difficult to understand?" The meaning of that verse is: Excluding the Noble Ones, who else is worthy of knowing the state of Nibbāna? Having known that state of Nibbāna well through the fourth Noble Path, they become free from taints (āsavas) immediately and attain peace through the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna); or, having known it well and becoming free from taints, they finally attain parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching by culminating it with the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala).

'Attamanā' means having a delighted mind. 'Abhinandun' means they greatly rejoiced. 'In this exposition' (imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṃ) refers to this sixteenth exposition. While it was being preached. The remaining words are clear.

Thus, in each of these sixteen expositions, for every sixty monks, the minds of nine hundred and sixty monks were liberated from the taints without clinging. In these sixteen instances, taking four truths at a time, sixty-four truths were preached in various ways according to the disposition of those to be led (veneyya).

## The explanation of the Dvayatānupassanā Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## The third chapter (vagga) is also finished according to the method of explaining the meaning, known by the name
## Mahāvagga.
228:
## 4. Aṭṭhakavagga
## 1. Kāmasuttavaṇṇanā

This sutta beginning with 'Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa' is the Kāma Sutta. What is the origin of its occurrence? While the Blessed One was residing in Sāvatthī, a certain Brahmin was plowing a field on the bank of the Aciravatī River, located between the city of Sāvatthī and the Jetavana Monastery, thinking, 'I shall sow barley.' While the Blessed One was entering for alms surrounded by the community of monks, He saw the Brahmin and, upon reflection, saw that 'This Brahmin's barley crops will be destroyed.' Again, reflecting on the perfection of his supporting conditions (upanissaya), He saw the Brahmin's supporting conditions for attaining the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Reflecting on 'When will he be able to reach it?', He saw that 'When the crops are destroyed and he is overcome by grief, he will reach it after hearing the Dhamma teaching.'

Then the Blessed One thought, 'If I approach the Brahmin at this very time, he will not think my advice is worth listening to. Brahmins have various diverse interests. Indeed, if I support and look after him from now on, his heart will become soft toward me, and then he will listen to my advice.' Thus, He approached the Brahmin and asked, 'Brahmin, what are you doing?' The Brahmin, thinking, 'This ascetic Gotama of such noble birth is exchanging friendly greetings with me,' became pleased with the Blessed One by that much alone and replied, 'Venerable Gotama, I am plowing the field to sow barley.' Then the Elder Sāriputta thought, 'The Blessed One has exchanged friendly greetings with the Brahmin. The Tathāgatas do not do this without cause or reason. I, too, shall exchange friendly greetings with him.' He approached the Brahmin and greeted him in the same way. Similarly, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and the remaining eighty Great Disciples did the same. The Brahmin became exceedingly delighted.

Then, one day while the crops were flourishing, the Blessed One, having finished His meal and traveling from Sāvatthī to the Jetavana Monastery, stepped off the path, went to the Brahmin, and said, 'Brahmin, your barley field is beautiful.' The Brahmin replied, 'Venerable Gotama, it is indeed beautiful. If it succeeds, I shall share it with you as well.' Then, after four months, the barley crops matured. While the Brahmin was making effort, thinking, 'I shall harvest today or tomorrow,' a great cloud arose and rained throughout the entire night. The Aciravatī River overflowed and swept away all the barley. The Brahmin was unhappy all night, and at dawn, he went to the riverbank. Seeing the destruction of all his crops, he was overcome with intense grief, thinking, 'I am ruined; how shall I live now?' The Blessed One also...
229:
At the time of dawn that same night, the Blessed One, surveying the world with His Buddha-eye, knew that 'Today is the time to preach the Dhamma to the Brahmin.' Following the routine of going for alms, He entered Sāvatthī and stood at the door of the Brahmin's house. When the Brahmin saw the Blessed One, he thought, 'The ascetic Gotama has come wishing to console me who am overcome by grief.' He prepared a seat, took the bowl, and invited the Blessed One to sit. Although the Blessed One already knew, He asked the Brahmin, 'Brahmin, why do you live with a distressed mind?' The Brahmin replied, 'Yes, Venerable Gotama, all my barley fields have been swept away by the water.' Then the Blessed One, saying, 'Brahmin, one should not be dejected when there is loss, nor should one be elated when there is success. Sensual pleasures (kāma) indeed both succeed and fail,' and knowing the suitable teaching for that Brahmin, He preached this sutta by way of Dhamma teaching. In this sutta, I shall explain only the connection of the meanings of the words briefly; the detailed explanation should be understood in the manner stated in the Mahāniddesa. As in this sutta, so also in all the suttas following this, it should be understood in the same way.

In that verse, 'kāmaṃ' refers to the sensuality of objects (vatthukāma), which are the phenomena of the three planes of existence such as pleasant forms and so on. 'Kāmayamānassa' means to one who desires. 'Tassa ce taṃ samijjhati' means if that object called 'kāma' succeeds for that being who desires it; it means if he obtains that object. 'Addhā pītimano hoti' means he certainly becomes one with a joyful mind. 'Laddhā' means having obtained. 'Macco' means a being. 'Yadicchati' means that which is desired.

'Tassa ce kāmayānassa' means to that person who desires sensual pleasures or who is driven by (longing for) sensual pleasures. 'Chandajātassa' means to one in whom craving (taṇhā) has arisen. 'Jantuno' means to a being. 'Te kāmā parihāyanti' means if those sensual pleasures decline and are destroyed. 'Sallaviddhova ruppati' means then he suffers as if pierced by an iron arrow or the like.

The summary of the third verse is: If a person avoids these sensual pleasures—either by suppressing the lust of desire (chandarāga) therein or by completely uprooting it—just as one avoids the head of a snake with one's foot. That monk, being mindful, completely overcomes the craving called 'visattikā' (the entangler), because it stands spreading throughout the entire world.
230:
776-8. The summary of the meaning of the three subsequent verses is as follows— Whosoever repeatedly clings to and lusts after these various sensual pleasures, such as fields like rice fields, property like house sites, gold known as kahāpaṇas, livestock like cattle and horses, women perceived as such, or relatives and kin, and other delightful forms and so forth—that person is oppressed, afflicted, and crushed by the defilements known as 'weakness' (abala). Or else, because of being devoid of the power of faith (saddhā-bala) and so forth, that weak person is oppressed even by weak defilements; the meaning is that they are oppressed because of their weakness.

Then, while that person, lusting for sensual pleasures, is guarding and seeking them, they are oppressed by manifest dangers such as lions, and unmanifest dangers such as bodily misconduct and so forth. Furthermore, suffering such as rebirth follows that person who is overcome by unmanifest dangers, just as water enters a broken boat.

Therefore, a being should always be mindful, practicing meditation such as mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), and should avoid sensual pleasures, shunning every kind of defilement-sensuality (kilesa-kāma) regarding objective-sensuality (vatthu-kāma) such as forms and so forth, by means of abandoning by suppression (vikkhamphana-pahāna) and abandoning by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). Thus, having abandoned those sensual pleasures, one should cross the fourfold flood (ogha) only by the path that brings about their abandonment; one would be able to cross it.

Then, just as a man, having bailed out a boat heavy with water, would reach the other shore without difficulty with the lightened boat; even so, having bailed out the water of defilements from the boat of the individual existence (attabhāva), one would reach the other shore with the lightened individual existence. Having reached Nibbāna, which is the further shore of all phenomena, one would go by attaining the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), and would attain final parinibbāna through the Nibbāna-element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Thus, the Teacher concluded the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Brahmin and the Brahmin lady were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala).
