## The Explanation of the Kāma Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
231:
## 2. Explanation of the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta
The sutta beginning with 'Satto guhāyaṃ' is the Guhaṭṭhaka Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja went to King Udena's park named Āvaṭṭaka on the bank of the Ganges in Kosambī, wishing to sit for the day-abiding in a cool place. That this Elder used to go there at other times as well, just as the Elder Gavampati went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven due to previous habit, should be understood according to the method mentioned in the explanation of the Vaṅgīsa Sutta. There, at the foot of a cool tree on the bank of the Ganges, he sat for the day-abiding, having entered into a meditative attainment (samāpatti). King Udena also went to play in the park on that very day, and after playing in the park for a large part of the day with dancing, singing, and so forth, he fell asleep with his head on the lap of a woman, being intoxicated with drink. The remaining women, saying 'The King is asleep,' got up and while gathering flowers, fruits, and so forth in the park, saw the Elder. Arousing a sense of shame and fear (hiri-ottappa), they cautioned one another, saying 'Do not make a noise,' and approached quietly. Having paid homage, they sat down surrounding the Elder. The Elder emerged from the attainment and taught the Dhamma to those women. They were delighted and listened, saying 'Sādhu, sādhu'.

The woman who was sitting with the King's head on her lap, thinking 'These women have abandoned me and are playing,' moved her thigh with a jealous heart and woke the King. The King woke up and, not seeing his harem, asked, 'Where are these low women?' She said, 'Those women, who have no respect for you, have gone saying, "We will delight with a recluse."' The King, being angry, went towards the Elder. When those women saw the King, some stood up, but some did not stand up, saying, 'Great King, we are listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the monk.' The King, being even more angry because of that, did not even pay homage to the Elder and asked, 'For what purpose have you come?' 'Great King, I have come for the sake of seclusion (viveka),' he replied. The King said, 'You say you have come for seclusion, yet you sit thus surrounded by a harem!' and then said, 'Tell me about your seclusion!' The Elder, though confident in speaking about seclusion, remained silent, reflecting, 'This King is not asking because he wishes to know.' The King said, 'If you do not tell me, I will have you bitten by red ants,' and while taking a nest of red ants from another Asoka tree, it fell scattered over himself. He wiped his body, took another nest, and came towards the Elder again. The Elder [thought], 'If this King [acts] against me...'
232: "If this king should wrong me, he would be headed for the states of deprivation (apāya)," thinking thus and out of compassion for the king, the Elder ascended into the air by psychic power and departed. At that time, the women said, "Great King, other kings, upon seeing such a monk, worship him with flowers and perfumes; but you, Great King, have endeavored to torment him with a nest of red ants, and have risen up to destroy your lineage." The king, realizing his fault, remained silent and asked the gardener, "Does the Elder come here on other days as well?" "Yes, Great King, he does," the gardener replied. "If so, inform me when he comes," the king instructed. One day, when the Elder arrived, the gardener informed the king. The king approached the Elder, asked him questions, and became one who has gone for refuge for life. On the day he was tormented with the nest of red ants, the Elder traveled through the air, then dived into the earth and emerged at the Buddha's Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber). The Blessed One, lying on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending in the lion's posture (sīhaseyya), saw the Elder and said, "Bhāradvāja, why have you come at an unseasonable time?" The Elder replied, "Yes, Blessed One," and reported the whole incident. Hearing this, the Blessed One said, "What benefit will talk of seclusion (viveka) be to that king who is greedy for sensual pleasures?" and while still lying on his right side, he spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the Elder. In that sutta, "satto" means one who is attached. "Guhāyaṃ" means in the body. The body is called a "cave" (guhā) because it is the dwelling place of wild beasts such as lust (rāga) and so on. "Bahunābhichanno" means one who is greatly shrouded by the many entanglements of defilements such as lust. By this term, the internal fetter (ajjhatta-bandhana) is meant. "Tiṭṭhanti" means those who remain by the power of lust and so on. "Naro" means a being. "Mohanasmiṃ pagāḷho": sensual pleasures are called "mohana" (that which causes delusion). In these sensual pleasures, devas and humans are deluded; it means being one who has plunged and sunk into those sensual pleasures. By this term, the external fetter (bahiddhā-bandhana) is meant. "Dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho so" means such a person is far from the three kinds of seclusion, such as physical seclusion (kāya-viveka); it means they are not near. Why? Because in this world, sensual pleasures are difficult to abandon. It means that in the world, it is not possible to abandon sensual pleasures easily. Thus, having concluded the first verse with "dūre vivekā hi tathāvidho so," he spoke the verse beginning with "icchānidānā" to reveal the nature of such beings once more. In that verse, "icchānidānā" means those who have craving (taṇhā) as their cause. "Bhavasātabaddhā" means those who are bound to the sweetness of existence, such as pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā). They are difficult to liberate.
233: Beings who have craving as their cause and are bound to the sweetness of existence, or to the things that are objects of sweetness in existence, are difficult to liberate. Others are not able to make them free. Or else, this is a statement of cause: those beings are difficult to liberate. Why? Because they are not to be liberated by others. If they were to be liberated, they would be liberated only by their own strength; this is the meaning. "Pacchā pure vāpi apekkhamānā" means longing for sensual pleasures that are in the future or the past. They long for these present sensual pleasures, as well as the two kinds of sensual pleasures mentioned before, the past and the future, with intense craving. The connection of these two phrases with the phrase "te duppamuñcā na hi aññamokkhā" should be understood; otherwise, it would not be known what those who long are doing or what has been done. 781-2. Thus, having concluded the first verse with "dūre vivekā tathāvidho" and having revealed the nature of such beings with the second verse, he now spoke the verse beginning with "kāmesu giddhā" to reveal their performance of evil deeds. The meaning of that verse is: those beings are greedy for sensual pleasures with the craving for enjoyment, and because they are repeatedly engaged in seeking them and so on, they are industrious; because they have reached delusion, they are deluded; because of ignorance, stinginess, and disregard for the words of the Buddha and others, they are difficult to give to (ungenerous). While established in unrighteousness (visama) such as bodily misconduct, when they reach the suffering of death at the time of the end, they wail, "What will become of us when we pass away from here?" Because they wail in this way, he said, "Sikkhetha... māhu dhīrā." Therein, "sikkhetha" means one should practice the three trainings (tisso sikkhā). "Idheva" means only in this Dispensation (sāsana). The rest is clear. Now, to show the ruin of those who do not act accordingly, he spoke the verse beginning with "passāmi." Therein, "passāmi" means I see with the physical eye and so on. "Loke" means in the realms such as the states of deprivation. "Pariphandamānaṃ" means quivering here and there. "Pajaṃ imaṃ" means this mass of beings. "Taṇhāgataṃ" means overcome by craving, meaning those who are made to fall into the states of deprivation. "Bhavesu" means in the sensual realms of existence and so on. "Hīnā narā" means people who perform base deeds. "Maccumukhe lapanti" means when they reach the final time, they wail in the jaws of death. "Avīta-taṇhāse" means those whose craving has not departed. "Bhavābhavesu" means in the sensual realms of existence and so on, or in great and small existences, meaning in repeated existences. Now, because those whose craving has not departed quiver and wail in this way, he spoke the verse beginning with "mamāyite" to exhort them in the removal of craving. Therein, "mamāyite" means in the object grasped as "mine" through craving and views. "Passatha" is addressed to the listeners. "Tattheva" means in that very place. The rest is clear. Thus, in this context, having shown the gratification (assāda) with the first verse, and having shown the danger (ādīnava) with the four subsequent verses, he now spoke the two verses beginning with "ubhosu antesu" to show the escape (nissaraṇa) along with its cause, and the benefit of escape; or, having shown the danger and impurity of sensual desire with all the verses, he now wished to show the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma). Therein, "ubhosu antesu" means in the two parts such as the causality of contact (phassa). "Vineyya" means having removed sensual desire. "Phassapariññā" means through the full understanding of contact such as eye-contact, or through the full understanding of all mental phenomena associated with that contact, and of those mental phenomena...
234:
Addressing the listeners, he said: "Etampi" means this danger as well. The rest is clear.

Thus, in this context, having shown gratification (assāda) with the first verse, and then the danger (ādīnava) with the following four verses, he now spoke the two verses beginning with "Ubhosu antesu" wishing to show the escape (nissaraṇa) along with its cause and the benefits of escape; or alternatively, having shown the danger, vileness, and defilement of sensual pleasures with all those verses, he now spoke them wishing to show the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma). In that verse, "Ubhosu antesu" (in both ends) refers to the two divisions such as contact (phassa) and the origin of contact. "Vineyya chandaṃ" means having removed lustful desire (chandarāga). "Phassaṃ pariññāya" means having fully understood contact such as eye-contact, or all mental phenomena associated with that contact following its sequence, and material phenomena by way of their bases, doors, and objects; thus, it means fully understanding the entire mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). "Anānugiddho" means being without greed for all things such as visual objects. "Yadattagarahī tadakubbamāno" means not performing an action that one would reproach oneself for. "Nalippatī diṭṭhasutesu dhīro" means that such a firm and wise person (dhīra) is not smeared by even one of the two types of smearing—the smearing of craving (taṇhā) and the smearing of views (diṭṭhi)—regarding things seen and heard; being unsmeared like the sky, he reaches supreme purity.

The summary meaning of the verse "Saññaṃ pariññā" is: not only contact, but also perception (saññā) such as the perception of sensual pleasure, or following the sequence of perception, having fully understood mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa) through the three types of full understanding as mentioned before, one should cross the fourfold flood (ogha) by this practice. Having thus crossed, the sage (muni) whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is not smeared because of abandoning the smearing of craving and views in the grasping of craving and views; having pulled out the thorns (salla) such as lust, and reaching the fullness of mindfulness, he wanders diligently (or, having pulled out the thorns by wandering diligently in the preliminary stage), he no longer longs for this world or the next, such as his own or another's existence. Because of the cessation of the final consciousness, he attains Parinibbāna like a fire without fuel. The Blessed One, wishing only to establish the lineage of the Dhamma, concluded the teaching with Arahantship as the climax. He did not cause the Path or Fruit to arise further through this teaching, because it was preached to an Arahant whose taints were already destroyed.

## In the Khuddaka-aṭṭhakathā named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Commentary on the Guhāṭṭhakasutta of the Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā is finished.
235:
## 3. Commentary on the Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasutta

The text beginning with "Vadanti ve duṭṭhamanā" is the Duṭṭhaṭṭhakasutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? First, I shall state the origin of the opening verse. The heretics (titthiyas), being envious and jealous of the great gain and honor (lābhasakkāra) that had arisen for the Blessed One and the community of monks, sent forth a female ascetic named Sundarī. This female ascetic Sundarī was a beautiful woman of the country, a white-clad ascetic. Having bathed well, dressed well, and being adorned with flowers and perfumes, she would listen to the Blessed One's Dhamma and then, at the time when the residents of Sāvatthī were leaving the Jetavana monastery, she would leave Sāvatthī and head towards the Jetavana monastery.

When people asked, "Where are you going?", she would say, "I am going to delight the ascetic Gotama and his disciples," and she would wander near the gatehouse of the Jetavana monastery. When the Jetavana gate was closed, she would return to the city, and at dawn, she would go to Jetavana again and wander near the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) as if picking flowers. When people who came to pay respects to the Buddha asked, "Why have you come?", she would say just anything. In this way, after about half a month had passed, the heretics killed Sundarī and buried her in a pit. At dawn, they made a great uproar saying, "We do not see Sundarī," and informed the King. With the King's permission, they entered the Jetavana monastery, pretending to search, and having exhumed the body from the place where it was buried, they placed it on a litter, carried it into the city, and cast reproaches. All this should be understood as it appears in the Udāna Pali.

On that day, at the time of dawn, the Blessed One, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye, knew, "Today the heretics will cause infamy (ayasa)." Considering, "Let not the people, believing their words and becoming disillusioned with one like me, head towards the states of misery (apāya)," he closed the door of the Fragrant Chamber and stayed only inside the Fragrant Chamber. He did not enter the city for alms. Although the monks saw the door closed, they entered the city as before. When the people saw the monks, they reviled them in various ways.

Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Blessed One of that matter and said, "Venerable Sir, the heretics have caused great infamy. It is no longer possible to live here. The island of Jambudīpa is vast; let us go elsewhere." When asked, "If infamy arises in that place too, where will you go, Ānanda?", he replied, "To another city, Blessed One." Then the Blessed One said, "Wait, Ānanda. This sound will last only seven days. After seven days, it will fall back only upon those who created the infamy," and he preached this verse beginning with "Vadanti ve duṭṭhamanā" to the Venerable Ānanda as the origin of the teaching.

In that verse, "Vadanti" means they truly speak with a corrupt mind, accusing the Blessed One and the community of monks. Alternatively, although there are those who usually speak truthfully, some have corrupt minds, while others have such a perception.
236:
The Blessed One said, "This infamy will fall only upon those who created it," and for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the Venerable Ānanda, he spoke this verse beginning with "Vadanti ve."

In that verse, "Vadanti" means they accuse the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks. Some speak with a malicious mind, truly intending to harm; others speak thinking it is true. The heretics have malicious minds, and those who hear and believe their words think it is true—this is the meaning. "Vādañca jātaṃ" refers to this sound of abuse that has arisen. "Muni no upeti" means that because of not having committed the act and because of not being provoked, the Buddha-muni does not approach (is not affected by) that abuse. For that reason, it is said, "Munī natthi khilo kuhiñcī"; it should be understood that for this Sage, there are no obstructions such as lust in any object.

After speaking this verse, the Blessed One asked Venerable Ānanda, "Ānanda, what do the monks say when they are thus reviled and insulted?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, they say nothing," the Blessed One said, "Ānanda, one should not remain silent everywhere thinking 'I am virtuous.' In the world, a wise man who does not speak cannot be distinguished from fools when mixed with them." Then, saying, "Ānanda, let the monks urge those people in this way," he spoke this verse for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma: "Abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upeti."

The Elder learned that verse and told the monks, "You should urge the people with this verse." The monks did so. Wise people remained silent. King Kosala also sent royal agents everywhere, caught the drunkards whom the heretics had bribed to kill Sundarī, and upon punishing them and learning the whole story, he rebuked the heretics. When the people saw the heretics, they threw stones and scattered dust on them, saying, "They brought infamy upon the Blessed One." Venerable Ānanda saw this and informed the Blessed One. The Blessed One spoke this verse to the Elder: "Sakañhi diṭṭhiṃ... vadeyya."

The meaning of that verse is: How can one transcend the view of the heretics, "By killing Sundarī and spreading blame among the Sakyan monks, we will receive offerings obtained by this means"? That infamy returned only to those heretics who were unable to transcend that view. Or, how can one who holds views such as eternalism transcend his own view, being led by that desire for views and established in that preference for views? Indeed, one should speak only according to what one fully knows of the views one has undertaken.

Then, after seven days had passed, King Kosala had the corpse removed and went to Jetavana Monastery in the evening. He paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, when such infamy arose, should I not have been informed?" The Blessed One said, "Great King, it is not proper for the Noble Ones to announce to others, 'I am virtuous, I am endowed with qualities'," and regarding that matter, he spoke the remaining verses beginning with "Ahaṃ sīlavā."
237:
One should speak only according to what one knows of those views that one has fully undertaken.

Then, after seven days had passed, King Kosala had the corpse removed and went to the monastery in the evening. He paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, when such infamy (loss of reputation) arose, should I not have been informed?" When he said this, the Blessed One said, "Great King, it is not proper for the Noble Ones to announce to others, 'I am virtuous, I am endowed with qualities'," and regarding the occurrence of that event, he spoke the remaining verses beginning with "Yo attano sīlavatāni."

In that verse, 'sīlavatāni' refers to virtues such as the Pātimokkha and ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) such as living in the forest. 'Anānupuṭṭho' means without being asked by others. 'Pāvā' means speaks. "Anariyadhammaṃ kusalā tamāhu yo ātumānaṃ sayameva pāvā" means: If a person praises himself in this way of his own accord, the wise say of his speaking, "This behavior is the practice of the ignoble (not the practice of the Noble Ones)."

'Santo' refers to one who is peaceful due to the subsiding of defilements such as lust, and likewise one whose mind is exceedingly peaceful. "ဣတိဟန္တိ သီလေသု အကတ္ထမာနော" means: One who does not boast of virtues in such a way as "I am endowed with virtue," etc. It means not speaking words that exalt oneself based on virtue. "Tamariyadhammaṃ kusalā vadanti" means: The wise, such as the Buddha, who are skilled in the aggregates (khandha), etc., say of that person's non-boasting, "This is the practice of the Noble Ones." "Yassussadā natthi kuhiñci loke" means: For that Arahant, the seven 'ussada' (prominences) such as lust do not exist anywhere in the world. The connection is: the wise say of that person's non-boasting, "This is the practice of the Noble Ones."

Having thus shown the practice of the Arahants, now wishing to show the King the practice of the heretics who hold wrong views, he spoke the words beginning with "Pakappitā saṅkhatā." In that verse, 'pakappitā' refers to views that are repeatedly conceived. 'Saṅkhatā' refers to views that are conditioned by causes. 'Yassa' refers to any person who holds wrong views. 'Dhammā' refers to the doctrines of wrong views. 'Purakkhatā' means being placed in the forefront. 'Santi' means they exist. 'Avīvadātā' refers to views that are not pure. "Yadattani passati āniśaṃsaṃ taṃ nissito kuppapaṭiccasantiṃ" means: For a person in whom these doctrines of wrong views are placed in the forefront and are impure, because he sees in himself the benefits such as gain and honor in the present, or a special destination in the hereafter through that wrong view, he relies on that peace which is liable to perish due to the perishing of the benefit...
238:
That person sees the benefits such as gain and honor occurring in the present life, and the excellence of the destination (gati) and so forth that will occur in the future life. Therefore, he remains dependent on that benefit and on the view characterized by perishability, conditioned arising, and conventional peace. Because of such dependence, he might exalt himself or disparage others with false virtues or faults.

By such dependence, those who adhere to views both take up and discard the Dhamma. In that verse, 'diṭṭhīnivesā' refers to the adherence to views known as the insistence that 'this alone is the truth.' 'Na hi svātivattā' means they are not easily overcome. It means that because one proceeds by concluding upon this or that learned and internalized doctrine among the sixty-two views, these adherences to views are difficult to overcome.

Therefore, because a person finds it difficult to overcome those adherences, in those very adherences to views, he discards and takes up various doctrines such as the goat-vow, the cow-vow, the dog-vow, the practice of fivefold heat, jumping from cliffs, the exertion of squatting, sleeping on a bed of thorns, and various doctrines concerning teachers, preaching, and sects. It is said to be like a monkey in the forest letting go of one branch to grab another. Because he is discarding and taking up in this way and his mind is not steady, he might bring about fame or ill-repute for himself or others based on non-existent virtues or faults.

The person who is endowed with wisdom that destroys all faults such as views is called 'dhona' (the cleansed one). For that Arahant called 'dhona,' there is no view conceived in any state of existence in the world. What does this mean? Because the Arahant, who is endowed with the quality of being 'dhona' and has shaken off all faults, has no views, and while sectarians fall into prejudice through deception or pride to conceal the evil deeds they have committed, how could the 'dhona'—having abandoned both deception and pride—be led by faults such as lust? By what name could he be designated in the present or in future destinations such as hell? He is 'anūpaya' (unattached), for he is unattached due to the absence of the two attachments of craving and views.

One who possesses those two, craving and views, is called 'upaya' (attached). Such an attached person has all views only in this life. In this context, 'upaya' refers to one who is dependent on craving and views. He arrives at a doctrine regarding phenomena, such as being 'lustful' or 'hateful.'
239:
He arrives at a doctrine regarding various phenomena. How and by what means could one speak of the unattached (anūpaya) Arahant who has abandoned craving and views? By what lust or by what hatred could one say he is 'lustful' or 'hateful'? The meaning is: how could that Arahant, who is thus irreproachable, be a concealer of evil like the sectarians? For that great person, there is truly no self-view (attadiṭṭhi) or annihilation-view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). There is no perception of self or perception of non-self, which are characterized by grasping or releasing craving and views. For what reason are they absent? Because that Arahant, in this very existence, has shaken off, abandoned, and dispelled all views with the wind of knowledge. Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship. Having heard this Dhamma, King Kosala was delighted, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Duṭṭhaṭṭhaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 4. Explanation of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta

This sutta beginning with 'Passāmi suddhaṃ' is the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? It is said that in the past, during the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, a certain householder living in Bārāṇasī went to the border regions with five hundred carts to collect merchandise. There, he made friends with a forest-dweller, gave him gifts, and asked, 'Friend, have you ever seen the core of sandalwood?' When he replied, 'Yes, master,' he entered the sandalwood forest with that forest-dweller, filled all the carts with sandalwood core, and said to the forest-dweller, 'Friend, when you come to Bārāṇasī, please bring some sandalwood core,' and then returned to Bārāṇasī.

Later, that forest-dweller also took sandalwood core and arrived at the householder's home. Seeing him, the householder performed all the duties of hospitality, and in the evening, had the sandalwood core ground, filled a casket, and sent him to the bathing place with his own men, saying, 'Go, friend, come back after bathing.' At that time, a festival was being held in Bārāṇasī. Then, the people of Bārāṇasī, having given alms early in the morning, in the evening...
240:
After giving alms, in the evening, wearing clean clothes and taking flowers, perfumes, and so on, they went to worship the Great Stupa of the Blessed One Kassapa. That forest dweller saw them and asked, "Where is the multitude going?" Hearing the words, "To the monastery to worship the stupa," he went there himself. There, seeing people making offerings at the stupa with various substances such as yellow orpiment and red arsenic, and not knowing how to create anything elaborate, he took that sandalwood and made a circular mark the size of a bronze plate upon the golden bricks of the Great Stupa.

Then, at the time of sunrise, rays of light emerged from that spot. Seeing this, he was inspired and made a prayer: "Wherever I may be reborn, may such rays arise from my chest." After passing away, he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Rays of light arose from his chest; his chest area shone like the orb of the moon, and he was known as the "Deity Candābha."

Having enjoyed such prosperity, alternating through the six celestial worlds, he spent one interval between Buddhas. When our Blessed One appeared, he was reborn in Sāvatthī in a family of wealthy Brahmins. Just as before, a circle of radiance like the orb of the full moon appeared on his chest. On the day of the naming ceremony, the Brahmins saw that circle and, being amazed, said, "This boy possesses the marks of great merit and fortune," and named him "Candābha."

When Candābha reached maturity, the Brahmins took him, adorned him, dressed him in a red cloak, and placed him on a chariot. Worshipping him as "Mahābrahmā," they proclaimed, "Whoever sees Candābha will obtain fame, wealth, and so on, and in the next life will go to heaven." They wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. Wherever they went, people came in crowds, saying, "Friends, this is one named Candābha; whoever sees him will obtain fame, wealth, and heavenly bliss," so that the whole of Jambudīpa was stirred. The Brahmins did not show him to those who came empty-handed, but only to those who came bringing a hundred or a thousand. Thus, carrying Candābha with them, the Brahmins eventually arrived at Sāvatthī.

At that time, the Blessed One, having set the noble Wheel of Dhamma in motion, had come to Sāvatthī in due course and was staying at the Jetavana monastery, preaching the Dhamma for the benefit of many. Then, when Candābha arrived in Sāvatthī, he became obscure like a small river entering the ocean; there was no one even mentioning the name "Candābha." In the evening, he...
241:
Seeing the multitude of people carrying flowers, perfumes, and so on, heading towards the Jetavana monastery, he asked, "Where are you going?" Hearing their words, "A Buddha has appeared in the world; he preaches the Dhamma for the benefit of many. We are going to Jetavana to hear that Dhamma," he also went there, surrounded by a group of Brahmins. At that time, the Blessed One was seated on the noble Buddha-seat in the Dhamma hall. Candābha approached the Blessed One, exchanged pleasant greetings, and sat on one side. At that very moment, his light disappeared. Indeed, in the presence of the Buddha's radiance, within a range of eighty cubits, no other light can prevail. Thinking, "My light is lost," he stood up from where he was sitting and prepared to leave.

Then a certain man said to him, "Friend Candābha, why is this? Are you leaving because you are afraid of the Ascetic Gotama?" "I am not leaving because I am afraid," he replied, "but rather, because of this person's power, my light no longer appears." He sat down again before the Blessed One and, observing the perfection of his physical form, rays, and marks from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair, he thought, "The Ascetic Gotama possesses great power. Only a small amount of light arose from my chest, yet with just that much, the Brahmins took me and wandered throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. For the Ascetic Gotama, who is endowed with such noble marks, no pride has arisen at all. Surely this one must be the Teacher of gods and humans, endowed with extraordinary virtues." With a heart full of great faith, he paid homage to the Blessed One and requested ordination. The Blessed One commanded a certain Elder, "Ordain him." That Elder ordained him and taught him the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (tacapañcaka kammaṭṭhāna). He began the practice of insight (vipassanā) and before long attained Arahantship, becoming famous as "Candābhatthera."

Concerning him, the monks started a discussion: "Friends, did those who saw Candābha obtain fame or wealth, go to heaven, or attain purity merely by that sight of a physical form through the eye-door?" The Blessed One, on that occasion, spoke this Sutta.

Therein, the meaning of the first verse is as follows: Monks, purity does not come from such a sight. Rather, a fool possessed by wrong views, seeing the Brahmin Candābha or another like him—who is impure because of the stains of defilements and is still diseased because the diseases of defilements have not been removed—perceives: "I see the pure, the supreme, the healthy one; and through that sight, which is called a [wrong] view, a person's complete purity occurs." He, perceiving thus and considering that sight as "supreme," continues to see purity in that sight...
242:
(That person) believes that vision to be "Path Knowledge" (maggañāṇa). However, that vision is not Path Knowledge. Therefore, He spoke the second verse beginning with "Diṭṭhena ce suddhi."

The meaning of that verse is: If the purification of defilements for a person occurs through that vision, which is called the seeing of forms, or if through that vision he can abandon suffering such as birth and so forth; if it were so, then he would be purified by an impure path other than the Noble Path, and he would be purified while still possessing "upadhi" (acquisitions/bases for rebirth) such as lust and so forth. But such a person cannot be purified. Therefore, the very view of those who speak thus indicates that it is a base wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi). It is as if that view itself says, "This person is one of wrong view." They speak in various ways according to their views, such as "The world is eternal" and so forth.

## "Na Brāhmaṇo" and so forth is the third verse. The meaning of that verse is: A Brahmin, so called because he has put away evil, is a Khīṇāsava (one whose taints are destroyed) who has attained the knowledge of the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) through the Noble Path. He does not claim purification through wrong knowledge arising from: what is seen (diṭṭha), such as forms regarded as highly auspicious; what is heard (suta), such as sounds of that nature; virtue (sīla), such as habits that should not be transgressed; practices (vata), such as the elephant practice and so forth; and what is sensed (muta), such as the touch of earth and so forth—all of which are distinct from the Noble Path Knowledge.

The remaining words were spoken to praise the virtues of that Brahmin. This is because that Brahmin is unstained by the merit of the three realms or by any evil. Because he has abandoned the view of self (atta-diṭṭhi) and any other views, he is called "one who has abandoned the self" (attañjaha). Because he no longer performs meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and so forth, he is said to be "one who does not perform [new karma] in this world" (na-y-idha pakubbamāno). Therefore, desiring to praise him in this way, He spoke [these words]. The connection of all the words with the preceding line should be understood as: The Brahmin who is unstained by merit and evil, who has abandoned the view of self, and who does not perform [new karma] in this world, does not claim purification through any other cause.

Having thus stated that a Brahmin does not claim purification through other causes, He now spoke the verse beginning with "Purimaṃ pahāya" to show that the views of those who claim purification through other practices cannot lead [to Nibbāna]. The meaning of that verse is: Although they claim purification through other practices, because they have not abandoned wrong views, they keep grasping and letting go. By that very view, they abandon former teachers and so forth and rely on others; followed and oppressed by craving called "ejā," they cannot cross over the various kinds of attachment (saṅga) such as lust. Being unable to cross over that attachment, they grasp and discard various teachings, just as a monkey grabs and lets go of one tree branch after another.
243:
The connection of the fifth verse is: The person mentioned as "Diṭṭhī hi naṃ pāva tathā vadānaṃ" is one who has undertaken [practices] by himself. In that context, "sayaṃ" means by oneself. "Samādāya" means having taken up (undertaken). "Vatāni" refers to practices such as the elephant practice. "Uccāvacaṃ" means changing from one teacher to another, being inconsistent or moving between the low and the high. "Saññasatto" refers to one who is attached to sensual perceptions (kāma-saññā) and so forth. "Vidvā ca vedehi samecca dhammaṃ" means the Arahant who knows the supreme Nibbāna has penetrated the Dhamma of the Four Truths through the "Vedas" which are the fourfold Path Knowledges. The remaining words are clear.

That Arahant of vast wisdom (bhūripañño), who has destroyed the taints, is called "visenibhūto" (one who has disbanded the army) because he stands having destroyed the army of Māra in all those things—whether seen, heard, or sensed. "Tam-eva-dassiṃ" refers to one who has such a pure vision. "Vivaṭaṃ carantaṃ" refers to one who wanders openly, having become unveiled through the removal of the shroud of craving and so forth. "Kenīdha lokasmiṃ vikappayeyya" means: by what conceptualization of craving or conceptualization of view could anyone in this world specifically conceive [of him]? Or, since lust and so forth mentioned previously have been abandoned by those individuals, how could they be specifically conceived? This is the meaning.

"Na kappayanti"—the connection and meaning of this verse is: Furthermore, such virtuous ones do not conceptualize or prioritize anything through the two types of conceptualization [craving and views]. Because they have attained the ultimate and absolute purity of the supreme goal, they do not speak of non-absolute purity—such as the views of non-action (akiriyavāda) or eternalism (sassatavāda)—as "absolute purity." "Ādānaganthaṃ gathitaṃ visajja" means: having cut with the sword of the Noble Path the four knots (gantha) bound within one's own mental continuum, which are called "ādānagantha" (knots of grasping) because they seize and hold onto forms and so forth. The remaining words are clear.

The verse "Sīmātigo" was spoken as a teaching based on a single individual. Its connection is the same as before, and it should be understood along with the explanation of the meaning as follows: Furthermore, such a person of vast wisdom is called "sīmātigo" (one who has gone beyond boundaries) because he has transcended the four boundaries of defilements, and he is called a "Brahmin" because he has put away evil. For such a person, there is no "grasping" (abhinivesa) of any phenomenon, whether by knowing through the knowledge of others' minds or the knowledge of past lives, or by seeing with the physical eye or the divine eye. Also, because of the absence of sensual lust, he is not called "lustful" (rāgī); because of the absence of lust for fine-material and immaterial realms...
244:
He is not called one who is stained by passion. Because for such a person, there is nothing in this world grasped as "this is supreme," the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship.

## In the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the Explanation of the Suddhaṭṭhaka Sutta is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta
The sutta beginning with "Paramanti diṭṭhīsu" is the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī, various sectarians (titthiyas) assembled and, declaring their own respective views, quarreled, saying, "This is supreme, this is supreme," and informed the King. The King had many people who were blind from birth assembled and ordered his ministers, "Show the elephant to these blind men." The ministers assembled the blind men, placed an elephant before them, and said, "Look!" Those blind men each touched a different part of the elephant. Then, when the King asked, "Friends, what is an elephant like?", the one who touched the trunk said, "Great King, an elephant is like a plow-pole." Those who touched the tusks and other parts rebuked the other, saying, "Friend, do not speak falsely before the King," and said, "Great King, an elephant is like a peg in a wall," and so on. When the King heard all this, he dismissed the sectarians, saying, "Your doctrine is just like these blind men's description of the elephant."

A certain monk on alms round learned of this event and informed the Blessed One. Based on that occurrence, the Blessed One addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, just as the men blind from birth, not knowing the elephant, touched various parts and quarreled, so too the sectarians, not knowing the Dhamma leading to liberation (vimokkhantikadhamma), grasp and touch various views and quarrel." Having said this, he spoke this sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma.

In that sutta, "Paramanti diṭṭhīsu parivbasāno" means taking one's own view as "this alone is supreme" and dwelling fixedly within it. "Yaduttari kurute" means making one's own teacher and so forth the most excellent. "Hīnāti aññe tato sabbamāha" means that, setting aside one's own teacher and so forth, one says of all others besides them, "These are inferior." "Tasmā vivādāni avītivatto" means that for that reason, he does not transcend disputes regarding views.
245:
The meaning of the second verse: Thus, one who cannot transcend disputes sees the aforementioned various benefits in himself, in what is called wrong view arising from these four bases: what is seen, heard, practiced (virtue and vows), and sensed. That person, having settled into those things such as what is seen and heard with his own view, thinking "this practice alone is supreme," sees all other teachers and doctrines besides his own as inferior.

The meaning of the third verse: For one who sees thus, relying on one's own teacher and seeing another's teacher as inferior—the wise call that a "tie" (gantha), meaning it is a "bond" (bandhana). Because that practice is a bond, a bhikkhu should not rely on or settle into what is seen, heard, sensed, or practiced (sīlabbata).

The meaning of the fourth verse: Not only should one not rely on wrong views such as what is seen or heard, but one should also not construct or produce further wrong views in the world that have not yet arisen. What kind of view should one not construct? One should not construct that wrong view which is fashioned by one's own intellect, by practices, or by knowledge such as the knowledge of attainments (samāpatti-ñāṇa). Furthermore, not only should one not construct wrong views, but one should also not, through conceit or through reasons such as birth and lineage, bring oneself near to wrong views by thinking "I am equal to him," nor should one think "I am inferior" or "I am superior."

The meaning of the fifth verse: Thus, without constructing wrong views and without being conceited, having abandoned the self and being without grasping, having given up the view previously held in this life and not grasping another, he does not form the two kinds of reliance—reliance on craving and reliance on views—even in that aforementioned knowledge. Not forming such reliance, he does not follow factions among beings who are divided by various views, and not being of a nature to follow through the power of desire and so forth, he does not believe in any of the sixty-two views, nor does he return to wrong views.

808-810. Now, to praise the virtues of the Arahant mentioned in this verse, he spoke the three verses beginning with "Yassūbhayante." In those verses, "ubhayante" refers to the things divided into contact and so forth as previously mentioned. "Paṇidhi" means craving that longs. "Bhavābhavāya" means for the sake of existence from one life to another repeatedly. "Idha vā huraṃ vā" means in this life, such as one's own existence, or in another life, such as the existence of another. "Diṭṭhe vā" means through the purity of what is seen; the same method applies to what is heard (suta) and so forth.
246:
The method is the same for 'heard' (suta) and so on. 'Perception' (saññā) refers to the views (diṭṭhi) that arise because of perception. "Dhammāpi tesaṃ na paṭicchitāse" means they do not hold the sixty-two types of wrong views, thinking "Only this is the truth, everything else is vain." "Pāraṅgato na pacceti tādī" means one who has reached the other shore, which is Nibbāna, does not return to the defilements already abandoned by various paths; and such a one is 'Tādī' (the Such) through five aspects. The rest is clear.

## the explanation of the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Jarā Sutta

"Appaṃ vata jīvitaṃ" (Short indeed is life) and so on is the Jarā Sutta. What is the occasion for its arising? Once, the Blessed One, having spent the rains retreat in Sāvatthī, considered the reasons for wandering through the countryside, such as maintaining the health of the Buddhas' bodies, prescribing training rules not yet established, taming those who should be tamed, and teaching Jātakas and so on according to the occasion; and then he set out for the countryside. Traveling in stages, he arrived at Sāketa in the evening and entered the Añjana Grove. The residents of Sāketa heard of this and, thinking "It is not the right time to see the Blessed One now," waited until the night had passed and dawn broke. Then, taking flowers, perfumes, and so on, they went to the Blessed One, performed offerings, paid homage, and exchanged pleasantries. They stood surrounding him until the time for the Blessed One to enter the village for alms. Then the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, entered for alms. A certain Brahmin Mahāsāla living in Sāketa saw him at the city gate while leaving the city. Upon seeing him, parental love for a son arose, and he came forward weeping, saying, "My son, I have seen you after a long time!" The Blessed One informed the monks, "Monks, let this Brahmin do as he wishes; do not stop him."

The Brahmin, like a cow yearning for its calf, came and embraced the Blessed One's body from the front, back, right, and left—all around—saying, "My son, I see you after a long time; we have been separated for a long time." If that Brahmin had not been allowed to do so, his heart would have split and he would have died. That Brahmin said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, I alone am able to give alms to the monks who have come with you; please favor only me." The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. The Brahmin took the Blessed One's bowl and, walking ahead, sent word to the Brahminī, "My son has come; prepare the seats." The Brahminī also did accordingly and, while standing and watching for the arrival, saw the Blessed One even on the way. Parental love for a son arose, and she said, "My son, it has been a very long time since I last saw you."
247: 'Please show favor only to me,' he requested. The Blessed One accepted by remaining silent. The Brahmin took the Blessed One's bowl, went ahead, and sent word to the Brahmin lady, 'My son has come, prepare the seats.' That Brahmin lady did accordingly and, while standing and waiting for the arrival, saw the Blessed One in the middle of the street. Parental love arose, and she said, 'My son, it has been a long time since I saw you.' She then held his feet, wept, invited him into the house, and served him carefully. When the meal was finished, the Brahmin took away the bowl. The Blessed One, knowing what was suitable for them, preached the Dhamma, and at the end of the discourse, both became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna). Then they requested the Blessed One, 'Venerable Sir, as long as the Blessed One dwells depending on this city, please take alms only at our house.' The Blessed One declined, saying, 'Buddhas do not go to only one fixed place in this way.' They then said, 'Venerable Sir, if that is so, even after wandering for alms with the community of monks, please perform the meal duties only here, preach the Dhamma, and then go to the monastery.' The Blessed One did so to favor them. People called that Brahmin and the Brahmin lady only as 'the Buddha's father' and 'the Buddha's mother.' That family also came to be known as the 'Buddha-kula' (Buddha's family).The Elder Ānanda asked the Blessed One, 'I know the parents of the Blessed One. Why do these people say, "I am the Buddha's mother, I am the Buddha's father"?' The Blessed One said, 'Ānanda, this Brahmin and Brahmin lady have been my parents continuously for five hundred births, my elder uncles for five hundred births, and my younger uncles for five hundred births. They speak this way only because of past affection.' He then spoke this verse:'Through previous association,Or by benefit in the present,Thus does that love arise,Like a lotus in the water.'Thereafter, the Blessed One, having stayed in Sāketa as long as he pleased, wandered again and went to Sāvatthī. That Brahmin and Brahmin lady also approached the monks, heard the appropriate Dhamma, reached the remaining three paths, and attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder. The Brahmins in the city assembled.
248:
The Brahmins in the city gathered, thinking, "We will pay respects to our relatives." Lay disciples who were Sotāpannas, Sakadāgāmis, and Anāgāmis, both male and female, also gathered, thinking, "We will pay respects to our fellow practitioners." All of them placed the bodies on a gabled palanquin and, honoring them with flowers, scents, and so forth, departed from the city.

The Blessed One, too, surveying the world with his Buddha-eye at dawn that day, knew of their passing away (parinibbāna). Realizing that "If I go there, many people will attain the Dhamma upon hearing the discourse," he took his bowl and robes, came from Sāvatthī, and entered the cemetery itself. People saw him and stood there after paying homage, thinking, "The Blessed One has come desiring to perform the funeral rites for his parents." The city-dwellers, honoring the gabled palanquin, brought it to the cemetery and asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, how should noble lay disciples be honored?" The Blessed One, intending to show that they were Asekha-munis (Arahants), said: "Just as Asekhas are honored, so should these noble lay disciples be honored," and spoke this verse:

"Those sages who are harmless,
Always restrained in body,
Go to the deathless state,
Where, having gone, they do not sorrow."

Looking at the assembly and desiring to preach a Dhamma suitable for that moment, he spoke this sutta.

In that sutta, "appaṃ vata jīvitaṃ idaṃ" means that this life of humans is very brief due to its short duration and the insignificance of its activities. This is the same method as stated in the Salla Sutta. "Oraṃ vassasatāpi miyyati" means one may die even within a hundred years, such as during the kalala stage and so forth. "Aticca" means having exceeded a hundred years. "Jarāsāpi miyyati" means one also dies of old age.

"Mamāyita" arises because of things cherished as "mine." "Vinābhāvasantamevidaṃ" means this life is of the nature of inevitable separation; it is impossible to exist without separation. "Māmaka" refers to one who has reached the designation of "my lay disciple," whether a Brahmin or a monk, or one who cherishes the Triple Gem such as the Buddha. "Saṅgata" means one who has been associated with or seen before. "Piyāyita" means one who is loved. "Nāmaṃyevāvasissati akkheyyaṃ" means all phenomena such as form (rūpa) perish; only the name remains for the purpose of designation and speech, such as "Buddharakkhita" or "Dhammarakkhita." "Munayo" refers to the sages whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). "Khemadassino" are those who see Nibbāna.
249:
The seventh verse was spoken to show the appropriate practice in this world oppressed by death. In that verse, "patilīnacarassa" means for one who practices by withdrawing the mind from various objects of craving. "Bhikkhuno" refers to a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) or a learner (sekha). "Sāmaggiyamāhu tassa taṃ, yo attānaṃ bhavane na dassaye" means they say this practice is suitable for that person who, by practicing thus, does not manifest himself (does not take birth again) in various planes of existence such as hell. The meaning is that by practicing in this way, he may be liberated from this death.

818-20. Now, to praise the virtues of the Arahant who is described as "not manifesting himself in existence," he spoke the following three verses. Therein, "sabbattha" means in the twelve sense bases (āyatana). In the phrase "yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ mutေသု vā," the connection should be understood as: "The Sage is not smeared by these things seen, heard, or sensed." In the phrase "dhono na hi tena maññati, yadidaṃ diṭṭhasutaṃ mutေသု vā," the connection should also be understood as: "He does not conceive (as 'I' or 'mine') because of that object seen or heard, nor does he conceive in things sensed." "Na hi so rajjati no virajjati" means he does not lust like foolish worldlings, nor is he "dispassioning" (in the process of removing lust) like virtuous worldlings and learners; rather, because his lust is entirely destroyed, he has reached the designation of "virāga" (the dispassionate one). The remaining words are clear in every respect. At the conclusion of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya).

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## The explanation of the Jarā Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## 7. Explanation of the Tissametteyya Sutta

"Methunamanuyuttassa" and so forth is the Tissametteyya Sutta. What is the origin (uppatti)? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying in Sāvatthī, two friends named Tissa and Metteyya went to Sāvatthī. In the evening, seeing a great crowd of people heading toward Jetavana, they asked, "Where are you going?" Then the people replied, "The Buddha has appeared in the world and is preaching the Dhamma for the benefit of many; we are going to Jetavana to hear it."
250:
“We too shall listen to the Dhamma,” they said and went. Having heard the beneficial Dhamma of the Blessed One, while sitting in the midst of the assembly, those two friends thought: “It is not possible to fulfill this Dhamma while living in the midst of a household.” Then, when the crowd had departed, they requested ordination from the Blessed One. The Blessed One commanded a certain monk, “Ordain these men.” That monk ordained them, gave them the meditation on the five parts of the body ending in skin (taca-pañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), and allowed them to dwell in the forest.

The monk Metteyya said to the monk Tissa, “Friend, our preceptor (upajjhāya) has gone to the forest; let us also go.” Tissa replied, “Friend, it is not yet suitable; I cherish seeing the Blessed One and hearing the Dhamma. You go alone,” and he remained behind. Metteyya went with the preceptor and, while practicing the monk's Dhamma in the forest, soon attained the fruit of Arahantship along with his teacher and preceptor.

Tissa's elder brother passed away due to illness. Hearing this news, he went to his village, where his relatives enticed and persuaded him to disrobe. Metteyya also returned to Sāvatthī with his teacher and preceptor. Then, the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat, wandered through the countryside and eventually arrived at that village. There, Metteyya paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I have a lay friend in this village; out of compassion, please wait for a moment.” He entered the village, brought the disrobed Tissa to the Blessed One, and standing in a suitable place, asked the Blessed One a question with the first verse for Tissa's benefit. Desiring to answer Metteyya, the Blessed One spoke the remaining verses. This is the origin of this Sutta.

In that commentary, ‘methunam-anuyuttassa’ means to one engaged in sexual intercourse. ‘Iti’ means thus. ‘Āyasmā’ is a term of endearment. ‘Tissa’ is the name of that Elder. Indeed, that Elder was known by the name Tissa. ‘Metteyya’ is the clan name (gotta). That Elder was well-known by his clan name. Therefore, in the account of the origin, it is said, “Two friends named Tissa and Metteyya.” ‘Vighāta’ means oppression or destruction. ‘Brūhi’ means “please tell.” ‘Mārisa’ is a term of endearment, meaning “Venerable sir who is free from suffering.” ‘Sutvāna tava sāsanaṃ’ means “having heard your word.” ‘Viveke sikkhi-ssāmase’ is said because he wished to request a Dhamma teaching for his friend. That disrobed Tissa was one who had already practiced the training.

‘Mussate vāpi sāsanaṃ’ means that the Dispensation, in terms of both scripture (pariyatti) and practice (paṭipatti), perishes. The word ‘vāpi’ is a mere expletive. ‘Etaṃ tasmiṃ anāriyaṃ’ means that whatever wrong practice (micchā-paṭipadā) exists in that person, this practice is not the practice of the Noble Ones (Ariyas).
251:
“Eko pubbe caritvānā” means having previously lived alone, either due to ordination or due to seclusion from the group. “The world calls that shaken vehicle low for a worldling” refers to the person who has disrobed. Just as one who rides an untrained and unsteady elephant vehicle harms the rider and falls into a precipice, so too, by practicing unsteady conduct such as bodily misconduct, one falls into hell and so on; and by the destruction of one's welfare, one falls into the precipice of rebirth. Thus, they are like a shaken vehicle. That worldling is also called “low.”

824-5. “Fame and reputation” (yaso kitti ca) refer to gain, honor, and praise. “Previously” (pubbe) means during the life as a monk. “For that disrobed one, that fame and reputation decline” means the decline of fame and reputation for that person. “Seeing this reason also” means seeing the existence of fame and reputation previously and their decline later. “One should train to abandon sexual intercourse” means one should practice the three trainings. For what reason? It is for the purpose of abandoning sexual intercourse. He who does not abandon sexual intercourse, through sensual thoughts... etc... is of such a nature. In that verse, “pareto” means being filled with the blame and oppression of others. “The sound of others” (paresaṃ nigghosaṃ) refers to the words of blame from preceptors and others. “Becomes dejected” (maṅku hoti) means becoming unhappy or dispirited.

The verses following this have clear connections. Among those verses, “weapons” (satthāni) refer to bodily misconduct and so on. These are called “weapons” because they cut oneself and others. Among those weapons of misconduct, this person is specifically urged, and he makes only the weapon of falsehood, saying, “I disrobed for this reason.” Therefore, it is said: “This indeed is his great entanglement; he plunges into falsehood.” In that phrase, “esa khvassa” is “esa kho assa.” “Great entanglement” (mahāgedho) means a great bond. If one asks what it is, it is plunging into falsehood. Plunging into that falsehood should be known as the great entanglement.

“Suffers like a fool” (mando-va parikissati) means that by committing taking life and so on, and experiencing suffering because of that, and by seeking and guarding wealth, one suffers like an extremely deluded person.

828-9. “Knowing this danger, the sage in this Dispensation, before and after...” means knowing the danger described as “the fame and reputation that were previously there decline for him,” in this Dispensation, from the previous state of a monk to the subsequent state of a monk...
252:
The Sage, having known the danger in the state of corruption, understood: "This practice of seclusion is the supreme practice of the Noble Ones." This means that because this practice is the supreme practice of the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas, one should train only in seclusion. "One should not think oneself superior because of that" means that one should not regard oneself as "I am superior" because of that seclusion; it means one should not become stubborn merely because of that seclusion.

"To the empty one" (rittassa) refers to one who is secluded and devoid of bodily misconduct and so forth. "They cherish the one who has crossed the flood" means that beings who are attached to the objects of sensuality cherish that Arahant who has crossed the four floods, just as those in debt cherish one who is free from debt. Thus, the Teacher concluded the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, the Elder Tissa reached the Fruit of Stream-entry, and later, having ordained, he realized the Fruit of Arahantship.
