## 8. Explanation of the Pasūra Sutta

"Purity is only here" and so forth is the Pasūra Sutta. What is the origin? It is said that while the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, there was a wanderer named Pasūra, a great debater. That wanderer Pasūra thought, "I am the foremost in debate in the whole of Jambudīpa; therefore, just as the rose-apple tree is the sign of Jambudīpa, so should there be renown for me." Having made a rose-apple branch his banner and finding no opponent in the whole of Jambudīpa, he eventually arrived at Sāvatthī. He made a mound of sand at the city gate, planted the branch there, and said, "Whoever is able to debate with me, let him destroy this branch," and then entered the city. A great crowd stood surrounding that place. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, having finished his meal, was leaving Sāvatthī. Seeing that situation, he asked many village boys, "O boys, what is this?" They told him everything. Saying, "If that is so, you pull it up and break it with your feet, and say, 'Let the one who desires a debate come to the monastery,'" he then departed.
253:
The wanderer, having wandered for alms and finished his meal, returned and saw the uprooted and broken rose-apple branch. He asked, "Who caused this to be done?" When it was said, "It was caused by Sāriputta, the son of the Buddha," he became delighted and said, "Today, let the wise see my victory and the defeat of the ascetic." To bring those who could examine the questions and reasons, he entered Sāvatthī and, wandering through the streets, crossroads, and squares, he proclaimed, "O people, let those who wish to hear the manifestation of wisdom in debate with the chief disciple of the Ascetic Gotama come forth!" Many people, both those who had faith in the Dispensation and those who did not, came forth, thinking, "We shall listen to the words of the wise." Then Pasūra, surrounded by a great crowd, went to the monastery, thinking, "When this is said, I will say that," and so forth. The Elder, thinking, "Let there not be high voices, loud noises, and the disturbance of many people in the monastery," prepared a seat at the gate-tower of Jetavana and sat down.

The wanderer approached the Elder and said, "O ascetic, did you cause my rose-apple banner to be broken?" When it was said, "Yes, wanderer, I caused it to be broken," he said, "O ascetic, let there be some conversation between us." When the Elder accepted, saying, "Let it be so, wanderer," he said, "O ascetic, you ask, and I shall answer." Then the Elder said to that wanderer, "O wanderer, is the asking difficult, or is the answering difficult?" He replied, "O ascetic, the answering is difficult; how could there be difficulty in asking? For anyone can ask anything." "If that is so, wanderer, you ask, and I shall answer." When this was said, the wanderer, with a mind full of wonder, thinking, "This monk is of good nature and caused the branch to be broken at the proper place," asked the Elder, "What is sensuality (kāma) for a man?" The Elder said, "Lustful intention (saṅkapparāga) is sensuality for a man." Hearing that, the wanderer, having a contrary perception of the Elder and wishing to charge him with defeat, said, "O ascetic, do you not say that manifold objects are the sensuality of a man?" "Yes, wanderer, it is true that I do not say so." Then the wanderer, having made him confirm it three times, addressed those who examine questions, saying, "O people, listen to the fault in the ascetic's doctrine." He then asked, "O ascetic, do your fellow practitioners live in the forest?" When it was said, "Yes, wanderer, they do," he asked, "While they live there in the forest, do they not think thoughts such as sensual thoughts?" When it was said, "Yes, wanderer, it is true that worldlings think them suddenly," he said, "If that is so, where is their state of being an ascetic? Are they not householders who enjoy sensual pleasures?" Having said this, he further spoke these words—
254:
“Those beautiful things in the world are not indeed sensual pleasures (kāma); lustful intention (saṅkappa-rāga) is called sensual pleasure. If one harbors unwholesome thoughts, even your fellow monk would become a consumer of sensual pleasures.”

Then, the Elder, wishing to point out the fault in the Wanderer’s doctrine, asked, “O Wanderer, do you say that lustful intention is not sensual pleasure for a man, but that beautiful and varied objects are?” “Yes, venerable sir,” he replied. Thereafter, the Elder made the Wanderer Pasūra confirm this three times and then addressed those investigating the problem, saying, “Friends, listen to the fault in the Wanderer’s doctrine.” He then asked, “Friend Pasūra, do you have a teacher?” “Yes, venerable sir, I do,” he replied. “Does that teacher see forms cognizable by the eye, or does he enjoy sounds and so forth?” “Yes, venerable sir, he enjoys them,” he replied. “If that is so, where is his status as a teacher? Is he not a consumer of sensual pleasures like a householder who stays at home?” Having said this, the Elder further spoke as follows:

“You say that those beautiful things in the world are indeed sensual pleasures, but you do not call lustful intention sensual pleasure. If he looks at delightful forms, your teacher too would be a consumer of sensual pleasures.

If he listens to delightful sounds,
If he smells delightful odors,
If he tastes delightful flavors,
If he touches delightful tangibles,
Your teacher too would be a consumer of sensual pleasures.”

When this was said, the Wanderer, having no rebuttal, thought, “This monk is a great debater; I will ordain under him and learn the texts of his doctrine.” He entered the city of Sāvatthī, sought a bowl and robes, and entered the Jetavana monastery. There, seeing the Elder Lāḷudāyī, who was golden-hued, well-proportioned, and inspiring in all aspects of his physical appearance and conduct, he thought, “This monk must be of great wisdom and a great debater,” and ordained under him. After defeating Lāḷudāyī with his own doctrine, he departed for the residence of the heretics in his original form and again proclaimed in Sāvatthī as before, “I will debate with the Samana Gotama.” Surrounded by a great crowd, he spoke words such as, “In this way, I will defeat the Samana Gotama...”
255:
The Wanderer Pasūra went to the Jetavana monastery, proclaiming his doctrine. The deity residing at the gatehouse of Jetavana thought, “This person is an unfit vessel (abhājanabhūta) for hearing the Dhamma,” and closed his mouth. That Wanderer Pasūra approached the Blessed One and sat down like a mute. People looked at his face, thinking, “Now he will ask, now he will ask,” and loud voices arose, saying, “Speak, O Pasūra! Speak, O Pasūra!” Then the Blessed One, saying, “What will Pasūra say?” spoke this Sutta for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma to the assembly gathered there.

In the first verse of that Sutta, the summary is as follows: These people of wrong views, referring to their own views, say, “Only here is there purity,” and do not speak of purity in other teachings. This being so, many recluses and brahmins, depending on their own teachers and so forth, and being those who say “This doctrine is auspicious” regarding their own views, are settled in their respective individual truths (pacceka-sacca) such as “The world is eternal.”

Being thus settled, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with “Te vādakāmā.” In that verse, “bālaṃ dahanti mithu aññamaññaṃ” means that both persons regard each other as fools, saying, “This one is a fool, this one is a fool.” “Vadanti te aññasitā kathojjaṃ” means that they, depending on their respective teachers and so forth, speak words of dispute with one another. “Pasaṃsakāmā kusalā vadānā” means that, desiring praise, both parties have the perception, “We are speakers of skillful doctrine, we are speakers of wise doctrine.”

Among those who speak thus, one is always as described in the verse “Yutto kathāyaṃ.” In that verse, “yutto kathāyaṃ” means one who is eager for contentious debate. “Pasaṃsamicchaṃ vinighāti hoti” means that one who desires his own praise becomes frustrated and disturbed by doubt even before the conversation begins, thinking, “How shall I defeat him?” and so forth. “Apāhatasmiṃ” refers to when the view is refuted by those investigating the questions, in such ways as, “Your speech is devoid of meaning, your speech is devoid of proper phrasing.” “Nindāya so kuppati” means that he becomes angry because of the blame that arises when his view is thus refuted. “Randhamesī” means one who seeks only the faults and openings of others.
256:
"Not only does he get angry, but indeed his view..." (this is the verse). In that verse, "parihīnamāhu apāhataṃ" means they say a speech that is devoid of meaning and phrasing, and thus rejected, is "deficient." "Paridevati" means because of that view, he laments, saying "I have considered it in another way," and so on. "Socati" means he grieves, focusing on things like "Victory belongs to him." "Upaccagā maṃ" is his lamentation in the manner of "He has surpassed me in the debate," and so on, which is excessive wailing.

"Ete vivādā samaṇesu": Here, "samaṇa" refers to wanderers outside the Dispensation. "Ugghātī nighātī hoti" means that in those views, by the power of victory and defeat, etc., one reaches elation (ugghāta) and depression (nighāta) of the mind, thus becoming one who is elated or depressed. "Virame kathojjaṃ" means one should abandon quarreling. "Na haññadatthatthi pasaṃsalābhā" means there is no other benefit in this dispute besides praise and gain.

836-7. The meaning of the sixth verse: Since there is no other benefit besides praise and gain, even if one obtains a great gain, one is praised in that view as "This is excellent." Having demonstrated that doctrine in the midst of the assembly, that person, due to the benefit of victory, reaches joy or laughs showing their teeth, and is puffed up with pride. Why? Because by attaining the benefit of victory, pride arises as desired. "Yā uṇṇati" etc., is the verse for such a proud person. In that verse, "mānātimānaṃ vadate paneso" means that person, not knowing that pride is a ground for destruction (vighātabhūmi), speaks only with pride and conceit.

Having thus shown the fault in the doctrine, now, not wishing to accept his doctrine, He spoke the verse beginning with "Sūro" (Hero). In that verse, "rājakkhādāya" means by the food provided by kings, or by royal provisions. "Abhigazzameti" shows that just as a person who eats royal provisions comes shouting, desiring an opposing hero, so too the one with a view comes searching for another with a view. "Yeneve so tena palehi" means go only to where that person is, by whose view you have courage. "Pubbeva natthi yadidaṃ yudhāya" shows that the mass of defilements that would arise for battle (dispute) no longer exists for Me from before; it was already abandoned at the foot of the Bodhi tree. The remaining verses have clear connections.

839-40. In those verses, "vivādayanti" means they dispute. "Paṭisenikattā" means an opponent. "Visenikatvā" means having destroyed the army of defilements. By the word "Pasūra," He addresses that wanderer. Those who have no defilements in this world, having abandoned defilements, cannot be approached for competition by one who thinks "Victory will be mine," just as foxes and others cannot compete with a lion; they will not be able to fulfill even a single word to compete with the Buddha who has abandoned defilements. This meaning is clear in all places.

The commentary on the Pasūra Sutta (Pasūra Sutta Vaṇṇanā) in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary named Paramatthajotikā is finished.
257:
"Labhetha" means "How will you obtain victory again?" By the word "Pasūra," He addresses that wanderer. "Yesīdha natthi" means "Those for whom there is none in this world."

"Pavitakkanti" means thinking thoughts such as "Will victory indeed be mine?" "Dhonena yugaṃ samāgamā" means one who has come into competition or comparison with the Buddha, who has shaken off (abandoned) defilements. "Na hi tvaṃ sakkhasi sampayātave" means that just as creatures like jackals compete with lions and the like, you will not be able to proceed even a single step or fulfill the competition itself by taking up a comparison with the Buddha who has abandoned defilements. All the remaining meanings and connections are indeed clear.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## The commentary on the Pasūra Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 9. Commentary on the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Disvāna taṇhaṃ" is the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta. What is the origin? At one time, while the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, at the time of dawn, surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, He saw the potential (upanissaya) for the Fruit of Arahantship in the Brahmin named Māgaṇḍiya and his wife, who lived in the market town of Kammāsadhamma in the Kuru country. At that very moment, He went from Sāvatthī to that place and sat in a certain forest grove not far from Kammāsadhamma, emitting a golden radiance.

The Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya also went to that forest at that moment to wash his face. Seeing the golden radiance, he looked here and there, wondering "What is this?" and seeing the Blessed One, he became delighted. It is said that his daughter was golden-colored; many kshatriya princes and others had asked for her but did not get her. The Brahmin held the view: "I will give her only to an ascetic who is golden-colored." When he saw the Blessed One, the thought arose: "This person is of the same color as my daughter; I will give her to him." Therefore, as soon as he saw Him, he was delighted. He went home quickly and said to the Brahmin lady: "Lady, lady, I have seen a man of the same color as our daughter. Adorn the girl; we shall give her to him."
258:
While the Brahmin's wife was bathing her daughter with scented water and adorning her with clothes, flowers, and ornaments, the time for the Blessed One's alms-round arrived. Then, the Blessed One entered the market town of Kammāsadhamma for alms.

The Brahmin and his wife, taking their daughter, went to the place where the Blessed One had been staying. Not seeing the Blessed One there, the wife looked here and there and saw the grass mat where the Blessed One had sat. By the power of the Buddhas' resolve, the place where they sit and the footprints they leave remain undisturbed and clear. The wife said to the Brahmin, "O Brahmin, this is that monk's grass mat." The Brahmin replied, "Yes, lady." "O Brahmin, if that is so, our purpose in coming will not be fulfilled," said the wife. When asked "Why, lady?", she replied, "O Brahmin, look, this grass mat is undisturbed; this is not a place used by one who enjoys sensual pleasures." The Brahmin said, "O lady, do not speak inauspicious words while we are seeking an auspicious matter."

Again, the wife wandered about looking here and there and, seeing the Blessed One's footprint, said to the Brahmin, "This is that monk's footprint." "Yes, lady," said the Brahmin. "O Brahmin, look at the footprint; this person is not one who is attached to sensual pleasures." When asked, "Lady, how do you know?", she spoke thus, wishing to show the power of her knowledge:

"The footprint of one with lust is elevated at the heel,
The footprint of one with hatred is dragged along,
The footprint of one with delusion is as if pressed down with force,
But the footprint of one who has drawn back the veil (of defilements) is like this."

Before their conversation was even finished, the Blessed One, having finished his meal, returned to that very forest grove. Seeing the physical form of the Blessed One, graced with noble marks and surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, the wife asked the Brahmin, "O Brahmin, have you seen this man before?" "Yes, lady," he replied. "Our purpose in coming will certainly not be fulfilled; it is impossible that one of such a nature would enjoy sensual pleasures."

While they were speaking thus, the Blessed One sat down on the grass mat. Then the Brahmin, holding his daughter with his left hand and the water vessel with his right, approached the Blessed One and said, "O monk, you are of golden complexion, and this maiden is also [of golden complexion]. She is suitable for you. I give this maiden to you to be supported as your wife." Saying this, he went near the Blessed One and stood there with the desire to give her. The Blessed One, without speaking to the Brahmin, as if conversing with another person...
259:
"...I give," saying this, he went to the Blessed One and stood there, wishing to give her. The Blessed One, without addressing the Brahmin, as if conversing with another person, spoke this verse beginning with "Disvāna taṇhaṃ" (Having seen Craving).

The meaning of that verse is: Even after seeing the daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga—who had assumed various beautiful forms and come with great allure to the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, there was not even a trace of desire for sexual intercourse in my mind. How much less would there be after seeing the form of this girl, which is filled with excrement and urine? I would not wish to touch her even with my foot, let alone live with her.

Then the Brahmin Māgandiya thought, "Those called monks renounce human sensual pleasures and go forth for the sake of divine sensual pleasures. But this monk does not even desire divine sensual pleasures, and he rejects even such a jewel of a woman. What indeed is his view?" To ask this, he spoke the second verse. In that verse, "such a jewel" refers to a divine female jewel, while "woman" refers to his own daughter. "View, virtue, practice, and livelihood" refers to his doctrine, morality, religious observances, and way of life. "How is the arising in existence?" means "How do you describe the arising (rebirth) in your own life?"

The two verses following this proceed in the manner of question and answer, so their connection is clear. Among them, the summary meaning of the first verse is: "Māgandiya, for me, there is no such thing as a fixed grasp or decision among the sixty-two types of wrong views, saying 'This alone is the truth, all else is false.' Why is that? Because, seeing the danger in wrong views, without grasping any view and while investigating the truths, I saw only Nibbāna, known as 'internal peace,' due to the state of tranquility of lust and so forth within the internal continuum."

The summary meaning of the second verse is: These wrong views are called "decisions" (vinicchaya) because they are grasped after being decided upon by various beings, and they are called "preconceptions" (pakappitāni) because they are constructed by their own conditions and so forth. "O Sage, you who do not grasp these wrong views and speak of this matter called 'internal peace,' please tell me: how is that state (Nibbāna) described by the wise? How is it made manifest by the wise?" (This is the question).
260:
Then the Blessed One, wishing to show the Māgaṇḍiya Brahmin the means by which the wise reveal that state of Nibbāna, as well as the path to Nibbāna along with its opposing factors, spoke the verse beginning with "Na diṭṭhiyā." In that verse, by the words "Na diṭṭhiyā" and so on, he rejects purification through views (diṭṭhi), hearing (suti), the knowledge of the eight attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti-ñāṇa), and the precepts and vows (sīlabbata) external to the Dispensation. Regarding the word "āha" in the phrase "suddhimāha," it should be understood that by connecting the word "āha" with the negative particle "na" in all instances and changing the person, the meaning is: "I do not say there is purification through views." The subsequent phrases should be understood in the same manner. Among those subsequent phrases, "adiṭṭhiyā nāha" means that he does not say there is purification apart from the Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) consisting of the ten bases. Similarly, "assutiyā" means apart from hearing the nine-fold Dhamma; "añāṇā" means apart from the knowledge of ownership of deeds (kammassakata-ñāṇa) and the knowledge in conformity with the truths (saccānulomika-ñāṇa); "asīlatā" means apart from the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla); and "abbatā" means apart from the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga). "Nopi tena" means that he does not say one is purified by even one of these, such as views alone; this is how the meaning should be understood.

"Ete ca nissajja anuggahāya" means abandoning those previously mentioned unwholesome states, such as views, by eradicating them, and not clinging to the subsequently mentioned wholesome states, such as non-view (Right View), by not allowing them to be mixed with craving and views. "Santo anissāya bhavaṃ na jappeti" means that a virtuous person who is peaceful through the calming of passion and so forth by this practice, not depending on any phenomenon such as the eye, is able to not long for or desire even a single state of existence. The intention is that this is his inner peace (ajjhattasanti).

When this was said, the Māgaṇḍiya Brahmin, not grasping the meaning of the words, spoke the verse beginning with "No ce kira." In that verse, the terms such as views are to be understood according to the method already stated. However, he spoke referring only to the unwholesome side in both instances. Connecting the word "āha" with the phrase "no ce kira," the meaning should be noted as: "If you do not say, if you do not preach." "Momuhaṃ" means extreme delusion or a state that causes delusion. "Paccenti" means they know.

Then the Blessed One, wishing to reject the question based on that wrong view of Māgaṇḍiya, spoke the verse "Diṭṭhiñca nissāya." The meaning of that verse is: Māgaṇḍiya, because you are repeatedly asking questions based on wrong views, you have come to such delusion regarding those very wrong views that you have firmly grasped. You do not see even a slight sign of suitability in this inner peace, the practice, or the Dhamma teaching that I have preached. For that reason, you perceive this Dhamma in a state of extreme delusion.

Having shown how Māgaṇḍiya fell into dispute due to his delusion regarding firmly grasped wrong views, the Blessed One now spoke the verse beginning with "Samo visesī" to show his own freedom from dispute, being free from delusion regarding those and other phenomena. The meaning of that verse is: A person who, through the three modes of conceit (māna) or through views, thinks "I am equal, superior, or inferior," would dispute with another person of such character because of that conceit and those views. But for one who does not tremble in these three modes of conceit, thinking "I am equal" or "I am superior" does not occur, nor does "I am inferior"—this is to be included as the remainder of the text. The meaning of the verse "Saccaṃ" is: Such a person who has abandoned conceit and views is called a "Muni" or a "Brāhmaṇa" like me, because he has barred evil.
261:
The meaning of that verse is: One who perceives in this way through the three modes of conceit or through views would dispute with that conceit, with that view, or with that person. For one like me, who does not tremble in these three modes of conceit, the thought "I am equal" or "I am superior" does not occur, nor does "I am inferior"—this is to be included as the remainder of the text.

There is still a little more to be said, namely the verse beginning with "Saccaṃ." The meaning of that verse is: For such a person who has abandoned conceit and views, and who is called a Brāhmaṇa like me because he has barred evil, why would he say "This alone is the truth"? What object would he speak of, or for what reason would he speak? Why would he dispute with that conceit, with that view, or with that person, saying "My view is true, your view is false"? In an Arahant like me whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), there is no occurrence of thinking "I am equal" in terms of equality, nor is there an occurrence of thinking in terms of the other two modes of conceit (superior or inferior) as being unequal. With whom would such a person engage in or spread dispute among those who hold similar views? Indeed, the Blessed One showed such a person with the verse beginning with "Okaṃ pahāya."

In that verse, "okaṃ pahāya" means abandoning the place of the consciousness that cognizes forms and so forth, by giving up desire and lust for those forms and so forth. "Aniketasārī" means not dwelling on the signs of forms and so forth, which are like a home, through the power of craving. "Gāme akubbaṃ muni santhavāni" means the sage does not form intimacies with laypeople in the village. "Kāmehi ritto" means being empty of sensual pleasures and thus being detached and separate from all desires due to the absence of desire and lust. "Apurekkharāno" means not bringing about a future state of existence. "Katham na viggayha janena kayirā" means one should not speak contentious words with people. Such an Arahant is as described in the verse beginning with "Yehi vivitto."

In that verse, "yehi" refers to those wrong views and so forth. "Vivitto vicareyya" means one should practice while being detached. "Na tāni uggayha vadeyya nāgo" means the Arahant, called a "Nāga" because he does not commit faults, should not grasp those wrong views and speak of them. "Jalambujaṃ" refers to the lotus born in the water, which has a thorny stalk. Just as that lotus is unsullied by water and mud, even so, the noble Arahant who speaks of inner peace is unsullied and unattached due to the absence of greed, both in sensual pleasures and in the world...
262:
"Anūpalitto" means being untainted by the two kinds of stains (craving and views) in both the two types of sensuality—objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defilement sensuality (kilesa-kāma)—and in the worlds such as the states of deprivation (apāya).

Furthermore, as there is more to be said, the verse beginning with "Na vedagū" is spoken. In that verse, "Na vedagū diṭṭhiyāyako" means that a person like me, who has reached the end of the four Vedas of the four paths, does not arrive at a view; he is neither one who goes by a wrong view nor one who trusts in that view as having essence. The etymology of that term is: one who goes (yāyati), thus he is a "goer" (yāyako). By the instrumental case, he goes by means of a wrong view, thus he is a "view-goer" (diṭṭhiyāyako). In the second sense, by the possessive case, there is the going of a view, thus he is also a "view-goer". "Na mutiyā sa mānameti" means that such a person does not come to pride through "thought" (muti), which is divided into thought-forms and so on. "Na hi tammayo so" means he is not "made of that" through the power of craving and views, nor does he make craving and views his refuge; indeed, this noble person is of such a nature. "Na kammunā nopi sutena neyyo" means that such a person is not to be led by karma, such as volitional formations of merit (puññābhisaṅkhāra), nor by learning (suta), such as purification through learning. "Anūpanīto sa nivesanesu" means that because that monk has abandoned the two kinds of approaches (upayāna), namely craving and views, he is not led into or attached to any of the objects that are the dwellings (nivesana) of craving and views. For such a person of this character, the verse beginning with "Saññāvirattassa" is spoken.

In that verse, "Saññāvirattassa" refers to one whose perception of sensuality and so on has been abandoned through meditation preceded by the perception of renunciation (nekkhamma-saññā). By this term, the "one liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) or the "one who uses tranquility as a vehicle" (samathayānika) is intended. "Paññāvimuttassa" refers to one who is liberated from all defilements through meditation preceded by insight (vipassanā). By this term, the "dry-insight practitioner" (sukkhavipassaka) is intended. "Those who have grasped perception and view wander about clashing in the world" means those who have grasped perceptions such as the perception of sensuality; these are specifically householders who are occupied with the basis of sensuality. And those who have grasped views; these are specifically those who have gone forth (monastics) who wander about clashing with one another regarding the basis of doctrine (dhamma). What remains unsaid in this Sutta should be understood according to the method already stated. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife went forth and attained Arahantship.

## the explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
263:
The explanation of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya Commentary is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Purābheda Sutta

The Sutta beginning with "Kathaṃdassī" is the Purābheda Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? The origin of this Sutta, as well as the five Suttas that follow it—namely, the Kalahavivāda Sutta, Cūḷabyūha Sutta, Mahābuūha Sutta, Tuvaṭaka Sutta, and Attadaṇḍa Sutta—and the Samma-paribbājanīya Sutta, should be understood generally by the same method already stated in the origin of the Samma-paribbājanīya Sutta. Specifically, however, just as during that Mahāsamaya occasion, the Buddha created an emanated Buddha (nimmita-buddha) to ask questions of himself in order to teach the Dhamma in a way suitable for the deities of lustful temperament, and thus spoke the Samma-paribbājanīya Sutta; so too, on that same Mahāsamaya occasion, knowing the thoughts of the deities in whom the thought had arisen, "What indeed should be done before the breakup of the body?", and for the sake of favoring those deities, he caused an emanated Buddha, surrounded by twelve hundred and fifty monks, to arrive through the air. He then had that emanated Buddha ask questions of himself and spoke this Sutta.

In the questions of that Sutta, first, that emanated Buddha asks about higher wisdom (adhipaññā) with the term "Kathaṃdassī" (how seeing), about higher virtue (adhisīla) with the term "Kathaṃsīlo" (how virtuous), and about the higher mind (adhicitta) with the term "Upasanto" (peaceful). The rest is clear.

In the answers, however, the Blessed One does not answer about higher wisdom and so on directly by their specific forms, but rather, because of the calming of those defilements through the power of higher wisdom and so on, one is called "peaceful" (upasanta). Desiring to show only the calming of those defilements in accordance with the inclinations of the various deities, he spoke the verses beginning with "Vītatāṇho" (one whose craving is gone). In that Sutta, the connection of the first eight verses with this verse, "Taṃ brūmi upasanto" (Him I call peaceful), should be understood. The connection of the subsequent verses with the very last phrase, "Sa ve santoti vuccatī" (He is truly called peaceful), should be understood.

According to the method of word-by-word commentary: "Vītatāṇho purā bhedā" means one whose craving has been abandoned even before the breakup of the body. "Pubbantamanissito" means one who does not depend on the former end (the past), which is divided into the past duration and so on. "Vemajjhenupasaṅkheyyo" means that even in the present duration, he is not to be reckoned by such ways as "one who is lustful" and so on. "Tassa natthi purakkhatam" means that because that Arahant lacks the two kinds of looking forward (preferences), there is no looking forward (longing) in the future duration; thus the connection of the meaning of this phrase with the phrase "Taṃ brūmi upasanto" should be understood here. This method applies in all places. From here on, however, I will not show the connection of meanings but will only provide the commentary on the terms that are not clear.

"Asantāsī" means one who does not tremble due to various instances of not receiving gains. "Avikatthī" means one who is not of a nature to boast about himself regarding virtue and so on. "Akukkuco" means...
264:
He is free from fidgeting with hands and feet, and so forth. 'Mantabhāṇī' means one who is accustomed to speaking after reflecting with wisdom. 'Anuddhato' refers to one who is free from restlessness (uddhacca). 'Sa ve vācāyato' means that the monk is restrained in speech and is accustomed to speaking words that are free from the four faults of verbal misconduct.

'Nirāsatti' means one who is without craving. 'Vivekadassī phassesu' means one who sees the seclusion from self and so forth in the present contacts such as eye-contact. He does not follow the lead of any of the sixty-two views.

'Patilīno' means one who has abandoned defilements such as lust and has withdrawn from them. 'Akuhako' means one who does not act to impress others through the three types of scheming (kuhana). 'Apihālū' means one who is not covetous by nature; it means being free from the craving of wishing (patthanā-taṇhā). 'Amaccharī' means one who is free from the five types of stinginess (macchera). 'Appagabbho' means one who is free from impudence such as physical rudeness. 'Ajeguccho' means one who is not loathsome but is always pleasant and agreeable due to being perfected in virtue and so forth. He is not engaged in slander (pisuṇavācā) which is committed in two ways.

'Sātiyesu anassāvī' means one who is free from the flow of craving for the sense pleasures which are the grounds for enjoyment. 'Saṇho' means one who is endowed with gentle bodily actions and so forth. 'Paṭibhānavā' means one who is endowed with the analytical insights of scriptural learning, questioning, attainment, and expression. 'Na saddho' means he does not have to believe the Dhamma he has realized himself through the words of others. Because lust has been exhausted, he has become dispassionate and does not feel passion again now.

He does not learn the Dhamma such as the Suttas out of a desire for gain. Being without opposition, he is non-opposing and does not fall into greed for tastes such as the primary flavors through craving.

'Upekkhako' means one who is endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā). 'Sato' means one who is endowed with mindfulness such as the mindfulness of the body (kāyānupassanā).

'Nissayānaṃ' refers to the supports of craving and views. 'Ñatvā dhammaṃ' means having known the Dhamma through aspects such as impermanence. 'Anissito' means one who does not depend on those supports of craving and views. By this, it is shown that there are no other supports besides the knowledge of the Dhamma. 'Bhavāya vibhavāya vā' means for eternalism or for annihilationism.
265:
Because of being free from attachment, he is no longer attached at this time. He does not learn the Suttas and so forth out of a desire for gain. Because of the absence of conflict, being without opposition, he does not reach the state of craving for tastes and so forth through craving (taṇhā). He is endowed with six-factored equanimity (saḷaṅgupekkhā). He is associated with mindfulness such as contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā). The supports called craving and views (diṭṭhi) do not exist for him. Having known the Dhamma through aspects such as impermanence (anicca), he has the nature of not relying on those supports of craving and views. Therefore, it shows the absence of other supports besides the knowledge that understands the Dhamma. He does not cling to the view of eternalism (sassata) or the view of annihilationism (uccheda). Such a person is called a 'peaceful one' (upasanta) by the Buddha. That monk has crossed over this great craving called 'visattikā' because of its spreading nature.

Now, wishing to praise that very peaceful person, the Buddha spoke the verse beginning with "He has no sons." In that verse, 'sons' refers to the four types of sons, such as those born of oneself (atraja). Here, it should be understood that possessions and so forth are referred to by the name 'sons' and so forth. Those sons do not exist for that monk, or because of the absence of those, it means sons and so forth do not exist. All worldlings (puthujjanas), whether devas or humans, as well as recluses and brahmins outside of this Dispensation (Sāsana), might speak of him as "one with lust" or "one with anger" due to the faults of lust and so forth. That fault of lust and so forth no longer exists before that Arahant. Therefore, for that reason, he does not tremble at words of blame. He does not speak with excessive conceit, placing himself among the superior, saying "I am superior." In the other two cases (equality and inferiority), it should be understood in the same way. Such a person does not reach the two kinds of conceptualizations (kappa) called craving-conceptualization and view-conceptualization. Why? Because the state of conceptualization (kappa) does not exist. Therefore, it means he is one whose conceptualizations are abandoned. 'Sakaṃ' refers to things possessed as "mine." He does not grieve over what is non-existent or because of impermanence. He does not follow after all things (dhammas) by the power of desire (chanda) and so forth. Such a person, supreme among men, is called 'peaceful' (santa). Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching by placing the fruit of Arahantship at the peak. At the end of the teaching, one hundred billion deities attained Arahantship. Those who reached the stages of Stream-entry (sotāpanna) and so forth were countless.

## The explanation of the Purābheda Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
266:
## 11. Kalahavivādasutta-vaṇṇanā

This discourse beginning with "Kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā" is the Kalahavivāda Sutta. What is the origin (uppatti) of this sutta? This sutta was also delivered during the Mahāsamaya. Knowing the thoughts of certain deities who wondered, "From what do the eight things such as quarrels arise?", the Buddha, following the previous method, had a created Buddha (nimmitabuddha) ask Him questions to make those things clear. Because the questions and answers are arranged in order in this sutta, all the verses have a clear connection.

The explanation of the obscure words in these verses should be understood as follows: "Kuto pahūtā kalahā vivādā" means from what cause do quarrels (kalaha) of body and speech, and disputes (vivāda) of speech which precede those quarrels, arise? "Paridevasokā sahamaccharā ca" means from where do lamentation, sorrow, and selfishness arise? "Mānātimānā sahapesuṇā ca" means from where do conceit, arrogance, and slander (pesuṇa) arise? "Te" refers to all eight aforementioned states of defilement. "Tadiṅgha brūhi" means "Please tell me that meaning I have asked; I entreat you." The particle "iṅgha" expresses a request.

"Piyappahūtā" means they arise from dear objects. The logic for this has already been stated in the Mahāniddesa. By the phrase "maccherayuttā kalahā vivādā", it is shown that the cause of quarrels, disputes, and so on is not only dear objects but also selfishness (macchariya). It should be understood that all those states are taught here with quarrel and dispute as the primary subjects. Just as selfishness exists in those states, slander also leads to disputes. Therefore, it is said: "Vivādajātesu ca pesuṇāni" (When disputes arise, slanders also occur).

"Piyāsu lokasmiṃ kutonidānā ye cāpi lobhā vicaranti loke" means: what is the source in the world for those dear things mentioned here as "piyā pahūtā kalahā"? Not only the dear things, but also the greed of those such as kings who wander about overcome by greed—what is the source of their greed? Thus, two meanings are asked with a single question. "Āsā ca niṭṭhā ca" refers to longing (āsā) and the fulfillment of that longing (niṭṭhā). "Ye samparāyāya narassa honti" refers to those things that lead to a person's future life or destination. This too is a single question.
267:
"Chandānidānāni" means states that have desire (chanda), such as sensual desire, as their cause. "Ye cāpi lobhā vicaranti" means those such as kings who wander about with greed; their greed also has desire as its cause. Thus, the two meanings are answered together. "Itonidānā" means they are indeed caused by desire. The grammatical derivation of the words "kutonidānā kutonidānā" should be understood according to the method stated in the Suciloma Sutta. "Vinicchayā" refers to making decisions through craving and making decisions through views. "Ye vāpi dhammā samaṇena vuttā" means other unwholesome states associated with anger (kodha) and so on, or unwholesome states of such nature, were taught by the Ascetic Buddha; from where do these states arise in abundance?

"Tamūpanissāya pahoti chando" means desire arises depending on the two objects of pleasant (sāta) and unpleasant (asāta), which are the feelings of pleasure and pain, through the power of wanting to join, wanting to separate, or longing. By this much, the question "From what source does desire arise in the world?" is answered. "Rūpesu disvā vibhavaṃ bhavañca" means seeing the passing away (vaya) and arising (uppāda) in material forms (rūpakkhandha). "Vinicchayaṃ kubbati jantu loke" means in the world of the four woeful planes and so on, this being makes decisions through craving because of the desire for possessions, and makes decisions through views in such ways as "my self has arisen." The logic for this has already been stated in the Mahāniddesa. By this much, the question "From where do decisions arise in abundance?" is answered.

"Etepi dhammā dvayameva sante" means these states such as anger arise only when the duality of pleasant and unpleasant is manifest. The manner of their arising has also been stated in the Mahāniddesa. By this much, the third question is also answered. Now, if anyone has doubt (kathaṃkathī) regarding these questions thus answered, the Buddha said "Kathaṃkathī ñāṇapathāya sikkhe" to show the way to abandon that doubt. It means one should practice the three trainings to attain the knowledge of the path and vision. Why? Because the Ascetic has taught the Dhamma only after knowing it. The Ascetic Buddha taught the Dhamma only after knowing it; there is no ignorance (aññāṇa) in Him regarding the Dhamma. It is only because of one's own lack of knowledge that one who does not know these teachings cannot know them; it is not due to a fault in the teaching. Therefore, one who has doubt should train for the path of knowledge; the Ascetic has taught the Dhamma only after knowing it.
268:
876-7. In the phrase "sātaṃ asātañca kutonidānā," by 'sāta' and 'asāta,' only pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) and painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) are intended. "Na bhavanti hete" means "na bhavanti ete" (these things do not occur). "Vibhavaṃ bhavañcāpi yametamatthaṃ etaṃ me pabrūhi yatonidānaṃ" means: "Tell me the meaning of the passing away (vibhava) and the arising (bhava) of pleasure and pain, and from what cause they arise." Here, an interchange of gender (liṅgavyattaya) has been made. The meaning is this: "There is this meaning regarding the passing away and arising of pleasure and pain; tell me from what cause that arises." In this context, 'vibhava' and 'bhava' should be understood as the view of annihilation (vibhava-diṭṭhi/uccheda-diṭṭhi) and the view of eternalism (bhava-diṭṭhi/sassata-diṭṭhi) which arise based on pleasure and pain. For this reason, in the section answering this question, it is stated in the Mahāniddesa: "The view of eternalism has contact as its cause; the view of annihilation also has contact as its cause." "Itonidānaṃ" means having contact (phassa) as its cause.

"Kismiṃ vibhūte na phusanti phassā" is a question: "When what is vanished do the five contacts, such as eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa), not touch?"

"Nāmañca rūpañca paṭicca" means depending on the associated mental phenomena (nāma) and the physical form (rūpa) which serves as the base and object (of contact). "Rūpe vibhūte na phusanti phassā" means when form is transcended, the five contacts do not touch.

"Kathaṃ sametassa" means for one practicing in what way? "Vibhoti rūpaṃ" means does form disappear or not arise? "Sukhaṃ dukhañca" refers to asking about form that is desirable or undesirable.

"Na saññasaññī" means for one practicing in such a way that form disappears, he is not one with normal perception (pakati-saññā). "Na visaññasaññī" means he is not one with abnormal perception (visaññā), such as one who is insane or distracted. "Nopi asaññī" means he is not without perception, such as one who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) or an unconscious being (asañña-satta). "Na vibhūtasaññī" means he is not one who has transcended perceptions of form according to the method of "with the complete transcending of perceptions of form" (sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ), i.e., one who has attained formless jhanas. For one practicing thus, form disappears. Not standing in these states such as 'saññasaññī,' it is said: "With a mind thus concentrated... he directs his mind toward the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana)." For such a person possessed of the formless path (arūpamagga-samangī), form disappears. "Saññānidānā hi papañcasaṅkhā" shows that even for one practicing thus, whatever perception exists, the conceptual proliferations (papañca) of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) which have that perception as their cause are not yet abandoned.
269:
882-3. (The created Buddha) asks: "Do the wise recluses and brahmins in this world say that the highest purity of a being is by this much measure (the formless attainments), or do they say there is another purity superior to these formless attainments?" 'Ettāvataggampi vadanti heke' means that some recluses and brahmins who hold the view of eternalism (sassata) and consider themselves wise, say that the highest purity is by this much measure of formless attainments. 'Tesaṃ paneke samayaṃ vadanti' means that among them, some who hold the view of annihilationism (uccheda) speak of the doctrine of annihilation. 'Anupādisese kusalā vadānā' means they are said to be skilled regarding Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna). Knowing that these holders of wrong views are relying on eternalism and annihilationism, and knowing those bases of reliance, the wise Buddha-muni, endowed with investigation and reflection, (knew this). 'Ñatvā vimutto' means having known the dhammas through aspects such as suffering (dukkha) and impermanence (anicca), he is liberated from defilements. 'Bhavābhavāya na sameti' means he no longer fully enters into repeated rebirth. Thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching by placing the fruit of Arahantship at the peak. At the end of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) similar to what was stated in the Purābheda Sutta.

## The explanation of the Kalahavivāda Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

## 12. Explanation of the Cūḷabyūha Sutta

885-6. The Cūḷabyūha Sutta begins with "Sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānā." What is the origin? This sutta was also spoken during that same Mahāsamaya for the purpose of clarifying the matter to certain deities who had the thought: "All these holders of views say 'we are of good views'; are these people really of good views and established only in their own views, or do they also adopt other views?" As in the previous method, the Buddha had a created Buddha (Nimmita-Buddha) ask him questions and then he spoke. In that sutta, the first two verses are only question verses. In those verses, 'sakaṃsakaṃdiṭṭhiparibbasānā' means living according to their own respective views. 'Viggayha nānā kusalā vadanti' means having grasped their views firmly and strongly, they each speak while professing, "We are skilled in this view."
270:
Those who profess, "We are experts," speak in various ways; they do not speak in one way only. "Whoever knows thus, he knows the Dhamma." Relying on that view, they say, "Whoever knows thus, he knows the Dhamma; the person who opposes this person's Dhamma is merely a fool." A "fool" (bāla) is a low person. "Unskilled" (akusala) means one who is ignorant.

887-8. Now there are three verses of response. These verses stand by expanding the meaning stated in the first half with the second half. Because of such expansion, and because it is shorter than the subsequent (Mahā)byūha Sutta, this sutta is named the "Cūḷabyūha Sutta" (Lesser Array). In those verses, "parassa ce dhammaṃ" refers to the view of another. "Sabbēva bālā" means that if this is the case, all these people are fools. Why? Because all of them remain firmly attached only to their own views. "Saṃsuddhapaññā kusalā mutīmā" means that while they do not debate with their own views and cannot be pure, remaining defiled, they [claim to] be those who have pure wisdom, are skilled, and are wise ones who know what is right and wrong. Alternatively, there is a reading "sandiṭṭhiyā ce pana vīvadātā." Its meaning is: if there were persons who are pure in their own views, possess well-purified wisdom, are skilled, and know what is right and wrong. If that were so, not even one among them would be a person of inferior wisdom. Why? Because for them too, the view is completed just as it is for others.

The summary meaning of the verse "Na vāhametaṃ" is: "I do not say that the words of those two fools who call each other 'fool' are true." Why? Because all of them have made their own respective views as "This alone is the truth, other views are empty." For that very reason, they regard others as "fools." Here, there are two readings: "tathiyaṃ" and "kathivaṃ."

In the question verse "Yamāhu," it refers to whichever "truth of views" they claim to be true.

In the response verse "Ekaṃ hi saccaṃ," the one truth is Nibbāna or the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). Regarding the truth that a being who knows it analytically would not dispute, it is said, "yasmiṃ pajā no vivade pajānaṃ." "Sayaṃ thunanti" means they speak for themselves.

In the question verse "Kasmā nū," "pavādiyāse" refers to those who hold doctrines. "Udāhu te takkamanussaranti" is a question: "Or do those who hold such views merely follow their own reasoning?"
271:
In the response verse beginning with "Na hēva," "aññatra saññāya niccāni" means setting aside the attachments to "permanence" based on mere perception. "Takkañca diṭṭhīsu pakappayitvā" means having generated one's own mere wrong thoughts (micchā-saṅkappa) within the doctrines. Because one who generates thought (vitakka) within doctrines also generates the doctrines themselves, it is stated in the Mahāniddesa: "They generate and produce views (diṭṭhigata)," and so on.

## 894-5.
Now, to show the perverted practice of those who follow mere reasoning (takka) when such various truths do not exist, the Buddha spoke the verses beginning with "Diṭṭhe sute." In those verses, "diṭṭhe" refers to the assumption of purity in what is seen (diṭṭhasuddhi). The same method applies to what is heard (suta), etc. "Ete ca nissāya vimānadassī" means that although one sees the disrespect (vimāna) toward one's own view—which is called purity—by relying on those wrong views, one remains fixed in one's own decision and, laughing, says, "The other is a fool, unskilled." Thus, even though seeing the disrespect, one remains in that decision of views and, being joyful and mirthful, habitually says, "The other is inferior and a fool."

This being so, the verse beginning with "Yenēva" was spoken. In that verse, "sayamattanā" means one's own self. "Vimāneti" means to disparage or blame. "Tadeva pāva" refers to that speech, or the view, or that person.

The meaning of the verse "Atisāradiṭṭhiyā" is: that person is full of and arrogant with such an overreaching wrong view. Intoxicated by that pride of views, thinking "I am completely perfect," he exalts himself in his mind, thinking "I am a wise man." Why? Because that view is completed according to his desire.

The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with "Parassa ce" is: to say a little more, if the person who remains in his own decision and laughs, saying "The other is a fool, unskilled," is called "inferior" by the words of that other person, then he himself becomes one of inferior wisdom along with that person. This is because that person also calls him a "fool" in return. In that case, that person's words would no longer be a standard. If one were to be a "Vēdagū" (one of consummate knowledge) and a wise man by oneself alone, then there would not be a single fool among the recluses (those with views). This is because all of them are wise men according to their own desires.
272:
The connection and meaning in the verse beginning with "Aññam ito" is as follows. Indeed, even if it is said, "If one is a wise man, a knower (vedagū), then there is no fool among the ascetics," someone might ask, "Why is there no fool among the ascetics?" To that, I shall give the answer: Since those sectarians (titthiyas) proclaim a doctrine other than this [dispensation], they have missed the path of purity and are incomplete; thus the various sectarians speak. Because those sectarians proclaim a wrong view other than this Buddha's dispensation, they have missed the path called purity and possess an incomplete view; this is what is meant by the various sectarians speaking in such a way. If it is asked, "Why do they speak with such delight in wrong views?" I shall answer: Those sectarians are intensely attached with the passion (rāga) for their own views. Because they are so intensely attached to the passion for their own views, those with wrong views proclaim their own views; this is the meaning.

899-900. Being thus intensely attached, the preceding verse says, "Purity is only here [in this life]." In that verse, "sakāyane" means in their own chosen wrong path. "Daḷhavādā" means they hold firm views. Among those who are accustomed to holding such firm views, which sectarian, being one who speaks firmly of his own chosen wrong path, would regard another in this group of sectarians as "this person is a fool"? Briefly, in that view, one would place others in the doctrines known as eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) and annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). In detail, in one's own chosen wrong path, which is divided into nihilism (natthika-diṭṭhi), theism (issaranimmāna-diṭṭhi), non-causality (ahetuka-diṭṭhi), and so on, how can a person who firmly says "only this my word is true" see another as a "fool" in accordance with the Dhamma within this sphere of wrong views? According to the view of that person with wrong views, everyone is indeed a wise person and one of good conduct. Despite this, that person who speaks of another as a fool with impure conduct is said to be engaging in dispute. That person, by saying of another, "This person is both a fool and of impure conduct," brings about a quarrel himself. Why is that? Because according to that person's doctrine, everyone would indeed be a wise person and one of good conduct.

Thus, standing by his conclusions in every way, that person with such views in the world arrives at a dispute by excessively judging for himself. Standing in wrong view and judging himself as well as his teachers and so on, he arrives at great dispute. Thus, knowing the fault in such conclusions and abandoning them through the Noble Path (ariya-magga), the being in the world no longer engages in dispute regarding any wrong conclusions; thus, the Buddha concluded the teaching with the culmination of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). At the end of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) similar to what was described in the Purābheda Sutta.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā
## The explanation of the Cūḷavyūha Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
273:
## 13. Mahāvyūha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

The sutta beginning with "Ye kecime" is the Mahāvyūha Sutta. What is the reason for its arising? This sutta was also taught during the Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya) to clarify the matter for certain deities who had the thought: "Do these people who are obsessed with wrong views receive only blame from the wise, or do they also receive praise?" [The Buddha] had them ask his own created Buddha-form according to the previous method. In that verse, "anvānayanti" means they bring back again and again.

Now, since those proponents of wrong views, while saying "Only this is the truth," may sometimes receive praise in some places, that fruit of the doctrine known as praise is small and is not capable of calming defilements such as lust (rāga). What then need be said of the second fruit, which is blame? Therefore, wishing to show this matter, [the Buddha] first spoke this verse of reply: "Appanhī etaṃ na alaṃ samāya, duve vivādassa phalāni brūmi" (For this is small and not enough for calming; I speak of two fruits of dispute), and so on. In that verse, "duve vivādassa phalāni" refers to the two fruits of blame and praise, or victory and defeat and other such things of a similar nature. "Etampi disvā" means having seen the danger in the fruits of dispute, such as that blame is indeed undesirable and that praise is also not capable of calming defilements. "Khemābhipassaṃ avivādabhūmiṃ" means a person who sees Nibbāna, which is not the ground for dispute, as security (khema).

Thus, without disputing, he spoke the verse beginning with "Yā kācimā". In that verse, "sammutiyo" means views/doctrines. "Puthujjā" means views arising among worldlings (puthujjanas). "So upayaṃ kimeyya" means in what way would that person approach even a single phenomenon (dhamma) among phenomena such as forms (rūpa) in the sense of something to be approached, or for what reason would he approach? "Diṭṭhe sute khantim-akubbamāno" means without forming an attachment to purity through seeing or hearing.

Regarding those who are outside of this Teaching, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sīluttamā". The meaning of that verse is: Some people, thinking that virtue (sīla) alone is supreme, speak of purity through mere restraint. Having undertaken and established themselves in vows such as the elephant-vow, etc., those who are led to [further] existence and are obsessed with existence say, "Purity for this teacher exists only in this view." Furthermore, those proponents of skill say, "We are skilled."
274:
Thus, among those who consider virtue alone as supreme, there is a person who practices with such a view. Regarding him, the verse beginning with "Sace cuto" was spoken. The meaning of that verse is: If he deviates from that practice of virtue, either due to the interference of others or due to his own inability to fulfill it, he fails in that unwholesome karma of clinging to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa) or wholesome karma such as merit-forming activities (puññābhisaṅkhāra), and he trembles. Not only does he tremble, but he also laments and yearns for purification through those rites and rituals. How? It is like a person separated from his home who is left behind by a caravan of merchants, and thus yearns for either his home or the caravan.

After showing the cause of trembling for those with the view of clinging to rites and rituals, the verse beginning with "Sīlabbataṃ vāpi pahāya sabbaṃ" was spoken regarding the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka). In that verse, "sabbaṃ" (all) refers to all unwholesome and mundane wholesome states. "Etaṃ suddhiṃ asuddhiṃ ti apatthayāno" means not desiring purification through the five strands of sensual pleasure and the like, nor the impurity characterized by unwholesome states. "Virato care" means one should practice having abstained from both [false] purification and impurity. "Santimanuggahāya" means without clinging to views (diṭṭhi).

Having shown the distress of those outside the Dispensation who believe in purification through restraint in rites and rituals, and the practice of the Arahant who has abandoned clinging to rites and rituals, the verse beginning with "Tamūpanissāya" is now spoken to show those outside the Dispensation who believe in purification in another way. The meaning of that verse is: There are also other recluses and brahmins. Depending on one or another of the loathsome practices, self-mortification, or purification through what is seen (diṭṭha-suddhi), etc., and having views that soar upwards through the view of non-action (akiriyadiṭṭhi), they speak of purification while having unextinguished craving for various lives (bhavābhava).

Among those who speak of purification while having unextinguished craving, even if one considers himself to have attained purification, because of his unextinguished craving, for one who yearns for various objects in various lives, yearnings (jappitāni) occur repeatedly. This is the meaning. Indeed, when craving is repeatedly indulged, it only increases craving. It means that not only do yearnings occur, but there is also trembling regarding the objects imagined through craving and views. Because craving is extinguished regarding various lives, for one who has no future falling away (cuti) or rebirth (upapatti) in this world, why would he tremble? How could there be yearning? This is the connection of this verse. The rest is to be understood as explained in the Niddesa.
275:
910-11. "Yamāhu" is a question verse. Now, since not even one of these doctrines is true, and they speak only out of mere view, the verse beginning with "Sakañhī" was spoken to show this matter. In that verse, "sammuti" refers to view (diṭṭhi).

While they thus claim their own doctrine to be perfect and call another's doctrine "inferior", the verse beginning with "Parassa ce vambhayitena hīno" was spoken regarding anyone. The meaning of that verse is: If one were inferior merely because of another's blame, no one among the doctrines would be particularly supreme. Why? Because many people speak of another's doctrine as inferior; all of them are firm in their own assertions and are dogmatists (daḷhavādā) regarding their own doctrine.

Furthermore, the verse beginning with "Saddhammapūjā" was spoken. Its meaning: Just as those sectarians praise their own systems, their "worship of the true Dhamma" (saddhammapūjā) proceeds in the same way. They show extreme respect to their teachers and so on. In that case, if they were the standard (pamāṇa), then all doctrines would be true. Why? Because their purification is individual (paccatta) to them; it is not achieved elsewhere, nor is it achieved in the ultimate sense (paramatthato). For those whose intellect is led by others' influence, it is merely a matter of clinging to a view within themselves.

Regarding the Brahmin who is undeceived and has barred evil (bāhitapāpa), the verse beginning with "Na brāhmaṇassa paraneyyamatthi" was spoken. Its meaning: For the Brahmin, because [the truth] is well-seen through the method such as "All conditioned things are impermanent," there is no knowledge to be led by another. Nor is there any grasping after deciding "This alone is the truth" among the views. For that reason, he has transcended disputes over views, and he does not regard any other doctrine as supreme, apart from the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on.

The connection and meaning of the verse beginning with "Jānāmi": Thus, while the ultimate Brahmin does not regard another doctrine as supreme, other sectarians, though knowing and seeing through knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) and so on, say "I know, I see it just so," and believe in purification through view. Why? Because if one among them saw the true meaning through that knowledge of others' minds, etc., what benefit would there be for him from that vision? What task would be accomplished by it? Would the full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā) be achieved, or would any of the tasks like abandoning the truth of the origin (samudaya-sacca) be achieved through full understanding? Because in every way, those sectarians have bypassed the Noble Path and speak of purification through other means. Bypassing those sectarians, the Buddhas and others also declare purification from defilements only through other means.

The connection and meaning of the verse "Passanto": There is still a little to be said. He who sees the meaning through knowledge of others' minds, etc., sees only mind and matter (nāmarūpa); he cannot see beyond that. Even when seeing mind and matter, he cannot know them specifically, but sees those mind and matter as permanent or as pleasant. As for seeing them as impermanent or suffering...
276:
... Is it accomplished by specifically knowing and completing one of the factors such as the abandonment of the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca)? This is because, in every way, those sectarians (titthiyas) bypass the Noble Path (ariya magga) and speak of purification through other means. The Buddhas and others also bypass those sectarians and speak of purification from defilements through other means.

The connection and meaning of the verse "Passaṃ naro" (A man seeing) should be understood thus: There is a little more to be said—whoever sees the meaning through the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) and so on, that person who sees is said to see mind and matter (nāmarūpa). Without seeing beyond that, they see those very things, mind and matter, as permanent (nicca) or as pleasant (sukha); they do not see them as impermanent (anicca) or as suffering (dukkha). When one sees in this way, let them see much or little of mind and matter as permanent and pleasant as they wish; however, the wise and skilled do not say that there is purification from defilements through such a vision.

The connection and meaning of the verse "Nivissavādī" (One who is dogmatically settled) should be understood thus: Even though there is no purification through that vision, one who is dogmatically settled in this way, saying "I know, I see, this is exactly so," or one who, relying on that vision and believing in purification through views, is dogmatically settled, saying "This alone is the truth," is not easily disciplined (subbinayo). Such a person is one who places at the forefront the wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) that has been thus conceptualized and constructed. Because they rely on a certain teacher and so on, they speak of beauty and purification only in that view, thinking of themselves, "I am one who speaks of complete purity, or one who sees complete purity." In that view, they see it as it truly appears to them. In seeing so, they see without deviation from their own view (diṭṭhi). The meaning is that they see that view exactly as it proceeds, and they do not wish to see it in any other way.

Regarding the sectarians who thus place conceptualized views at the forefront, the verse "Na brāhmaṇo kappamupeti saṅkhā" (A Brahmin does not enter into conceptualization through reckoning) was spoken. In that verse, "saṅkhā" means having reflected and known. "Nāpi ñāṇabandhū" refers to one who has craving and views as kinsmen, which are not abandoned by the knowledge of attainments (samāpattiñāṇa) and so on. The word-analysis (vigraha) is: because there is no kinsman made for him by knowledge, he is "nāpi ñāṇabandhu". "Sammutiyo" refers to the conventions or views of those who hold views. "Puthujjā" refers to views arising among worldlings (puthujjanas). "Uggahaṇanti manye" means others regard it as grasping; it means others grasp those conventions.

There is a little more to be said—the verse "Vissajja ganthāni" (Having released the bonds) was spoken. In that verse, "anuggaho" refers to one who is free from grasping. Because that person does not have such grasping, they are called "anuggaha". Or, because they do not grasp, they are called "anuggaha". There is a little more to be said.
277:
Furthermore, there is more to be said—the verse "Pubbāsave" (Past taints) beginning with "So evarūpo" was spoken. In that verse, "pubbāsave" refers to the defilements (kilesas) that arise by taking past objects such as forms (rūpa) and so on as the object. "Nave" refers to the defilements that arise by taking present objects such as forms and so on as the object. "Na chandagū" means not going by the power of desire (chanda) and so on. "Anattagarahī" means not blaming oneself by way of what has been done or not done.

Being thus one who does not blame oneself, the verse beginning with "Sa sabbadhammesu" (He among all things) was spoken. In that verse, "sabbadhammesu" refers to the sixty-two types of views, in such divisions as "Whatever is seen," and so on. "Pannabhāro" refers to a person who has laid down the burden. "Na kappeti" means being without conceptualization, not making the two kinds of conceptualization (kappa). "Nūparato" means they are not merely endowed with stillness like a virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana) or a trainee (sekha). "Na patthiyo" refers to one who is free from craving. Craving is called "patthiyā" because it desires; because that Arahant does not have the craving that desires, they are called "na patthiyo". The remaining words are clear in their respective places and thus are not mentioned further. In this way, the Buddha concluded the teaching with Arahantship as the peak. At the end of the teaching, the realization (abhisamaya) occurred just as described in the Purābheda Sutta.

## The Explanation of the Mahāvyūha Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 14. Explanation of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta

What is the origin of the Tuvaṭaka Sutta beginning with "Pucchāmi taṃ" (I ask you)? This Sutta was also spoken at that same Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya) to reveal the matter to certain deities who had the thought, "What is the practice for the attainment of Arahantship?" As in the previous method, the Buddha had a created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha) ask him questions and then he preached it.

In the opening verse of that Sutta, in the word "pucchāmi", the questioning is analyzed by way of wanting to make known what is not yet seen, and so on. "Ādiccabandhu" refers to the kinsman of the lineage of the Sun. "Vivekaṃ santipadañca" refers to seclusion and the state of peace, Nibbāna. "Kathaṃ disvā" means having seen by what cause, or having what kind of vision.

Then the Blessed One, because of seeing in what way he extinguishes the defilements, and having such a vision he attains final peace (Parinibbāna), therefore, to make that matter clear...
278:
The Blessed One, wishing to urge that assembly of deities (devas) toward the abandonment of defilements, spoke five verses in various ways, beginning with "Mūlaṃ papañcasaṅkhāyā."

Among those verses, the summary of the first verse is as follows: Because they have the nature of fabricating, the tendencies of proliferation (papañca) themselves are called 'papañcasaṅkhā'. The root of these tendencies of proliferation are the defilements such as ignorance (avijjā). One should completely cease through wisdom the root of those proliferation-tendencies, as well as all notions of "I am" (asmi) that arise. To abandon the cravings (taṇhā) that arise within one's own continuity, one should train by being mindful at all times.

Thus, having taught the discourse associated with the Three Trainings (sikkhā) through the first verse alone, culminating in Arahantship, he then spoke the verse beginning with "Yaṃ kiñci" to teach by way of abandoning conceit (māna). In that verse, "Yaṃ kiñci dhammamabhijaññā ajjhattaṃ" means one should know any of one's own qualities, such as high birth and so on. Alternatively, "Atha vāpi bahiddhā" means one should also know the qualities of teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya) who are external. "Na tena thāmaṃ kubbethā" means one should not create conceit (strength/pride) based on those qualities.

Now, wishing to show the method of not acting with conceit to that person, he spoke the verse beginning with "Seyyo na tena." The meaning of that verse is: Through that conceit, one should not think "I am better," "I am lower," or "I am equal." A person endowed with those qualities such as high birth should not remain dwelling on them, differentiating oneself through such ways as "I am one who went forth from a high family."

Having thus taught by way of abandoning conceit, he now spoke the verse beginning with "Ajjhattameva" to teach by way of the calming of all defilements. In that verse, "Ajjhattamevūpasame" means one should calm all defilements such as greed (rāga) within oneself. "Na aññato bhikkhu santimeseyya" means that, setting aside the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on, a monk should not seek peace (santi) through any other means. "Kuto nirattā vā" means why would one seek that which is useless? (One should not seek it).

Now, wishing to show the steadfastness (tādibhāva) of an Arahant whose defilements have been calmed within his own continuity, he spoke the verse beginning with "Majjhe yathā." The meaning of that verse is: For example, whether situated in the middle of the great ocean, which is said to be the middle part between the upper and lower portions and measures four thousand yojanas, or in the middle of Mount Sineru, waves do not arise and that place remains unshaken...
279:
...just as it remains unshaken, so an Arahant, free from craving (aneja), remains unshaken amidst worldly conditions (lokadhamma) such as gain (lābha). Such a monk of such a nature should not allow the eruption of defilements such as greed (rāga) to occur anywhere.

Now, the created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha), rejoicing in this Dhamma teaching which was delivered culminating in Arahantship, and wishing to ask about the initial practice (paṭipadā) for that Arahantship, spoke the verse beginning with "Akittayī." In that verse, "Akittayī" means he has preached or declared. "Vivaṭacakkhū" refers to the Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes that are open and unobstructed. "Sakkhidhammaṃ" means the Dhamma realized by oneself, personally witnessed. "Parissayavinayaṃ" means the removal of the dangers which are the defilements. "Paṭipadaṃ vadehi" means "please speak the practice now." Addressing the Blessed One as "Bhaddante," he says, "May you be blessed." Alternatively, it means "Please speak your noble (bhadda) practice." He asks about that same practice by dividing it into "Pātimokkhaṃ atha vāpi samādhiṃ." With the word "Paṭipadaṃ," he asks about the Path (magga). With the other words, he asks about virtue (sīla) and concentration (samādhi).

929-30. Then, because sense restraint (indriya-saṃvara) is the protection of virtue, and because this teaching delivered in this sequence is suitable for those deities, the Blessed One began the verse starting with "Cakkhūhi" to show the practice starting from sense restraint. In that verse, "Cakkhūhi neva lolassa" means one should not be fickle with the eyes by way of looking at things that should not be seen and so on. "Gāmakathāya āvaraye sotaṃ" means one should close the ears to animal talk (tiracchānakathā). "Phassena" refers to the contact with the pain of illness. "Bhavañca nābhijappe" means one should not long for existences such as the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava) for the sake of removing that pain of illness. "Bheravesu ca na sampavedheyya" means one should not tremble at the terrifying dangers such as lions and tigers which are the causes of that pain; or it means one should not tremble at the objects of the remaining nose-faculty and mind-faculty. In this way, complete sense restraint is spoken of. Alternatively, having shown sense restraint with the previous words, with this word he shows that "while living in the forest, one should not tremble even upon seeing or hearing something terrifying."

"Laddhā na sannidhiṃ kayirā" means having rightfully obtained any of those requisites such as almsfood, one should not store them up, thinking, "It is always difficult to obtain for one living in a forest monastery."
280: A monk who delights in meditation should not be restless with his feet. He should dispel remorse (kukkucca) such as fidgeting with hands and so on. He should not be negligent by being respectful in this Dhamma. He should abandon laziness, deceit, laughter, and physical and mental playfulness. He should also abandon things associated with adornment. 934-7. He should not practice or perform Atharvana magic, the science of dreams, or the science of marks such as those of gems. He should not practice the art of knowing animal sounds like those of deer, nor should he engage in slander. He should not engage in buying and selling with the five fellow-practitioners, whether through deception or through desire for profit. He should live in such a way that he does not give rise to defilements that cause blame, so that other ascetics and brahmins cannot blame him. In the village, he should not be attached through socializing with laypeople. He should not speak flatteringly to people out of desire for gain. He should not speak words concerning requisites like robes, or words intended for obtaining those requisites. 938-9. He should not be led into false speech for the sake of livelihood. Even if he hears many unpleasant words from those monks or worldlings such as kings, having been provoked or harassed by others, he should not retaliate. Why? Because the virtuous do not retaliate. Knowing all this Dhamma as stated, investigating and reflecting, he should know Nibbāna as the peace from lust and so on. If it is asked why one should not be negligent, he spoke the verse beginning with 'Abhibhū hi so'. In that verse, 'Abhibhū' means the overcomer of forms and so on. 'Anabhibhūto' means one who is not overcome by those forms and so on. He saw the Dhamma directly, not following others. Always paying homage, he should practice the three trainings. The remaining meanings are clear in all places.
281:
By the words "Not restless with the eyes" (cakkhūhi neva loloti), etc., the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (indriyasaṃvara-sīla) is shown. By "of food and drink" (annānamatho pānānaṃ), etc., the virtue regarding the use of requisites (paccayapaṭisevana-sīla) is shown by way of rejecting hoarding. By abstaining from sexual intercourse, lying, slander, and so forth, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha (pātimokkhasaṃvara-sīla) is shown. By "Atharvana spells, dreams, signs" (āthabbaṇaṃ supinaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ), etc., the virtue of livelihood purification (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) is shown. By the words "Let him be a meditator" (jhāyī assa), concentration (samādhi) is shown. By "the monk investigating" (vicinaṃ bhikkhū), wisdom (paññā) is shown. By "always mindful, let him train" (sadā sato sikkhe), all three trainings (sikkhā) are again shown in brief. By "Then in seats and beds, with little noise, let the monk dwell; he should not indulge in much sleep" (atha āsanesu sayanesu, appasaddesu bhikkhu vihareyya, niddaṃ na bahulīkareyyā), etc., the acceptance of factors that support virtue, concentration, and wisdom, and the removal of factors that hinder them, are taught. Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the complete practice to the created Buddha (nimmitabuddha), concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahatship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) similar to that mentioned in the Purābheda Sutta.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## the Commentary on the Tuvaṭaka Sutta of the Suttanipāta is finished.
## 15. Commentary on the Attadaṇḍa Sutta

"Fear arises from one's own rod" (attadaṇḍā bhayaṃ jātaṃ), etc., is the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. What is its origin? As described in the origin of the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta, the Buddha, knowing the dispute between the Sakyans and Koliyans regarding water, thought, "My kinsmen are quarreling; I shall stop them." Standing between the two armies, the Blessed One spoke this Sutta.
