In that Sutta, the meaning of the first verse is: Whatever fear arises in the world, whether in the present life or in the future life, all that fear arises from the "rod" of one's own misconduct (duccarita). Even though this is so, look at the people quarreling—look at these people, such as the Sakyans, who are quarreling, harming, and oppressing one another. Thus, having rebuked those people who were acting in opposition and wrongly, in order to generate spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in them by showing his own right practice...
282:
(Even though it occurred due to misconduct,) look at these people, such as the Sakyan princes, who have fallen into strife. Look at their mutual quarreling, harming, and oppressing. Having thus rebuked this multitude of people who were acting in opposition to one another and whose conduct was perverted, and wishing to show his own good conduct, the Buddha said, "I shall preach about the sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) just as I experienced it when I was a Bodhisatta in the past," in order to instill spiritual urgency in that multitude. This is the meaning.

Now, wishing to show the manner in which the Bodhisatta experienced that spiritual urgency, he spoke the verse beginning with "Phandamānaṃ." In that verse, "phandamānaṃ" means a being trembling due to craving and so forth. "Appodake" means in a place with little water. "Aññamaññehi byāruddhe disvā" means seeing various beings at odds with one another. "Maṃ bhayamāvisī" means a terrifying fear entered me.

"Samantamāsāro loko" means that the world all around, starting from hell, is pithless, devoid of any permanent essence. "Disā sabbā sameritā" means all directions are shaken by the nature of impermanence. "Icchaṃ bhavanamattano" means desiring a shelter for oneself. "Nāddasāsiṃ anositaṃ" means I did not see any place that was not occupied by aging and so forth.

"Osānetveva byāruddhe, disvā me aratī ahū" means seeing beings whose minds were afflicted and who were oppressed by aging and so forth, only at the end of youth and such, and only because of the destruction that comes with the end, I felt dissatisfaction (arati). Then, in those beings, I saw the dart (salla) of lust and so forth. "Hadayaniissitaṃ" means based in the mind.

If one asks, "What kind of power does that dart have?", he spoke the verse "Yena sallena otiṇṇo." In that verse, "disā sabbā vidhāvatī" means it runs to all directions of misconduct, as well as to all the cardinal and intermediate directions such as the East. "Tameva sallamabbuyha, na dhāvati na sīdati" means having pulled out that dart of lust and so forth, one no longer runs to those directions, nor does one sink in the four floods (ogha).

Regarding beings pierced by this dart of lust and so forth which has such great power, he spoke the verse "Tattha sikkhānugīyanti, yāni loke gadhitāni." The meaning of that verse is: In the world, people crave to obtain the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, they are called "gadhitāni" (things craved). Alternatively, they are called "gadhitāni" because they have been indulged in for a long time. Because of that craving for sensual pleasures, many arts (sikkhā) such as elephant-craft are taught or learned. Look at how much this world is negligent! Therefore, a wise man of good family should not have a mind that is obsessed with those craved sensual pleasures or those arts such as elephant-craft. Rather, by seeing impermanence and so forth, he should penetrate the truth and, being weary of sensual pleasures in every way, he should practice only for his own Nibbāna (extinction of suffering).
283:
Regarding beings pierced by the dart of lust and so forth, he spoke the verse "Sikkhānugīyanti yāni loke gadhitāni." The meaning of that verse is: In the world, people crave to obtain the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, they are called "gadhitāni." Alternatively, they are called "gadhitāni" because they have been indulged in for a long time. Because of that craving, many arts (sikkhā) such as elephant-craft are taught or learned. Look at how much this world is negligent! Therefore, a wise man of good family should not have a mind that is obsessed with (or attached to) those craved sensual pleasures or those arts. Rather, by seeing impermanence and so forth, he should penetrate the truth and, being weary of sensual pleasures in every way, he should practice only for his own Nibbāna (peace).

Now, wishing to show how one should practice for the sake of Nibbāna, he spoke the verse beginning with "Sacco siyā." In that verse, "sacco" means being endowed with truth of speech, truth of knowledge, and truth of the path. "Rittapesuṇo" means one who has abandoned backbiting. "Vevicchaṃ" means stinginess (macchariya). "Niddā tandiṃ sahe thīnaṃ" means one should overcome these three things: drowsiness, physical laziness, and mental sloth. "Nibbānamanaso" means one whose mind is inclined toward Nibbāna.

950-51. "Sāhasā" means the various acts of violence or arbitrary behavior committed by a lustful person through his passionate nature. "Purāṇaṃ nābhinandeyya" means one should not delight in past forms and so forth. "Nave" refers to those (forms, etc.) occurring in the present. "Hiyyamāne" refers to those that are perishing. "Ākāsaṃ na sito siyā" means one should not be dependent on craving. Indeed, craving is called "ākāsa" (sky/space) because it is boundless regarding forms and so forth.

If one asks, "For what reason should one not depend on the sky (craving)?", he spoke the verse beginning with "Gedhaṃ brūmi." The meaning of that verse is: I call this craving, known as 'sky,' "gedha" (greed) because of its craving for forms and so forth. Furthermore, I call it "ogha" (flood) in the sense of oppressing, "ājava" (impulse) in the sense of rushing forward, "jappana" (muttering) because it causes one to mutter "this is mine, this is mine," "ārammaṇa" (attachment) in the sense of being difficult to release, and "pakampana" (agitation) because it causes trembling. I also say that this craving is the "mud of sensuality" (kāmapaṅka) which is difficult to cross because it binds the multitude of people and is hard to overcome.

When it is said, "One should not be dependent on the sky," if one asks, "What is this sky?", the answer is, "I call it greed (gedha)." In this way, the connection of that verse should be understood. The word-arrangement (padayojanā) in that verse is: Greed is called "ākāsa." Likewise, that which is called the "great flood" (mahogha), I call that (greed). I also call it "ājava," "jappana," "ārammaṇa," and "pakampana." That "mud of sensuality" which is difficult to cross in the world together with its gods, I call that (greed).

Being one who does not depend on that craving known as 'sky' which has synonyms such as greed, he spoke the verse beginning with "Saccā avokkamma." The meaning of that verse is: A Brahmin (noble person) who stands on the high ground of Nibbāna, having reached the state of a Sage (muni) by attaining sagehood (moneyya) without departing from the three kinds of truth mentioned before. Such a person is called "santa" (peaceful) because he has relinquished all sense-bases (āyatana).
284:
Furthermore, He spoke the verse beginning with "Sa ve vidvā." In that verse, "ñatvā dhammaṃ" means having known the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma) through the method of impermanence and so forth. "Sammā so loke iriyāno" means that because of abandoning the defilements that cause improper conduct, that person is one who lives and practices appropriately in the world according to the cause.

Regarding the person without longing, He spoke the verse beginning with "Yo'dha kāme." In that verse, "saṅgaṃ" refers to the sevenfold attachment. One who abandons that attachment and has no lust is said to be "nājjheti" (does not increase covetousness).

Therefore, for anyone among you who wishes to be of such a nature, I speak the verse beginning with "Yaṃ pubbe." In that verse, "yaṃ pubbe" refers to the mass of defilements and past kamma that arise based on past formations (saṅkhāra). "Pacchā te māhu kiñcanaṃ" means let there be no impediments such as lust that arise based on future formations. "Majjhe ce no gahessasi" means if you do not grasp or take hold of present phenomena such as visual forms.

Thus, by saying "you will live at peace," He showed the attainment of Arahantship, and now He spoke the subsequent verses by way of praising the Arahant. Among those verses, in the verse beginning with "Sabbaso," "mamāyitaṃ" means the act of making something "mine," or the absence of objects that are grasped as "this is mine." "Asatā ca na socati" means not grieving due to non-existent causes or unpleasant causes. "Na jīyati" means not reaching a state of decline.

958-9. Furthermore, He spoke the verse beginning with "Yassa natthi." In that verse, "kiñcanaṃ" refers to any phenomenon such as visual forms. Furthermore, He spoke the verse beginning with "Aniṭṭhurī." In that verse, "aniṭṭhurī" means one who is not envious (anissukī). Some teachers also read it as "Aniddhurī." "Sabbadhi samo" means one who is equal toward all beings, meaning one who is equanimous (upekkhako). What is meant is: I say that the person who does not grieve, thinking "I have nothing," who is unshakable when questioned, who is not envious, not greedy, without craving, and equal in all things—I declare these four benefits in that person.

Furthermore, He spoke the verse beginning with "Anejassa." In that verse, "nisaṅkhati" means the absence of any formation among meritorious formations and so forth. Because that formation is not constructed, or there is no construction, it is called "nisaṅkhati." "Viyārambhā" means various...
285:
...efforts such as meritorious formations and so forth. "Khemaṃ passati sabbadhi" means seeing only safety (fearlessness) in all phenomena.

Seeing thus, He spoke the verse beginning with "Na samesu." In that verse, "na vadate" means not speaking of oneself as equal, inferior, or superior among those who are equal, inferior, or superior, by the power of conceit such as "I am equal." "Nādeti na nirassati" means not taking or discarding any phenomenon among visual forms and so forth. The rest is clear in all places. Thus, He concluded the teaching by crowning it with Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, five hundred Sakyan princes and Koliyan princes were ordained through the "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination, and the Blessed One, taking those monks, entered the Mahāvana forest.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the explanation of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 16. Explanation of the Sāriputta Sutta

The Sāriputta Sutta, beginning with "Na me diṭṭho," is also called the "Therapañha Sutta." What is the origin? The origin of this sutta is: starting from the merchant of Rājagaha obtaining a block of sandalwood, having a bowl made from that sandalwood placed in the sky, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja taking the bowl by psychic power, the prohibition of psychic powers for the disciples in that matter, the sectarians (titthiyas) wishing to perform miracles with the Blessed One, the performance of the miracle, the Blessed One's journey to Sāvatthī, the sectarians following Him, King Pasenadi of Kosala approaching the Buddha in Sāvatthī, the appearance of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, the prevention of the four assemblies' efforts to perform miracles to defeat the sectarians and the performance of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), the Blessed One who had performed the miracle going to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the preaching of the Dhamma there for three months, and the descent from the celestial world to the city of Saṅkassa as requested by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera—expanding on these stories and the Jātakas in between, the Blessed One, being worshipped by the deities of ten thousand world-systems, descended to the city of Saṅkassa by the central jeweled stairway and stood at the base of the stairway.
286:
## 
“Those wise ones who are intent on meditation, who delight in the peace of renunciation, who are mindful and enlightened—even the gods love them.” This was spoken while this Dhammapada verse was being taught. At that time, the Buddha, wishing to perform a miracle, performed the miracle, traveled to Sāvatthī, followed by the heretics. In Sāvatthī, King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Buddha. The Kaṇḍa mango tree became famous. The Buddha forbade the fourfold assembly from attempting to perform miracles to defeat the heretics and instead performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) Himself. After performing the miracle, He ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and preached the Dhamma there for the three months of the rains retreat. At the request of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, He descended from the celestial realm to the city of Saṅkassa. These and other stories were taught in detail, interspersed with Jātaka tales. Being worshipped by gods from ten thousand world systems, the Buddha descended to the city of Saṅkassa via the central ruby staircase and stood near the staircase.

Venerable Sāriputta was the first of all to pay homage to the Buddha standing on the staircase. Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā paid homage, followed by the rest of the multitude. Then the Buddha thought: “In this assembly, Moggallāna is known as foremost in psychic powers, Anuruddha in the divine eye, and Puṇṇa as a Dhamma speaker. But this assembly does not know Sāriputta as foremost in any particular quality. I shall reveal Sāriputta’s quality of wisdom.” Then He asked the Elder a question. The Elder answered all the questions asked by the Buddha—questions concerning ordinary persons (puthujjana), trainees (sekha), and non-trainees (asekha). Then the multitude knew that Venerable Sāriputta was “foremost in wisdom.”

Then the Buddha said, “Sāriputta is not only foremost in wisdom now; he was also foremost in wisdom in the past,” and He related a Jātaka. In the past, more than a thousand ascetics lived at the foot of a mountain, subsisting on roots and fruits. Their teacher fell ill, and his attendants cared for him. The senior disciple said, “I will bring suitable medicine; attend to the teacher diligently,” and went to the human settlement. Before the senior disciple returned, the teacher passed away. Thinking, “The teacher is about to pass away now,” the disciples asked him about his attainment. Referring to the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana), he said, “There is nothing.” The disciples took it to mean, “The teacher has no attainment.” Later, when the senior disciple returned with the medicine and saw that the teacher had passed away, he asked, “Did you ask the teacher anything?” They replied, “Yes, we did. He said ‘There is nothing,’ meaning he attained nothing.” The senior disciple said, “By saying ‘There is nothing,’ the teacher was making known the Sphere of Nothingness. The teacher should be honored.”

“Even if more than a thousand fools gather and weep for a hundred years, a single wise man who understands the meaning of what is said is far better.”

Thus the Buddha related the Jātaka. For the benefit of his five hundred co-resident disciples, Venerable Sāriputta spoke eight verses, beginning with “Na me pubbe,” concerning suitable lodgings, resorts, duties, and practices. The Buddha, wishing to explain the meaning, then taught the remaining verses. In those verses, “Na me pubbe” means before this descent to the city of Saṅkassa. “Viditavattato” means because of having good conduct. “Tusitagaṇimāgato” means because of coming from the Tusita heaven to the mother’s womb.
287:
After the Buddha had related the Jātaka, Venerable Sāriputta, for the benefit of his five hundred co-resident disciples, spoke eight verses of praise, beginning with “Na me diṭṭho ito pubbe,” to ask about suitable lodgings, resorts, virtue, and duties. The Buddha, explaining that meaning, taught the remaining verses.

In those verses, “ito pubbe” means in the time before this descent to the city of Saṅkassanagara. “Vagguvado” means one with pleasant speech or one with good conduct. “Tusitā gaṇimāgato” means “Tusitā āgato” because of passing away from the Tusita realm and coming to the mother’s womb, and “gaṇī” because of being a leader of a group (teacher). Or it means one who has come as a leader from the delightful heaven called Tusita, or one who has come as a teacher of the delightful group of Arahants.

In the second verse, “sadevakassa lokassa yathā dissati” means as he appears to the world of gods, so he appears to humans. Or “yathā vā dissati” means he sees according to the truth, without distortion. “Cakkhumā” means the Buddha who is endowed with the supreme eye of omniscience. “Eko” means being solitary (unrivaled) through the state of monkhood and so forth. “Ratiṃ” means delight in renunciation and so forth.

In the third verse, “bahūnamidha baddhānaṃ” means many disciples such as kings in this Dispensation. Disciples are called “baddhā” (bound) because their conduct is bound to (dependent on) the teacher. “Atthi pañhena āgamaṃ” means “I have come with a desire for [answers to] questions,” or “There is the coming of those who desire questions,” or “The coming is for the sake of questions.”

In the fourth verse, “vijigucchato” means for one who is weary of rebirth and so forth. “Rittamāsanaṃ” means a secluded couch or seat. “Pabbatānaṃ guhāsu vā” means in the caves of mountains; this should be connected with “for one who resorts to a secluded seat.”

In the fifth verse, “uccāvacesu” means in the low and the high (inferior and superior). “Sayanesu” means in lodgings such as monasteries. “Kīvanto tattha bheravā” means how many causes of fear are there in that place? There is also a variant reading “kuvanto,” which means wailing, but it does not fit the context.

In the sixth verse, “katī parissayā” means how many dangers and obstacles? “Agataṃ disaṃ” refers to Nibbāna. It is called “Agata” (unreached) because it has not been reached before, and it is called “Disā” (direction/quarter) because it is to be pointed out as such.
288:
Therefore, it is said, "the place not gone to before (Nibbāna)." *Abhisambhave* means should overcome (overwhelm). *Pantamhī* means at the end (at the edge of the forest).

968-9. In the seventh verse, "*Kyāssa vyappathayo assu*" means what kind of words would that monk's words be? In the eighth verse, "*Ekodi nipako*" means a wise person with a concentrated mind.

Thus, the Venerable Sāriputta, having praised the Blessed One with three verses, asked five verses regarding the lodgings, the resort for alms, and the practice of virtue etc., for the benefit of five hundred disciples. To clarify that matter, the Blessed One began the answer with the method starting with "*Vijigucchamānassa*." Among those verses, the meaning of the first verse is: "Sāriputta, for a monk who loathes (the suffering of the round) through birth etc., who resorts to a secluded seat and bed, and who desires enlightenment (Sambodhi), I will tell you the comfortable dwelling (phāsuvihāra) and the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (anudhamma), just as one who knows would speak; thus I speak."

In the second verse, "*Pariyantacārī*" refers to one who practices within the four limits such as virtue. "*Ḍaṃsādhipātānaṃ*" refers to the danger of gadflies and other flies. The other flies are called "*adhipāta*" because they fly from here and there to bite. "*Manussaphassānaṃ*" refers to the danger of contact with humans such as thieves.

In the third verse, "*Paradhammikā*" refers to all those who are outsiders, excluding the seven types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika). "*Kusalānuesī*" refers to one who constantly seeks wholesome states.

In the fourth verse, "*Ātaṅkaphassena*" means by the contact of disease. "*Sītaṃ atuṇhaṃ*" refers to cold and heat. Even if that person is touched by many such conditions as disease, it is "*bahudhā*" (in many ways). "*Anoko*" refers to one who has no home (abode) for kamma-forming consciousness (abhisaṅkhāravijñāṇa) etc.

Thus, having answered the meaning asked in the three verses starting with "*Bhikkhuno vijigucchato*," the Blessed One now, wishing to answer the meaning asked in the method starting with "*Kyāssa vyappathayo*," spoke the verse starting with "*Theyyaṃ na kāre*." In that verse, "*phasse*" means...
289:
When one knows the turbidity or impurity of the mind, one should dispel all that impurity, calling it "*kaṇhapakkha* - the dark side."

One should also stand having uprooted the root, such as ignorance, of that anger and excessive pride. This means that when overcoming such things as love and hate, one should overcome them certainly; one should not exert effort slackly in that overcoming.

Leading with wisdom, being endowed with noble joy, one should endure the four things that cause lamentation mentioned in the subsequent verse.

"What shall I eat?", "Where shall I eat?", "I slept poorly this night, where shall I sleep tonight in the coming night?"—one should discard these four thoughts, two related to almsfood and two related to lodging, and be one who practices without anxiety and without craving.

Having obtained food known as almsfood at the time of almsround, or clothing known as robes at the time of robes, lawfully and properly, one should know the measure in both receiving and using them. This means one should know the measure in this Dispensation (Sāsana) or for the sake of contentment (santoṣa). That monk should be well-guarded regarding those four requisites, one who dwells restrained, one who guards the postures, and one who guards the doors of body, speech, and mind. There is also a reading "*yaticārī*," which has the same meaning. "*Rusito*" means one who is angry or provoked (struck).

Being devoted to Jhana by developing unarisen Jhana and by practicing arisen Jhana, and having a concentrated mind by producing the equanimity of the fourth Jhana, one should cut off thoughts such as sensual thoughts and remorse (*kukkucca*).
290:
One should cut off thoughts such as sensual thoughts, the basis of those thoughts such as the perception of sensual pleasures, and restlessness such as the fidgeting of hands. When admonished with words by persons such as a preceptor, one should be mindful and welcome that admonishment. One should speak words arising from wisdom. One should not speak excessively, transgressing the limits of time and the limits of virtue. One should not speak words concerning lineage and entourage that are blameworthy among people, nor should one give rise to such intention.

Now, hereafter, for the sake of disciplining the five stains such as lust for form, one should, being established in mindfulness, train in the three trainings. One who trains thus can endure lust regarding contacts such as forms, but should not endure other states.

Furthermore, as that person trains progressively for the sake of disciplining those five sense objects, He [the Buddha] spoke the verse beginning with "Etesu dhammesu". In that verse, "etesu" refers to states such as forms. That monk, at the time said to be the time for developing concentration when the mind is restless, repeatedly investigates and contemplates all conditioned things by way of impermanence and so forth, and with a concentrated mind, should dispel the darkness of delusion and so on. There is no doubt in this; the remaining words are clear in all respects.

Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks attained Arahantship, and thirty crores of devas and humans attained the realization of the Dhamma.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Sāriputta Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## The Fourth Chapter, known by name as the Aṭṭhakavagga, is also finished according to the method of explaining the meaning.

5. Pārāyanavagga, 1. Vatthugāthā. The words beginning with "Kosalānaṃ purā rammā" are the verses stating the introductory story of the Pārāyanavagga. The reason for the arising of those introductory verses is as follows: In the past, a certain master carpenter living in the city of Bārāṇasī was a peerless master in his craft. That master carpenter had sixteen disciples. Each disciple also had one thousand resident pupils. Thus, this group of masters and disciples, numbering more than seventeen thousand, all made their living depending on the city of Bārāṇasī. They would go to the foot of the mountains, take trees, and right there at the foot of the mountains, they would complete various types of palaces. Then, forming rafts, they would bring them to the city of Bārāṇasī by the Ganges River. If the King desired them, they would assemble and give the King palaces of one story, two stories, three stories, four stories, five stories, six stories, or seven stories...
291:
## 5. Pārāyanavagga
## Explanation of the Vatthugāthā
"Kosalānaṃ purā rammā" and so forth are the introductory verses of the Pārāyanavagga. The origin of those introductory verses is as follows: In the past, it is said, a certain master carpenter living in Bārāṇasī was a peerless master in his craft. That master carpenter had 16 disciples, and each disciple had a thousand resident pupils. Thus, this group of masters and disciples, numbering over seventeen thousand, all made their living depending on Bārāṇasī. They would go near the mountains, take trees, and right there near the mountains, they would complete various kinds of palaces. Then, forming rafts, they would bring them to Bārāṇasī by the Ganges. If the King was in need, they would assemble and give the King palaces ranging from one story to seven stories. If the King did not want them, they would sell them to others and support their wives and children.

Then one day, the master thought, "It is not possible to make a living forever by the work of a carpenter; this work is difficult in old age." He called his disciples and said, "Dear sons, bring trees that have no heartwood, such as the cluster fig (udumbara)." The disciples agreed and brought them. The master made a wooden bird out of that wood, entered inside the bird, and fitted a mechanism. Then, the wooden bird flew into the sky like a king of Garuḍas, soared above the forest, and descended in front of the disciples. Then the master said to the disciples, "Dear sons, by making wooden bird-vehicles like this, it is possible to take the sovereignty of the whole of Jambudīpa. Dear sons, you also make these bird-figures; we shall make a living by taking sovereignty. It is very painful to live by the craft of carpentry." The disciples did as the master said and informed the master.

Then the master asked, "Dear sons, which kingdom shall we take?" The disciples said, "Master, we will take the kingdom of Bārāṇasī." The master said, "Dear sons, it is not proper; do not like this idea. For even if we take Bārāṇasī, we will not be free from the talk of being carpenters, such as 'Carpenter King' or 'Carpenter Viceroy.' Jambudīpa is very vast; let us go elsewhere."

Then, together with their wives and children, they mounted the wooden bird-vehicles, prepared their weapons, and headed towards the Himalayas. Entering a city in the Himalayas, they descended right at the King's palace. Those carpenters seized the sovereignty in that city and consecrated the master as King. He became famous as "King Kaṭṭhavāhana." That city also received the name "Kaṭṭhavāhana City" because it was taken by him. Likewise, the entire district became known as "Kaṭṭhavāhana District." That King Kaṭṭhavāhana was a righteous king. Likewise, the Viceroy was also a righteous person. The ministers also...
292:
The entire country also became prosperous. King Kaṭṭhavāhana was a righteous king; likewise, the sub-king and the sixteen disciples appointed to ministerial positions were also righteous. That kingdom, being supported by the king through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu), became exceedingly prosperous, wealthy, and free from danger. The townspeople and countryfolk, saying, "We have obtained a good king, and we have also obtained a good royal retinue," cherished the king and his retinue very much.

Then one day, merchants from the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), bringing merchandise, arrived at the city of Kaṭṭhavāhana and, carrying gifts, went to see the king. The king asked them everything, "From where have you come?" When they replied, "Your Majesty, we come from the city of Bārāṇasī," the king inquired about everything regarding that city and said, "Establish a friendship between your king and me." The merchants agreed, saying, "Very well."

The king gave provisions to those merchants, and when it was time for them to return, he sent them off with respectful instructions once more. When those merchants returned to Bārāṇasī, they informed their king. The King of Bārāṇasī had a drum beaten to announce, "From this day forward, I grant exemption from taxes to merchants coming from the kingdom of Kaṭṭhavāhana," and saying, "May King Kaṭṭhavāhana be my friend," the two kings became friends without ever having seen each other. King Kaṭṭhavāhana also had a drum beaten in his city, announcing, "From this day forward, I grant exemption from taxes to merchants coming from the city of Bārāṇasī, and they must also be provided with provisions."

After that, the King of Bārāṇasī sent a message to King Kaṭṭhavāhana, saying, "If any wonder worthy of being seen or heard arises in that country, please let me see it and hear of it as well." King Kaṭṭhavāhana sent a reply to him in the same manner. While the two kings were living according to this agreement, once there appeared to King Kaṭṭhavāhana woolen blankets (kambala) that were extremely valuable, very soft, and in color like the rays of the morning sun. Seeing those blankets, the king thought, "I will send them to my friend," and had ivory carvers make eight ivory caskets. He placed the blankets in those caskets, then had lacquer workers make the exterior look like lacquer balls. He then placed those eight lacquer balls into a large casket, wrapped it with cloth, sealed it with the royal seal, and dispatched ministers, saying, "Give these to the King of Bārāṇasī."

He also sent a letter saying, "This gift should be viewed in the middle of the city, surrounded by the assembly of ministers." Those ministers went and presented them to the King of Bārāṇasī. The king had the letter read, convened the ministers, and in the royal courtyard in the middle of the city, broke the seal, removed the wrappings, and opened the casket. Seeing the eight lacquer balls, he thought, "My friend has sent me lacquer balls as if giving them to playing children," and he examined one of the lacquer balls. That lacquer ball, being dry, cracked. At that moment, the lacquer fell away, and the ivory casket appeared, opening up and looking very beautiful. The King of Bārāṇasī opened that ivory casket, and seeing the blanket inside, he opened the remaining caskets as well. It was the same in all the caskets. Each blanket was sixteen cubits in length and eight cubits in width.
294:
'I present this gift.' Upon hearing these words, the various neighboring kings came to receive it and escorted it as far as the border of King Kaṭṭhavāhana’s realm.

King Kaṭṭhavāhana also, having heard the news, came to receive it. Honoring the gift in the same manner, he brought it into the city and assembled his ministers and citizens. In the royal courtyard, he removed the cloth wrapping, opened the chest, and seeing the casket, he opened all the caskets in succession. Upon seeing the inscription on the gold plate, he was filled with joy, thinking, 'My friend has sent me a jewel of a gift that is exceedingly rare to obtain even in a hundred thousand aeons.' He thought, 'How marvelous! I have heard what was never heard before: "The Buddha has arisen in the world." If only I could go and behold the Blessed One and listen to the Dhamma!' He then addressed his ministers, 'It is said that the jewels of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha have appeared in the world. What do you think should be done?' The ministers replied, 'Great King, please remain here; we shall go and learn of the situation.'

Then, sixteen senior ministers with a retinue of sixteen thousand followers paid homage to the King and departed, saying, 'If the Buddha has indeed arisen in the world, there will be no returning; if He has not yet arisen, we shall return.' The King’s nephew also paid homage to the King and said, 'I too shall go.' The King said, 'Dear son, if you find that the Buddha has arisen there, return and inform me.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and departed. All of them traveled, resting for one night at each stage, and reached the city of Bārāṇasī. However, before they arrived, the Blessed One had already attained Parinibbāna. They wandered through the entire monastery asking, 'Who is the Buddha? Where is the Buddha?' and seeing the prominent disciples, they questioned them. The disciples told them, 'The Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna.' They lamented, saying, 'Alas! Though we have traveled a long distance, we did not even get to behold Him.' They then asked, 'Venerable sirs, is there any instruction given by the Blessed One?' The disciples replied, 'Yes, lay devotees, there is: one should be established in the Three Refuges, observe the Five Precepts, keep the Uposatha consisting of eight factors, give alms, and go forth into the homeless life.' Hearing this, they all went forth as monks, leaving behind only the minister who was the King's nephew.

The nephew took the relics of use (paribhoga-dhātu) and set out toward the kingdom of Kaṭṭhavāhana. The relics of use refer to the Bodhi tree, the alms-bowl, the robes, and so forth. He also brought back a water-strainer and a Thera who was a bearer of the Dhamma (Suttas and Abhidhamma) and a bearer of the Vinaya. Reaching the city in due course, he informed the King, 'The Buddha arose in the world and has attained Parinibbāna,' and he related the instructions given by the Blessed One. The King approached the Thera, listened to the Dhamma, and had a monastery built and a stupa erected...
295:
Having established [a stupa], planted a Bodhi tree, and being established in the Three Refuges and the five perpetual precepts, he observed the eightfold Uposatha and gave gifts such as alms. Having lived out his lifespan, he was reborn in the sense-sphere heaven. Those sixteen thousand also went forth, and having passed away as worldlings (puthujjana), they became the retinue of that same king.

Having spent the interval between two Buddhas in the celestial realm, they passed away from the heaven before our Blessed One had arisen. The teacher was born as the son of the chaplain (purohita) to the father of King Pasenadi of Kosala, named 'Bāvarī'. He was endowed with three marks of a Great Man and was a master of the three Vedas. After his father's death, he stood in the position of chaplain. The remaining sixteen thousand and sixteen people were also reborn in Brahmin families in that same city of Sāvatthī. Among them, the sixteen chief disciples studied the arts under Bāvarī, while the other sixteen thousand studied under those chief disciples. Thus, they all gathered together once again. King Mahākosala passed away, and then Pasenadi was consecrated as king. Bāvarī was also his chaplain. The king gave Bāvarī the wealth and other possessions given by his father. Indeed, in his youth, the king had studied the arts under Bāvarī himself.

Then Bāvarī addressed the king: 'Great King, I shall go forth [into the homeless life].' The king said: 'Teacher, while you are here, it is as if my father were still here; please do not go forth yet.' [Bāvarī] replied: 'Enough, Great King, I shall go forth.' Being unable to prevent him, the king requested: 'Please go forth in the royal garden where I may see you in the evening and morning.' The teacher, together with his sixteen thousand followers and sixteen chief disciples, went forth as ascetics and lived in the royal garden. The king attended to him with the four requisites and used to go to pay respects to the teacher every evening and morning.

Then one day, the disciples said to the teacher: 'Living near the city is a great obstacle (palibodha). Teacher, let us go to a place far from the crowds. Living in a remote dwelling is of great benefit to those who have gone forth.' The teacher agreed, saying 'Very well,' and informed the king. Although the king tried to prevent them three times, he was unable to do so. He gave two hundred thousand coins and commanded two ministers: 'Build a hermitage and give it to the group of sages in whatever place they desire.' Then the teacher, surrounded by the sixteen thousand and sixteen matted-hair ascetics and receiving the support of the ministers, [departed] from the northern province...
296:
(Bāvarī) set out towards the southern region. Venerable Ānanda, when reciting the introduction to the Pārāyanavagga at the time of the Council, spoke these verses.

In those verses, 'Kosalānaṃ pura' means from the city of the Kosala country, namely Sāvatthī. 'Ākiñcañña' means the state of having nothing (akiñcana), which refers to being secluded from the obstacles of possessions and equipment.

'So assakassa visaye, aḷakassa samāsane' means that Brahmin lived in a place near both King Assaka and King Aḷaka, in the nearby territory, in the middle of the two countries. 'Godhāvarī kūle' means on the bank of the Godhāvarī River. In the place where the Godhāvarī River divides into two, it forms an island three yojanas in size, which is entirely covered with wood-apple (kapittha) trees. It is the place where sages such as Sarabhaṅga lived in ancient times.

Having seen that place, the Brahmin Bāvarī informed the ministers: 'This place was the dwelling of former recluses; it is suitable for those who have gone forth.' To acquire the land for the hermitage, the ministers gave one hundred thousand coins to King Assaka and one hundred thousand to King Aḷaka. Those ministers gave that [three-yojana] area as well as another area of about two yojanas, totaling about five yojanas. That place was situated between the borders of the two kings' realms. The ministers had a hermitage built there, brought wealth from Sāvatthī and elsewhere, established an alms-village, and then departed. 'Uñchena ca phalena ca' means by means of gathering alms with a bowl and by forest roots and fruits. Therefore, it is said: 'Depending on that very place, a prosperous village arose.'

In that context, 'tassa' refers to the bank of the Godhāvarī River, or to that Brahmin. This genitive case 'tassa' is used in the sense of the accusative, meaning 'depending on that (place)' (taṃ upanissāya). 'Tato jātena āyena, mahāyaññamakappayi' means that from agriculture and so on in that village, a revenue of one hundred thousand coins arose. Taking that revenue, the householders went to King Assaka and said: 'May the Great King accept this revenue.' The king said: 'I do not wish to accept it; take it to the teacher (Bāvarī) instead.' The teacher, too, did not take it for himself but performed a sacrifice of giving. In this way, the ascetic Bāvarī gave alms every year.
297:
"Mahāyaññanti" - The meaning of the verse is: That Bāvarī, while performing the sacrifice of giving every year in this manner, once performed that great sacrifice in one year, departed from that village, and returned again to the hermitage. Having entered the hermitage and gone into the leaf-hut, he sat reflecting repeatedly on the gift, thinking, "It was well given." While he had thus returned, another brahmin arrived, sent by a young brahmin woman who did not wish to work in the house, saying, "O brahmin, this Bāvarī gives away a hundred thousand [pieces of wealth] annually by the banks of the Godhāvarī; go and ask for five hundred from him and bring me a slave girl."

987-8. "Ugghaṭṭapādo" refers to one whose soles rub against each other due to walking, or one whose feet strike heel against heel, ankle against ankle, or knee against knee. "Sukhañca kusalaṃ pucchi" means he asks about happiness and health, saying, "O brahmin, are you happy? Are you free from illness?"

989-91. "Anujānāhi" means agree or believe. "Sattadhā" means in seven ways. "Abhisaṅkharitvā" means taking cow dung, flowers, kusa grass, etc., quickly going to the door of Bāvarī's hermitage, smearing the ground with cow dung, scattering flowers, spreading grass, washing the left foot with water from a pitcher, walking about seven steps, and rubbing the sole of his foot—this refers to performing such a deceptive act. "Bheravaṃ so akittayi" means he uttered a terrifying word; the meaning is that he recited this verse: "If, when I am begging..." "Dukkhito" means one who has become unhappy.

992-4. "Ussussati" means he withers, thinking that the man's words might sometimes be true. "Devatā" refers only to the deity residing in the hermitage. "Muddhani muddhapāte vā" means either on the head or in the falling off of the head.

995-6. "Bhotī carahi jānāti" means "O goddess, if you know." "Muddhādhipātañca" means the falling off of the head. "Ñāṇamettha" means "I have the power of knowledge regarding this falling off of the head."

"Purā" refers to the time when he was twenty-nine years of age. While the brahmin Bāvarī was living on the banks of the Godhāvarī, after eight years had passed, the Buddha appeared in the world. "Apacco" means lineage or offspring.
298:
"Sabbābhiññābalappatto" means attaining power through all higher knowledges, or attaining all higher knowledges and strengths. "Vimutto" means a mind that is liberated through the process of taking an object.

1001-3. "Sokassa" means that Bāvarī has sorrow. "Pahūtapañño" means possessing great wisdom. "Varabhūrimedhaso" means possessing excellent and vast wisdom, or excellent wisdom that delights in the truth. "Vidhuro" means one who is free from burdens; "appaṭimo" means one who is incomparable.

1004-9. "Mantapārage" means those who have reached the end of the Vedas. "Passavho" means "behold" or "see." "Ajanataṃ" means to those who do not yet know. "Lakkhaṇā" refers to the marks. "Byākkhātā" means preached or detailed. "Samattā" means complete or fulfilled. "Dhammena manusāsati" means he instructs according to the Dhamma.

"Jātiṃ gottañca lakkhaṇaṃ" means "How long since he was born?"—referring to my birth (age), lineage, and marks. "Mante sisse" refers to the Vedas studied by me and my disciples. "Manasāyeva pucchatha" means "Ask these seven questions only with the mind."

1013-8. "Tissametteyyo" refers to this single person by way of name and clan. "Dubhayo" means both. "Paccekagaṇino" means those who have separate groups of followers. "Pubbavāsanavāsitā" means those whose minds are perfumed by the habit of merit from the practice of duties having gone forth in the dispensation of the Blessed One Kassapa in the past. "Puramāhissatiṃ" refers to the city named Māhissatī. The meaning is that they entered that city; this should be understood in all places. "Gonaddhaṃ" is the name of the city Godhapura. "Vanasavhayaṃ" refers to the city of Pavana; some teachers say "Vanasāvatthī." Thus, for those sixteen matted-hair ascetics who reached Kosambī from Vanasāvatthī, and Sāketa from Kosambī, there was a retinue of about six leagues.

Then the Blessed One reflected: "The matted-hair disciples of Bāvarī are coming, increasing the great crowd; their faculties are not yet mature, nor is this place suitable. However, the Pāsāṇaka Shrine in the Magadha country is suitable for them."
299:
At that time, the Blessed One thought, "When I teach the Dhamma, there will be the realization of the Dhamma by the great multitude; many people coming from all the cities will also arrive." Surrounded by the community of monks, he set out from Sāvatthī towards Rājagaha. Those ascetics also came to Sāvatthī, entered the monastery, and while searching, "Who is the Buddha? Where is the Buddha?", they went to the foot of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). Seeing the footprints of the Blessed One, they reflected, "The footprint of one with lust is elevated... the footprint of the Buddha who has removed the veil of ignorance is like this," and they came to the conclusion, "He is indeed the Omniscient Buddha."

The Blessed One, in due course, entered cities such as Setavya and Kapilavatthu, increasing the faith of the people, and proceeded to the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya. The ascetics also left Sāvatthī at that very moment, entered all those cities, and arrived at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya itself. Referring to this, it is said: "To Kosambī, to Sāketa, and to the noble city of Sāvatthī, to Setavya and Kapilavatthu," and so on.

In that context, "Māgadhaṃ puraṃ" means Rājagaha, the capital of the Magadha country. "Pāsāṇakaṃစေတိယ" refers to a place that was formerly a dwelling of devas on top of a large rock. When the Blessed One appeared, it became a monastery. That monastery is called "Pāsāṇaka Cetiya" according to its former designation.

"Tasitovudaka" means that those ascetics followed the Blessed One with great speed, traveling in the morning the distance usually covered in the evening, and in the evening the distance usually covered in the morning. When they heard, "The Blessed One is in this place," they became exceedingly joyful and ascended that shrine. Therefore, it is said, "They quickly ascended the mountain."

"Ekamantaṃ ṭhito haṭṭho" means that upon seeing the Blessed One residing within the great pavilion created by Sakka at that Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, the Blessed One greeted them in a friendly manner, saying, "Are the ascetics well?" and so on. They also exchanged greetings, saying, "Venerable Gotama, we are well," and so on. Then Ajita, the senior disciple, stood to one side with a joyful heart and asked the questions he had conceived in his mind.

In that context, "Ādissa" refers to "How old is he?" "Jammana" means asking, "Tell us the lineage of our teacher." "Pārami" means reaching the end or completion.

1026-7. "Vīsaṃ vassasataṃ" means one hundred and twenty years. "Lakkhaṇe" refers to the Treatise on the Marks of a Great Man. It means being completely proficient in other treatises such as the Itihāsas. Alternatively, taking the subsequent word, it should be connected as "He has reached perfection (pāramī) in those treatises." "Pañcasatāni vāceti" means he himself teaches the mantras to five hundred youths who are naturally lazy and of little wisdom. "Sadhamme" refers to their own Brahmanical Dhamma, the knowledge of the Three Vedas.
300:
"Anavaya" means without remainder (complete). Alternatively, taking the subsequent word, it should be understood as "one who has reached the end, the perfection (pāramī)" in those treatises. "Pañcasatāni vāceti" means he himself teaches the mantras to five hundred youths who are naturally lazy and of little wisdom. "Sadhamma" means in their own Brahmanical Dhamma, the scriptures of the Three Vedas.

"Lakkhaṇānaṃ pavicayaṃ" means the detail of the marks. It is the question, "What are those three marks on the body of that Blessed One?"

1030-31. "Pucchañhī" refers to the person who asks. "Kametaṃ paṭibhāsati" means to which person among devas and others does this question occur?

1032-33. Thus, after hearing the answers to the five questions, the Brahmin, wishing to ask the remaining two questions, said, "The head and the splitting of the head." Then the Blessed One, wishing to answer those questions, spoke the verse, "Ignorance is called the head." In that verse, because ignorance, which is the state of not knowing the Four Noble Truths, is the summit (head) of Saṃsāra, it is said, "Ignorance is the head." Because the knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga-vijjā) is endowed with faith, mindfulness, concentration, the desire to act (chanda), and energy (vīriya) that arise together with it, and because it has reached the state of having a single taste among the faculties, it causes that head of ignorance to split. Therefore, it is said, "Knowledge causes the head to split," and so on.

1034-8. "Tato vedena mahatā" means reaching a state of being supported by great rapture (pīti) that arose from hearing these answers, a state of not being discouraged, and a state of joy and delight of body and mind. After paying homage, he spoke this verse beginning with "Bāvarī." Then the Blessed One, out of compassion for that Brahmin Bāvarī, spoke the verse beginning with "Sukhito." Having spoken it, he gave the invitation of omniscience, saying, "And for Bāvarī." In that verse, "Sabbesaṃ" means for all sixteen thousand disciples without remainder. "Tatြ pucchi tathāgataṃ" means that either at that Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, or in that assembly, or among those invited, Ajita asked the first question. The meaning in all the remaining verses is clear.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka,
## the explanation of the introductory verses (Vatthugāthā) of the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

5-Pārāyanavagga, 2-Ajitasutta. He asks the question beginning with "By what is the world enveloped?" In that context, "Nivuto" means enveloped or covered. For example, like a vessel with a lid. "Kukkuccaṃ abhipannaṃ" refers to what is smeared with the state of remorse (kukkucca). "Pamādā nappakāsati" means not shining due to stinginess or negligence.
301:
## 1. Ajitasutta-vaṇṇanā
In that question, "nivuta" means obstructed or covered. "Kissābhilepanaṃ brūsi" means asking, "What do you say is the smearing of this world?"

"Vevicchā pamādā nappakāsati" means that because of stinginess (macchariya) and because of negligence (pamāda), the world does not shine. Indeed, stinginess does not allow one to be manifest through virtues such as generosity (dāna), and negligence does not allow one to be manifest through virtues such as morality (sīla). "Jappābhilepanaṃ" means craving is the smearing of this world, just as monkey-glue is the smearing that sticks to a monkey. "Dukkha" refers to the suffering of birth (jāti) and so forth.

"Savanti sabbadhi sotā" means that the streams of craving and so forth flow in all the sense bases (āyatana) such as forms (rūpa). "Kiṃ nivāraṇaṃ" asks, "What is the obstruction of those streams? What kind of protection is there?" "Saṃvaraṃ brūhi" means, "Speak of the restraint known as the obstruction of those streams." By this, he asks about partial abandonment (sāvasesappahāna). "Kena sotā pidhiyyare" asks, "By what Dhamma are these streams closed or cut off?" By this, he asks about abandonment without remainder (anavasesappahāna).

"Sati tesaṃ nivāraṇaṃ" means that mindfulness (sati) associated with insight (vipassanā), which seeks the destinations of wholesome states, is the obstruction of those streams. "Sotānaṃ saṃvaraṃ brūmi" means, "I call that very mindfulness the restraint of the streams." "Paññāyete pidhiyyare" means that by the Path-wisdom (maggapaññā) which penetrates impermanence (anicca) and so forth in forms and other objects, these streams are completely closed.

In the question verse "Paññā ceva," the summary meaning should be understood as: "Venerable Sir, the wisdom and mindfulness mentioned by you, and all the remaining mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa)—where do all these cease? Please answer this question I have asked."

In the answer verse, however, since wisdom and mindfulness are included within "mind" (nāma) itself, they are not mentioned separately. The summary meaning here is: "Ajita, regarding the question you asked me, 'Where does this cease?', I shall tell you where mind and matter cease without remainder. With the cessation of that consciousness (viññāṇa), simultaneously and without before or after, mind and matter cease here in this Nibbāna." In this Nibbāna, when consciousness ceases, this mind-and-matter ceases. Because of the cessation of consciousness, the cessation of that mind-and-matter occurs. It means it is impossible to exist beyond that cessation.
302:
By these words, the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca) is shown by the phrase "Suffering is a great fear for that person." The Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca) is shown by the phrase "The streams flow in all places." The Truth of the Path (maggasacca) is shown by the phrase "They are closed by wisdom." The Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca) is shown by the phrase "Ceases without remainder." Having heard the Four Truths in this way, but not yet having attained the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya), he wished to ask again about the practice of the trainee (sekha) and the non-trainee (asekha), and thus spoke the verse beginning with "Ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse."

In that verse, "saṅkhātadhammā" is a designation for Arahants who have investigated and scrutinized things through the power of impermanence and so forth. "Sekhā" refers to the remaining Noble individuals who are still training in morality (sīla) and other virtues. "Puthū" refers to the many (seven types of) trainees. It means, "O Wise One, please tell me the practice of those trainees and non-trainees about whom I have asked."

Then, because a trainee must abandon all defilements beginning with the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchandanīvaraṇa), the Blessed One showed the practice of the trainee with the half-verse beginning with "Kāmesu." The meaning of that verse is: one should not be greedy for sensual objects (vatthukāma) or the defilement of lust (kilesakāma), and while abandoning bodily misconduct and states that defile the mind, one should not be defiled in mind. As for the non-trainee (asekha), because they have repeatedly weighed all formations (saṅkhāra) through the power of impermanence and so forth, they are skilled (kusala) in all things; being mindful through the mindfulness of body (kāyānupassanāsati) and so forth, and having destroyed self-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) and others, they have reached the state of a monk (bhikkhu) and practice in all postures. Therefore, the Blessed One showed the practice of the non-trainee with the half-verse beginning with "Kusalo." The remaining meaning is clear in all places.

In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahantship as the climax. At the end of the teaching, the ascetic Ajita, together with his thousand disciples, was established in Arahantship. For many other thousands of beings, the Dhamma-eye (sotāpattimagga-ñāṇa) arose. Simultaneously with the attainment of Arahantship, the ascetic requisites of the venerable Ajita and his thousand disciples, such as antelope skins, matted hair, and bark garments, disappeared. All of them became "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks, possessing miraculous bowls and robes, with hair two finger-breadths long, and they sat with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to the Blessed One.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya,
## The Commentary on the Ajita Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
303:
## 2. Commentary on the Tissametteyya Sutta

This sutta beginning with 'Kodha santussito' is the Tissametteyya Sutta. What is its origin (uppatti)? The origin of all these suttas is by the power of questioning. Since the Blessed One had invited them, saying, 'The opportunity is given, ask [your questions],' those brahmins asked about their respective doubts. And as each was asked, the Blessed One answered them. Thus, it should be understood that these suttas originated by the power of questioning.

When the questions of Ajita were concluded, the brahmin Mogharāja began to ask, 'How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see him?' Knowing that Mogharāja’s faculties (indriya) were not yet mature, the Blessed One rejected him, saying, 'Wait a while, Mogharāja; let another ask.' Then Tissametteyya, wishing to ask about his own doubt, spoke the verse beginning with 'Kodha'. In that verse, 'Kodha santussito' means: who in this world is content? 'Iñjitā' refers to the agitations of craving and views. 'Ubhantamabhiññāya' means having known both ends. 'Mantā na lippatī' means he is not smeared [by defilements] through wisdom.

1048-9. Wishing to explain the meaning to Tissametteyya, the Blessed One spoke the two verses beginning with 'Kāmesu'. In those verses, 'Kāmesu brahmacariyavā' means one who leads the holy life regarding sense pleasures; it means one who, seeing the danger in sense pleasures, is endowed with the noble holy life of the Path. By this much, he shows the state of contentment (santusita). With the words 'vītatāṇho' (devoid of craving) and so on, he shows the state of imperturbability (aniñjita). In that verse, 'saṅkhāya nibbuto' means one who is quenched by the quenching of lust and so on, after investigating phenomena by way of impermanence and so forth. The remaining meanings are clear according to the method already stated in various places.

Thus, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin also, together with a thousand disciples, was established in Arahantship. The Dhamma-eye (the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry) arose for many thousands of others. The rest is just as previously stated.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Commentary on the Tissametteyya Sutta of the Sutta Nipata is finished.
304:
## 3. Commentary on the Puṇṇaka Sutta

This Puṇṇaka Sutta beginning with 'Anejaṃ' was also spoken after rejecting Mogharāja, just as in the previous method. In that verse, 'mūladassāvī' means one who habitually sees the roots of unwholesome and so on. 'Isayo' refers to the matted-hair ascetics named sages (isī). 'Yaññaṃ' refers to the objects to be offered. 'Akappayiṃsu' means they sought.

'Āsīsamānā' means longing for forms and so on. 'Itthattaṃ' means longing for existence in this human life; it means desiring the state of being human and so forth. 'Jaraṃ sitā' means those who are dependent on old age. In this context, by the cause of old age, the entire suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭa-dukkha) is meant. Therefore, it shows that while depending on the suffering of the round and being unable to escape from that suffering, they sought the sacrifice.

In the verse, 'Kaccissu te bhagavā yaññapathe appamattā, atāruṃ jātiñca jarañca mārisā,' the sacrifice itself is called 'yaññapatha' (the path of sacrifice). The meaning is: 'O Blessed One, were those people, being diligent in sacrifices and performing them, able to cross over the suffering of the round?'

'Āsīsanti' means they long for the attainment of forms and so on. 'Thomayanti' means they praise the sacrifices and so on in such ways as 'It is well-sacrificed, it is purely given.' 'Abhijappanti' means they utter words for the sake of attaining forms and so on. 'Juhanti' means they give. 'Kāmābhijappanti paṭicca lābhaṃ' means that based on the attainment of forms and so on, they repeatedly long for sense pleasures; they say, 'Oh, would that it were ours!' and it means they increase craving therein. 'Yājayogā' means those devoted to sacrifice. 'Bhavarāgarattā' means that by such longings and so on, they are either stained by the lust for existence, or being those who have lust for existence and performing such longings and so on, they were unable to cross over the suffering of the round such as rebirth.

1054-5. 'Atha ko carahi' means 'If those people could not cross, who else can cross now?' 'Saṅkhāya' means having investigated with wisdom. 'Paroparāni' means other existences and one's own existence, such as the individualities of others and the individuality of oneself. 'Vidhūmo' means a person free from the 'smoke' of bodily misconduct and so on. 'Anīgho' means a person free from the 'thorns' of lust and so on. 'Atāri so' means such an Arahant has crossed over rebirth and old age. The remaining matter here is quite clear.

The Blessed One concluded the teaching of this sutta also by making Arahantship the pinnacle. At the conclusion of the teaching, this brahmin also, together with a thousand disciples, was established in Arahantship. The Dhamma-eye, the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry, became manifest to many thousands of others.
305:
In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, this Brahmin, along with a thousand disciples, was established in Arahantship. For many hundreds of others, the Dhamma-eye (the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry) arose. The rest is just as previously stated.

## In the Paramatthajotikā, the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya
## In the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the Explanation of the Punnaka Sutta is finished.
## 4. Explanation of the Mettagū Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Pucchāmi taṃ" is the Mettagū Sutta. Therein, "maññāmi taṃ vedaguṃ bhāvitattaṃ" means: "I consider this Venerable One as a Vedagū (one who has reached Nibbāna through the knowledge of the Path) and as one with a developed mind (bhāvitatta)."

In the word "apucchasi", the letter "a" is merely a particle used for completing the verse; the meaning is simply "you asked". "Pavakkhāmi yathā pajānanti" means: "I shall teach just as one who knows explains." "Upadhinidānā pabhavanti dukkhā" means: "With the acquisitions (upadhi) such as craving as the cause, various sufferings such as birth arise."

Regarding the sufferings that arise with acquisitions as the cause, He spoke the verse beginning with "Yo ve avidvā". Therein, "pajānanti" refers to one who knows formations (saṅkhāra) by way of impermanence and so forth. "Dukkhassa jātippabhavānupassī" refers to one who repeatedly sees that the cause of birth in the suffering of the round of existence is "upadhi" (acquisitions).

"Sokapariddavañca" means sorrow and lamentation. "Tathā hi te vidito esa dhammo" means: "In whatever way beings know, by way of making them known in those various ways, this Dhamma is known by you."

1060-61. "Kittayissāmi te dhammaṃ" means: "I will teach you the Dhamma of Nibbāna and the Dhamma of the practice leading to Nibbāna." "Diṭṭhe dhamme" means in the Dhamma of suffering and so forth that is to be seen in the present, or in this very existence. "Anītiham" refers to the Dhamma that is directly realized by oneself (not based on hearsay from others). "Yaṃ viditvā" means: "Having known by contemplating that Dhamma in the way of 'all formations are impermanent' and so forth." "Tañcāhaṃ abhinandāmi" means: "I desire your words which illuminate the Dhamma of the kind mentioned." "Dhammamuttamaṃ" means: "I also greatly delight in that supreme Dhamma."
306:
In the phrase "above, below, and across in the middle", "above" (uddhaṃ) refers to the future time, "below" (adho) refers to the past time, and "across in the middle" (tiriyañcāpi majjhe) refers to the present time. "In these [times], dispel craving (nandi), the attachment to views (diṭṭhi-nivesana), and kammic consciousness (abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa); having dispelled them, one should not remain in existence." If this is done, one would not remain in either of the two types of existence. Thus, the word "panujja" should be connected to the sense of "dispel"; however, in the sense of "having dispelled", the connection is "one should not remain in existence". It means that having dispelled that craving, attachment, and consciousness, one would not remain in either of the two types of existence.

1063-4. To the person who, having dispelled those things, does not remain in existence, He spoke the verse beginning with "Evaṃvihārī". Therein, "idheva" means in this very Dispensation (Sāsana), or in this very existence. In the phrase "sukittitaṃ gotamanūpadhikaṃ", "anūpadhikaṃ" refers to Nibbāna. Referring to that Nibbāna and addressing the Blessed One, he said: "O Gotama, the Nibbāna Dhamma which is free from acquisitions (upadhi) has been well proclaimed."

It is not only suffering that is abandoned—He spoke the verse beginning with "Te cāpi". Therein, "aṭṭhitaṃ" means respectfully or constantly. "Taṃ taṃ namassāmi" means: "Therefore, I pay homage to you." "Sameccā" means having approached. He said "Nāga" as a way of addressing the Blessed One.

Now, although it was known by that Brahmin that "the Blessed One has certainly abandoned suffering", the Blessed One, without revealing Himself, wishing to advise as a person who has abandoned suffering, spoke the verse beginning with "Yaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ". The meaning of that verse is: "The person whom you, knowing, would recognize as: 'This person is a Brahmin because he has expelled evil (bāhita-pāpa); he is a Vedagū because he has reached [the goal] through knowledge (veda); he is Akiñcana because of the absence of possessions (kiñcana); and he is unattached to the world of sensual pleasures and existence because of his non-attachment to sensual pleasures and existence.'" Certainly, that person has crossed this fourfold flood (ogha); having crossed to the other shore, he is without thorns (akhila) and without doubt.

Furthermore, He spoke the verse beginning with "Vidvā ca yo". Therein, "idha" means in this Dispensation or in this existence. "Visajja" means having relinquished. The rest of the meaning is clear in all places.
307:
In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahatship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as previously described.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Mettagū Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 5. Explanation of the Dhotaka Sutta

1068-9. The sutta beginning with "Pucchāmi taṃ" is the Dhotaka Sutta. Therein, "vācābhikaṅkhāmi" means "I greatly desire [your] words." "Sikkhe nibbānamattano" means one should train in higher virtue (adhisīla) and so forth for the sake of the extinguishing of one's own lust (rāga) and other defilements. "Ito" means from my mouth (from me).

When this was said, the Brahmin Dhotaka, with a delighted mind, praising the Blessed One and wishing to request liberation from doubt, spoke the verse beginning with "Passāmahaṃ." Therein, "passāmahaṃ devamanussaloke" means "I see in the world of gods and humans." "Taṃ taṃ namassāmi" means "I pay homage to such a person." "Pamuñca" means "let [me] be liberated."

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show him that liberation from doubt depends on oneself through the means of crossing the flood, spoke the verse beginning with "Nāhaṃ." Therein, "nāhaṃ sahissāmi" means "I am not able (I cannot, or I will not strive [to liberate another])." "Pamocanāya" means "for the sake of liberation." "Kathaṃkathiṃ" refers to one who has doubt. "Taresi" means "one should cross."

1072-5. When this was said, the Brahmin Dhotaka, even more delighted, praising the Blessed One and wishing to request instruction, spoke the verse beginning with "Anusāsa brahme." Therein, "brahmā" is a term for what is noble. Addressing the Blessed One with that word, he said, "O Noble One, instruct me." "Vivekadhammaṃ" refers to the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the seclusion from all conditioned things (saṅkhāra). "Abyāpajjamāno" means not falling into various [unwholesome] states. "Idheva santo" means being right here in this very life. "Asito" means independent (anissita), not clinging through craving or views. The next two verses follow the same method as explained in the Mettagū Sutta. However, the difference is that "dhammaṃ" (the Dhamma) is used in that sutta, while "santiṃ" (peace) is used in this sutta.
308:
In the first half of the third verse as well, it is just as previously explained. In the second half, "saṅgo" means a place of attachment, or clinging. The rest is clear in every respect.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahatship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as previously described.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Explanation of the Dhotaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 6. Explanation of the Upasīva Sutta

The sutta beginning with "Eko ahaṃ" is the Upasīva Sutta. Therein, "mahantamoghaṃ" means the great flood. "Anissito" means not depending on or clinging to either a person or a thing (dhamma). "No visahāmi" means "I am not able." "Ārammaṇaṃ" means support (nissaya). "Yaṃ nissito" means depending on which person or thing.

Now, since that Brahmin has attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana) but does not recognize even that peaceful support, the Blessed One, wishing to show him both that support and the higher path of escape (Nibbāna), spoke the verse beginning with "Ākiñcaññaṃ." Therein, "pekkhamāno" means entering and emerging from that attainment of the sphere of nothingness with mindfulness, and seeing it through the aspect of impermanence (anicca) and so forth. "Natthīti nissāya" means taking the attainment that occurs as "there is nothing" as an object. "Tarassu oghaṃ" means "cross the fourfold flood through the insight (vipassanā) that proceeds from that point onwards as appropriate." "Kathāhi" means through doubts (kathaṃkathā). "Taṇhakkhayaṃ nattamahābhipassa" means "see Nibbāna clearly, making it manifest day and night." By this verse, he explains to him the dwelling in happiness in this very life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).

1078-9. Now, having heard the words "having abandoned sense-pleasures" (kāme pahāya), and seeing the sense-pleasures he himself has abandoned through suppression (vikkhambhana), he spoke the verse beginning with "Sabbesu." Therein, "hitvā maññaṃ" (hitvā aññaṃ) means having abandoned the other six attainments below that. "Saññāvimokkhe parame" means in the sphere of nothingness, which is the highest among the seven deliverances of perception (saññāvimokkha). Tiṭṭhe...
309:
He asks whether that person remains in that Brahma-realm of Nothingness (Ākiñcaññāyatana) without departing. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to grant a stay of only sixty thousand aeons (kappas) for that person, spoke the third verse.

Having heard about that person's stay in that realm, he now wishes to ask about that person's state of eternalism (sassata) or annihilation (uccheda), and thus spoke the verse beginning with 'Tiṭṭhe ce'. In that verse, 'pūgampi vassānaṃ' means a collection of numerous years. There is also a reading 'pūgampi vassāni'; in that case, the genitive case should be changed to the nominative case by way of grammatical substitution. Alternatively, for this word 'pūga', the meaning 'many' should be stated. Some also read it as 'pūgāni', but the former reading is the most excellent. In that same verse, 'tattheva so sīti siyā vimutto' means: would that person, right there in that realm of Nothingness, be liberated from various sufferings and reach the state of coolness? Would he reach Nibbāna and remain as an eternal being? 'Cavetha viññāṇaṃ tathāvidhassa' means: or would the consciousness of such a person attain Parinibbāna without clinging? Thus he asks about annihilation (uccheda). Or would it be for the purpose of taking rebirth? Thus he also asks about that person's rebirth.

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the Parinibbāna without clinging of a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) born in that realm of Nothingness, without falling into the characteristics of annihilation or eternalism, spoke the verse beginning with 'Accī yathā'. In that verse, 'atthaṃ paleti' means he goes to rest (disappears). 'Na upeti saṅkhaṃ' means he does not come under the designation 'he has gone to such and such a place'. 'Evaṃ muni nāmakāyā vimutto' means: in this way, the Sekhamuni (a sage in training) born in that realm of Nothingness is already liberated from the form-body (rūpakāya) by nature. Having attained the fourth path (Arahattamagga) in that realm and having fully understood the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), he is further liberated from the name-body (nāmakāya). Becoming an Arahant liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta), he reaches the state of rest called Parinibbāna without clinging. He no longer comes under designations (saṅkhā) such as 'Khattiya' or 'Brāhmaṇa' and so forth.

Now, having heard the words 'atthaṃ paleti', the brahmin Upasīva could not properly grasp the meaning and spoke the verse beginning with 'Atthangato so'. The meaning of that verse is: Has that person gone to rest and no longer exists, or is he truly eternal, free from disease, and unchanging? O Great Sage, please explain this well to me. Why? Because this Dhamma is known by you.

The Blessed One taught this sutta culminating in the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala). At the end of the teaching, the realization of the Dhamma occurred just as previously mentioned.

## The Commentary on the Upasīva Sutta is finished.
310:
Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that such a thing (eternalism or annihilation) cannot be said to that brahmin Upasīva, spoke the verse beginning with 'Atthangatassa'. In that verse, 'atthangatassa' means of one who has attained Parinibbāna without clinging. 'Na pamāṇamatthi' means there is no measure such as form (rūpa), etc. 'Yena naṃ vajju' means that by which they might speak of that person, such as lust (rāga), etc. (those do not exist). 'Sabbesu dhammesu' means in all phenomena such as the aggregates (khandhas), etc. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta culminating in the fruit of Arahatship. At the end of the teaching, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred as previously mentioned.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## In the Sutta Nipāta Commentary, the explanation of the Upasīva Sutta is finished.
## 7. Commentary on the Nanda Sutta

1084-5. 'Santi loke' and so forth is the Nanda Sutta. In that sutta, the meaning of the first verse is: People in the world such as kings, etc., referring to Ājီvakas, Nigaṇṭhas, and others, say 'There are sages (munis).' 'Tayidaṃ kathaṃsu' means: Do they call one a sage because he is endowed with knowledge (ñāṇūpapanna) arisen through knowledge of attainments (samāpatti-ñāṇa), etc.? Do they speak of such a person? Or do they call one a sage because he is endowed with a life of various hardships (lūkhajီvita)? Then, the Blessed One, rejecting both of those and wishing to show the true sage, spoke the verse beginning with 'Na diṭṭhiyā'.

1086-7. Now, to remove doubt in the views of those who say 'Purity is through views (diṭṭhi), etc.', he asks the verse beginning with 'Ye kecime'. In that verse, 'anekarūpena' means through various ways like omens and festivals (kotūhalamaṅgala), etc. 'Tattha yatā carantā' means living guarded by their own views in that belief. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show that there is no purity in that way, spoke the second verse.

1088-90. Hearing 'They cannot cross over,' he now wishes to hear about the one who has crossed over and asks the words beginning with 'Ye kecime'. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show those who have crossed over birth and old age (jāti-jarā) by means of crossing the flood (ogha), spoke the third verse. In that verse, 'nivutā' means covered or enveloped. 'Yesīdha' should be broken down as 'yesu idha'. Here, 'su' is just a particle. 'Taṇhaṃ pariññāya' means having fully understood craving (taṇhā) through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). The remaining words are clear in all respects according to the method previously mentioned.
311:
In this way, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahantship as its culmination. At the end of the teaching, the brahmin Nanda, greatly rejoicing in the words spoken by the Blessed One, uttered a verse: "I greatly rejoice in this Dhamma." In this sutta as well, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred just as previously described.

## In the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The explanation of the Nanda Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Hemaka Sutta

1091-4. "Ye me pubbe" etc., is the Hemaka Sutta. Therein, "ye me pubbe viyākaṃsu" means those teachers such as Bāvarī who previously explained their own views to me. "Huraṃ gotamasāsanā" means (views) prior to the dispensation of the Buddha Gotama. "Sabbaṃ taṃ takkavaḍḍhanaṃ" means all those views only increase thoughts of sensual desire (kāma-vitakka) and so forth. "Taṇhānigghātanaṃ" refers to the destruction of craving (Nibbāna where craving is eliminated).

Then, wishing to teach that Dhamma to the brahmin Hemaka, the Blessed One spoke two verses beginning with "Idha". In those verses, "etadaññāya ye satā" means those who, having gradually understood the way to reach this deathless state of Nibbāna through insight (vipassanā) in such ways as "all conditioned things are impermanent," and who are mindful through the mindfulness of body (kāyānupassanā-sati) and so forth. "Diṭṭhadhammābhinibbuta" means they are completely cooled because they have realized the Dhamma and because defilements such as lust (rāga) have been extinguished in this very life. The remaining meanings are clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, with Arahantship as its culmination. At the end of the teaching, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred just as previously described.

## In the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The explanation of the Hemaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
312:
## 9. Commentary on the Todeyya Sutta

"Yasmiṃ kāmā" etc., is the Todeyya Sutta. Therein, "vimokkho tassa kīdiso" is a question asking what the nature of that person's liberation (vimokkha) is. Now, wishing to show the brahmin Todeyya that there is no other liberation, the Blessed One spoke the second verse. In that verse, "vimokkho tassa nāparo" means there is no other liberation for him; only this destruction of craving is liberation.

1097-8. Although it was said that "only the destruction of craving is liberation," he did not understand that meaning and asked again: "Is that person without longing or is he still longing?" In that verse, "uda paññakappī" asks whether he still conceives thoughts of craving or thoughts of views through knowledge such as the knowledge of attainment (samāpatti-ñāṇa). Then, the Blessed One, wishing to explain that meaning, spoke the second verse. In that verse, "kāmabhave" means in sensual pleasures and in existence. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, with Arahantship as its culmination. At the end of the teaching, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred just as previously described.

## In the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The explanation of the Todeyya Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Kappa Sutta

"Majjhe sarasmiṃ" etc., is the Kappa Sutta. Therein, "majjhe sarasmiṃ" is said to mean in the middle of Saṃsāra, because there is no sign by which the beginning or the end can be known. "Tiṭṭhataṃ" means for those who are staying. "Yathāyidaṃ nāparaṃ siyā" means in such a way that this suffering (dukkha) would not occur again.

1101-2. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to clarify that meaning, spoke three verses. In those verses, "akiñcanaṃ" is the opposite of having impediments (kiñcana). "Anādānaṃ" is the opposite of grasping (ādāna). It means the stilling of impediments and grasping. "Anāparaṃ" means that which has no other part or comparison, the supreme (Nibbāna). "Na te mārassa paddhagū" means...
313:
