Those persons do not become the followers, attendants, or disciples who follow in the footsteps of Māra. The rest is clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, with Arahantship as its culmination. At the end of the teaching, the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) occurred just as previously described.

## In the Commentary of the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The explanation of the Kappa Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Jatukaṇṇi Sutta

1103-4. "Sutvānahaṃ" etc., is the Jatukaṇṇi Sutta. Therein, "sutvānahaṃ vīramakāmakāmiṃ" means having heard of the Buddha who is heroic and desireless because he does not desire sensual pleasures, in such ways as "Itipi so bhagavā" etc. "Akāmamāgamaṃ" means I have come to question the Blessed One who is free from desire. "Sahajanetta" refers to the Buddha who possesses the eye of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) which is co-arisen. "Yathātacchaṃ" means as it truly is. "Brūhi me" is said as he requests again. When requesting, one might speak even a thousand times; what need is there to mention twice? "Tejī tejasā" means being endowed with majesty and overwhelming with majesty. "Yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ jātijarāya idha vippahānaṃ" means I wish to know in this very life that Dhamma which is the abandoning of birth and old age.

1105-7. Then, the Blessed One, teaching that Dhamma to the brahmin Jatukaṇṇi, spoke three verses. In those verses, "nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato" means seeing Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna as the state of security (khema). "Uggahitaṃ" means grasped through the power of craving and views. "Nirattaṃ vā" means that which should be discarded or released. "Mā te vijjittha" means let it not be for you. "Kiñcanaṃ" refers to impediments such as lust (rāga); let those impediments such as lust not arise specifically for you. "Pubbe" refers to defilements that have arisen based on past conditioned things (saṅkhāra). "Brāhmaṇa" is how the Blessed One addresses the brahmin Jatukaṇṇi. The rest is clear in all respects.
314:
In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, with Arahantship as its culmination. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as before.

## The Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā
## The Commentary on the Jatukannī Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Bhadrāvudha Sutta
1108-1109. "Okañjahaṃ" and so forth is the Bhadrāvudha Sutta. Therein, "okañjahaṃ" means abandoning attachment (ālaya). "Taṇhacchidaṃ" means cutting the mass of craving. "Anejaṃ" means being unshakable amidst the worldly conditions (lokadhamma). "Nandijjaham" means abandoning the longing for future forms and so on. Indeed, it is craving alone that is spoken of here in various ways by way of praise. "Kappañjahaṃ" means abandoning the two kinds of conceptualizations (taṇhā-kappa and diṭṭhi-kappa). "Abhiyāce" means "I entreat greatly." "Sutvāna nāgassa apanamissanti ito" means "Having heard the words of the Naga (the Blessed One), many people will depart from this Pāsāṇaka Shrine." "Janapadehi saṅgatā" means those who have gathered here from provinces such as Anga. "Viyākarohi" means "Please preach the Dhamma."

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to teach the Dhamma in accordance with Bhadrāvudha's inclination, spoke two verses. Therein, "ādānattaṇhaṃ" means the craving for grasping that takes hold of forms and so on; it means craving and clinging (taṇhupādāna). "Yaṃ yaṃhi lokasmimupādiyanti" means whatever (kamma-abhisaṅkhāra) they grasp among these divisions such as the aggregates. "Teneva māro anveti jantun" means that Māra, in the form of the rebirth-linking aggregates arising from the volitional formations produced with clinging as a condition, follows that being.

"Tasmā pajānaṃ" means "Therefore, knowing these dangers in formations by way of impermanence and so on." "Ādānasatte iti pekkhamāno pajaṃ imaṃ maccudheyye visattanti" means "Looking at this generation of beings who are attached to forms and so on, called 'ādāna' because they are to be grasped, and who are stuck in the realm of Death throughout the whole world." Or else, looking at the persons who are settled in grasping, and this generation of beings who, because of the cause of grasping, are stuck in the realm of Death, in order to transcend that realm of Death...
315:
...looking at them as being unable [to transcend], [the verse says] "one should not produce anything (kiñcana) in the whole world." The rest of the words are clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, with Arahantship as its culmination. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as before.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Patha named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Commentary on the Bhadrāvudha Sutta in the Suttanipāta Commentary is finished.
## 13. Commentary on the Udaya Sutta

1112-1113. "Jhāyinti" and so forth is the Udaya Sutta. Therein, "aññāvimokkha" refers to asking about the liberation realized through the power of wisdom. Then, since the brahmin Udaya was an attainer of the fourth jhana, the Blessed One, wishing to show him liberation through knowledge in various ways by way of the jhana he had attained, spoke two verses. Therein, "pahānaṃ kāmacchandānaṃ" means that for one who brings about the first jhana, there is the abandoning of sensual desire; thus, He speaks of that first jhana also as "liberation through knowledge." In this way, all the terms should be connected.

"Upekkhāsatisaṃsuddhaṃ" means well-purified by the equanimity and mindfulness of the fourth jhana. By the words "dhammatakkapurejavaṃ," He speaks of the liberation of Arahantship attained by staying in that liberation of the fourth jhana and practicing insight (vipassanā) into the jhana factors. For, the "Dhamma-thought" (dhammatakka), consisting of right intention and so on associated with the Path, is the precursor to the liberation of Arahantship. Therefore, He said: "dhammatakkapurejavaṃ." "Avijjāya pabhedanaṃ" means that because it arises depending on Nibbāna, which is called the shattering of ignorance, He calls that very liberation through knowledge "the shattering of ignorance" by way of metonymy (kāraṇopacāra), attributing the cause to the effect.

1115-1116. Having heard of Nibbāna spoken of by the words "shattering of ignorance," and wishing to ask, "By the abandoning of what is that [Nibbāna] spoken of?", he spoke the verse beginning with "Kiṃsu saṃyojano." Therein, "Kiṃsu saṃyojano" means "What is the fetter?" "Vicāraṇaṃ" means "What is the cause of wandering (vicaraṇa)?" "Kissa vīppahānena" means "By the abandoning of what thing of such a name [is Nibbāna spoken of for that being]?"
316:
Then the Blessed One, wishing to explain that meaning, spoke the verse beginning with "Nandisaṃyojano" (The fetter of delight). In that verse, "vitakkassa" (of thought) means that thoughts such as sensual thoughts would occur to that person.

1117-8. Now, wishing to ask about the path to that Nibbāna, he spoke the verse beginning with "Kathaṃ satassa" (How for one mindful). In that verse, "viññāṇaṃ" refers to karmic-formative consciousness (abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa). Then, wishing to teach the path to the brahmin Udaya, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Ajjhattañca" (And internally). In that verse, "evaṃ satassa" means for a person who is thus mindful and clearly comprehending. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the attainment of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as before.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Udaya Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 14. Explanation of the Posāla Sutta

1119-20. "Yo atītaṃ" (Who the past) and so forth is the Posāla Sutta. In that sutta, "yo atītaṃ ādisati" means that the Blessed One refers to the past lives of himself and others, in various ways such as "even one birth". "Vibhūtarūpasaññissa" means for a person who has completely transcended the perception of form. "Sabbakāyappahāyino" means for a person who has abandoned the entire form-body by means of abandonment through substitution of opposites (tadaṅga) and suppression (vikkhambhana), meaning one who has abandoned rebirth in the form-existence. "Natthi kiñcīti passato" means for one who sees "there is nothing" by practicing insight into the absence of consciousness, meaning one who has attained the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana). "Ñāṇaṃ sakkānu pucchāmi" means addressing the Blessed One as "Sakka" and saying, "I ask about the knowledge of that person; what kind of knowledge should be asked about?" "Kathaṃ neyyo" means how should he be led, or how should the higher path-knowledge be produced for him?

Then the Blessed One, demonstrating his own unimpeded knowledge regarding such persons, spoke two verses to explain that knowledge. In those verses, "viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo sabbā abhijānaṃ tathāgato" means the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, who specially knows all the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti), which are four by way of karmic formations and seven by way of rebirth. "Tiṭṭhantamenaṃ jānāti" means by way of karmic formations...
317:
...knows that person who is standing, thinking, "In the future, this person will have such a destination (gati)." "Vimuttaṃ" means a person whose mind is inclined towards the sphere of nothingness and so forth. "Tapparāyaṇaṃ" means a person who has that sphere of nothingness as his final resort, being intent on that meditative state.

"Ākiñcaññasambhavaṃ ñatvā" means having known the karmic formations that produce the sphere of nothingness, and knowing, "In what way does this person have an impediment (palibodha)?" "Nandī saṃyojanaṃ iti" means that for that person, there is that delight called lust for the formless (arūparāga); knowing that delight as a fetter. "Tato tattha vipassati" means then, having emerged from the attainment of the sphere of nothingness, he observes that attainment with insight by way of impermanence and so forth. "Etaṃ ñāṇaṃ tathaṃ tassa" means that for such a person practicing insight, the knowledge of the path of Arahantship that arises in due order is true and unerring. "Vusīmato" means for one who has lived the holy life. The remaining words are clear in all respects.

Thus the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was the attainment of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) just as in the previous suttas.

## In the Commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya named Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Posāla Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## 15. Explanation of the Mogharāja Sutta

"Dvāhaṃ sakka" (Twice, O Sakka) and so forth is the Mogharāja Sutta. In that sutta, "dvāhaṃ" means "I, for two times". That brahmin Mogharāja had previously asked the Blessed One twice, at the end of the Ajita Sutta and the Tissametteyya Sutta. However, the Blessed One did not answer, as he was waiting for the ripening of Mogharāja's faculties (indriya). Therefore, he said, "Dvāhaṃ sakka apucchissaṃ" (Twice, O Sakka, I have asked). "Yāvatatiyañca devīsi vyākarotīti me sutaṃ" means "I have heard that the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Blessed One, who is a divine seer (devīsi) who seeks out [the end of] defilements, and who is asked for the third time in accordance with the Dhamma, explains clearly." It is said that Mogharāja heard this while he was on the banks of the Godhāvarī River. Therefore, he said, "Vyākarotīti me sutaṃ" (I have heard that he explains).

"Ayaṃ loko" means the human world. "Paro loko" means the remaining worlds, excluding the human world. "Sadevako" means excluding the Brahma world...
318:
The world associated with the remaining devas by rebirth (uppattideva) and devas by convention (sammutideva) is called "the world together with its devas." Alternatively, the phrase "the Brahma world together with its devas" or "in the world together with its devas" is merely an illustration of this method. By that statement, the entire world of the aforementioned varieties should be understood.

"One with such supreme vision" (abhikkantadassāviṃ) means one who sees the highest in this way; it shows that he is capable of seeing the inclinations (āsaya), dispositions (adhimutti), destinations (gati), and tendencies (parāyana), etc., of the world together with its devas.

"Look upon the world as empty" (suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu) means to look upon the world as empty for two reasons: either by way of noting the lack of mastery [over phenomena] or by way of contemplating the voidness of conditioned things (saṅkhāra). "Having removed the view of self" (attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca) means having uprooted the view of a personal identity (sakkāyadiṭṭhi). The remaining words are clear in all respects.

In this way, the Blessed One taught this sutta as well, culminating in Arahatship. At the conclusion of the teaching, there was a realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) similar to what has been previously stated.

## In the Khuddaka Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Commentary on the Mogharāja Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta is finished.
## 16. Piṅgiya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

"I am old" (jiṇṇo'hamasmi), etc., is the Piṅgiya Sutta. Therein, "I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded" means that the brahmin was overcome by old age, being two hundred years old by birth; he was also weak, so that when he thought, "I will step here," he actually stepped elsewhere; and his former healthy complexion was ruined. Therefore, he said, "I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded."

"May I not perish in the midst, being bewildered" means: "May I not perish while still ignorant in the midst [of life] without having realized Your Dhamma." "The abandonment of birth and old age in this teaching" means: "Right here at Your feet or at the Pāsāṇaka Cetiya, I wish to know the Dhamma of Nibbāna, which is the abandonment of birth and old age; please preach that Dhamma to me."

Now, because the brahmin Piṅgiya spoke the verse "I am old" due to his attachment to the body, the Blessed One, in order to remove his affection for the body...
319:
...spoke the verse beginning with "Seeing people suffering because of forms" (disvāna rūpesu vihaññamāne). In that verse, "because of forms" (rūpesu) means due to the cause of form, because of the condition of form. "Suffering" (vihaññamāne) means being oppressed by punishments and so forth. "People are afflicted because of forms" (ruppanti rūpesu) means that people are changed and oppressed by eye diseases and so forth, and solely because of the cause of form.

1129-30. Although the brahmin Piṅgiya heard the practice taught by the Blessed One culminating in Arahatship, he did not attain the special distinction because of the weakness of old age. He then praised the Blessed One again with the verse beginning with "The four directions" (disā catasso) and requested a Dhamma teaching. Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the practice culminating in Arahatship once more, spoke the verse beginning with "Beset by craving" (taṇhādipanne). The rest of the words are clear in all respects.

This sutta was also taught by the Blessed One culminating in Arahatship. At the conclusion of the teaching, Piṅgiya was established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). It is said that he thought from time to time, "My uncle Bāvarī has not had the opportunity to hear such a teaching of diverse and brilliant inspired speech." Because of that distraction of affection, he was unable to reach Arahatship. However, his disciples, the one thousand matted-hair ascetics, reached Arahatship. All of them became "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks, possessing bowls and robes created by psychic power.

## In the Khuddaka Nikāya Commentary named Paramatthajotikā,
## the Commentary on the Piṅgiya Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta is finished.
## Pārāyanatthutigāthā Vaṇṇanā

After this, the Elders who conducted the Council (saṅgītikāra), wishing to praise the teaching, spoke the verses beginning with "The Blessed One said this" (idamavoca bhagavā). Therein, "said this" (idamavoca) means he spoke this Pārāyana Sutta. "To the sixteen attendants" (paricāraka-soḷasānaṃ) means to the sixteen brahmins together with Piṅgiya, who were the attendants of Bāvarī, or it means to the sixteen attendants of the Buddha, the Blessed One. They themselves were the brahmins. At that time, the assembly of sixteen [groups] sat in the front, back, left, and right directions, each extending six leagues (yojana), making a total of twelve leagues in a straight line. "Requested" (ajjhiṭṭho) refers to the Buddha who was requested. "Having understood the meaning" (atthamaññāya) means having understood the meaning of the Pali text. "Having understood the Dhamma" (dhammaññāya) means having understood the Pali text itself. "Pārāyana"—thus applying this name to this Dhamma discourse, to those brahmins...
320:
Reciting the names of the Brahmins, they said, "Ajita, Tissa-metteyya... they have approached the Buddha, the Excellent One."

1131-7. In those verses, 'sampannacaraṇaṃ' means being endowed with the Pātimokkha virtue and so forth, which are the foundational causes for Nibbāna. 'Isi' refers to the Great Seer (Mahesi), the Buddha. The remaining words are clear. After that, 'brahmacariyamacariṃsu' means they practiced the holy life, which is the Path. Therefore, 'Pārāyana' means the way (ayana) to the further shore, which is Nibbāna.

## Commentary on the Pārāyanānugīti Verses

In the phrase 'pārāyanamanugāyissaṃ', there is this connection: When the Blessed One taught the Pārāyana, sixteen thousand matted-hair ascetics attained Arahantship. For the remaining fourteen crores of devas and humans, there was the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). This was said by the ancient teachers thus:

"Then, at the delightful Pāsāṇaka Shrine, during the Pārāyana assembly,
the Buddha led fourteen crores of beings,
to the deathless Nibbāna."

When the Dhamma teaching was finished, the people who had come from various places returned to their own villages and towns by the power of the Blessed One. The Blessed One also went to Sāvatthī, surrounded by many thousands of monks, including the sixteen attendants. Then the monk Piṅgiya paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall go to inform the Brahmin Bāvarī about the arising of the Buddha; for I have promised him." Then, permitted by the Blessed One, he went to the banks of the Godhāvarī river by means of knowledge-travel (ñāṇagamana) and then approached the hermitage on foot. While the Brahmin Bāvarī was sitting and watching the road, he saw him from afar coming in the guise of a monk, without the matted hair and other requisites of an ascetic, and he came to the conclusion: "A Buddha has arisen in the world." He asked the arriving Piṅgiya, "Piṅgiya, has a Buddha arisen in the world?"

"Yes, Brahmin, He has arisen. Staying at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine, He taught us the Dhamma. I shall teach that Dhamma to you." Then the Brahmin Bāvarī, with great honor, worshipped him along with his followers and prepared a seat. Sitting there, the Elder Piṅgiya spoke the words beginning with "pārāyanamanugāyissaṃ".

In that verse, 'anugāyissaṃ' means "I shall recite in accordance with the words taught by the Blessed One." 'Yathā addakkhi' means "He saw by means of the uncommon knowledge through which He Himself penetrated the Four Noble Truths." 'Nikkāmo' means...
321:
...one who has abandoned sensual desires. There is also a variant reading 'nikkamo', meaning one who possesses energy, or one who has emerged from the side of unwholesomeness. 'Nibbano' means one who is free from the forest of defilements, or simply free from craving. "For what reason would He speak a lie?" This shows that He has abandoned those defilements that would cause one to lie. By this, he arouses the Brahmin's enthusiasm to hear the Dhamma.

1139-41. 'Vaṇṇūpasañhitaṃ' means endowed with qualities. 'Saccavhayo' means being possessed of the true name "Buddha". 'Brahme' is an address to that Brahmin. 'Kubbanakaṃ' refers to a small amount of words. 'Bahupphalaṃ kānanamāvaseyya' means one should approach and dwell in a forest filled with various kinds of many fruits. 'Appadasse' refers to those with little wisdom, such as Bāvarī. 'Mahodadhi' refers to a great mass of water, such as Lake Anotatta.

1142-4. 'Yeme pubbe' refers to these people who existed in the past. 'Tamanudāsino' means those who dwell having dispelled the darkness. 'Bhūripaññāṇo' means one who has the banner of wisdom. 'Bhūrimedhaso' means one who has extensive wisdom. 'Sandiṭṭhikamakālikaṃ' means having a fruit that is to be seen by oneself and a fruit that is to be obtained without delay. 'Anītikaṃ' means being free from the danger of defilements.

1145-50. Then the Brahmin Bāvarī spoke two verses beginning with "kiṃ nu tamhā". Thereafter, Piṅgiya, wishing to show that he does not stay away from the presence of the Blessed One, spoke the words beginning with "nāhaṃ tamhā". "I see that Buddha with my mind as if with my eyes. I pass the night even while paying homage. In whichever direction the Buddha resides, in that very direction I bow." This shows that his mind is bent, inclined, and leaning towards that Buddha.

'Dubbalathāmakassa' means one who has little strength, or one who is weak and lacking in energy. It means "because of that weakness, the body does not go," or "it does not go to where the Buddha is." There is also a reading 'na pareti', which has the same meaning. 'Tattha' means in the presence of the Buddha. 'Saṅkappayantāyā' means by the movement of the thinking mind. 'Tena yutto' shows being joined, intensely joined, and repeatedly joined with the place where the Buddha is.

'Paṅke sayāno' means one sleeping in the mud of sensual pleasures. 'Dīpā dīpaṃ upapplavim' means "I have approached from one teacher to another as a support." 'Athaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ' means "I, while wandering about holding such wrong views, saw the Buddha at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine."

At the end of these verses, knowing the maturity of the faculties of Piṅgiya and Bāvarī, the Blessed One, while staying in Sāvatthī, emitted a golden-hued radiance. Piṅgiya sat praising the qualities of the Buddha to Bāvarī.
322:
Due to the lack of strength and the decline of energetic power, because of such weak capability, the body cannot go; it cannot go to the place where the Blessed One is. There is also a variant reading "na pareti," which has the same meaning. By going with the intention of the mind to the presence of the Blessed One, one is associated with the place where the Blessed One resides, intensely associated, and repeatedly associated.

"Paṅke sayāno" means sleeping in the mud of sensual pleasures. "Dīpā dīpaṃ upapplavim" means approaching from one teacher to another as a refuge. "Athaddasāsiṃ sambuddhaṃ" means that I, while wandering about holding such wrong views, then saw the Blessed One at the Pāsāṇaka Shrine.

At the end of this verse, knowing the ripening of the spiritual faculties (indriya) of Pingiya and Bāvarī, the Blessed One, while staying in Sāvatthī itself, emitted a golden radiance. While Pingiya was sitting and praising the virtues of the Buddha to Bāvarī, he saw that radiance and looked around, wondering, "What is this?" Seeing the Blessed One as if He were standing right in front of him, he informed the Brahmin Bāvarī, "The Buddha has come." The Brahmin also rose from his seat and stood with his hands in anjali. The Blessed One, spreading His radiance and showing Himself to the Brahmin, and knowing what was suitable for both of them, addressed Pingiya alone and spoke this verse beginning with "As was Vakkali."

The meaning of that verse is: Just as the Elder Vakkali was one released through faith (saddhā-adhimutta) and reached Arahantship by making faith the precursor; and just as Bhadrāvudha, who was one of the sixteen disciples, and Gotama of Āḷavī reached Arahantship through faith; in the same way, you too should release your faith. Then, being one who is intensely resolved in faith, and by beginning insight (vipassanā) in the manner of "All conditioned things are impermanent," etc., you will reach Nibbāna, the further shore of the realm of death. Thus, He concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. At the end of the teaching, Pingiya was established in Arahantship and Bāvarī in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). The five hundred disciples of the Brahmin Bāvarī also became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna).

1154-5. Now, Pingiya, wishing to make known his own devotion, spoke the verse beginning with "Esa bhiyyo." In that verse, "paṭibhānavā" means being endowed with the analytical insight of ready wit (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). "Adhideve abhiññāya" means knowing the qualities that make one a supreme deity. "Parovaraṃ" means the low and the high, meaning he knew all things that cause oneself and others to become supreme deities. "Kaṅkhīnaṃ paṭijānatant" refers to those who, while having doubt, claim "we are without doubt."

"Asaṃhīraṃ" means being unable to be destroyed by lust (rāga) and so forth. "Asaṃkuppaṃ" means being of a nature that is indestructible and unchangeable. Both these terms refer to Nibbāna. "Addhā gamissāmi" means that I shall certainly reach that Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). "Na mettha kaṅkhā" means I have no doubt regarding this Nibbāna.
323:
I no longer have any doubt in this Nibbāna. Thus, please regard me as one whose mind is resolved upon and inclined towards Nibbāna, the Elder Pingiya requested. By this instruction of the Blessed One, "In the same way, you too should release your faith," he generated faith in himself, and having been liberated from defilements by making faith the precursor, he spoke to the Blessed One to manifest that state of being resolved through faith: "Thus, please regard me as one whose mind is resolved." The meaning here is: "Just as You have told me, please regard me as one who is so resolved."

## Thus, in the Commentary on the Khuddaka entitled Paramatthajotikā,
## The Explanation of the Sutta of the Sixteen Brahmins (Soḷasabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā) of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
## The fifth chapter, known by the name Pārāyanavagga, is also finished according to the method of the explanation of the meaning.

## Concluding Remarks (Nigamanakathā)
By this much, that which was stated:
"Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most supreme among those worthy of homage,
By one who has abandoned even slight misconduct in the Khuddaka Nikāya,
That Sutta Nipāta preached by the Lord of the World,
Who seeks the liberation of the world,
I shall perform the explanation of its meaning."

Herein, the explanation of the meaning of the Sutta Nipāta, which is comprised of five chapters beginning with the Uragavagga and consists of seventy suttas beginning with the Uragasutta, has been completed. Therefore, it is said:

"Wishing for the long endurance of the True Dhamma,
Whatever merit I have obtained by performing this explanation of the meaning of the Sutta Nipāta,
By the power of that merit, may all these people,
Quickly reach growth, increase, and abundance,
In the Dhamma made known by the Noble Ones."

(In terms of the extent of the scriptures to be studied, there are approximately forty-four recital sections (bhāṇavāra).)
324:
Adorned with supreme and pure faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with the collection of virtues such as morality, conduct, uprightness, and gentleness; capable of plunging into the thicket of one's own and others' doctrines; possessed of the maturity of wisdom; having the power of unimpeded knowledge in the Teacher's Dispensation consisting of the three Pitakas along with their commentaries; a great grammarian; endowed with the beauty of sweet and noble speech arising from the happiness produced by the perfection of the vocal instrument; a speaker of what is fit and proper; a speaker of the supreme; a great poet; well-established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with qualities such as the six higher powers (abhiññā) and the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); a lamp of the lineage of the Elders; an ornament of the lineage of the Elders residing at the Mahāvihāra; possessed of vast and pure wisdom; the Elder who is given the name Buddhaghosa by the venerable teachers—this Sutta Nipāta Commentary named Paramatthajotikā, composed by him:

May it remain in the world for as long as,
Showing the way to the purification of wisdom,
To the sons of good family who seek liberation from the world,
As long as the very name "Buddha" of the Pure-minded One, the Unshakable One,
The Supreme One in the world, the Seeker of all virtues,
Continues to exist and endure in the world.

## The Explanation of the Sutta Nipāta Commentary is finished.
